past this, slow parchment drying hurts the cup, one importer says

steps.title: Ferment first (often)
steps.text: Many slow-dry lots start with a sealed ferment; Elida Estate's ASD naturals spend about five or six days sealed in tanks or bags.

steps.title: Spread thin, in shade
steps.text: The coffee goes onto raised beds, often shaded, or onto covered patios, spread thinly and turned.

steps.title: Lose water slowly
steps.text: Drying runs for weeks rather than days, down to about 10–12% moisture.

steps.title: Rest before milling
steps.text: Esmeralda then bags its dried coffee for at least 30 days to let it stabilize.

records.layers: Any, but the best-known slow-dried coffees are naturals and anaerobic naturals, dried with the whole fruit still on.

cup.common: No single flavor of its own; producers use it for clean, even drying, and one importer says slow, even drying helps coffee keep its quality longer.
cup.text: Esmeralda says its raised beds let air circulate for clean, evenly dried coffee. Coffee Review scored two of Elida Estate's anaerobic slow-dry naturals 93 and 94.
cup.why: The parchment shell and a gentle pace buffer the bean against harsh, uneven drying, and very fast drying is bad for coffee. In a lab study, beans dried with nightly pauses, like sun drying, took about eight days instead of five but ended with much the same sugars, so the authors concluded sugars can't explain quality differences between the two. Pace matters differently at each stage: a Coffee Research Foundation scientist in Kenya says drying must be fast at first, while the parchment is soaking wet and microbes can taint it, then slow and cool in the middle (“white”) stage so the parchment doesn't crack.
cup.prized: Even drying and a coffee that holds its quality. A Geisha natural dried in a dark room won best natural Geisha at Best of Panama 2020.
cup.watch: Too slow is a problem too: coffee that doesn't dry quickly enough can ferment out of control or grow mold, and one importer says parchment drying for more than 30 days shows problems in the cup. In Kenyan trials where drying stretched to 12–20 days in thick 4–8 cm layers, all the coffee came out poor, possibly because of the long drying and thick layers.

byCoffee.text: Elida Estate's ASD Catuaí natural spent six days sealed and 60 days drying, and scored 94 at Coffee Review.
Finca Hartmann's dark-room drying produced the Black Jaguar natural Geisha from Guarumo farm, best natural Geisha at Best of Panama 2020.

spectrum.label: Over-fermented or moldy if it stays wet too long

story.text: Ratibor Hartmann of Finca Hartmann in Panama began drying coffee in drawers in a dark room with a dehumidifier and fans; by 2021 he'd been experimenting for almost ten years.
A dark-room-dried natural Geisha won best natural Geisha at the Best of Panama competition.
Coffee Review described anaerobic slow-dry naturals as drying 60 days or more and credited Wilford Lamastus of Elida Estate with popularizing them.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: In published sources, deliberate slow drying is mainly a Panamanian specialty practice: Hacienda La Esmeralda's raised-bed lots (about 29 days) and Elida Estate's anaerobic slow-dry naturals (60 days or more, popularized by Wilford Lamastus). Ratibor Hartmann of Finca Hartmann dries coffee in a dark room with a dehumidifier and fans, away from sun and heat, though no drying time is given. No published figure says how much coffee is dried this way.

Research is more cautious about long drying: trials reported by Kenya's Coffee Research Foundation found poor quality when drying ran to 12–20 days in thick layers, and one importer says parchment that takes more than 30 days to dry shows problems in the cup.

sections.title: A balancing act
body: Dry too slowly and the coffee can ferment out of control or mold; dry too fast and it suffers too: coffee left unturned in hot sun can overheat, and one importer calls very fast drying of bare beans harsh and uneven. The parchment shell itself slows drying and shields the bean from strong sun and day–night temperature swings.

records.name: Thermal shock
records.summary: A warm rinse, then a cold one, after a long ferment.
records.lede: After a long, controlled fermentation, the coffee is rinsed in warm water and then straight away in cold water. Perfect Daily Grind credits it to Diego Bermúdez of Finca El Paraíso in Cauca, Colombia. Producers say the swing “opens” the beans to take in aroma and then “seals” it in, but the roaster that explains this theory says research is still needed.

facts.label: the warm rinse (104 °F)
the cold rinse (54 °F)
El Paraíso's altitude (6,330–6,430 ft)
El Paraíso's Cup of Excellence top-10 finish

steps.title: Sanitize the cherries
steps.text: Ripe cherries are washed in ozonated water, sometimes with UV light, to cut down wild microbes.

steps.title: Sealed ferment
steps.text: Whole cherries ferment in sealed steel tanks, in some lots flushed with CO2 and seeded with yeasts selected from wild samples.

steps.title: Pulp and ferment again
steps.text: The cherries are pulped and the coffee ferments again with its mucilage.

steps.title: Warm rinse
steps.text: The coffee is rinsed in, or heated in its juices to, about 40–50 °C (104–122 °F).

steps.title: Cold rinse
steps.text: It then goes straight into cold water at about 10–12 °C (50–54 °F), which producers say stops the fermentation.

steps.title: Controlled drying
steps.text: El Paraíso lots then dry in machines at gentle heat, about 34–42 °C (93–108 °F), down to 10–11% moisture.

records.layers: It varies. In El Paraíso's double-ferment lots the shock comes after pulping, on parchment still coated in mucilage; other lots shock the whole cherries, before pulping or before a sealed ferment.

cup.common: Very intense, perfumed fruit, sometimes so intense that people suspect something was added.
cup.text: Roasters list notes like freeze-dried strawberry, cotton candy and violet, or citrus, orange blossom, peach, mango, passion fruit and lychee. One roaster's education director says the processing has an intensive impact on flavor.
cup.why: Unproven. The producers' working theory is that heat opens the beans' pores so they take in esters (fruity aroma compounds) from the fermentation juice, and cold closes them again; the quick swing may also halt enzymes, as blanching does to vegetables. The roaster that explains this says scientific research is still needed.
cup.prized: Big, clear aromatics, and roasters credit the step with a clean, consistent cup and with stopping fermentation before it goes too far.
cup.watch: The intensity led many to suspect that one El Paraíso release was infused with additives; the roaster selling it says the flavor came only from processing. Because the shock is one step among sanitizing, added yeast, sealed ferments and machine drying, it's hard to know how much of the flavor it causes.

byCoffee.text: Diego Bermúdez's double-washed thermal-shock Castillo was sold with notes of citrus, orange blossom, peach, mango, passion fruit, honey, lychee, strawberry, raspberry and plum; a neighboring Bermúdez farm's Castillo, processed by Diego, with freeze-dried strawberry, cotton candy and violet.

Wilton Benítez's lots, which follow a koji ferment with a bean-sealing step using hot and cold water, scored 94–95 with Coffee Review in 2023 and 2024, with lychee, bergamot and jasmine and a creamy or syrupy mouthfeel.

story.text: The Bermúdez family started Finca El Paraíso in Piendamó, Cauca.
El Paraíso won a regional competition, its way into specialty coffee.
Diego Samuel Bermúdez placed 10th in Colombia's Cup of Excellence with a washed Bourbon that scored 89.76.
He placed 24th with an anaerobic washed Castillo, and won the body and exotic categories of the coffee federation's Colombia, Land of Diversity contest.
Trade writers were describing thermal shock as his creation: a rinse at about 40 °C, then one at about 12 °C.

After disqualifying four lots, Best of Panama's organizers called “co-fermented” and “thermal shock” deceptive terms; Coffee Review's editor said they needed to explain how the alteration was confirmed.

sections.title: Who invented it
body: Perfect Daily Grind credits Diego Bermúdez. One roaster's education director credits him together with Wilton Benítez, and describes both sanitizing cherries and adding yeast strains selected from wild samples. Bermúdez co-founded a processing company, INDESTEC, with his brother and cousin, and the family now runs several more farms.

sections.title: Recipes differ
body: Lots sold as thermal shock don't follow one recipe. One roaster's listing describes washing whole cherries in 50 °C (122 °F) water, sealing them for 80 hours at 35 °C (95 °F) and spraying on a Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast; another producer shocks before pulping in a washed process.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Most thermal-shock lots on the market come from Cauca, Colombia, where it started: Diego Bermúdez's El Paraíso, in the village of Los Arados at about 1,930 m (6,330 ft), and a neighboring farm run by a relative, Finca El Paraíso Villa Esperanza, whose coffee he processes. Wilton Benítez's Granja Paraíso 92 in Piendamó, Cauca, uses hot and cold water in its koji lots, and other producers, such as Paola Trujillo with an SL28, have made their own versions.

sections.title: On the bag
body: “Thermal shock”, “thermo shock” or “heat shock” (one listing reads “double anaerobic fermentation, heat shock, washing”). Lots are often named after a fruit, such as Bermúdez's Red Plum and Lychee releases, and Coffee Review describes Benítez's step as sealing the beans through “impacts of hot and cold water”.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: The main risk is to trust. The flavors are intense enough that many drinkers suspected Bermúdez's Red Plum of being infused, and in 2024 Best of Panama's organizers called “thermal shock” a deceptive term, without saying how they confirmed that the lots they disqualified had been altered.

Because the shock is one step among sanitizing, added yeast, sealed ferments and machine drying, no one has shown how much of the flavor it causes, and the roaster that explains the theory says research is still needed.

records.name: Washed

cup.common: A clean, bright cup with clear acidity, where the coffee's origin and variety come through plainly.
cup.text: Importers describe washed coffees as clean and crisp, with caramel-like sweetness and pronounced acidity. A 2015 research review found wet-processed coffees more aromatic and acidic, and less bitter, burnt or woody, than dry-processed ones.
cup.why: The fruit comes off first, so microbes work on the sticky mucilage for 12–72 hours in a tank instead of for weeks around the seed, and the parchment dries in roughly one to two weeks. The seed changes too: lab studies find washed beans start germination-like activity within about a day of pulping, using up simple sugars (they end with roughly 5–10 times less glucose and fructose than naturals) and building amino acids, raw material for flavor in the roast.
cup.prized: Clarity: a cup in which place and variety are easy to taste. Kenya's best washed lots, for example, are prized for bright acidity with citrus, blackcurrant and berry.
cup.watch: A ferment left too long turns sour and alcoholic and can leave over-fermented 'stinker' beans. Separately, washed coffees left underdeveloped in the roast can taste sour or thin.

byCoffee.text: Kenyan mills ferment overnight, then up to 36 more hours, wash, and soak the parchment in clean water for 12–48 hours before drying. The best lots are known for bright citrus, blackcurrant and berry acidity, sometimes leaning winey.
Washed Ethiopians can have sparkling, citrusy acidity, with florals and sweet spice in the aroma, says one importer; the same coffees dried in the fruit lean toward berry and dried fruit.
Washing can bring out the variety's floral and citrus side, one roaster says; natural and honey Geshas can carry more fruit, sweetness and ferment.

Washing stations (the first private one opened in 2001, and over 200 since) are credited with greatly improving Rwanda's coffee. One importer's washed lots run floral and clear, with bright lemon acidity.

spectrum.label: Tangy, lactic from a long or sealed ferment

steps.title: Sort and pulp
steps.text: Cherries are floated to skim off unripe and overripe fruit, then a machine strips the skin and fruit flesh.

steps.title: Ferment in tanks
steps.text: The sticky mucilage left on the parchment ferments as microbes break it down. Dry tanks are usually done within a day; tanks under water can take longer, and Colombia's protected-name rules give about 14–18 hours in water-filled tanks. It varies with climate, water and microbes.

steps.title: Wash (and soak)
steps.text: The loosened mucilage is rinsed off. In Kenya the clean parchment then soaks under fresh water before drying.

steps.title: Dry the parchment
steps.text: Parchment dries on patios, raised beds or in machines until the seed is about 11–12% water. Weather and method change the time a lot.
steps.hours: about 6–15 days in the sun; about 29 on one estate's slow-drying raised beds; 18–36 h in a mechanical dryer

steps.title: Rest, then hull
steps.text: The dry parchment rests before a dry mill strips it off.
steps.hours: 30 days or more at one Panama estate

records.layers: Parchment only. The skin, fruit flesh and mucilage are all off before drying, so the seed dries in its papery parchment shell.

story.text: Washed processing reached southern Ethiopia, which until then had dried all its coffee in the fruit.
Rwanda's first private washing station opened in Huye, run by the Maraba cooperative; more than 200 followed.
Colombia's coffee research centre, Cenicafé, presented Ecomill, a washing system using 0.3–0.5 litres of water per kilo of dry parchment instead of 4–20 litres.
Colombia relaxed export rules that had long favored standard, clean-profiled wet-processed coffees, opening the door to naturals and experimental lots.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup set up a Traditional Washed category that excludes anaerobic, carbonic, inoculated, extended and co-fermented coffees.

facts.label: typical tank ferment, often about a day
ferment in water-filled tanks under Colombia's protected-name rules

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Washing is the norm for most Arabica-growing countries. Colombia is the world's biggest producer of washed Arabica, and its protected name, Café de Colombia, is defined as washed Arabica. In the International Coffee Organization's long-standing coffee groups (set under its agreements up to 1994), Brazil, Ethiopia and Paraguay form the “Brazilian Naturals”, and most other Arabica exporters sit in one of the two “milds” groups (Colombia, Kenya and Tanzania in one; Central America, Mexico, Peru, Rwanda, Burundi, India and others in the other), which the ICO describes as wet-processed. Countries that grow mainly Robusta, such as Indonesia and Uganda, are grouped with the Robustas even though they also grow Arabica.

In East Africa, Kenya grows almost only Arabica and processes it by the wet method, washed processing dominates Burundi's production, and Rwanda's specialty trade grew around washing stations (the first private one opened in 2001; more than 200 followed). Ethiopia is the exception: only about 20–30% of its coffee was washed in 2021.

Washed coffee is rare in Brazil: in a 2019 survey of growers, 85% made naturals, 14% pulped the skin off before drying, and only 1% also fermented in tanks. Practically all Robusta is dry-processed. In Indonesia, Sumatra and Sulawesi traditionally wet-hull, while Java, Bali and Flores have historically washed. Even in Colombia, specialty lots are diversifying: of 63 Colombian single-farm coffees Coffee Review tasted in 2021, 45% were conventionally washed, about 30% were naturals (“not in the Colombia tradition”) and almost 25% were anaerobic or carbonic-maceration variations.

sections.title: Water and waste
body: Washing takes water and leaves wastewater with a high organic load that has to be treated. Cenicafé puts conventional fermenting and tank washing at roughly 4–20 litres per kilo of dry parchment; its Ecomill system (2013) cuts that to 0.3–0.5 litres.

In Costa Rica, strict water-treatment rules pushed mills to eco-pulpers and mechanical demucilagers (machines that scrub the mucilage off), which can use as little as 200 litres per fanega of cherry, against about 3,000 litres for the traditional washed method.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Washed, fully washed, wet-processed and lavado all name this method; the ICO's glossary treats wet-processed and washed coffee as the same thing. In Burundi, “fully washed” means processed at a washing station with a second soak after fermentation, while “washed” coffee is often processed on the farm.
“Semi-washed” is not the same: in Brazil it means some, but not all, of the mucilage was scrubbed off by machine before drying, and in Indonesia it means wet-hulled.

records.name: Wet-hulled

cup.common: A heavy, low-acid cup with earthy, herbal and savory notes, often with dark chocolate.
cup.text: Importers describe earthy, herbal and savory flavors with dark chocolate and nuts. At its best, one adds, the earthiness is clean and humus-like, with raw-sugar or molasses sweetness.
cup.why: The parchment is stripped while the bean is still about 25–50% water, and the bare seed then dries fast, exposed to the weather; importers tie the signature flavor to this processing, not just to the islands. Sumatran lots that are hulled dry instead come out brighter and lighter in body.
cup.prized: Clean earthiness with a little green herb or moss, real sweetness, and even, slow drying on clean patios.
cup.watch: Bare, damp beans pick up dirt and humidity easily: watch for dirt-like or rubbery flavors, vegetal bitterness, crushed beans and harsh, uneven drying. Dark roasting can hide such defects.

byCoffee.text: Wet-hulling is traditional here: smallholders sell damp parchment within hours of washing, partly because cloudy, rainy weather makes slow drying in parchment hard. One importer names Aceh and the Lake Toba area, including Lintong, among its sources.
Traditionally wet-hulled too, though some estates, such as Toarco's Pedemeran plantation, have used washed processing.
Its old estates in East Java (Jampit, Blawan, Kayumas) have historically fully washed their coffee instead.

steps.title: Pulp and ferment
steps.text: Smallholders pulp the cherries and ferment them overnight in bags, tubs or tanks.

steps.title: Wash, dry briefly
steps.text: The mucilage is washed off and the parchment dries for just a few hours, then is sold while still around half water.

steps.title: Hull while damp
steps.text: The mill may dry it a little more, then strips the parchment at about 25–50% moisture (sources differ), far wetter than the 10–12% at which most coffee is hulled.

steps.title: Dry the bare beans
steps.text: The bare green beans dry on tarps or patios; at the port they're often flash-dried to 11–12% before export.
steps.hours: about 12–15 days (one importer); picking to shipping can take under a month

records.layers: Parchment for a short while, then nothing. The skin and mucilage come off first, the parchment is stripped while the bean is still damp, and the bare seed finishes drying.

facts.label: moisture at hulling (sources differ), against 10–12% for most coffee
drying the bare beans, on average (one importer)
when it most likely began, in Aceh
picking to shipping can take

story.text: Sumatra processed its coffee the two common ways, washed and natural.
Japanese interest in Sumatran coffee led to the introduction of wet-hulling, Cafe Imports says; Sucafina says it most likely began in Aceh in the late 1970s, and its exact origins are unclear.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Sources describe wet-hulling as specific to Indonesia. Sumatra and Sulawesi have traditionally wet-hulled all their coffee, and the classic profile comes from North Sumatra and Aceh; importers name the Gayo highlands, Takengon and Bener Meriah, and Lintong near Lake Toba.

Java's old estates, Bali and Flores have historically washed their coffee, and newer projects in Flores and Timor-Leste are washed, though some buyers now ask for wet-hulled lots from Bali and Flores. No published figure gives wet-hulling's share of Indonesian output.

records.name: Yeast-inoculated
records.summary: A chosen yeast strain is added to steer the ferment.
records.lede: Instead of relying on whatever microbes are on the fruit, the producer adds a starter culture, usually a known yeast strain. The added yeast tends to crowd out the wild ones, which makes the ferment more predictable. Research is young and mostly small trials, so the flavor claims are still largely producers' and suppliers' own.

facts.label: the species behind one major supplier's coffee yeasts
more yeast than a wild ferment, in a 2021 trial
producers sent yeast kits by one Brazilian project in 2020
yeast dose on cherries in one roaster-listed lot

steps.title: Clean the cherries
steps.text: Some producers wash cherries in ozonated water, sometimes with UV light, so fewer wild microbes compete.

steps.title: Add the yeast
steps.text: A measured dose of a known strain goes onto the cherries or into the tank of pulped coffee.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: The added yeast multiplies and, in one trial, used up the sugars faster and more completely than wild microbes did.
steps.hours: 36 h in one washed trial · up to 120 h in sealed ones

steps.title: Finish and dry
steps.text: The coffee is then washed or dried; trials have inoculated both pulped (washed) and whole-fruit (natural) coffee.

records.layers: Either: trials have inoculated pulped coffee with its mucilage in a washed ferment, and whole fruit in natural and sealed ferments.

cup.common: Usually a cleaner, more predictable version of the base process rather than one signature flavor; each strain is sold for a different effect.
cup.text: One yeast supplier markets a strain for fruit and mouthfeel and another for brightness and citrus. In Brazilian robusta trials, one added yeast brought fruity, almond, chocolate and nutty notes that consumers could pick out.
cup.why: The added yeast takes over: in a 2021 Australian trial it reached about 100 times the yeast count of a wild ferment, used the sugars faster and more completely, and left two to three times more glycerol, alcohols, esters and acids in the green beans.
cup.prized: Consistency: ferments left to chance can be hard to predict, and starter cultures promise more control. In one agronomist's trials, added yeasts outcompeted the native microbes and gave cleaner cups.
cup.watch: The taste gains are small or unproven: in that 2021 trial most differences weren't statistically significant. A producer in one Brazilian project says lots from different varieties, altitudes and processes all ended up with similar sensory profiles.

byCoffee.text: In Brazilian trials on Conilon (Brazilian robusta), one added yeast raised cupping scores by more than a point, and another raised them by over 3 points in a 120-hour sealed ferment.
In a 2021 Australian trial on Bourbon, a mix of two yeasts gave the top score, 82.0, against 80.3 for the uninoculated ferment.
A Syngenta–Nucoffee project with Brazil's Federal University of Lavras uses yeasts isolated from coffee itself and reports more than 1,000 lots scoring 80–90 points.
In a 2023 study, yeasts added to sealed ferments gave cups above 80 points, with the best at 86.5 (Torulaspora delbrueckii on pulped coffee), and notes of citrus, caramel, honey and chocolate.

spectrum.label: Different lots end up tasting alike

story.text: Brazilian studies in 2014 and 2015 were among the few early trials of adding yeast to coffee's wet ferment, a 2021 paper notes.
In an article Lallemand sponsored, an agronomist trialling its LalCafé yeasts (all Saccharomyces cerevisiae) reported more consistent ferments and cleaner cups.
A Brazilian project sent 383 kits of coffee-derived yeasts to 323 producers, after more than 20 years of research on over 3,000 microbes.
An Australian trial found inoculated yeasts dominated the ferment and doubled or tripled key compounds in the beans, though most taste differences weren't significant.
Brazilian studies found yeast-started sealed ferments all scored above 80, and that ferments started with Saccharomyces cerevisiae outscored unfermented coffee.

sections.title: Not the same as co-fermenting
body: Inoculation adds microbes, usually a known yeast; co-fermenting adds fruit, spices or other ingredients. US rules don't require co-fermentation additives to be listed, and one importer calls clear disclosure of processes and additives best practice.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Brazil leads the research, and its Nucoffee Artisans project, run by Syngenta–Nucoffee with the Federal University of Lavras, sent 383 microorganism kits to 323 producers in 2020, in regions such as Cerrado Mineiro; one producer says they use yeasts isolated from coffee itself. In Colombia, agronomist Mauricio Villegas has trialled Lallemand's commercial yeasts, Cauca's thermal-shock producers add yeasts selected from wild samples, and Cofinet's fruit co-ferments in Quindío add a wine yeast. A 2021 trial was run in Australia.

sections.title: On the bag
body: “Yeast-inoculated”, “inoculated” or “yeast fermentation”; one Colombian exporter calls its version a “Honey – Yeast Inoculation Process”. When a wine yeast goes in with fruit, as in Cofinet's peach lot, it's sold as a co-ferment. The strain is rarely named, though one listing says a Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast was sprayed on.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: The gains are often small: most taste differences in one trial weren't statistically significant, and a Brazilian producer found lots of different varieties, altitudes and processes ended up with similar profiles. Like any ferment, it can still go too far, especially when warm: over-fermented coffee can taste of spoiled wine, with reddish beans that smell of rotting fruit. And “special yeast” has been offered for flavors critics doubt a yeast could make: in 2018 a competitor credited a strong cinnamon flavor to one, and Saša Šestić doubted it could occur naturally.

records.name: Campo das Vertentes
records.summary: A mild Minas highland: very sweet, with chocolate and nuts
records.lede: A protected coffee origin (Indicação de Procedência, granted in 2020) covering 17 municipalities in Minas Gerais, around Santo Antônio do Amparo, São João del-Rei and Campo Belo. Its climate is mild: cool, rainy summers and, in its higher parts, very cold winters. The protected name covers green, roasted and ground Arabica.

facts.label: protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)
municipalities in the protected area
altitude of the area (1,600–3,300 ft)
points needed for the origin seal

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names, Brazil's agriculture ministry catalog and the protected name's own rules all describe it as very sweet, with a balanced body and hints of chocolate and nuts.
cup.prized: Coffee sold under the origin seal must score at least 80 points and be free of astringency, woody taste and foreign flavors or aromas.

story.text: Records show coffee farms here by the 1860s; until the mid-1900s they grew on a small scale, mostly for the farm families' own use.
A national coffee-renewal plan brought contour planting, nursery-raised seedlings and chemical fertilizer.
In the 2007 Minas Gerais state quality contest, samples from here clustered in the early rounds but had mostly dropped out by the later ones.
Brazil's patent office, INPI, granted the protected origin name on 24 November.
Its producers joined 12 other protected Brazilian coffee regions in a marketing agreement with BSCA, the Brazilian Specialty Coffee Association.

grows.text: Arabica only. The protected name allows naturals, pulped naturals (cereja descascado: skin off, sticky fruit left on while it dries), demucilaged and fermented-and-washed coffees, and controlled fermentation. No published source gives their shares here; across Brazil, 85% of growers in a 2019 survey made naturals. No source names the main varieties.

sections.title: The protected name
body: The growers' association ACAVE (Associação dos Cafeicultores do Campo das Vertentes) holds the name, and a council of its members runs the seal. Its 17 municipalities are Bom Sucesso, Camacho, Campo Belo, Cana Verde, Candeias, Carmo da Mata, Conceição da Barra de Minas, Ibituruna, Nazareno, Oliveira, Perdões, Ritápolis, Santana do Jacaré, Santo Antônio do Amparo, São Francisco de Paula, São João del-Rei and São Tiago.
INPI's technical sheet says the region is moving toward sweeter, more aromatic specialty Arabica, which it says can sell for 30–40% more than a conventional sack.

sections.title: The land
body: Rolling plateaus at about 500–1,000 m (1,600–3,300 ft), rising above 1,500 m (4,900 ft) in the Serra da Mantiqueira to the east. Coffee may be picked by hand or by machine.

area.note: Only the 17 municipalities of the protected origin, around Santo Antônio do Amparo, São João del-Rei and Campo Belo.

records.name: Cerrado Mineiro
records.summary: Flat, mechanized savanna farms and Brazil's first protected coffee origin
records.lede: A high, flat savanna plateau in western Minas Gerais, where coffee grows at 800–1,300 m (2,600–4,300 ft) on mostly large, highly mechanized farms. In 2005 it became Brazil's first protected coffee origin, and in 2013 its first Denominação de Origem, the tier under which Brazil's patent office requires the coffee to show set traits of flavor and aroma.

facts.label: municipalities in the protected area
coffee producers (2025)
growing altitude (2,600–4,300 ft)
of Minas Gerais's coffee

harvest.text: Picked from May to September, in the dry season; the low humidity at harvest lowers the risk of unwanted fermentation. In 2026 picking began in the first week of May, and about 90% of the area was done by September (Conab).

grows.text: Until recently growers planted mostly Catuaí, Mundo Novo and Bourbon, EPAMIG says, but regional nurseries estimated in 2021 that 70–80% of the seedlings bought in the previous three years were newer varieties such as MGS Paraíso 2, Arara and Catucaí; no source gives today's shares. Naturals lead, as in most of Brazil, and the protected name also allows pulped naturals (cereja descascado), demucilaged and fermented-and-washed coffee.

cup.text: The region's official profile, as Senar/MG cites it from Brazil's agriculture ministry, runs from caramel to nut aromas, with delicately citric acidity and a chocolate flavor. Embrapa-linked researchers add a moderate body and a long, sweet finish, and the protected name's technical sheet describes the typical cup as caramel, chocolate and nuts with evident citric acidity, a dense body and a long finish.
cup.why: Distinct seasons help: rain falls mostly from October to March, so the harvest comes in dry weather. Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names also credits uniform ripening and a concentrated harvest.
cup.prized: Clean coffee scoring at least 80 points on the Specialty Coffee Association's cupping form, the bar for the Denominação de Origem seal.

story.text: Farmers found that liming the acidic savanna soil, to balance its pH, made large-scale farming possible.
Growers filed their first request for a protected origin name.
It became Brazil's first geographical indication for coffee.
It became Brazil's first coffee Denominação de Origem.
Heat, dry spells, frost and scarce, uneven rain cut the harvest 13.8%, to 4.6 million 60-kg bags (Conab).
Conab's Triângulo, Alto Paranaíba and Noroeste region, which takes in the Cerrado, expected 8.9 million bags, up 86.5% on the poor 2025 crop.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Coffee here grows in full sun on flat land, and a 2007 Coffee & Conservation review called it the most mechanized coffee growing in the world, with little hand picking. Because the dry season is long, most farms irrigate at least part of their coffee, often with center-pivot sprinklers.

In 2026 Conab noted that the Triângulo holds the Minas Gerais municipalities with the highest share of irrigated coffee, though in the October–November 2025 drought many growers lacked the water to irrigate, which cut the irrigated fields' potential.

sections.title: The protected name
body: The Denominação de Origem, held by the Federação dos Cafeicultores do Cerrado in Patrocínio, was granted on 31 December 2013. Its area was drawn in 1995 by an ordinance (Portaria 165/95) of IMA, Minas Gerais's state agriculture institute, and covers the Triângulo Mineiro and Alto Paranaíba and parts of the Alto São Francisco and Noroeste, all above 800 m (2,600 ft).

Seal coffee must be Arabica from that area, cup clean at 80 points or more, and be processed on the farm as a natural, pulped natural, demucilaged or fermented-and-washed coffee; roasted coffee may not be blended with other species.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for “Região do Cerrado Mineiro” and its origin seal. In 2025 about 1,300 of the region's producers were cleared to use the seal, on 102,000 of its 234,000 hectares of coffee.
Patrocínio, home of the growers' federation, is the region's hub. Other towns you may see include Monte Carmelo, Carmo do Paranaíba, Araguari and Coromandel.

area.note: Only the protected Região do Cerrado Mineiro in western Minas Gerais: 55 municipalities in the Triângulo Mineiro and Alto Paranaíba and parts of the Alto São Francisco and Noroeste.

records.name: Espírito Santo
records.summary: Brazil's Conilon (Robusta) heartland, with mountain Arabica up high
records.lede: Brazil's Robusta heartland: about 70% of the country's Robusta, called Conilon here, grows in this state, which also grows Arabica in its mountains. Its protected coffee names include Conilon from Espírito Santo, Montanhas do Espírito Santo and Caparaó, which it shares with Minas Gerais.

facts.label: of Brazil's Robusta (2026/27 forecast)
60-kg bags in 2026, about 12.1 million of them Conilon
where its Conilon grows (up to 2,000 ft)
mountain Arabica, Montanhas do Espírito Santo (1,600–4,600 ft)

harvest.text: Conilon, in the north, is picked from April, mostly in May and June, and finishes in August or September; mountain Arabica, in the south, starts in April and can run into October (Conab, 2026). By late May 2026 the Conilon harvest was 15–25% done, ahead of most Minas Gerais Arabica (Cepea).

grows.text: About three-quarters Conilon, a Brazilian type of Coffea canephora, the species behind Robusta (12.1 of 16.5 million bags in 2026), mostly dried whole as naturals, the usual way with canephora in Brazil. Mountain Arabica is mainly wet-processed (washed or semi-washed), with some naturals. No source ranks the Arabica varieties.

cup.text: For Conilon, Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names says lower farms give a full body with chocolate and almond, and higher ones floral and fruity notes. Mountain Arabica from Montanhas do Espírito Santo is described with bright acidity and a chocolate and sugarcane aroma; StoneX adds sweetness and aromatic complexity. The agriculture ministry's catalog says washed Montanhas lots lean toward molasses, red fruit and caramel, and naturals toward wine, yellow fruit and chocolate.

feel.acidity: low in Conilon; bright in mountain Arabica

cup.why: Altitude sorts the cup here: for both Conilon and mountain Arabica, the protected-name descriptions tie fruitier, more floral or more unusual notes to higher farms.
cup.watch: Lower Montanhas lots can turn woody, cereal-like and astringent, and Conilon in general tends to be more bitter and less aromatic than Arabica.

story.text: Conilon growing began in the state.
Montanhas do Espírito Santo and Caparaó each gained Denominação de Origem status, and Conilon from Espírito Santo a protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência).
Cool, wet weather trimmed Robusta yields even as Brazil headed for a record crop.
Conab put the Conilon crop at about 12.1 million bags, down 14.3%, as older plantings dropped flowers after the record 2025 loads, while Arabica rose 33% to 4.4 million bags.

sections.title: Two coffees, one state
body: Most of the state's coffee is Conilon, a Brazilian type of Coffea canephora, the species behind Robusta. Its mountains grow Arabica, mostly on small family farms: StoneX counts 16 municipalities above 400 m in Montanhas do Espírito Santo, and says the misty, humid climate leads growers to washed or semi-washed processing.
Caparaó, a mountain area shared with Minas Gerais, has many small family farms, and its coffee is picked by hand.

sections.title: The protected names
body: Conilon from Espírito Santo covers canephora grown up to 600 m (2,000 ft), mostly lower, where average temperatures run 22–26 °C; the ministry's catalog gives it 2.2% caffeine. Montanhas do Espírito Santo covers Arabica at 500–1,400 m (1,600–4,600 ft) with 18–22 °C averages, picked mostly by hand.

Caparaó spans 16 municipalities around the Caparaó mountains: ten in Espírito Santo (Dores do Rio Preto, Divino de São Lourenço, Guaçuí, Alegre, Muniz Freire, Ibitirama, Iúna, Irupi, Ibatiba and São José do Calçado) and six in Minas Gerais.

area.note: The whole state. Caparaó's protected area also takes in six municipalities across the border in Minas Gerais.

records.name: Mantiqueira de Minas
records.summary: Mountain coffee that often ranks in Brazil's Cup of Excellence top ten
records.lede: The Minas Gerais side of the Serra da Mantiqueira mountains, part of the wider Sul de Minas region, with coffee at about 1,000–1,400 m (3,300–4,600 ft). Its name comes from the Tupi word Amantikir, “crying mountains,” for its many springs, and its coffees often finish in the top ten of Brazil's Cup of Excellence.

facts.label: growing altitude (3,300–4,600 ft)
municipalities in the protected area
growers, 82% of them small farmers (2021)
upgraded to Denominação de Origem

harvest.text: Picked from May to September.

grows.text: No source ranks varieties here. Brazil's trees are mostly Catuaí and Mundo Novo (EPAMIG); the region's specialty lots described by BeanScene and Melbourne Coffee Merchants were red and yellow Bourbon and Yellow Catucaí. Naturals and pulped naturals (skin off, sticky fruit left on to dry) both reach contest finals; no source gives the split.

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names sums it up as sweet with slightly citric acidity. A SAGA lot of red and yellow Bourbon from five smallholders was described with citrus, floral and fruity notes, a creamy, dense body and a long finish (BeanScene, 2021).
cup.why: StoneX credits hot days and cold nights, which slow ripening and, it says, make the coffee sweeter and more aromatic. Embrapa researchers point to mild temperatures plus dry spells while the cherries ripen and are picked.
cup.prized: Competition lots: Melbourne Coffee Merchants notes its coffees often finish in Cup of Excellence's top ten.

story.text: In a Minas Gerais state quality contest, Carmo de Minas was the hot spot for finalist samples, both naturals and pulped naturals.
It won a protected origin name based on its tradition and reputation.
The name was upgraded to a Denominação de Origem.
São Gonçalo do Sapucaí hosted the first festival of Mantiqueira de Minas specialty coffees.

sections.title: Towns and farms
body: Carmo de Minas is the name you'll see most; Barista Hustle calls it a microregion of Mantiqueira. One farm there, Pé de Cedro, has 25 of its 35 hectares in coffee at 1,000–1,200 m; one of its lots was a natural Yellow Catucaí.
A specialty coffee tourism route runs through Carmo de Minas and São Lourenço.

sections.title: The protected name
body: The Denominação de Origem covers 25 municipalities: Baependi, Brasópolis, Cachoeira de Minas, Cambuquira, Campanha, Carmo de Minas, Caxambu, Conceição das Pedras, Conceição do Rio Verde, Cristina, Dom Viçoso, Heliodora, Jesuânia, Lambari, Natércia, Olímpio Noronha, Paraisópolis, Pedralva, Piranguinho, Pouso Alto, Santa Rita do Sapucaí, São Gonçalo do Sapucaí, São Lourenço, São Sebastião da Bela Vista and Soledade de Minas. Aprocam, the Mantiqueira coffee growers' association, represents the region.
The agriculture ministry's 2021 catalog gives the protected area 57,000 hectares of coffee, about 1.37 million 60-kg bags a year, and an altitude of 900–1,500 m (2,950–4,900 ft).

area.note: Only the 25 municipalities of the Mantiqueira de Minas Denominação de Origem, on the Minas Gerais side of the Serra da Mantiqueira, within Sul de Minas.

records.name: Matas de Minas
records.summary: Hilly, once-forested southeast Minas: small family farms, citrus and caramel
records.lede: The hilly southeast of Minas Gerais, around the city of Manhuaçu, on land once covered by Atlantic rainforest. Coffee grows at about 600–1,200 m (2,000–3,900 ft), mostly on small family farms. In 2026 Conab's Zona da Mata, Rio Doce and Central region, which takes it in, was the state's second-biggest, with about 27% of its crop (9.7 of 35.6 million bags).

facts.label: municipalities
of its ~51,000 coffee farms are under 20 ha (2022)
growing altitude (2,000–3,900 ft)
protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)

harvest.text: Picked from April to September, mostly by hand because the land is so steep. In 2026 rain fell across almost the whole region during the harvest and lowered the quality of many lots. Growers here usually strip the trees early rather than sweep up fallen coffee, a job a labor shortage has largely ended (Conab).

grows.text: Arabica only. No source ranks varieties here; Brazil's trees are mostly Catuaí and Mundo Novo (EPAMIG). The protected name allows naturals, pulped naturals, demucilaged and fermented-and-washed coffee; state contest entries include both naturals and pulped coffees, and in the 2022 3 Corações Florada Premiada contest Matas de Minas was among the regions with the most finalists in the washed ('via úmida') Arabica category. No source gives the overall split.

cup.text: A Federal University of Viçosa study of state contest lots from 2016, 2017 and 2019 found citrus aromas, medium sweetness with caramel and fruity flavors, pronounced acidity, a full body and a long finish. Itatiaia adds a chocolatey aroma, and StoneX describes a medium to full body and high sweetness. The protected name's own profile: sweet, with citrus, caramel and chocolate, an intense floral and citrus aroma, a full to very full body, delicate, balanced acidity and a long finish.
cup.why: Altitude seems to help: in that study, higher farms tended to score higher, though the authors call it a trend, not a firm result.
cup.prized: Contest lots: in those contests naturals averaged above 84 points and pulped coffees above 83, with tops of 90.80 and 91.58.
cup.watch: Damp air. In the 2007 state contest many early entries came from here but few reached the late rounds, which researchers linked partly to fermentation risk from humidity and to small family farms on slopes. Rain at harvest remains a risk: in 2026 it lowered the quality of many lots (Conab).

story.text: Coffee spread here from the Paraíba do Sul valley, and its plantations drove much of the growth of Brazil's coffee industry.
A grower from the region became its first finalist in the Ernesto Illy coffee quality prize.
A regional origin seal was created.
On 15 December it won a protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência).
In the Florada Premiada contest it had more washed Arabica lots selected than any other region.

sections.title: Small farms on slopes
body: Most growers are families with small plantings of 3–20 hectares, and about 71% of the region's coffee land sits on slopes, according to the Viçosa study. Royal Coffee describes rolling, uneven terrain suited to small and medium farms.
Coffee towns here include Manhuaçu, Araponga, Espera Feliz, Caratinga and São João do Manhuaçu.

sections.title: The protected name
body: The Conselho das Entidades do Café das Matas de Minas, based in Manhuaçu, holds the name. It covers 64 municipalities in eastern Minas Gerais, among them Manhuaçu, Caratinga, Carangola, Muriaé, Viçosa, Araponga, Espera Feliz and Alto Caparaó, and INPI's sheet credits the region with about 36,000 coffee growers, 80% of them small family farmers.
Seal coffee must be Arabica grown above 600 m (2,000 ft), processed and stored inside the area, dried to 10.5–11.5% moisture, and score at least 80 points.

area.note: Only the 64 municipalities of the protected origin in eastern Minas Gerais, from Viçosa and Muriaé to Manhuaçu, Caratinga and Carangola.

records.name: Alta Mogiana
records.summary: São Paulo hill country near Franca: creamy, chocolatey and nutty
records.lede: Hill country in northern São Paulo state along the Minas Gerais border, around Franca, with coffee at about 900–1,280 m (2,950–4,200 ft). It has been tied to coffee for over a century and has held a protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência) since 2013.

facts.label: growing altitude (2,950–4,200 ft)
protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)
municipalities in São Paulo and in Minas Gerais
average summer and winter temperature

harvest.text: Picked from May to August, by hand or machine; the growers' association prefers picking each plot at peak ripeness. In 2026 dry, hot weather helped ripening and picking around Franca, Conab reported.

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names describes a velvety, creamy body, a strong fruity aroma, soft chocolate and nut notes and medium, balanced acidity. The protected name's rules add a long aftertaste with caramel sweetness and bittersweet chocolate, and a 2021 SAGA lot showed caramel and a hint of toasted almond.
cup.why: Revista Cultivar (2009) credits its altitude and climate with slow, even ripening; Barista Hustle notes its cool climate and high elevations.

story.text: Coffee arrived with the spread of the railways.
Low prices, frost and plant-health problems discouraged many growers and sharply cut the coffee area.
Across 25 Mogiana municipalities, coffee land roughly doubled to 111,000 hectares while sugarcane nearly quadrupled to 234,700, an Embrapa satellite study found.
Alta Mogiana gained its protected origin name.
Conab reported very good quality around Franca after a dry, hot ripening season, while rain at ripening hurt other areas.

sections.title: Coffee holds the hills
body: Sugarcane has spread fast in northeastern São Paulo, but it is hard to harvest by machine on slopes steeper than 12%, so coffee keeps the hilly ground. The Embrapa study also credits professional growers with strong technical support.
Franca hosted the region's 2009 coffee quality contest. Other Alta Mogiana towns include Pedregulho, Altinópolis, Batatais and Cristais Paulista.

sections.title: The protected name
body: AMSC, the Alta Mogiana specialty coffee growers' association in Franca, holds the name. It covers 16 municipalities in São Paulo (Altinópolis, Batatais, Buritizal, Cajuru, Cássia dos Coqueiros, Cristais Paulista, Franca, Itirapuã, Jeriquara, Nuporanga, Patrocínio Paulista, Pedregulho, Restinga, Ribeirão Corrente, Santo Antônio da Alegria and São José da Bela Vista) and 7 in Minas Gerais (Capetinga, Cássia, Claraval, Ibiraci, Itamogi, São Sebastião do Paraíso and São Tomás de Aquino).
Only Arabica qualifies, and INPI's sheet describes the region as known for "bebida mole" (literally "soft cup") coffee.

grows.text: Mostly Catuaí and Mundo Novo, says INPI's technical sheet; the agriculture ministry's catalog also names Bourbon and Obatã. The protected name covers naturals and pulped naturals (cereja descascado); no source gives the split, though across Brazil 85% of growers in a 2019 survey made naturals.

area.note: Only the 23 municipalities of the protected origin: 16 in São Paulo around Franca and 7 across the border in Minas Gerais.

records.name: Oeste da Bahia
records.summary: Irrigated, mechanized Cerrado coffee in western Bahia, above 700 m
records.lede: Coffee in western Bahia grows above 700 m (2,300 ft), about 800 m (2,600 ft) on average, in the Cerrado, the tropical savanna of central Brazil. All of it is irrigated, mostly by center pivot, on large, highly mechanized farms, and commercial growing only began in 1994.

facts.label: growing altitude (2,300 ft+)
protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)
municipalities in the protected area
of the coffee irrigated

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names describes a pleasant flavor and fragrance, a slightly fruity, floral aroma, excellent sweetness and good acidity. The protected name's own profile adds a full body, mild sweetness and a long aftertaste.
cup.why: A long dry season at harvest helps picking and drying, and the warm, frost-free climate, 22–26 °C on average, gets about 3,000 hours of sun a year.

story.text: The first records of coffee growing here date from the early 1900s: small plots, mostly in humid valleys, with some coffee already sold in Barreiras.
The first experimental rain-fed plantings were made.
Commercial irrigated coffee growing began.
Oeste da Bahia gained a protected origin name, granted in May.
Conab counted 6,500 hectares of irrigated Arabica in Bahia's Cerrado, expected to yield 250,000 bags, down 5.7% in an off-year of coffee's two-year bearing cycle.

harvest.text: No source gives exact months. The dry season lasts 4–6 months, with rain mostly from October to April, which favors picking and drying; the 2026 harvest was over by August (Conab).

grows.text: Arabica only. The protected name allows naturals, pulped naturals (cereja descascado), demucilaged and fermented coffee, dried on patios and finished in mechanical dryers. No source gives the split or names the main varieties.

sections.title: Growing it
body: The water comes from rivers and the Urucuia aquifer, and Conab says the coffee is grown only under irrigation, mostly by center pivot, by large, highly mechanized growers. StoneX notes Bahia's warm temperatures and some of Brazil's highest yields: in 2012 the region averaged 41.5 bags per hectare against a national 24.55 (Conab figures cited by oriGIn).

sections.title: The protected name
body: ABACAFÉ, the western Bahia coffee growers' association, holds the name. It covers land at 700 m or more in 11 municipalities: Formosa do Rio Preto, Santa Rita de Cássia, Riachão das Neves, Barreiras, Luís Eduardo Magalhães, São Desidério, Catolândia, Baianópolis, Correntina, Jaborandi and Cocos. In the 2017 farm census Barreiras, Cocos and Luís Eduardo Magalhães were Bahia's three biggest Arabica municipalities, and São Desidério was sixth.

area.note: Only land at 700 m or more in 11 municipalities of western Bahia, around Barreiras and Luís Eduardo Magalhães.

records.name: Rondônia
records.summary: Amazon Robusta, holder of the first canephora Denominação de Origem
records.lede: A western Amazon state on the Bolivian border where nearly all the coffee is Coffea canephora, the species behind Robusta, grown mostly on small family farms. Its coffee is known as Robustas Amazônicos (Amazonian Robustas), and in 2021 its Matas de Rondônia area won the world's first Denominação de Origem for this species.

facts.label: world's first Denominação de Origem for canephora coffee
municipalities in the Matas de Rondônia DO
growing altitude (600–1,300 ft)
families farming coffee (2024)

harvest.text: In 2026 Rondônia's harvest ran ahead of the rest of Brazil: by late May it was 50% to over 60% done, the most advanced of any region (Cepea), and 98% of the area was picked by the end of August (Conab).

grows.text: Nearly all canephora: about 92% of coffee land was planted with Robustas Amazônicos, clonal crosses of Conilon and Robusta, in 2023. Naturals are the usual process for canephora in Brazil; specialty growers add controlled fermentation and drying on raised beds.

cup.text: Embrapa researcher Enrique Alves describes mild sweetness and acidity, a velvety body and a lasting aftertaste, with notes of nuts, chocolate and dried fruit; any bitterness tends toward cacao nib. Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names adds woody, spicy and herbal notes.
cup.why: Embrapa says the character comes from more than four decades of genetics, environment and farming working together, as growers selected crosses between canephora's two botanical groups, Conilon and Robusta.
cup.prized: Clean, sweet lots judged on the Fine Robusta tasting protocol, where Embrapa sets its quality bar for clones at over 80 points.
cup.watch: Canephora in general tends to be fuller-bodied but more bitter, less aromatic and less acidic than Arabica, and careless drying, with too much heat or mold, hurts the cup.

story.text: The first Arabica demonstration field, of Mundo Novo, was probably planted near what is now Ji-Paraná, as settlers arrived.
Conilon and Robusta were brought to new farm settlements.
Embrapa released BRS Ouro Preto, a multi-clone Conilon cultivar for the western Amazon.
Matas de Rondônia won its Denominação de Origem in June.
About 92% of the state's coffee land was planted with Robusta amazônico (IBGE figures).
Conab expected 2.9 million bags from 43,155 hectares, up 24%, at 66.7 bags per hectare.

sections.title: What Robusta means here
body: Arabica and Robusta are two different coffee species. Robusta's proper name is Coffea canephora, and Brazil grows two main botanical groups of it, Conilon and Robusta. Rondônia's farmers have crossed and selected the two over the years, and those plants make up about 80% of the coffee in Matas de Rondônia, whose Denominação de Origem covers 15 municipalities, including Cacoal, Alta Floresta d'Oeste, Rolim de Moura and São Miguel do Guaporé.

Canephora has long been seen as the lesser species because it tends to be more bitter and less acidic than Arabica. Careful picking, controlled fermentation and better drying are changing that: Embrapa uses a Fine Robusta tasting protocol, and in a 2022 national contest Matas de Rondônia had more canephora lots selected than any other region. Embrapa also measures less caffeine in these coffees, 1.4–1.8%, than in standard Conilon.

sections.title: Indigenous growers
body: Aruá and Tupari families in the Rio Branco Indigenous Land have grown coffee in their villages for about 15 years. In 2018 they began training with Embrapa, picking only ripe cherries and drying them on raised beds; one of their lots was described with caramel, malt and nuts, a silky body and a sweet finish.

sections.title: Farming now
body: Conab's 2026 survey describes growers replacing old clones such as P50 and 03 with more productive, hardier plants suited to the local climate, spreading drip irrigation, and planting more densely to raise yields and make machine harvesting easier. Their yield, 66.7 bags per hectare, is more than twice Minas Gerais's 31.

area.note: The whole state; the Matas de Rondônia Denominação de Origem covers 15 of its municipalities, around Cacoal and Rolim de Moura.

records.name: Sul de Minas
records.summary: Southern Minas, the state's biggest coffee region
records.lede: The south and southwest of Minas Gerais, where coffee grows at about 800–1,400 m (2,600–4,600 ft), mostly on small farms. It is the state's biggest coffee region: in 2016 it produced 37% of all Brazil's coffee, and for 2026 Conab expected 15.9 of Minas Gerais's 35.6 million bags from its Sul e Centro-Oeste region.

facts.label: 60-kg bags in 2026, Conab's Sul e Centro-Oeste region
of Brazil's coffee output in 2016
growing altitude (2,600–4,600 ft)
first coffee farms

harvest.text: Picked from April to September. Rain slowed the 2026 harvest: by late May only about 10% was in, according to Cepea. Picking peaked in July and August, June rain knocked coffee to the ground, and Conab expected it to finish at the end of September.

cup.text: Embrapa-linked researchers describe a medium body, citric acidity and a sweet finish, and StoneX notes high acidity and sweetness. Itatiaia says the mountain coffees add fruit, caramel, chocolate and almond, while southwest lots lean floral and citrus.

story.text: The first coffee was planted in Aiuruoca, Jacuí and Baependi, in the Sapucaí and Grande river valleys.
Railroads, after decades of poor transport, set off a new coffee boom.
State investment and incentives, and growing cooperatives, built up the sector.
The region had 52% of Minas Gerais's coffee land, about 523,500 hectares, and produced 37% of Brazil's coffee.
Conab expected 15.9 million bags from 555,472 hectares in its Sul e Centro-Oeste region, up 32% on 2025, after a long early drought and harvest-time rain.

sections.title: Where it's traded
body: Varginha is the region's logistics and export hub, home to many exporters and warehouses. It, Guaxupé and Três Pontas rank among Brazil's top ten towns for coffee storage, and Alfenas and Muzambinho host big coffee companies' facilities.
The region is also home to Cooxupé, which StoneX calls the world's largest coffee cooperative.

grows.text: No source ranks varieties for the region; Brazil's trees are mostly Catuaí and Mundo Novo (EPAMIG). Naturals lead across Brazil (85% of growers in a 2019 survey, 14% making pulped naturals), and no regional split is published.

area.note: Only the south and southwest of Minas Gerais (the state's Sul de Minas planning region), which takes in Mantiqueira de Minas. Conab reports it together with the Centro-Oeste as "Sul e Centro-Oeste".

records.name: Antioquia
records.summary: Colombia's second-biggest producer, and home of Urrao's Chiroso.
records.lede: Antioquia, the department around Medellín, is Colombia's second-largest coffee producer, at about 2.1 million bags a year, grown at roughly 1,300–2,200 m (4,300–7,200 ft). Migrating antioqueño growers helped carry coffee to other parts of the country. For specialty buyers, one name to look for is Urrao, a high town where the Chiroso variety is commonly found.

facts.label: where coffee grows (4,300–7,200 ft)
of Colombia's coffee, about 2.1 million bags a year (2020)
coffee-growing families, farming 1.55 ha each on average (2022 figure)
planted with coffee in 2021

harvest.text: Main crop September–December and mitaca (the smaller second crop) April–June, says Barista Hustle. The growers' federation likewise counts Antioquia's first-half picking as its mitaca.

grows.text: Almost all washed on the farm, as across Colombia: Barista Hustle says most Antioquia growers process their own coffee and sell it as parchment. No published source gives the department's variety mix; nationally, rust-resistant varieties such as Castillo covered 88% of coffee land in 2025, up from 83% in 2020. Chiroso from Urrao, and naturals like a Colombia-variety lot from the Santa Barbara Estate, are small specialty niches: one 2021 estimate put all of Colombia's natural, honey and anaerobic exports at about 15,000 bags a year.

cup.text: Antioquia has no protected regional profile of its own. Its best-known specialty coffee, Chiroso, tends to be described as aromatic, floral, bright and tea-like (Sweet Maria's); Sey Coffee found bright citrus, orange-oil aromatics, jasmine and a sweet, tea-like finish in an Urrao lot and compared it to Ethiopian coffees.

story.text: Records mention coffee plants in Antioquia, grown as medicine.
Growers make the first attempt at commercial coffee.
97% of Antioquia's coffee growers have their own depulper, the machine that strips the fruit from the seed before washing.
Production grows fast in the first half of the century.
In November, a family farm at 1,950 m (6,400 ft) in Urrao harvests its first Chiroso.

sections.title: Urrao and Chiroso
body: Chiroso, named after a rural Colombian word for something long or stretched out, grows around Urrao. Despite the bag name Bourbon Chiroso, genetic work links it to Ethiopian landraces.

Most Antioquia growers process their coffee on the farm and sell it as parchment (dried, still in its papery hull) through cooperatives. Cenicafé's regional Castillo line for Antioquia is Castillo El Rosario, and one of its trial sites was the El Rosario station in Venecia, Antioquia.

sections.title: Farms on the bag
body: Barista Hustle pictures a coffee farm near Jericó. The importer Mercanta buys from the Santa Barbara Estate, five sister farms around Santa Bárbara, Fredonia and Amagá that grew from a small farm Pedro Echavarría started in the 1980s; the family experiments with processing, and one listed lot is a natural (dried in the fruit) Colombia-variety coffee from 1,850 m (6,070 ft).

records.name: Cauca
records.summary: Sunny southwestern mountains: bright, clean coffee with caramel aromas.
records.lede: Cauca is a southwestern department of high mountains and volcanic soils, where Indigenous, Afro-descendant and mestizo families grow coffee at about 1,400–2,100 m (4,600–6,900 ft). Its protected regional profile credits long hours of sun and steady weather all year, with the mountains shielding farms from Pacific wind and damp. Inzá and Piendamó are coffee towns whose names appear on specialty lots; Piendamó is home to Diego Bermúdez's Finca El Paraíso, known for thermal-shock lots (fermented coffee rinsed in hot, then cold water).

facts.label: where coffee grows (4,600–6,900 ft)
protected regional origin name granted
lots entered in the Best Coffee of Cauca contest (2025)
record price there, for a Piendamó grower's lot (2025)

harvest.text: Main crop April–July and mitaca (the smaller second crop) November–January, says Barista Hustle; Juan Valdez puts the main crop a little earlier, March–June. Either way, Cauca picks most of its coffee in the first half of the year, as Nariño does.

grows.text: Almost all washed on the farm; Inzá growers ferment and wash in the same tank and dry under cover. Barista Hustle says the old Caturra and Typica have gradually given way to rust-resistant Castillo and Colombia. Thermal-shock and other experimental lots, like those from Finca El Paraíso, are a small specialty niche: one 2021 estimate put all of Colombia's natural, honey and anaerobic exports at about 15,000 bags a year.

cup.text: Cauca's protected regional profile describes high acidity, a medium body and a clean, soft cup with sweet and floral notes over strong caramel aromas; Juan Valdez likens its sweetness to a basket of fruit. Sweet Maria's tasted panela (unrefined cane sugar), brown sugar, raisin and cinnamon in an Inzá lot that arrived in 2025.
cup.why: The regional profile credits long hours of sunshine, steady weather all year and high mountains that block wind and humidity from the Pacific.

story.text: In August, Café de Cauca becomes a protected regional origin name, months after Nariño's.
A Castillo lot from Cauca places third at Colombia's Cup of Excellence.
The Best Coffee of Cauca contest draws 223 lots and sends 16 to auction; a Piendamó grower's lot sets a record US$42 a pound.

sections.title: Towns on the bag
body: Inzá lots come from farms at about 1,400 m (4,600 ft) to over 2,000 m (6,550 ft), where growers traditionally ferment and wash in the same tank, then dry the coffee in covered rooms for two weeks or more. Piendamó is home to Diego Bermúdez's Finca El Paraíso and produced the 2025 contest record; one roaster lists a thermal-shock lot from El Tambo, about 28 km from the capital Popayán. Intelligentsia buys Pink Bourbon from Finca Juan Martín in the Sotará area.

records.name: The Coffee Axis
records.summary: Caldas, Risaralda and Quindío: Colombia's old coffee heartland, medium-bodied and bright.
records.lede: The Coffee Axis (Eje Cafetero) is Colombia's central coffee belt: Caldas, Risaralda and Quindío, with wider definitions adding northern Tolima and northern Valle del Cauca, and sometimes southwestern Antioquia. Old Caldas, which then took in Risaralda and Quindío, was the country's biggest producer in the early 1900s, but production has since shifted southwest toward Huila, Cauca and Nariño. Its coffee cultural landscape has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2011.

facts.label: where coffee grows across the three (3,900–7,200 ft)
grown in old Caldas in 1932
of coffee in Caldas in 2021, down from 220,000 in 1960
plants per hectare in Quindío, the most intensively farmed department (2019)

harvest.text: Caldas picks its main crop August–December and Risaralda September–December, each with a small mitaca (second crop) in April–May. Quindío picks all year: its north peaks September–December and its south March–May, and in 2021 the growers' federation said half of its municipalities were in their main crop in the first half of the year.

grows.text: Washed on the farm, as almost all Colombian coffee is. Cenicafé, the growers' federation's research centre in Chinchiná, Caldas, bred regional Castillo lines for these departments, and rust-resistant varieties like Castillo covered 88% of Colombia's coffee land in 2025; no published source splits the three departments' trees by variety.

cup.text: Juan Valdez, the growers' federation's brand, describes a strong coffee with character: a pronounced aroma, pronounced acidity and a medium body. The Coffee Axis has no protected regional profile of its own.

story.text: The first commercial coffee plantations go in, in what is now Caldas.
Caldas is carved out of Cauca and Antioquia, taking in today's Risaralda and Quindío.
Old Caldas grows more than a million bags of coffee.
Quindío and Risaralda split off from Caldas as departments of their own.
On 25 June UNESCO lists the Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia: six areas in 51 coffee municipalities of Caldas, Quindío, Risaralda and Valle del Cauca.
Caldas has about 60,000 hectares of coffee, after decades of decline.

sections.title: The three departments
body: Caldas, with its capital Manizales, has the widest altitude range and the heaviest rain, 2,100–5,500 mm a year. Risaralda, on a plateau between the central and western ranges of the Andes, has about 19,000 coffee-growing families (2022 figure). Quindío is the most technified, meaning densely planted and intensively farmed.

Cenicafé's regional Castillo lines here include Castillo Naranjal (for Caldas, Quindío, Risaralda and Valle), Castillo El Rosario and Castillo Paraguaicito; a 2006 Cenicafé study grew Castillo lines at the Maracay station in Quimbaya, Quindío.

sections.title: The UNESCO landscape
body: The World Heritage listing covers six areas in 51 coffee municipalities of Caldas, Quindío, Risaralda and Valle del Cauca, with 95,503 farms, more than 79,000 coffee growers and 172,000 hectares of coffee, by the growers' federation's 2021 count. The federation calls it the world's only living, productive coffee cultural landscape.

area.note: Caldas, Risaralda and Quindío are outlined in full. Wider definitions add northwestern Tolima, northern and eastern Valle del Cauca and southwestern Antioquia (Wikipedia), or northern Tolima and northern Valle del Cauca (Barista Hustle); those edges are not outlined.

records.name: Huila
records.summary: Colombia's biggest coffee department: sweet, balanced, with caramel notes.
records.lede: Huila is a department in Colombia's southwest where coffee grows between about 1,000 and 2,200 m (3,300–7,200 ft), often under heavy cloud. It is now the country's largest coffee producer, and a 2015 study put about a third of its coffee at specialty grade, the quality tier specialty roasters buy. Its lots and Nariño's regularly lead Colombia's Cup of Excellence, the best-known national quality competition.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,300–7,200 ft)
of its coffee graded specialty, in a 2015 study
of sun a day under the cloud cover
protected regional origin name granted

harvest.text: Barista Hustle gives August–December for the main crop and March–June for the mitaca, the smaller second crop. That is the pattern in the south, around San Agustín. Northern Huila runs the other way round, with its main crop in the first half of the year, so farms only 100 km apart can be in different harvests. In Cenicafé trials in 2018–2020, La Plata picked most of its coffee in the first half of the year, while Garzón, Pitalito, Algeciras and Acevedo picked most in the second.

grows.text: Almost all washed on the farm, as across Colombia. No published source gives Huila's variety split: Workshop Coffee found red and yellow Caturra growing alongside Castillo on a 4-hectare farm, and nationally rust-resistant varieties like Castillo covered 88% of coffee land in 2025. Pink Bourbon, Papayo and Bourbon Ají are rarer specialty varieties tied to Huila.

cup.text: Huila's protected regional profile describes a balanced, sweet cup with a medium-to-full body and an intense fruity, caramel-like aroma. Juan Valdez, the growers' federation's own brand, adds herbal notes to the fruit.
cup.why: The regional profile points to cloud that cuts direct sun to about 3.5 hours a day and to steady daytime temperatures; Juan Valdez says the cloud shields the cherries from intense sun so they ripen in a balanced, sweet way.
cup.prized: Huila and Nariño lots regularly top Colombia's Cup of Excellence, says Barista Hustle.

story.text: Coffee is first planted in Huila.
Huila's 4,471 coffee farms grow about 48,000 bags a year, around 1.5% of Colombia's crop.
Cheap land draws smallholder families as big farms are split up and sold; some bring know-how from the Coffee Axis.
Café de Huila becomes a protected regional origin name.
The Huila Coffee 2025 competition draws 156 lots, and a Pitalito grower's lot sets a record of US$65 a pound.

sections.title: Towns and varieties
body: Pitalito and Acevedo are the towns most tied to the Papayo variety, with farms in Bruselas, near Pitalito, and in Oporapa. Workshop Coffee based its 2013 buying trip in San Agustín, at the department's southern tip.
Huila is also where Pink Bourbon was first identified and where Bourbon Ají comes from, says the importer Sucafina.

sections.title: Breeding for Huila
body: Huila hosted 43% of Cenicafé's national variety trials, and from 2016 to 2021 the research centre tested new rust-resistant lines on farms at 1,300–1,700 m (4,250–5,600 ft) in Garzón, Pitalito, La Plata, Algeciras and Acevedo, to build a regional variety for the department.

records.name: Nariño
records.summary: Colombia's high far south: bright, citric and sweet.
records.lede: Nariño, in Colombia's far south, grows its coffee high: about half of its farms are above 1,800 m (5,900 ft). Over roughly 30 years it has gone from nearly unknown among specialty buyers to perhaps the best quality reputation in the country, says Barista Hustle. In 2011 it became the first Colombian region with its own protected origin name.

facts.label: where coffee grows (4,300–7,500 ft)
of its farms lie above 1,800 m (5,900 ft)
Colombia's first regional protected origin name
bags a year, about a fifth of Huila's (2022 figures)

harvest.text: Barista Hustle gives a single picking season, May–September. The growers' federation counts Nariño's first-half picking as its main crop, as it does Cauca's. Lot listings fit that: Royal Coffee gives May–July for La Unión, and a 2020 study of Castillo farms in La Unión, Sandoná, La Florida and Consacá sampled the main harvest in April–June.

cup.text: Nariño's protected regional profile describes high acidity, a medium body, sweet notes and a clean, soft cup with a very pronounced aroma; Juan Valdez adds citric notes. Barista Hustle sums it up as notable acidity, sweetness and complex flavour. Sey Coffee tasted ripe stone fruit and lively citrus acidity in a washed Caturra from Buesaco.
cup.why: Cool temperatures slow ripening, which both the regional profile and Juan Valdez link to more sugar in the bean. The farms sit near the equator under strong, direct sun, on volcanic soils.
cup.prized: Nariño lots regularly top Colombia's Cup of Excellence, says Barista Hustle.

story.text: In February, Café de Nariño becomes Colombia's first protected regional origin name.
In January, StoneX reports the Nariño coffee committee expecting first-half output about 30% above a year earlier.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: The coffee lands center on Pasto, the department capital, with the Galeras volcano above it. Nariño grows far less than Huila, about 600,000 bags a year against roughly five times that.

sections.title: Small farms, high and slow
body: Farms are very small: Sey Coffee's Buesaco lot came from three growers with 1–1.5 hectares of Caturra each, at 2,000–2,200 m (6,550–7,200 ft). Royal Coffee's La Unión lot pooled 20 small producers at 1,700–2,200 m (5,600–7,200 ft), each of whom picks, pulps, ferments, washes and dries at home.

Sey says the cool, dry heights slow ripening, which it links to more complex sugars and brighter acidity; its Buesaco lot fermented dry in tanks for 13–16 hours and dried on raised beds for 12–18 days.

grows.text: Washed on very small family farms, often in each grower's own small wet mill; one La Unión lot was dried on patios and raised beds inside solar dryers. No published source gives the variety split; lots list Caturra, Castillo, Colombia and Typica, and nationally rust-resistant varieties like Castillo covered 88% of coffee land in 2025.

records.name: Santander
records.summary: Shade-grown under native forest; balanced, herbal and lightly citric.
records.lede: Santander is where Colombian coffee first took hold: in the 1800s it flourished here and in neighbouring Norte de Santander, before Antioquia and the rest of the country took the lead. Much of it now grows under the shade of native forest, which keeps temperatures even, and it gained its protected origin name in 2014. A 2022 review says it has the highest share of rust-resistant varieties of any department.

facts.label: protected regional origin name granted
grown under trees, much of it native forest
of improved seed requested in 2025, the most of any department

harvest.text: Barista Hustle gives October–December for Santander's harvest. In the first half of 2021 the growers' federation listed only a small part of the department as picking, in its mitaca (the smaller second crop). The federation's 1932 coffee census had put the harvest at August–October, with no second crop.

cup.text: Santander's protected regional profile describes a clean, balanced cup with a medium-to-full body, medium acidity, and sweet, herbal and fruity flavours with a light citrus edge. Juan Valdez also stresses its pronounced aroma and herbal notes. Tasting notes on two Santander blends lean nutty and chocolatey: Otus Coffee lists chocolate milk, hazelnut, brown sugar and sweet citrus, and InterAmerican lists chocolate, nuts and lime.
cup.why: Shade keeps temperatures even, says the regional profile; Juan Valdez adds that the forest protects the coffee from high heat.
cup.watch: Royal Coffee New York finds that Santander's and Boyacá's lower, warmer farms give less complex coffee, a classic breakfast-blend cup.

story.text: Coffee flourishes first in Santander, Norte de Santander and Cundinamarca.

Large Santander estates, built on credit in the late 1800s, fall into financial crisis after the Thousand Days' War and falling prices, and production grows instead in Antioquia and across the country.
The growers' federation starts the research behind a protected name, led by Cenicafé with the Santander growers' committee.
Café de Santander becomes a protected regional origin name.
The growers' federation opens a regional coffee hub here in November, a COP 4.22 billion investment, and pilots carbon credits for smallholders' agroforestry farms (farms that mix coffee with trees).

grows.text: Washed, and much of it grown under shade. A 2022 review says Santander has the highest share of rust-resistant varieties, such as Castillo, of any department; one cooperative blend from southern Santander mixes Caturra and Castillo.

sections.title: Shade and cooperatives
body: Santander coffee grows mostly under trees, much of it native forest, in what a 2022 review calls a shade-grown technified system: dense, modern plantings kept under shade. InterAmerican Coffee credits the department with more advanced shading practices, even temperatures and a concentrated harvest.

One cooperative blend from COOPSANTANDER growers in southern Santander was a washed mix of Caturra and Castillo grown at 1,200–1,750 m (3,950–5,750 ft). InterAmerican buys a blend from growers around Bucaramanga, the capital, through its sister exporter.

records.name: Sierra Nevada
records.summary: Shaded coffee on a coastal mountain range: chocolate and nuts.
records.lede: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is an isolated mountain range on Colombia's Caribbean coast, with peaks of about 5,700 m (18,700 ft) only 42 km from the sea. Coffee grows at about 500–1,900 m (1,600–6,200 ft), much of it shaded by remaining forest, and many growers are Indigenous Arhuaco families. Its protected origin name, granted in 2017, covers 33 municipalities in Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira.

facts.label: where coffee grows (1,600–6,200 ft)
municipalities in three departments under its protected name
of growers are Arhuaco, says Colombia's tourism site
the year it became a UNESCO biosphere reserve

harvest.text: One long picking season, September–February, says Barista Hustle, with no mitaca (second crop) listed; InterAmerican gives September–December for ASOARHUACO's coffee. The growers' federation's 1932 census also recorded a single harvest in Magdalena, November–January.

grows.text: Washed and grown under shade; the Arhuaco association ASOARHUACO's coffee is certified organic, washed and dried on raised beds. Cenicafé bred a regional Castillo line for these departments, Castillo Pueblo Bello; no published source gives the variety mix.

cup.text: The protected regional profile describes a clean, balanced cup with an even, medium-to-full body, medium acidity, chocolate-like flavours and a sweet, nutty aroma. Juan Valdez puts it as hazelnut with lingering chocolate.
cup.why: The regional profile points to strong light, low rainfall, high humidity and coffee grown entirely in shade.

story.text: Forest clearing begins to cut the range's water supply; two rivers have since dried up completely.
UNESCO makes the Sierra Nevada a biosphere reserve.
Café de la Sierra Nevada becomes a protected regional origin name, covering coffee areas in Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Colombia's tourism site says about 70% of the growers are Arhuaco, an Indigenous people, and Barista Hustle says more than a tenth of the area's population lives in Indigenous reserves. Growers use the remaining native forest as shade for their coffee, which helps protect that forest.

The protected name also takes in some coffee areas outside the range itself, in the eastern Andes near the Venezuelan border. Cenicafé bred a regional Castillo line for these departments, Castillo Pueblo Bello.

sections.title: Cooperatives on the bag
body: ASOARHUACO, the association of Arhuaco producers, has about 1,000 members who grow coffee and cocoa under shade trees with organic certification; InterAmerican lists its coffee at 1,200–1,500 m (3,950–4,900 ft) and tastes tropical fruit, brown sugar and grapefruit with a delicate body. Asoanei, another Arhuaco cooperative, had 400 members in 2015 and sought fair-trade and organic certification.
Four Indigenous peoples live in the range, the Arhuaco, Kogi, Wiwa and Kankuamo; the Arhuaco call it the Heart of the World. Cenicafé runs a research station at Pueblo Bello, in Cesar.
