area.note: Only the coffee lands of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, where the three departments meet; the protected name also takes in some coffee areas in the eastern Andes near the Venezuelan border.

records.name: Tolima
records.summary: Third-biggest coffee department: citrus and fruit, with lively acidity.
records.lede: Tolima is Colombia's third-largest coffee producer, with coffee at about 1,000–2,000 m (3,300–6,600 ft). Its north belongs to the Coffee Axis, while its southern municipalities, around Planadas, have become the most important for specialty buyers. A warm climate gives it two flowerings a year, and it gained its protected origin name in 2017.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,300–6,600 ft)
Colombia's third-largest coffee department
record at the Tolima international coffee fair (2025)
protected regional origin name granted

harvest.text: Barista Hustle gives March–June for the main crop and October–December for the mitaca, the smaller second crop. The growers' federation counts central and southern Tolima's first-half picking as the main crop. The regional profile credits a warm climate with two flowerings a year.

grows.text: Washed on the farm, as across Colombia: ASOPEP's members in Planadas pulp, ferment, wash and dry their coffee in their own small mills, and its lots are sun-dried. No published source gives the variety split; Planadas lots list Caturra, Castillo, Colombia and Typica, and nationally rust-resistant varieties like Castillo covered 88% of coffee land in 2025.

cup.text: Tolima's protected regional profile describes medium-high acidity, a clean, soft, balanced cup, sweet flavours and citrus and fruit; Barista Hustle reads it as fairly high acidity and body with many fruity and citrusy flavours. Juan Valdez calls it smooth and balanced, sweet from the aroma on.

story.text: The first coffee trees are planted in Tolima.
Growers in Planadas found ASOPEP, an organic producers' association, with 165 members.
Café de Tolima becomes a protected regional origin name.
At the third Tolima international coffee fair, 20 of 642 lots go to auction and one sets a record US$72 a pound.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Planadas, in the far south, is the third-largest coffee municipality in all of Colombia. The Nevado del Tolima volcano rises in the north. A 2015 study of hundreds of samples from Tolima, Huila, Cauca, Nariño and Norte de Santander found Tolima's the least like the others.
Cenicafé, the federation's research centre, selected a regional Castillo line for Tolima, Castillo La Trinidad.

sections.title: Planadas and ASOPEP
body: Planadas, in Tolima's southernmost corner, has thousands of smallholders who grow coffee on small plots among shade trees, bananas, maize, beans and sugarcane. Armed conflict and coca long isolated them, and Royal Coffee says the violence has eased in recent years.

ASOPEP, the Planadas organic growers' association, runs a dry mill and a cupping lab that doubles as a coffee and cacao school; Royal Coffee lists its coffee at 1,400–2,100 m (4,600–6,900 ft), picked April–July and October–January, with tropical fruit and nutty notes.

records.name: Brunca
records.summary: Early-ripening Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus; mild to citrus-sweet cups.
records.lede: Brunca covers the coffee cantons of Pérez Zeledón, Coto Brus and Buenos Aires, and Royal Coffee's 2020 origin profile put it at about 20% of Costa Rica's crop. It ripens early, so the national harvest starts here, and in 2025 ICAFE, the national coffee institute, split it into two regions named Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop, in Royal Coffee's 2020 origin profile
where it grows (2,000–5,600 ft)
top score in the honey and natural category at the 2025 Taza de la Excelencia, a Pérez Zeledón Gesha
split into Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus regions

harvest.text: Picked from August to February. ICAFE counts Brunca as the early-ripening zone where Costa Rica's harvest begins.

grows.text: ICAFE, the national coffee institute, names Caturra and Catuaí as Costa Rica's main varieties and says wet (washed) processing has long been the main method; no count for Brunca itself is published. Its recent competition winners are Geshas: washed lots, a black honey, and the 2025 winner of the combined honey and natural category.

cup.text: 1Zpresso's guide says Brunca varies widely: lower farms tend toward smoother cups, higher ones toward more sweetness, complex citrus and jasmine-like aromatics. Café Britt describes complex citrus ranging from very mild to very sweet, and Royal Coffee calls the profile milder and full-bodied.
cup.why: Altitude: farms run from 600 to 1,700 m (2,000–5,600 ft), and 1Zpresso links the sweeter, more citric cups to the higher ones.
cup.prized: Competition Geshas: Pérez Zeledón lots won both the washed and the honey and natural categories at the 2025 Taza de la Excelencia, and La Torre's black-honey Gesha placed second in its category at the 2024 Cup of Excellence with 92.00 points.

story.text: La Torre, Jhon Alvarado Abarca's farm, places second in the honey and natural category of the Cup of Excellence with a black-honey Gesha at 92.00 points.
Coto Brus's estimated harvest was 15,000 fanegas (Costa Rica's bushel-like harvest unit) above 2019/20, and Pérez Zeledón's was rising too.
Pérez Zeledón Geshas won the washed category (Vista Paraíso, 90.63 points) and the honey and natural category (La Cusuka, 91.22) at the Taza de la Excelencia, Costa Rica's national quality contest.
ICAFE split Brunca into two regions, Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus.
ICAFE figures reported by CR Hoy showed coffee land growing in Pérez Zeledón and, after an earlier fall, expanding again in Coto Brus, while the country as a whole kept losing it.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Pérez Zeledón, Coto Brus and Buenos Aires are the cantons to look for. Coto Brus is higher and more humid and depends on coffee; Buenos Aires lies in the foothills of La Amistad International Park; Pérez Zeledón, the canton around San Isidro de El General, was among Brunca's first coffee areas.

sections.title: Split in two (2025)
body: El Financiero reported that ICAFE split Brunca because Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus differ socially and in their topography and altitude, and lie far apart; Coto Brus, for example, relies more on Indigenous labour. Both are raising their output, especially Coto Brus. The report does not say which of the two new regions takes in Buenos Aires.

sections.title: Grades
body: Royal Coffee's 2020 profile says most of Brunca's coffee grows at lower elevations and is graded HB or GHB (Hard Bean or Good Hard Bean) rather than SHB (Strictly Hard Bean, grown above about 1,200 m · 3,900 ft), which it links to a milder, fuller-bodied cup.

area.note: Since 2025 ICAFE treats Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus as separate regions. El Financiero doesn't say which one takes in Buenos Aires, but ICAFE's electoral regions with the same two names (2006 decree) group Buenos Aires with Coto Brus.

records.name: Central Valley
records.summary: Where Costa Rican coffee began, around San José, Heredia and Alajuela.
records.lede: The Central Valley (Valle Central) surrounds San José, Heredia and Alajuela, on the central plateau where Costa Rican coffee growing began in 1779. Royal Coffee's 2020 profile put it at about 15% of the crop, but the city keeps spreading over its farms and the harvest has been shrinking; in 2025 ICAFE folded the Tres Ríos region into it.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop, in Royal Coffee's 2020 origin profile
coffee first grown on the central plateau (Meseta Central)
where about 80% of its coffee grows (3,300–4,600 ft); the rest reaches 1,900 m (6,200 ft)
fanegas: the 2023/24 harvest against 2019/20

harvest.text: Picked from November to February. The valley has well-defined rainy and dry seasons.

grows.text: ICAFE, the national coffee institute, names Caturra and Catuaí as Costa Rica's main varieties and says wet (washed) processing has long been the main method; no count for the valley itself is published. Cafe Imports singles out some of the country's best naturals here.

cup.text: Café Britt describes a balanced cup with hints of chocolate and fruit and a subtle honey aroma; Royal Coffee calls the region's profile more citric and sweet.

feel.body: medium to full, depending on altitude

cup.prized: Cafe Imports says some of Costa Rica's best natural-process coffees (dried inside the whole cherry) come from here.

story.text: Coffee growing in Costa Rica began on the Meseta Central, the central plateau around San José.
The harvest came in 103,000 fanegas (Costa Rica's bushel-like harvest unit) below 2019/20, part of a downward trend over the last six harvests.

Hacienda Colima–Volcán Azul placed second among washed coffees at the Taza de la Excelencia, with 90.09 points; La Nación listed it under the Central Valley, though the 2024 Cup of Excellence listed the same estate under the West Valley.
ICAFE merged Tres Ríos, a few kilometres east of the capital, into the Central Valley region.
ICAFE figures reported by CR Hoy showed Costa Rica's coffee land down from nearly 103,000 ha in 2005 to 82,500 ha in 2025, with urban growth around the capital among the main causes.

sections.title: City versus coffee
body: CR Hoy reported in 2026 that housing, industry and commerce have taken coffee land in Heredia and Alajuela, that Guadalupe and Moravia no longer produce coffee, and that ICAFE still needs a new census to measure the loss. In 2025 ICAFE's promotion manager, Andrés Piedra, said it hopes places such as Tres Ríos, Heredia, Alajuela and Puriscal can hold on to their production.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Perfect Daily Grind's 2022 tour of the valley names San Rafael, Barva and San Isidro in Heredia, Desamparados in San José, and the slopes of the Poás volcano, home of Starbucks' experimental farm Hacienda Alsacia. Since 2025 Tres Ríos, in La Unión canton, is part of this region, though the Tres Ríos name can still be used.

area.note: ICAFE's Valle Central region as its 2006 electoral rules list it: every canton of Heredia province; San José and the cantons around and west of it (including Puriscal, Mora, Santa Ana, Escazú and Turrubares); Alajuela and Poás; and La Unión, home of Tres Ríos, merged in 2025. Desamparados is kept because Perfect Daily Grind tours its hills as part of the valley, though ICAFE's list puts it under Los Santos. Coffee grows only in part of these cantons; CR Hoy says Guadalupe and Moravia no longer grow any.

records.name: Guanacaste
records.summary: Low farms across three provinces; soft acidity, round body.
records.lede: The Guanacaste coffee region spreads across parts of three provinces, Guanacaste, Puntarenas and Alajuela, and in Alajuela it centres on San Carlos and Sarapiquí. Its farms sit fairly low, at 600–1,300 m (2,000–4,300 ft), often under shade trees, and in 2025 ICAFE merged it into its Zona Norte (northern zone) region.

facts.label: where it grows (2,000–4,300 ft)
share of the crop: Royal Coffee (2020) puts the three regions it doesn't profile, Guanacaste among them, at a small fraction
average temperature (79 °F), the warmest region in 1Zpresso's guide

harvest.text: Picked from July to February.

cup.text: 1Zpresso's guide describes softer acidity, a moderate body and a round mouthfeel, sometimes with a salty edge and a bittersweet finish. Café Britt similarly notes a smooth body, light acidity and distinct bitter and salty notes. Coopeldos, a cooperative in Tilarán, sells a sweet, chocolatey coffee with fruit and a hint of spice, medium to intense acidity and a soft body.

sections.title: Where coffee grows
body: 1Zpresso's guide places the region between the Central Volcanic Range and the Guanacaste range, across parts of Guanacaste, Puntarenas and Alajuela provinces, centred in Alajuela on San Carlos and Sarapiquí; with an average of 26 °C (79 °F), shade trees are common to protect the coffee from heat. Costa Rica's agriculture ministry (MAG) lists Abangares, Tilarán, Santa Cruz, Hojancha, Nicoya and Nandayure as the coffee cantons it serves in Guanacaste province (2024).

sections.title: Now part of Zona Norte
body: In 2025 ICAFE folded Guanacaste into its Zona Norte region, so coffee from places like Nandayure now shares a region with places like San Carlos.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Wikipedia's table of the regions lists San Carlos, Sarapiquí, the Nicoya Peninsula and Puntarenas under Guanacaste.

Coopeldos, a cooperative in Tilarán, grows its coffee at 800–1,250 m (2,600–4,100 ft). A 2008 history by Brunilda Hilje Quirós and Margarita Torres Hernández traces coffee in Tilarán from 1900 to 1994, as an example of a region left out of official histories.

grows.text: ICAFE, the national coffee institute, names Caturra and Catuaí as Costa Rica's main varieties and says wet (washed) processing has long been the main method. No published source describes Guanacaste's own variety or process mix.

story.text: ICAFE merged Guanacaste into its Zona Norte region, so coffee from Nandayure now shares a region with San Carlos.

area.note: Built from sources: San Carlos and Sarapiquí (1Zpresso, Wikipedia), the Guanacaste cantons where MAG supports coffee growers, and Puntarenas, which Wikipedia lists as a sub-area. Farms sit at 600–1,300 m (2,000–4,300 ft), so only the higher parts of these large cantons grow coffee. Since 2025 ICAFE calls the region Zona Norte.

records.name: Orosi
records.summary: Smallest harvest; a humid valley with chocolaty, elegant cups.
records.lede: Orosi is a valley in Cartago province where coffee is the leading industry, its hillsides lined with coffee and sugar cane. It makes the smallest harvest of Costa Rica's regions, and in 2025 ICAFE joined it to Turrialba; even together they remain the smallest.

facts.label: where it grows (3,300–4,600 ft)
of rain a year, May to November
harvest of any region, even after joining Turrialba in 2025
elevation of Orosi town (3,450 ft)

harvest.text: Picked from September to March by 1Zpresso's guide, though in 2020 ICAFE said picking in Orosi starts as early as July.

cup.text: 1Zpresso's guide says Orosi leans chocolaty, with an elegant acidity balancing its sweetness and body; Café Britt calls its coffees smooth and balanced.

sections.title: Growing it
body: The valley is humid, with about 2,500 mm of rain a year, and protected forest around it. 1Zpresso's guide links Orosi to larger beans and notes more than a century of coffee growing here.

sections.title: Now part of Turrialba
body: In 2025 ICAFE joined Orosi to the Turrialba region; El Financiero reported that coffee from Turrialba, Orosi and Cachí shares similar traits, and that even combined it remains the region with the lowest production. The Orosi name can still be used in promotion.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Orosi is a district of Paraíso canton, at about 1,050 m (3,450 ft), with Tapantí National Park at the head of the valley. Cachí, another Paraíso town at 1,049 m (3,442 ft), sits among coffee plantations by Lake Cachí, a reservoir on the Reventazón River, across the water from Ujarrás.

grows.text: ICAFE, the national coffee institute, names Caturra and Catuaí as Costa Rica's main varieties and says wet (washed) processing has long been the main method. No published source describes Orosi's own mix.

story.text: ICAFE folded Orosi into the Turrialba region.

area.note: The Orosi valley and Cachí, both in Paraíso canton, Cartago province. Since 2025 ICAFE counts Orosi as part of the Turrialba region.

records.name: Tarrazú
records.summary: Costa Rica's best-known region: high, sweet and brightly acidic.
records.lede: Tarrazú, in the mountains about 70 km south of San José, is Costa Rica's best-known coffee region and its biggest in Royal Coffee's 2020 profile, with about 40% of the crop. Most of it grows high enough to be graded SHB (Strictly Hard Bean, the top altitude grade). Locally the area is called Los Santos, and since 2025 that is also the name ICAFE, the national coffee institute, uses for the region.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop, in Royal Coffee's 2020 origin profile
where it grows (3,900–6,200 ft)
winning lots at the 2024 Cup of Excellence
protected origin name granted for three cantons

harvest.text: Picked from November to March. Rain falls from May to November and the dry season runs December to April; Café Britt says these clear seasons ripen the cherries evenly.

grows.text: Caturra and Catuaí are the everyday varieties, as across Costa Rica. Gesha, grown here since 2012, now leads the competition tables: 22 of the 34 winning lots at the 2024 Cup of Excellence were Geshas. Washed coffee is the long-standing base; the micromills also make many honey and natural lots, and some experimental ferments.

cup.text: Café Britt and a guide from grinder maker 1Zpresso both describe Tarrazú as tending toward chocolate, orange, vanilla and dried fruit; 1Zpresso adds a honey-like sweetness and jasmine-like aromatics.
cup.why: Announcing the 2019 protected name, the government credited the high altitude and late ripening for the coffee's very high acidity and very good body and aroma.
cup.prized: Competition lots: all three top coffees at the 2020 Taza de la Excelencia, Costa Rica's national quality contest, came from Tarrazú, two of them honey-processed (dried with some of the sticky fruit still on the seed). At the 2024 Cup of Excellence it supplied 25 of the 34 winning lots, led by Geshas from Santa Teresa (washed, 92.04) and Don Cayito (honey, 93.62).

story.text: Farmers began growing coffee in the high valley around San Marcos.
La Candelilla, in La Sabana de San Marcos, opened as Costa Rica's first micromill, a small mill a farm builds to process its own coffee.
Gesha production began in the region.
The government handed over a denomination of origin (a protected place name) covering the cantons of Tarrazú, Dota and León Cortés.
ICAFE renamed its region Los Santos, because only the council that runs the denomination may use the name Tarrazú.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Most of the land is high: in 2019, 85% of Los Santos coffee land grew SHB beans, at 1,200–1,650 m (3,900–5,400 ft), and Perfect Daily Grind's 2022 tour puts farms at about 1,400 m to just over 2,000 m (4,600–6,600 ft). 1Zpresso's guide notes slightly acidic sedimentary soils and coffee grown under companion shade trees.

Most farms are small, about 2.5 ha on average by Café Britt's count, and a growing number run their own micromills; much coffee goes through cooperatives: Royal Coffee counts Coop Dota and Coop Tarrazú, with Coop Naranjo in the West Valley, at more than 8,000 members together.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for San Marcos de Tarrazú, the main town, and nearby Santa María (de Dota) and San Pablo, which also supply specialty coffee. The protected Tarrazú name covers three cantons (counties): Tarrazú, Dota and León Cortés. InterAmerican Coffee notes that this legal area is smaller than the area long sold as Tarrazú, so some coffee once labeled Tarrazú no longer qualifies.

sections.title: At harvest
body: Café Britt says the population of Los Santos nearly triples during the harvest, and that most farms grow their coffee under a mix of native and imported shade trees.

area.note: The three cantons of the protected Tarrazú name (2019). InterAmerican Coffee notes that coffee long sold as Tarrazú also came from beyond them; since 2025 ICAFE calls its region Los Santos.

records.name: Tres Ríos
records.summary: The 'Bordeaux of Costa Rica', shrinking under urban growth.
records.lede: Tres Ríos sits a few kilometres east of San José, near the Irazú volcano, and has long been nicknamed the Bordeaux of Costa Rica. As the city spread over its farms, production fell, and in 2025 ICAFE folded it into the Central Valley region, though the Tres Ríos name can still be used to promote coffee.

facts.label: where it grows (3,900–5,400 ft)
merged into the Central Valley region
the volcano whose minerals enrich its soil
Strictly Hard Bean, the top altitude grade (Royal Coffee, 2020)

harvest.text: Picked from November to March.

cup.text: Cafe Imports describes a smooth, milder, easy-drinking profile with toffee sweetness and soft citrus. 1Zpresso's guide notes a refined, balanced acidity, a long finish and a fuller body.
cup.why: Its flavor is credited to fertile soil enriched with minerals from the Irazú volcano, balanced by rain and warm summers.
cup.watch: Urban growth has closed dozens of its coffee farms.

sections.title: Now part of the Central Valley
body: In June 2025 El Financiero reported that ICAFE had merged Tres Ríos into the Central Valley because it had become a small region: urban growth had replaced coffee plots and production had fallen. ICAFE's promotion manager, Andrés Piedra, said the Tres Ríos name can still be used in promotion.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Tres Ríos is in La Unión canton, Cartago province. Along with Tres Ríos itself, the communities of Concepción and San Ramón still grow coffee for the specialty market.

grows.text: ICAFE, the national coffee institute, names Caturra and Catuaí as Costa Rica's main varieties and says wet (washed) processing has long been the main method. No published source describes Tres Ríos's own mix.

story.text: Royal Coffee's origin profile calls Tres Ríos the smallest of the regions it covers, with almost all its coffee graded SHB.
ICAFE merged Tres Ríos into the Central Valley region because urban growth had replaced its coffee plots.
CR Hoy reported that Tres Ríos has lost its small coffee farms and that only the largest remain.

area.note: Tres Ríos is in La Unión canton, Cartago province; since 2025 it is part of ICAFE's Central Valley region.

records.name: Turrialba
records.summary: Low, early-picking valley by an active volcano; gentle, light cups.
records.lede: Turrialba is a low region, at 500–1,400 m (1,600–4,600 ft), in a valley beside the active Turrialba volcano. It is among the first in Costa Rica to pick each year, from as early as July, and its coffee is known for a gentle, light cup. In 2025 ICAFE folded Orosi into it.

facts.label: where it grows (1,600–4,600 ft)
when picking can start, among the country's earliest
share of the crop: Royal Coffee (2020) puts the three regions it doesn't profile, Turrialba among them, at a small fraction

harvest.text: Picked from July to March, one of the earliest starts in Costa Rica.

cup.text: Café Britt describes mild acidity, a light body and a soft aroma, and 1Zpresso's guide a gentle, lighter cup with delicate aromatics.
cup.why: Café Britt says the active Turrialba volcano heavily shapes the flavors here.

story.text: ICAFE said picking would start from July in Turrialba and Orosi, as well as in the early-ripening Brunca region.
Aquiares Estate's natural Centroamericano (H1) is among the Cup of Excellence's National Winner lots, with 87.42 points.
ICAFE merged Orosi into the Turrialba region; El Financiero noted that Turrialba's harvest had trended down over the previous six seasons.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Turrialba averages about 23 °C (73 °F), with roughly 2,800 mm of rain a year, on volcanic and alluvial (river-laid) soils, and 1Zpresso's guide says some of Costa Rica's earliest coffee farms were here.

sections.title: CATIE's coffee collection
body: Turrialba is home to CATIE, the agricultural research centre whose international coffee collection holds about 2,000 kinds of coffee plants, among them Arabica, Robusta (Coffea canephora), Liberica and wild coffees from Ethiopia and Sudan.

grows.text: ICAFE, the national coffee institute, names Caturra and Catuaí as Costa Rica's main varieties and says wet (washed) processing has long been the main method; no count for Turrialba is published. Aquiares Estate has competed with a natural Centroamericano, a modern F1 hybrid.

area.note: Turrialba canton and neighbouring Jiménez canton (home of Juan Viñas, a long-established Turrialba-region grower), Cartago province; coffee grows only on their middle slopes, about 500–1,400 m (1,600–4,600 ft). Since 2025 ICAFE's Turrialba region also takes in Orosi (Paraíso canton).

records.name: West Valley
records.summary: Western slopes; orange, peach and honey; many competition winners.
records.lede: The West Valley (Valle Occidental) runs along the western slopes of Costa Rica's central mountains, on fertile volcanic soil, around towns like Naranjo and Grecia. Royal Coffee's origin profile gives it about a fifth of the country's crop (20% in 2020, 21% on its current page), and Cafe Imports notes that a high share of Costa Rica's Cup of Excellence winners come from here.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop, in Royal Coffee's origin profile (2020)
where it grows (2,300–5,200 ft)
finalists at the 2020 Taza de la Excelencia, the national quality contest
winning lots at the 2024 Cup of Excellence, most of them fermentation or honey lots

harvest.text: Picked from October to February.

grows.text: 1Zpresso's guide says the region grows mainly Caturra and Catuaí, with smaller pockets of Villa Sarchi, while Cafe Imports finds plenty of Villa Sarchi and Villalobos and more and more SL28 and Gesha. Gesha and a variety listed as San Roque turn up among the 2024 Cup of Excellence winners. Washed coffee is Costa Rica's long-standing norm; the region's specialty lots lean to honeys (semi-lavado) and, lately, fermentation experiments.

cup.text: Café Britt and 1Zpresso's guide describe West Valley coffees as ranging from orange and peach to honey and vanilla, and 1Zpresso adds chocolate-like notes. One roaster's red-honey lot from Naranjo (red honey leaves all the sticky fruit on the seed while it dries) is sold as bright, sweet and fruit-forward. Perfect Daily Grind's 2022 tour singles out Naranjo for floral coffees, and Erasmo Arrieta, a Taza de la Excelencia judge, describes orange- and tangerine-like sweetness and acidity, with peach in the Geishas.
cup.prized: Cafe Imports notes a high share of the country's Cup of Excellence winners here, plenty of the Costa Rican varieties Villa Sarchi and Villalobos, and some newer, experimental ones such as SL28 and Gesha.
cup.why: Perfect Daily Grind's 2022 tour credits the air currents that cross toward the Central Valley, the hills and the Poás volcano; 1Zpresso's guide points to fertile volcanic soils and many microclimates.

story.text: Villa Sarchi, a dwarf mutation of Bourbon, was found in north-western Alajuela province; it is still grown in small pockets here.
West Valley coffees made up 14 of the 26 finalists at the Taza de la Excelencia.
West Valley farms take 7 of the 34 winning lots at the Cup of Excellence, four of them in the experimental (fermentation) category.
El Financiero reported that the urban growth behind Tres Ríos's decline is starting to be felt here too, in places like Grecia.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Naranjo, a canton in Alajuela province, is one of the West Valley's standout coffee names; Perfect Daily Grind's 2022 tour also names Zarcero, San Ramón and Atenas, and Grecia is another of the region's coffee towns. Coop Naranjo is one of the country's large cooperatives.

area.note: ICAFE's Valle Central Occidental region as its 2006 electoral rules list it: Naranjo, Grecia, Sarchí (Valverde Vega), Palmares, San Ramón, Atenas, Zarcero (Alfaro Ruiz), San Mateo and Orotina, all in Alajuela province. Coffee grows only in the higher parts of these cantons.

records.name: Guji
records.summary: Southern Oromia's fruity naturals and washed lots, once sold as Sidamo.
records.lede: Guji is a zone of Oromia in southern Ethiopia, next door to Yirgacheffe and Sidama. It was long treated as part of Sidamo and has only fairly recently been recognised as a coffee area of its own, known for complex, fruity coffees, washed and natural.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,600–6,900 ft)
one Royal Coffee natural, from Deri Kidame, grew at 1,900–2,300 m (6,250–7,550 ft)
Uraga, Kercha, Hambela, Odo Shakiso, Adola and Bule Hora

harvest.text: Royal Coffee's Guji lots list October to January or November to February, depending on the lot.

grows.text: Both washed and natural, says Coffee Hunter; no published source gives the split. Of the six Guji lots among the 2021 Cup of Excellence winners, four were naturals, one honey and one anaerobic, from local landraces (some entered as Typica), Kurume and 74110.

cup.text: Coffee Hunter calls Guji complex, balanced and fruity, and 1Zpresso describes bright citrus and berry-like acidity with fruit-forward sweetness. Royal Coffee New York says its naturals tend to be fruit-forward with a medium body; in three Coffee Review write-ups of Guji coffees, cocoa nib showed up alongside the fruit each time.
cup.why: 1Zpresso credits fertile volcanic soils and big swings between day and night temperatures.
cup.prized: The Roasters Pack says the West Guji zone, home of the Kurume and Dega landraces, is known for some of Ethiopia's highest-quality coffee, with floral, citric cups.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Guji is a zone of Oromia, not part of the Sidama Region. Its coffee used to be sold in the exchange's Sidamo category, and some lots still carry both names, like Royal Coffee New York's “Ethiopia Natural Sidamo Guji G4”.
Woreda (district) names such as Hambela, Uraga, Kercha or Odo Shakiso often follow. Shakiso also has a washing station of that name, and Coffee Hunter photographs cherry sorting at Buku.

sections.title: Guji and West Guji
body: West Guji Zone, with its seat at Bule Hora, was later formed from nine districts and two towns taken from Borena and Guji zones, so bags may say Guji, West Guji or East Guji. Coffee Hunter's six Guji coffee woredas are Uraga, Kercha, Hambela, Odo Shakiso, Adola and Bule Hora.

story.text: In September, Guji Zone is created from the upland woredas of Borena Zone, with its seat at Negele (Nagele).
At Ethiopia's first Cup of Excellence, West Guji lots are among the winners.
A natural from Odo Shakiso places third at the Cup of Excellence and sells for about US$94–95 a pound; six of the 33 winning lots are from Guji.

area.note: Coffee Hunter's six Guji coffee woredas (Hambela appears as Hambela Wamena). The 2016 boundaries predate West Guji Zone: there, Bule Hora sits in Borena zone and the other five in Guji zone.

records.name: Harrar
records.summary: Eastern naturals: heavy, winey, blueberry and chocolate, more like Yemen.
records.lede: Harrar is the coffee of Ethiopia's dry eastern highlands, named for the old walled city of Harar. It is almost always natural (dried in the fruit) and tends to be heavy and winey, closer in style to Yemen's coffees than to Ethiopia's southern and western ones.

facts.label: almost always, dried inside the fruit
of the main regions Royal Coffee New York compares
longberry, shortberry and Mocha (peaberry)
where InterAmerican's Harrar Grade 4 grew (4,950–6,950 ft)
of Ethiopia's coffee came from East and West Hararghe in 2005, about 12,000 t

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York); InterAmerican gives October–February for its Harrar. Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

grows.text: Almost always natural, dried in the fruit (Cafe Imports, Coffee Review); UNIDO also says natural processing is more common in Harar. The trees are local landraces sold as heirloom.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes intense, winey fruit like blueberry and blackberry jam with a little spice and a heavy body, and Cafe Imports finds it distinctly chocolatey and nutty. Coffee Review says Harrars resemble Yemen's coffees more than southern or western Ethiopia's. In Coffee Review's tastings, one Harrar showed blueberry, brown sugar, vanilla and cherry blossom (2017), another molasses, dark chocolate and pear (2016).
cup.why: 1Zpresso says the dry, cool climate suits natural processing, and Cafe Imports links the chocolate and nut tones to that drier climate.
cup.prized: The best show an intense blueberry or blackberry aroma, and roasters use it in espresso blends for its aromatics.
cup.watch: Drying in the fruit can tip into ferment: even a 93-point Harrar Coffee Review tasted in 2000 was noted as close to fermented.

story.text: West Hararghe grows 8,364 t of coffee and East Hararghe 3,654 t, about 3.7% and 1.6% of Ethiopia's crop, by the statistics agency's count.
A coffee research sub-centre opens at Mechara, West Hararghe, at about 1,800 m (5,900 ft).
The US trademark office turned down Ethiopia's “Harrar” application, part of a 2005–2007 push to register Harrar, Sidamo and Yirgacheffe in 34 countries.
The US office accepted Ethiopia's rebuttal on Harrar; by mid-2007 the three names held 28 registrations, including in Canada, the EU, Japan and the US.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Sweet Maria's speaks of a greater Harar or Hararghe region. Traders sort Harrar by bean: longberry, shortberry and Mocha, meaning peaberry, a cherry that grew one round seed instead of two.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Harrar coffee grows in the semi-arid highlands around the walled city of Harar, in the East and West Hararghe zones of Oromia; UNIDO's Harar coffee zone also takes in Arsi.

area.note: East and West Hararghe zones of Oromia (spelled Harerge in the data). Coffee grows in their highlands, not across the lowland parts. Harar city's own small region (Hareri) is not included, and UNIDO also counts Arsi in the Harar coffee zone.

records.name: Jimma
records.summary: Western zone known for naturals; home of Ethiopia's coffee research center.
records.lede: Jimma is a coffee zone in western Ethiopia's Oromia region, and the Limu coffee area sits inside it. It is best known for natural (dried-in-the-fruit) coffees, and the town of Jimma is home to the Jimma Agricultural Research Center, which released numbered selections like 74110.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,600–6,900 ft)
Jimma Agricultural Research Center founded (sources differ on the exact year)
release of 74110, 74112 and other early Jimma selections
districts Coffee Hunter groups under Limu and Jimma

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

grows.text: Best known for naturals (1Zpresso); washed coffee is made too, and in a 2015 study the higher Gera site gave the best washed coffee. No published source gives the split. The trees are mostly local landraces, as across Ethiopia, plus selections from the research centre in Jimma town: a 2021 Cup of Excellence natural from Gera was 74110.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes Jimma's naturals as tropical-fruited, with honey sweetness and wine-like aromatics, a full body and lively acidity.
cup.why: In a 2015 study by Jimma researchers, the Jimma site (1,753 m, 5,750 ft) gave the best natural coffee of three south-western sites, while the higher Gera site (1,940 m, 6,350 ft) gave the best washed coffee.

story.text: The Jimma Agricultural Research Center was founded to improve Ethiopian coffee and coordinate research nationally.
A research sub-centre opens at Gera, on 280 ha at about 1,900 m (6,250 ft); UNIDO lists the main Jimma centre, from 1967, at 1,753 m (5,750 ft).
Selections 74110, 74112, 74140 and 74158 were released; a Royal Coffee New York Guji lot lists 74110 and 74112 today.
A natural 74110 from Gera places 18th at Ethiopia's Cup of Excellence.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Coffee Hunter says the zone is politically defined as Jimma and puts Limu's woredas inside it, so bags may say Jimma, Limu or a woreda such as Gera or Goma. Cafe Imports spells it Djimma, and Sweet Maria's lists Agaro and Gera among western coffee areas.

area.note: Jimma Zone of Oromia, including the Limu woredas. Coffee Hunter's Limu–Jimma trade name also takes in six woredas outside Jimma zone (Ale, Bedelle, Chora, Dedesa, Noppa and Yayu; in Ilubabor zone in the 2016 data), which are not outlined.

records.name: Kaffa
records.summary: Southwestern forests where wild Arabica grows; the Gesha woreda is here.
records.lede: Kaffa (Keffa) is a forested zone in southwestern Ethiopia, often called the birthplace of Arabica: coffee still grows wild there, in deep forest at about 1,400–2,100 m (4,600–6,900 ft). Coffee Hunter places the Gesha woreda (district), home of the Gesha variety, in this zone.

facts.label: where its forest coffee grows (4,600–6,900 ft)
Kafa forests named a UNESCO biosphere reserve
farm-gate coffee price in Kaffa, Bench Sheko and Sheka, October 2020 (Limu Seka, Gera and Gomma: 23–28)

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

grows.text: Wild and semi-wild forest coffee and smallholder landraces; no published source gives the washed–natural split. Coffee Review's three write-ups of Gimbo lots (2024–2025) were all washed, one of them a Geisha, and the Tega & Tula estate, which has two washing stations, sells washed forest coffee.

story.text: The traveller Paul Soleillet listed coffee among the main goods traded at Bonga, once the capital of the Kingdom of Kaffa.
The coffee that became the Gesha variety was collected from Ethiopian forests near a mountain usually written Gesha.
Building began on a National Coffee Museum in Bonga.
UNESCO named the Kafa Biosphere Reserve, protecting forest where wild Arabica grows.
On 23 November, after a referendum, Kaffa and five other zones leave the Southern Nations region to form the South West Ethiopia Peoples' Region, with Bonga as its capital.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: You'll see Kaffa, Keffa or Kafa. Ethiocoffee groups Kaffa's coffee with Bench Maji's and Illubabor's as wild and semi-wild types. Older sources put the zone in the Southern Nations region (SNNPR); its main town, Bonga, is now the capital of the South West Ethiopia Peoples' Region, and a trading centre for coffee, honey and cardamom.

sections.title: Forest coffee and farms
body: Coffee still grows wild in Kaffa's mountain rainforest, and about 30 cooperatives market that forest coffee; UNIDO names a Kafa Forest Coffee Farmers' Cooperative Union. Coffee Review's Gimbo lots came from smallholders.

There are also estates: the Tega & Tula farm, just over 500 ha straddling those two villages, grows at about 1,700–2,000 m (5,600–6,550 ft), has two washing stations and drying beds, and sells washed Kaffa forest coffee, dried in the sun.

cup.text: Little is published on a Kaffa style. Coffee Review's write-ups of washed lots from Gimbo found florals (star jasmine, lilac, orchid), grapefruit, lychee and cocoa nib; Quantum Roasters describes a washed forest coffee from Tega & Tula as very floral, with lime, bergamot, caramel and berry.

area.note: Keffa Zone as in the 2016 boundaries, when it was part of the Southern Nations region (SNNPR) and had ten woredas, among them Gesha and Gimbo. Since November 2021 it has been part of the South West Ethiopia Peoples' Region, now with 13 woredas.

records.name: Limu
records.summary: Western washed coffees: sweet, clean and gentle, sometimes lemony.
records.lede: Limu is a coffee area in western Ethiopia's Oromia region, inside the zone politically defined as Jimma; its woredas (districts) include Limu Kossa and Limu Seka. It is best known for clean washed coffees with gentle acidity and a rounded sweetness.

facts.label: typical altitude (3,950–6,250 ft)
of the main regions Royal Coffee New York compares
farm-gate coffee price in Limu Seka, Gera and Gomma, October 2020

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

grows.text: Sources disagree on which process leads: Coffee Hunter and 1Zpresso call Limu a washed-coffee area, while Royal Coffee New York says it is still mostly dried in the fruit. The trees are mostly local landraces, as across Ethiopia; no published source gives Limu's variety mix.

cup.text: Coffee Hunter calls Limu sweet, smooth and clean with subtle acidity, and 1Zpresso adds floral and spicy undertones and a rounded sweetness. Algrano, a green-coffee marketplace, says it can taste very lemony.
cup.watch: Sources disagree on how it's processed: Coffee Hunter and 1Zpresso call Limu a washed-coffee area, while Royal Coffee New York says it is still mostly dried in the fruit, so check the process on the bag.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Coffee Hunter maps Limu and Jimma together and splits the Limu trade name into two groups of woredas. Category A: Gera, Goma, Gumay, Kersa, Limu Kossa, Limu Seka, Mena, Seka Chekorsa and Shebe Sambo. Category B: Ale, Bedelle, Chora, Dedesa, Noppa and Yayu. So a bag may say Limu, Jimma or a woreda name.
Watch for a namesake: a 2021 Cup of Excellence lot listed as Limmu came from a woreda of that name in East Welega zone, not from Jimma's Limu.

story.text: Ethiopia's coffee research centre at Jimma opens, on 183 ha at 1,753 m (5,750 ft); UNIDO files its location as Jimma/Limu.
A coffee research testing site opens at Agaro, in the Limu–Jimma coffee area, at 1,630 m (5,350 ft).

area.note: The two Limu woredas of Jimma zone (spelled Limu Kosa in the data). The Limu trade name covers more: Coffee Hunter adds seven other woredas (Gera, Goma, Gumay, Kersa, Mena, Seka Chekorsa, Shebe Sambo) and six more (Ale, Bedelle, Chora, Dedesa, Noppa, Yayu), which are not outlined.

records.name: Sidama
records.summary: Its own region since 2020; floral and citric; washed and natural both common.
records.lede: Sidama is a highland area of southern Ethiopia, in the Rift Valley, that became its own regional state in 2020; older bags call it Sidamo, the name Ethiopia trademarked. Sources disagree on whether washed or natural coffee leads there; it tends toward citrus and florals.

facts.label: washed, by 1Zpresso’s count (other sources say mostly natural)
typical altitude (4,900–7,200 ft)
voted yes in 2019 to make Sidama its own region
became Ethiopia's tenth regional state, on 18 June

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

grows.text: Sources disagree on which process leads: 1Zpresso puts it at about 60% washed and UNIDO names Sidama as a washed-coffee area, while Royal Coffee New York says Sidama's coffee is still mostly dried in the fruit; naturals swept the 2024 Cup of Excellence. The trees are local landraces plus selections from the Jimma research centre, which made up nearly all of Sidama's winning lots in 2021 and 2024, mostly 74158 and 74112.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes bright, citrus-led acidity and delicate sweetness, often with jasmine, bergamot and stone fruit; Wikipedia's overview singles out lemon, citrus and berries. Its naturals tend to be fruitier and fuller with softer acidity.
cup.why: 1Zpresso points to fertile volcanic soil, clear rainy seasons and large day–night temperature swings, and says its good water supply supports all the washing.
cup.prized: Sweet Maria's says areas once blended into bulk Sidama, such as Bensa and Chire, now stand out on their own.
cup.watch: Royal Coffee New York finds Sidama naturals fruit-forward and sweet but sometimes less delicate, and notes they must dry evenly to avoid defects.

story.text: The Sidama Coffee Farmers Cooperative Union was founded; Trade Aid called it Ethiopia's second-largest union in 2023.
The US trademark office turned down Ethiopia's “Sidamo” application; after a challenge, it was granted in February 2008.
In a November referendum, 98.5% of voters backed making Sidama a region of its own.
On 18 June Sidama left the Southern Nations region (SNNPR) and became Ethiopia's tenth regional state.
Sidama lots take 27 of the 29 Cup of Excellence places, all naturals; the winner, a 74158 from Basha Bekele, sells for US$445 a pound.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Sidamo is the older spelling and the old province name, and it is the one Ethiopia trademarked, so you'll see both. It has also been used loosely: Wikipedia lists Yirgacheffe and Guji as kinds of Sidamo, and Guji was sold in the exchange's Sidamo category. Today Guji is a zone of Oromia and Yirgacheffe is in Gedeo zone, both outside the Sidama Region.
Village and station names often follow the region: Sweet Maria's names Bensa and Chire, and Coffee Hunter shows the Bombe washing station.

sections.title: In the Cup of Excellence
body: Sidama led Ethiopia's Cup of Excellence, the national quality competition, in 2020, 2021 and 2024. In 2020 the first winner was a sun-dried natural from Nigussie Gemeda, scoring 91.3. In 2021 Sidama took 16 of 33 winning lots, led by Tamiru Tadesse's anaerobic 74165 from Bensa at US$150 a pound, and in 2024 it took 27 of 29.
The winning lots name woredas such as Bensa, Arbegona, Bona Zuria and Bura.

area.note: The 2016 boundaries show Sidama Zone of the Southern Nations region; on 18 June 2020 that zone became the Sidama Region, with Hawassa as its capital, and it is now split into four zones plus Hawassa city.

records.name: Yirgacheffe
records.summary: Ethiopia's best-known washed coffee: floral, citric and tea-like.
records.lede: Yirgacheffe is a town and woreda (district) in Gedeo zone in southern Ethiopia, and on bags the name stands for a wider coffee area around it. It is the best-known of Ethiopia's washed coffees, famous for floral and citrus tones.

facts.label: typical altitude (6,250–7,200 ft)
districts Coffee Hunter groups under the Yirgacheffe name
Yirgacheffe's price rise by 2007, to $2 a pound, as its trademark drew attention

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

grows.text: Mostly washed: 1Zpresso and UNIDO both name it a washed-coffee area, and Coffee Hunter lists washed as its usual process. Naturals are common too; both Gedeo lots among the 2021 Cup of Excellence winners were naturals of the Jimma selection 74112. The trees are mostly local landraces sold as heirloom.

cup.text: Yirgacheffe tends toward bright citrus and pronounced florals with a crisp, tea-like finish, say Coffee Hunter, 1Zpresso and Coffee Review. Cafe Imports finds its microregions differ: stone fruit and citrus in Adado, near-tropical fruit in Aricha, fruit tea in Kochere, toffee and almond in Chelchele.
cup.why: It is grown high, mostly at 1,900–2,200 m (6,250–7,200 ft), and mostly washed, the method Royal Coffee New York links to its delicate, clean, floral cups.
cup.prized: Coffee Review calls a really fine Yirgacheffe extraordinary, yet it usually sells at everyday specialty prices.
cup.watch: Sweet Maria's finds the quality uneven, partly because coffee from neighbouring areas was often sold under the famous name.

story.text: The Yirgacheffe Coffee Farmers Cooperative Union is founded; by UNIDO's 2025 count it has 28 member cooperatives with more than 45,000 farmers.
Ethiopia filed trademarks for Yirgacheffe, Sidamo and Harrar in 34 countries, and the US approved Yirgacheffe first.
The new Ethiopian Commodity Exchange (ECX) began selling most coffee pooled by region and grade, so lots could rarely be traced past the region.
From March, the exchange allowed washing stations to sell directly, which Cafe Imports expected to improve traceability.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Coffee Hunter lists eight woredas under the Yirgacheffe name, among them Kochere, Gedeb and Wenago, and Cafe Imports profiles microregions such as Adado, Aricha, Chelchele, Kochere and Konga. A label like “Yirgacheffe Aricha Gr1 Natural” reads region, place, grade, process.
Older sources treat Yirgacheffe as part of Sidamo, and 1Zpresso notes it was once part of the Sidama zone. It sits in Gedeo zone, outside the Sidama Region created in 2020.

The legal boundary for selling coffee as Yirgacheffe reaches a little beyond Gedeo, says Royal Coffee, taking in Gelana Abaya and other neighbouring parts of Oromia; Coffee Hunter's eight woredas are Wenago, Kochere, Yirgacheffe, Gedeb, Bule, Dilla Zuria, Gelana and Abaya. Yirgacheffe itself is a single woreda, just north of Kochere.

area.note: The eight woredas Coffee Hunter lists under the Yirgacheffe name. In the 2016 boundaries Gedeb appears as Kochere Gedeb; the first six are in Gedeo zone, while Gelana and Abaya are Oromia woredas (in Borena zone in that data) that the legal Yirgacheffe boundary also takes in.

records.name: Acatenango
records.summary: Shade-grown coffee on Fuego's ashy slopes, cooled by Pacific breezes.
records.lede: Acatenango is the valley among the Acatenango and Fuego volcanoes. Anacafé says coffee grows here under dense shade, up to about 2,000 m (6,500 ft), in coarse, sandy soil that Fuego's constant eruptions keep rich in minerals. Pacific breezes and clearly marked seasons let farms dry their coffee in the sun.

facts.label: temperatures (57–88 °F), the widest swing in Anacafé's figures
of rain a year (48–72 in)
a natural Geisha from Acatenango at the 2025 Cup of Excellence

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

grows.text: No published source ranks Acatenango’s varieties: Sample Coffee names Bourbon, Caturra and Catuaí, and the Geisha naturals that place in the Cup of Excellence are a small, high-priced share. Almost all washed, as across Guatemala, where Cafe Imports lists washed or mechanically demucilaged (fruit scrubbed off by machine) coffee as the norm and 1Zpresso calls naturals less common. Anacafé says the Pacific breezes and marked seasons let farms dry coffee in the sun.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a marked acidity, a fragrant aroma, a balanced body and a clean, lingering finish; it names no specific flavors. Global Coffee Report's 2011 profile, written with Anacafé, also stresses the acidity and the long finish.

story.text: El Platanar y Anexos, a Caturra and Catuaí farm at 1,524 m (5,000 ft) in Acatenango, places 14th at the Cup of Excellence.
Two natural Geishas from Acatenango, from Los Jutes and La Cookies, place third and fourth among the competition's natural and honey exotics.
Two naturals from Chimaltenango, the department Acatenango belongs to, make the winners' list again.

area.note: Only the area around the municipality of Acatenango, in Chimaltenango department, in the valley among the Acatenango and Fuego volcanoes. No published source gives the region’s exact boundary.

sections.title: Next to Antigua
body: Global Coffee Report places the Acatenango Valley just on the other side of the volcano from Antigua, with coffee grown up to 2,000 m (about 6,500 ft) under dense shade and nearly constant ash from Fuego.

records.name: Antigua
records.summary: A sunny volcano valley, now an EU-protected coffee name.
records.lede: Antigua is the valley around Guatemala's old colonial capital, ringed by the Agua, Fuego and Acatenango volcanoes. Anacafé, the national coffee association, describes it as sunny and low in humidity, with cool nights and the least rain of its eight regions. Its name was registered as a denomination of origin in Guatemala in 2011, and the EU protected it in October 2026.

facts.label: of rain a year (32–48 in), the least of the eight regions
humidity
denomination of origin registered in Guatemala
EU registers “Café Antigua” as a protected geographical indication

harvest.text: Picked about January to mid-March, by Anacafé-based guides. APCA, the growers' association, gives a wider window, November to April.

grows.text: APCA, the growers’ association, names Bourbon, Caturra and Catuaí; no figure gives their shares. Washed and sun-dried: Global Coffee Report describes Finca San Sebastián’s coffee picked crimson-red, fermented slowly and washed with fresh water, and says Antigua’s clearly marked seasons let farms dry their coffee in the sun.

cup.text: Anacafé calls Antigua elegant and well balanced, with a rich aroma and a very sweet taste. The EU's 2026 description of Café Antigua lists honey, caramel, apple and toasted-nut aromas, a full body, and a lasting acidity that is neither sharp nor bitter.
cup.why: Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids notes that dry weather while the fruit ripens and is picked usually makes coffee sweeter, and Antigua gets the least rain of Anacafé's regions.
cup.prized: Sweetness and balance. Cafe Imports calls Antiguas sweet, smooth and good for blending.
cup.watch: Cafe Imports describes them as mild and on the lower-acid side.

story.text: Salvador Falla founds Finca San Sebastián, a mainly Bourbon farm his great-grandson Estuardo still ran in 2011.
The Antigua name gets its first trademark registration, according to a 2003 WIPO presentation.
Antigua's first certification program starts, by the same account.
Coffee Review notes that the growers' association does not count coffee from Fuego's Pacific-facing slopes, just outside the valley, as Antigua.
In December, Guatemala's registry certifies Antigua's denomination of origin as entry number 1 in its first book; the state holds the title.

On 8 October the EU registers “Café Antigua” as a protected geographical indication, on an application from the Asociación de Productores de Café Genuino Antigua, which says it began the process in 2021.

sections.title: Buying genuine Antigua
body: APCA, the Antigua growers' association, says it is made up of 40 farms, and points to a certificate of origin as the buyer's guarantee that a coffee is Genuine Antigua.
The EU protection covers green and roasted coffee, whole bean or ground, produced in Sacatepéquez department, and allows both Arabica and Robusta (Coffea canephora).

sections.title: How high is Antigua?
body: It depends who you ask. Anacafé puts the region at 1,520–1,710 m (5,000–5,600 ft); APCA says 1,400–2,000 m (4,600–6,600 ft); Cafe Imports says most farms sit at 1,300–1,600 m (4,300–5,200 ft).

sections.title: On the bag
body: Cup of Excellence lots from Sacatepéquez include Hacienda Carmona, a washed Bourbon grown at 1,783 m (5,850 ft) in Antigua Guatemala (2012), and Granja El Tempixque, a washed Catuaí from San Miguel Dueñas (2025), one of the department's municipalities.

area.note: The EU’s 2026 protected name Café Antigua covers coffee from Sacatepéquez department, outlined in full. Coffee Review noted in 2003 that the growers’ association did not count a coffee from Fuego’s nearby, Pacific-facing slopes as official Antigua.

records.name: Atitlán
records.summary: Smallholder coffee on the volcano slopes around Lake Atitlán.
records.lede: Atitlán's coffee grows around Lake Atitlán, about 90% of it on the slopes of three volcanoes, says Anacafé. Its soil is the richest in organic matter of Guatemala's five volcanic regions, and the lake's daily Xocomil winds shape the local climate. Much of the coffee comes from small Indigenous Kaqchikel and Tz'utujil growers.

facts.label: grown on the slopes of three volcanoes
of rain a year (72–92 in)
humidity

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

cup.text: Anacafé describes Atitlán as very aromatic, with a bright citrus acidity and a full body. Cafe Imports adds nut and chocolate notes balanced by lemony acidity, with some florals.
cup.why: Cafe Imports links the nutty, chocolatey side to the windy, wet climate around the lake.

story.text: Coffee Review finds most Atitlán samples organic, from smallholder cooperatives often cut off by rough terrain.
Two Atitlán naturals place in the Cup of Excellence: a Ruiru 11 from San Lucas Tolimán and a Pacamara from Santiago Atitlán.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for municipalities such as Santiago Atitlán and San Lucas Tolimán. Finca Pampojila in San Lucas Tolimán placed again in 2026, listed under Sololá department, with a natural Ruiru 11.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Global Coffee Report describes many small Kaqchikel and Tz’utujil growers with a long artisanal tradition, and Coffee Review found in 2003 that most Atitlán coffees were organic and came from smallholder cooperatives. 1Zpresso places most of the coffee on the slopes of the three volcanoes on the lake’s south side.

grows.text: No published source names Atitlán’s main varieties, so the list starts with Guatemala’s common ones. Cafe Imports names Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí, Typica, Maragogype and Pache as Guatemala’s common varieties, and 1Zpresso calls Caturra and Catuaí its foundation and also lists the rust-resistant Catimor, Sarchimor and Anacafé 14 among the main ones. Pacamara and Ruiru 11 naturals from Santiago Atitlán and San Lucas Tolimán place in the Cup of Excellence. Almost all washed, as across Guatemala, where Cafe Imports lists washed or mechanically demucilaged (fruit scrubbed off by machine) coffee as the norm and 1Zpresso calls naturals less common.

area.note: Sololá, the department around Lake Atitlán, is outlined in full. Coffee grows mostly on the volcano slopes south of the lake, in municipalities such as Santiago Atitlán and San Lucas Tolimán. Anacafé also uses seven administrative regions for its field services, which group departments differently: its Region II puts Sololá with Suchitepéquez, Retalhuleu and parts of Quetzaltenango and Chimaltenango (USDA, 2021).

records.name: Cobán
records.summary: Guatemala's rainforest region: rain, mist and fresh-fruit cups.
records.lede: Cobán is Guatemala's rainforest region, in the center of the country: cloudy, cool and wet all year. Anacafé says it has two seasons, rainy and rainier, and a fine mist locals call chipi-chipi hangs over hills of limestone and clay soil.

facts.label: of rain a year (120–160 in), second only to San Marcos
humidity, the highest in Anacafé's figures
temperatures (59–68 °F)
leaf-rust incidence in Anacafé’s Region VI, which includes Alta Verapaz: the lowest of its seven regions (USDA, 2021)

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a pleasant aroma, a fine, well-balanced body and distinct fresh-fruit notes. An older profile adapted from Anacafé material calls it medium-bodied, with light acidity.

story.text: German immigrants first plant coffee here at the end of the 19th century, says Global Coffee Report's 2011 profile.

During World War II, under US pressure, Guatemala deports many of its German residents to US detention camps and takes over their properties; descendants of German coffee families such as the Dieseldorffs still grow and sell coffee around Cobán.
A washed Centroamericano H1 from Finca Vinaros in Alta Verapaz, the department around Cobán, wins a Cup of Excellence place with 87.05 points.

sections.title: The weather
body: Coffee Review describes Cobán's weather as moist and Caribbean-influenced, and Perfect Daily Grind says the coffee grows mostly in mountains reached by tropical air from the Atlantic.

sections.title: Cloud forest
body: Global Coffee Report calls Cobán the wettest coffee region, with close to 4,000 mm (about 160 in) of rain a year, though Anacafé’s own figures put San Marcos higher, at up to 5,000 mm (200 in). As the rain increases, it says, pine and cypress forest gives way to tree ferns and mosses.

grows.text: No published source names Cobán’s main varieties, so the list starts with Guatemala’s common ones. Cafe Imports names Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí, Typica, Maragogype and Pache as Guatemala’s common varieties, and 1Zpresso calls Caturra and Catuaí its foundation and also lists the rust-resistant Catimor, Sarchimor and Anacafé 14 among the main ones. A washed Centroamericano H1, a rust-resistant hybrid, from Alta Verapaz placed in the 2026 Cup of Excellence. Almost all washed, as across Guatemala, where Cafe Imports lists washed or mechanically demucilaged (fruit scrubbed off by machine) coffee as the norm and 1Zpresso calls naturals less common.

area.note: Alta Verapaz, the department around the city of Cobán, is outlined in full. Anacafé also uses seven administrative regions for its field services, which group departments differently: its Region VI adds Baja Verapaz and El Estor in Izabal (USDA, 2021).

records.name: Fraijanes
records.summary: A high volcanic plateau dusted by ash from Pacaya.
records.lede: Fraijanes is a high plateau whose soil gets an occasional light dusting of ash from Pacaya, which Anacafé calls Guatemala's most active volcano. Morning cloud and dew clear quickly and the dry season is sunny, so coffee is dried in the sun. Fraijanes is also a municipality in Guatemala department, at about 1,585 m (5,200 ft).

facts.label: of rain a year (60–120 in)
temperatures (54–79 °F)
harvest, the earliest finish of the eight regions

harvest.text: Picked about December to February.

grows.text: Wikipedia’s article on the municipality lists Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí and Pache; no source ranks them. Almost all washed, as across Guatemala, where Cafe Imports lists washed or mechanically demucilaged (fruit scrubbed off by machine) coffee as the norm and 1Zpresso calls naturals less common. Anacafé says the sunny dry season lets farms dry coffee in the sun.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a bright, persistent acidity, plenty of aroma and a defined body, but names no specific flavors. In 2003 Coffee Review could find only one Fraijanes sample and called an Intelligentsia Fraijanes assertively acidic.

story.text: Coffee Review calls Fraijanes a very old, well-established high plateau with a sunny harvest season, but says few of its coffees reach the US.

Global Coffee Report describes Fraijanes as hemmed in by a growing city and facing labour shortages, contamination and crime, and profiles San Agustín Las Minas, a Rainforest Alliance farm that treats its own and the nearby city's wastewater, which would otherwise reach Lake Amatitlán untreated.

area.note: Only the area around the municipality of Fraijanes, in Guatemala department near Guatemala City. No published source gives the region’s full extent.

records.name: Huehuetenango
records.summary: Guatemala’s highest, driest non-volcanic region and its Cup of Excellence leader.
records.lede: Huehuetenango is Guatemala's mountainous northwest, on the Mexican border. Anacafé calls it the highest and driest of the country's three non-volcanic regions, kept free of frost by hot, dry winds from Mexico's Tehuantepec plain. It dominates the Cup of Excellence, the national competition and auction for the year's best lots: in 2026, farms there took 16 of the 27 winning places.

facts.label: Cup of Excellence winning places in 2026
top 2026 bid, for a lot of El Injerto's natural Geisha
soils, not volcanic ones
of rain a year (48–56 in)

harvest.text: Picked about January to April.

grows.text: 1Zpresso names Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí and Typica as the most often grown; no figure gives shares, and the Geishas and Pacamaras that fill Cup of Excellence lists are a small, high-priced share. Washed has historically dominated, 1Zpresso says, with naturals newer; most farms process their own cherries on site.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a fine, intense acidity, a full body and pleasant wine-like notes. Cafe Imports finds crisp apple-like (malic) and citrus acidity with toffee sweetness, and calls Huehue the most fruit-forward and complex of Guatemala's coffees.
cup.why: The dry Tehuantepec winds keep frost away, which lets cherries on high farms ripen slowly, 1Zpresso explains.
cup.prized: Roasters often prefer them to Antiguas, Coffee Review noted in 2003, calling the region an insider's favorite.
cup.watch: Natural (dried-in-the-fruit) lots vary more from lot to lot than washed ones, 1Zpresso notes.

story.text: Coffee Review calls Huehuetenango an insider's favorite; many of its samples come from small organic cooperatives.
El Injerto, Arturo Aguirre's farm, is already an eight-time Cup of Excellence winner, Global Coffee Report notes.
A washed Geisha from La Gran Manzana wins the washed-exotics category with 91.15 points; one lot sells for $143.10 a pound.
El Injerto's natural Geisha scores 91.86, the competition's highest, and one of its lots sells for $449.10 a pound.

sections.title: Where it's grown
body: Because the region is remote, nearly every producer processes their own coffee, and its many rivers and streams let mills sit almost anywhere, Anacafé says. Global Coffee Report notes the area was once a Mam Maya kingdom.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Lots often name a municipality rather than the department. 2025 Cup of Excellence winners came from La Libertad (home of El Injerto), San Pedro Necta, Cuilco and Unión Cantinil, and the same farms were listed under Huehuetenango in 2026.

area.note: Huehuetenango department, outlined in full. Anacafé also uses seven administrative regions for its field services, which group departments differently: its Region V pairs Huehuetenango with Quiché (USDA, 2021).

records.name: Nuevo Oriente
records.summary: Smallholder coffee in the east, on old volcanic ground; chocolatey.
records.lede: Nuevo Oriente is a small region on Guatemala's eastern edge, bordering Honduras; Prensa Libre places it in Chiquimula department. It sits on a former volcanic range whose soil is metamorphic rock, balanced in minerals. Coffee has been grown here since the 1950s, almost all by small producers, in what was once one of the country's poorest, most isolated areas.

facts.label: when small farms began growing coffee here
of rain a year (72–80 in)
soil that holds water through the dry season
100 lb bags of green coffee per hectare a year (2016/17–2020/21) in Anacafé’s Region VII, which includes Chiquimula and Zacapa: the highest yields of its seven regions (USDA)

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

grows.text: No published source ranks the region’s varieties; this list comes from one importer’s regional lot (StoneX), which blends Caturra, Catuaí, Villa Sarchí, Sarchimor and Marsellesa. Almost all washed, as across Guatemala, where Cafe Imports lists washed or mechanically demucilaged (fruit scrubbed off by machine) coffee as the norm and 1Zpresso calls naturals less common.

cup.text: Anacafé calls Nuevo Oriente well balanced and full-bodied, with a chocolaty flavor. An importer's regional lot (StoneX) lists milk chocolate with orange and lemon acidity and a medium body.
cup.why: Cafe Imports links its full, balanced cup to cloudy, rainy weather with steady temperatures and little sun.

story.text: Small producers start growing coffee on the old volcanic range; almost all of it is still smallholder coffee.
Global Coffee Report says recent plantings here helped lift Guatemala’s production, on red clay and metamorphic soils that often yield double the national average.
USDA reports that Anacafé’s Region VII, which includes Chiquimula and Zacapa, is the country’s most productive, at 29 bags per hectare in 2020/21.

area.note: Chiquimula, where Prensa Libre (citing Anacafé) places the region, is outlined in full. A Spanish Wikipedia summary says it also takes in parts of Izabal, Zacapa, Jutiapa and El Progreso, which are not outlined. Anacafé also uses seven administrative regions for its field services, which group departments differently: its Region VII is Zacapa, Chiquimula and parts of Izabal and Petén (USDA, 2021).

records.name: San Marcos
records.summary: The hottest, rainiest region, with delicate floral cups.
records.lede: San Marcos, in Guatemala's Pacific-facing mountains, is the warmest and wettest of Anacafé's eight regions, with up to 5,000 mm (200 in) of rain a year. The rains arrive earliest here, so coffee flowers first. Because rain at harvest time is unpredictable, much of the coffee is started in the sun and finished in a Guardiola, a mechanical dryer.

facts.label: of rain a year (200 in), the most of the eight regions
temperatures (70–81 °F), the warmest region
to flower in Guatemala, because the rains start earliest
leaf-rust incidence in Anacafé’s Region I, San Marcos and Quetzaltenango: the highest of its seven regions (USDA, 2021)

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

grows.text: Washed, as across Guatemala, and often finished in a Guardiola dryer because rain can fall at harvest; most farms have their own mills. Honeys and naturals are a newer niche with their own category in Anacafé’s 2025 competition for San Marcos and Quetzaltenango. No published source names the varieties San Marcos grows most.

cup.text: Anacafé describes delicate floral notes in the aroma and the cup, a pronounced acidity and a good body. Global Coffee Report's 2011 profile, credited to Anacafé, says the same.
cup.watch: Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids found a 2003 San Marcos (a Green Mountain Dos Marías) assertively acidic.

story.text: Most San Marcos coffee reaching the US comes from one farm, Dos Marías, run by the Asturias family, Coffee Review reports.
Global Coffee Report profiles Agapito Orozco, who farms 10 hectares under avocado, jocote and chalum shade, as his father and grandfather did.
Anacafé holds its 11th coffee competition for Quetzaltenango and San Marcos, with categories for the regional coffee and for processes such as honeys and naturals.

sections.title: How it's grown
body: Most farms have their own processing mills, Anacafé says. 1Zpresso links the region's fertile soil to the nearby Tajumulco volcano.

area.note: San Marcos department, outlined in full. Anacafé also uses seven administrative regions for its field services, which group departments differently: its Region I pairs San Marcos with Quetzaltenango, and the two hold a joint regional competition.

records.name: Agalta
records.summary: Northern and eastern Honduras: family farms, tropical fruit, caramel and chocolate.
records.lede: Agalta is the coffee region of Olancho, Yoro, Atlántida and Colón, in the profile of IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, which calls it Tropical Agalta; El Heraldo gives the same four departments and altitudes of up to 1,700 m (5,600 ft). Most of its farms are family-owned, says Coffeeness. Sources disagree on the weather: Perfect Daily Grind describes a more tropical climate, while Coffeeness describes a drier microclimate in a rain shadow, an area mountains shelter from rain.

facts.label: departments: Olancho, Yoro, Atlántida and Colón, per IHCAFE’s profile and El Heraldo
(3,600–4,600 ft) per IHCAFE and PDG; Coffeeness says 1,200–1,600 m (3,900–5,250 ft)
of rain a year (53–77 in), per IHCAFE

grows.text: No published source ranks Agalta’s varieties, so the rust-resistant ones lead, as they do nationally: IHCAFE said in 2017 that 60% of Honduras’s coffee area was improved, rust-resistant plants (Lempira, IHCAFE 90, Parainema). IHCAFE’s regional profile names Bourbon, Caturra and Typica, and Coffeeness adds Catuaí, Pacas, Lempira and IHCAFE 90. Mostly washed, as across Honduras, where Coffee Review says wet processing is the norm and a growing number of producers are trying naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes diverse tropical fruit, a caramel and chocolate fragrance, a delicate but pronounced acidity and a sweet finish. Coffeeness finds it sweet and chocolate-led with a hint of spice and medium body, and says washed lots have a lively acidity and a crisp, clean finish.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, places Agalta in Olancho, Yoro, Atlántida and Colón, at 1,100–1,400 m (3,600–4,600 ft), 14–22 °C (57–72 °F) and 1,350–1,950 mm (53–77 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra and Typica. It describes tropical fruit, a caramel and chocolate fragrance and a sweet aftertaste. Coffee Hunter also puts Agalta in the north and east; Coffeeness instead puts it in Olancho, El Paraíso and parts of Francisco Morazán.

story.text: No lot from Olancho, Yoro, Atlántida or Colón places in either year’s Cup of Excellence, where Santa Bárbara, Lempira and other western departments take most places.

area.note: IHCAFE’s regional profile and El Heraldo’s 2018 guide both place Agalta in Olancho, Yoro, Atlántida and Colón, outlined in full; IHCAFE’s introduction names only Yoro and Olancho. Coffee grows in the mountains of these large departments, not across them. Coffeeness instead puts Agalta in Olancho, El Paraíso and parts of Francisco Morazán.

records.name: Comayagua
records.summary: Central Honduras: bright, creamy cups and the country's top 2016 yields.
records.lede: The Comayagua region is central Honduras, covering the departments of Comayagua and Francisco Morazán, home of the capital, Tegucigalpa. Coffeeness describes hot days, cool nights, moderate rain and well-balanced loamy soil, and heavy investment in processing equipment. Comayagua department was the country’s largest producer in the 2024/25 harvest, by the count of IHCAFE, the national coffee institute.

facts.label: quintals (100 lb sacks) from Comayagua department in 2024/25, about 16% of the national crop and the most of any department
quintals (100 lb) of green coffee per manzana (1.72 acres) in 2016, the country’s best yield
a washed Geisha from Francisco Morazán, third among 2026’s Cup of Excellence exotics
what that Geisha sold for

grows.text: No published source ranks the region’s varieties, so the rust-resistant ones lead, as they do nationally (60% of the coffee area in 2017, by IHCAFE). IHCAFE’s regional profile names Bourbon, Caturra and Typica, Coffeeness Pacas, Catuaí, Bourbon and IHCAFE 90, and El Heraldo’s 2023 guide adds Lempira; Geishas from Francisco Morazán place in the Cup of Excellence. Mostly washed, as across Honduras, where Coffee Review says wet processing is the norm and a growing number of producers are trying naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots. Coffeeness says honey and washed lots give cleaner, more consistent cups here.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes a sweet, citrusy fragrance, bright acidity and a creamy, rich body. Coffeeness finds tropical fruit and balanced acidity, and says honey and washed lots give cleaner, more consistent cups.

story.text: Comayagua posts the country's highest average yield, 30.19 quintals of green coffee per manzana, by IHCAFE's count.
PDG's Comayagua profile cites José Abel Girón Dubón's Pacamara from Finca Las Botijas, washed champion of Project Origin's Best of Honduras auction at 91.34 points and $29.10 a pound.
IHCAFE’s 2024/25 harvest report ranks Comayagua department first, with 986,429 quintals; with Copán and Lempira it makes up 46% of the national crop.
El Pino's washed Geisha from Francisco Morazán scores 90.39 at the Cup of Excellence and sells for $84.60 a pound.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,100–1,400 m (3,600–4,600 ft), 14–22 °C (57–72 °F) and 1,350–1,700 mm (53–67 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra and Typica. It describes a sweet, citrusy fragrance, a vibrant acidity with citrus and sweet flavors, and a creamy body. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 1,100–1,700 m (3,600–5,600 ft) and adds Lempira.

area.note: IHCAFE’s regional profile and El Heraldo say the region encompasses Comayagua and Francisco Morazán, outlined in full. Both also count part of Comayagua department in the Montecillos region.

records.name: Copán
records.summary: Western Honduras by Guatemala: chocolate, caramel and a creamy body.
records.lede: Copán is Honduras's western coffee region, taking in Copán, Ocotepeque and part of Santa Bárbara, along the borders with Guatemala and El Salvador. Its temperatures swing more than almost anywhere in the country, with lows of 11.5 °C (53 °F), and most of its coffee is grown in shade. It can be sold under the protected regional name Honduran Western Coffees (HWC).

facts.label: lows (53 °F); possibly the country's coolest region
Honduran Western Coffees, a protected regional name it shares with Opalaca
departments: Copán, Ocotepeque and part of Santa Bárbara
quintals (100 lb sacks) from Copán department in 2024/25, second only to Comayagua

grows.text: No published source ranks Copán’s varieties, so the rust-resistant one leads, as these do nationally (60% of the coffee area in 2017, by IHCAFE). IHCAFE’s regional profile names Bourbon, Caturra and Catuaí, and Coffeeness adds Typica and IHCAFE 90. Mostly washed, as across Honduras, where Coffee Review says wet processing is the norm and a growing number of producers are trying naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 regional guide describes a sweet aroma, chocolate, caramel and citrus, a delicate acidity, a bold, creamy body and a long, balanced finish. Coffeeness finds chocolate and nut with medium body and acidity, and calls it ideal for espresso.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits the high elevations, which slow the ripening of the cherries.
cup.prized: Sasa Sestic, interviewed for the PDG guide, finds Copán coffees often work well in blends.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives November to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,000–1,500 m (3,300–4,900 ft), 12–22 °C (54–72 °F) and 1,300–2,300 mm (51–91 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra and Catuaí. It describes chocolate flavor, a round, balanced body and a long, pleasant aftertaste. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives a wider 1,000–1,700 m (3,300–5,600 ft) and 16–24 °C (61–75 °F), and adds a sweet aroma.

sections.title: Volume, not competitions
body: Copán is one of Honduras’s biggest producers, but no lot from Copán or Ocotepeque placed in the 2025 or 2026 Cup of Excellence, where neighbouring Santa Bárbara and Lempira took most places. Coffee Review counts Copán, with Opalaca and Montecillos, among the three regions along the Guatemalan and Salvadoran border that give Honduras’s highest and most admired coffees.

story.text: Santa Rita, Copán, is the most productive municipality in the country in the 2023/24 harvest, at 25.09 sacks per manzana, IHCAFE’s figures show.

Copán department is the second-largest producer of the 2024/25 harvest; La Prensa’s report of IHCAFE’s figures puts the western departments of Copán, Lempira and Ocotepeque at 42.9% of the national crop.

area.note: Copán and Ocotepeque are outlined in full. IHCAFE’s profile and El Heraldo add Santa Bárbara (northern Santa Bárbara, IHCAFE says), and IHCAFE’s introduction also names Lempira and Cortés; those parts are not outlined.

records.name: El Paraíso
records.summary: By Nicaragua: Parainema country, and a 2017 Honduran price record.
records.lede: El Paraíso is southeastern Honduras, on the Nicaraguan border, and relatively warm at 16–22.5 °C (61–73 °F). It is known for Parainema, a rust-resistant variety that IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, released in 2004. In 2017 a Parainema from Finca El Laurel here won the Cup of Excellence and sold for $124.50 a pound, a Honduran record at the time.

facts.label: the 2017 Cup of Excellence winner, a Parainema: a Honduran record then
that lot's score, grown at 1,400 m (4,600 ft)
temperatures (61–73 °F), warm for Honduran coffee
