grows.text: No published source ranks El Paraíso’s varieties. Parainema leads here because Perfect Daily Grind and Cup of Excellence results tie the region to it; IHCAFE’s profile names Catuaí and Caturra, El Heraldo’s 2023 guide adds Pacas, Parainema and Lempira, and nationally rust-resistant varieties covered 60% of the coffee area in 2017. Mostly washed, as across Honduras, where Coffee Review says wet processing is the norm and a growing number of producers are trying naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes sweet, citric, smooth cups with grape, mango and tropical fruit, a floral acidity and a creamy body; its winning Parainema showed green apple, jasmine, peach and blueberry. Coffeeness describes something gentler: nutty and brown-sugar sweet, medium-bodied, with low acidity.

story.text: IHCAFE releases Parainema, a rust-resistant selection from the Sarchimor line T5296.
Oscar Daniel Ramírez Valerio's Parainema from Finca El Laurel wins the Cup of Excellence with 91.81 points and sells for $124.50 a pound.
Laurel #3 places second in the Cup of Excellence's Parainema category with 89.47.
El Laurel places sixth among the Parainemas, with 87.68.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,100–1,400 m (3,600–4,600 ft), 16–22 °C (61–72 °F) and 950–1,950 mm (37–77 in) of rain a year, with Catuaí and Caturra. It describes citrus flavors, a sweet fragrance, a smooth body and a lingering aftertaste. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 1,100–1,700 m (3,600–5,600 ft) and adds Pacas, Parainema and Lempira.

area.note: IHCAFE places the region in El Paraíso department and some adjacent areas of Choluteca and Francisco Morazán, and El Heraldo in El Paraíso, Francisco Morazán and part of Choluteca; only El Paraíso is outlined.

records.name: Montecillos
records.summary: Home of Café de Marcala, Honduras's first protected origin name.
records.lede: Montecillos lies in southwestern Honduras along the Salvadoran border, around the Montecillos mountains. Cold nights at altitude slow the ripening of the cherries, Perfect Daily Grind writes, and the region is home to Café de Marcala, Honduras's first denomination of origin, a legally protected place name.

facts.label: Honduran denomination of origin: Café de Marcala
top score of the 2025 Cup of Excellence, a washed Geisha from La Paz
top bid for that Geisha

grows.text: No published source ranks Montecillos’s varieties. IHCAFE’s regional profile names Bourbon, Catuaí, Caturra and Pacas; Coffeeness leads with Catuaí and adds Lempira; nationally rust-resistant varieties covered 60% of the coffee area in 2017. Geishas and Parainemas from La Paz place in the Cup of Excellence. Mostly washed, as across Honduras, where Coffee Review says wet processing is the norm and a growing number of producers are trying naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots. Coffeeness says Montecillos farmers favor honey processing.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes citrus, peach, apricot and caramel, a velvety body and a sparkling acidity it calls tartaric (the acid found in grapes). Coffeeness finds sweet citrus with an apple-like acidity.
cup.why: PDG credits the altitude and cold nights, which let the cherries ripen more slowly.

story.text: Marcala becomes a registered appellation of origin, which Coffee Review calls the first in Central America; its area overlaps the Copán, Opalaca and Montecillos regions.
A washed Geisha from La Salvaje in La Paz wins the exotic category of the Honduran Cup of Excellence with 91.59, the competition's top score.
La Paz places again, with a washed Geisha from the same producer, Fabio Antonio Caballero García, and a natural Parainema from Liquidambar.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for “Marcala” or “Café de Marcala”, the protected name, and for La Paz, a department Coffeeness places in Montecillos. Coffeeness also puts Intibucá and Lempira here, which PDG assigns to Opalaca.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, places Montecillos in La Paz, Comayagua, southern Santa Bárbara and Intibucá, at 1,200–1,600 m (3,950–5,250 ft), 12–21 °C (54–70 °F) and 1,300–2,300 mm (51–91 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Catuaí, Caturra and Pacas. It describes fruity, sweet fragrances, a vibrant, bright acidity, orange and peach, and a velvety body. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 14–22 °C (57–72 °F) and 1,200–1,700 mm (47–67 in).

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to April; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

area.note: El Heraldo puts all of La Paz department in Montecillos, outlined in full. The region also takes in parts of Comayagua and Santa Bárbara (southern Santa Bárbara, IHCAFE says) and, by IHCAFE’s profile, Intibucá; Coffeeness names La Paz, Intibucá and Lempira. Those parts are not outlined.

records.name: Opalaca
records.summary: Fruit-forward mountain coffee and many Cup of Excellence winners.
records.lede: Opalaca covers much of Santa Bárbara, Intibucá and Lempira, and takes its name from the Opalaca mountains; Coffeeness describes a cool, humid climate with heavy rain. These three departments now supply most Cup of Excellence winners, the national competition and auction for the year's best lots: in 2026, 24 of the 30 winning places came from them.

facts.label: 2026 Cup of Excellence places from Santa Bárbara, Lempira and Intibucá
2025 Cup of Excellence places from Santa Bárbara alone
top 2026 bid, for a washed Geisha from El Pimporro in Intibucá
quintals (100 lb sacks) from Lempira department in 2024/25, third in the country; it was first in 2023/24

grows.text: No published source ranks Opalaca’s varieties. IHCAFE’s profile names Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí and Typica, and nationally rust-resistant varieties covered 60% of the coffee area in 2017; Cup of Excellence lots from these departments are mostly Geisha, Parainema, Pacas and Typica, with the odd IHCAFE 90. Mostly washed, as across Honduras, where Coffee Review says wet processing is the norm and a growing number of producers are trying naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes tropical fruit, grape and berry with a fine, delicate acidity; Sasa Sestic adds mango, florals and strong aromas. Coffeeness calls it wine-like and complex, with apple-like acidity and milk chocolate.
cup.prized: Geishas, Pacas and traditional Typicas. The 2026 Cup of Excellence's best traditional lots were washed Typicas from Lempira and washed Pacas from Santa Bárbara.

story.text: Jorge Lanza, a producer from Santa Bárbara, wins the Honduran Cup of Excellence.

El Heraldo’s report of IHCAFE’s 2023/24 figures names Lempira the top-producing department, and Las Vegas, in Santa Bárbara, the source of the best-quality coffee and of the 20th Cup of Excellence’s winner.
Santa Bárbara farms take 22 of the 30 Cup of Excellence places, and a natural Typica from Finca Dariela in Lempira tops the traditional category with 90.50.
A washed Geisha from El Pimporro in Intibucá wins with 90.50 points and sells for up to $90 a pound; washed Typicas from Lempira top the traditional category.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Competition lists and many bags name the department: Santa Bárbara, Lempira or Intibucá. PDG splits Santa Bárbara between Opalaca and Copán, so a Santa Bárbara coffee could come from either region.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,100–1,600 m (3,600–5,250 ft), 19–21 °C (66–70 °F) and 1,350–1,900 mm (53–75 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí and Typica. It describes an aromatic, balanced cup with a fine, delicate acidity, grape and blackberry, a smooth body and a sweet aftertaste. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 1,100–1,700 m (3,600–5,600 ft) and 16–22 °C (61–72 °F).

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives November to February; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

area.note: IHCAFE names Santa Bárbara, Lempira and Intibucá, outlined in full; PDG says the region takes in much of them, and El Heraldo only part of Santa Bárbara. IHCAFE also puts northern Santa Bárbara in the Copán region and southern Santa Bárbara and Intibucá in Montecillos, so these departments are shared.

records.name: Embu
records.summary: Mount Kenya's southeastern slopes: juicy, sweet, berry and caramel.
records.lede: Embu is a county on Mount Kenya's southeastern slopes, where many people work as coffee farmers. 1Zpresso describes its coffees as juicy and full, with bright fruit acidity and pronounced sweetness.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,900–6,550 ft)
average temperature
rain a year
Embu coffee sold at the Nairobi auction, 2025/26 season to July 2026

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to December. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

grows.text: Fully washed is the norm, often with a soak after washing, as at Rianjagi. Most Kenyan lots blend SL28 and SL34 with Ruiru 11 and, more and more, Batian, since farms are too small to keep them apart (Sucafina, 2020); Royal Coffee (2026) calls Batian Kenya's most-planted tree. No county shares are published.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes bright fruit acidity and pronounced sweetness, with berry, citrus, floral, honey and caramel-like notes, juicy and full. Melbourne Coffee Merchants found its Rianjagi peaberry sweet, with complex florals, green grape and rosehip tea.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: Coffee Hunter's Kavutiri factory belongs to the Murue Farmers' Cooperative Society: 980 members in Runyenjes division at about 1,700 m (5,600 ft), whose cherry is pulped, fermented overnight in tiled tanks, washed in river water and dried on raised beds. Royal Coffee's Kathakwa factory gathers 1,050 smallholders at 1,600–1,700 m (5,250–5,600 ft) and picks from October to December.

sections.title: Inside a factory
body: Rianjagi, Melbourne Coffee Merchants' supplier near Manyatta, sits at 1,605–1,625 m (5,270–5,330 ft) and takes cherry from about 1,100 of its society's 2,100 members, whose farms average under a quarter hectare. Cherry is picked and delivered the same day, sorted by a cherry clerk, pulped and sorted by density in water. It then ferments dry for 12–24 hours, is washed in river water, graded in channels and soaked for 24–48 hours.
The parchment dries on raised beds for one to three weeks, down to 11–12% moisture, then rests about a month before milling.

story.text: Many of today's growers farm land their parents bought after agricultural reform let smallholders grow cash crops such as coffee.
The Rianjagi factory and its farmers' cooperative society were set up near Manyatta, on the Rupingazi River.
Kenya's old provinces were dissolved; Embu, once part of Eastern Province, is now a county.
Embu's coffee sold for Sh1.6 billion at the Nairobi auction by July 2026, well behind Murang'a, Nyeri and Kirinyaga, which each sold over Sh4 billion.

records.name: Kiambu
records.summary: Estate country north of Nairobi: tropical fruit, bright and full.
records.lede: Kiambu is the county just north of Nairobi, and unlike most of Kenya, where cooperatives grow most coffee, it is dominated by large estates, many owned by multinational companies. Its coffee is mostly washed, and 1Zpresso finds vivid tropical fruit in it.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,900–6,900 ft)
large estates dominate here, unlike most of Kenya
rain a year
under coffee in June 2022, the most of any county (Ministry of Agriculture)
auction sales in 2025/26 to July 2026, fifth among counties

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives September to December, a little earlier than the Mount Kenya counties. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

grows.text: Mostly fully washed, but some estates here also sell sun-dried naturals, such as Oaklands and Tatu near Ruiru; those estates list SL28, SL34, Ruiru 11 and K7, and Tatu also Batian. In Kenya's smallholder cooperatives most lots blend SL28 and SL34 with Ruiru 11 and, more and more, Batian, since farms are too small to keep them apart (Sucafina, 2020); Royal Coffee (2026) calls Batian Kenya's most-planted tree. No county shares are published.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes vivid tropical fruit, bright acidity and a refreshing but full mouthfeel. Estate naturals taste different: Royal Coffee lists cherry, raisin and chocolate for Oaklands' natural.
cup.watch: Royal Coffee says the big estates favour mechanised, higher-yield farming, which can come at the cost of cup quality.

sections.title: Estates on the bag
body: Kiambu lots often come from estates or small grower groups. Melbourne Coffee Merchants imports Muhathi Estate, 5 ha at 1,720 m (5,650 ft) in the Aberdare foothills near the Komothai river. Sample Coffee, a roaster, sells lots from the Ngewa-Komothai growers, about 30 producers at 1,600–2,000 m (5,250–6,550 ft) near the Gatamaiyo Forest Reserve, each with a small wet mill of their own.

sections.title: Estates, naturals and housing
body: Royal Coffee calls Kiambu, next to Nairobi, a coffee powerhouse with an extensive community of coffee mills, exporter warehouses and quality labs. Its estates include Oaklands, near Ruiru at 1,575 m (5,170 ft), which sells a sun-dried natural of SL28, SL34, K7 and Ruiru 11, and Tatu Estate, 120 ha at 1,570 m (5,150 ft), run by Kofinaf, which Coffee Hunter calls Kenya's leading coffee producer at about 8.5% of yearly output.
Kiambu still has the most coffee land in Kenya, but its farmland is being rapidly subdivided for real estate (Business Daily, 2024), and around Ruiru many coffee estates have already become housing.

story.text: Ruiru 11 was released from the coffee research station at Ruiru, a Kiambu town that gives the variety its name.
Kiambu had about 20,369 ha under coffee, more than any other county, by Ministry of Agriculture figures.
Business Daily reported farmland being rapidly subdivided for housing, threatening the county's tea and coffee.
Kiambu ranked fifth at the Nairobi auction, with Sh3.46 billion in sales by July 2026.

records.name: Kirinyaga
records.summary: Mount Kenya's eastern slopes: floral, cranberry and blackcurrant, full-bodied.
records.lede: Kirinyaga is the county east of Nyeri, on Mount Kenya's eastern slopes, with volcanic soil and a mix of steep mountainsides and gentler hills. Its coffees tend to be floral and lively, with cranberry and blackcurrant notes and a full body.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,250–6,250 ft)
rain a year
Kerugoya, the largest town (5,079 ft); coffee and tea grow on the higher ground
clean coffee sold at the Nairobi auction, 2025/26 to July 2026

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to January. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

grows.text: Fully washed coffee from smallholder cooperative factories is the norm. Most Kenyan lots blend SL28 and SL34 with Ruiru 11 and, more and more, Batian, since farms are too small to keep them apart (Sucafina, 2020); Royal Coffee (2026) calls Batian Kenya's most-planted tree. No county shares are published.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes floral aromas, cranberry and blackcurrant, lively acidity and a full body.
cup.why: Royal Coffee credits the volcanic soil close to Mount Kenya.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: The Rungeto Farmers' Cooperative Society runs the Karimikui, Kii and Kangoi factories. InterAmerican puts Karimikui's 1,400 farmers at 1,600–1,800 m (5,250–5,900 ft), with cherry pulped, fermented overnight, washed and dried on raised tables for 8–14 days. Driftaway sells a blend from the Kii and Kairu factories, run by Rungeto and by the far larger Baragwi society (16,892 members). Baragwi's Guama factory topped Coffee Review's 2016 list of 30 coffees with 97 points, Business Daily reported.

Coffee Hunter's Gakuyu-ini factory, run by the Thirikwa Farmers Cooperative Society, takes cherry from 900 smallholders, whose farms average under a hectare, near Kerugoya and Kianyaga on Mount Kenya's southern slopes. The mill sits at 1,600 m (5,250 ft) and the farms around it at 1,500–1,900 m (4,900–6,250 ft); its lots mix Ruiru 11, Batian, SL34 and SL28.

story.text: The Baragwi society's Guama factory topped Coffee Review's list of the year's 30 best coffees with 97 points, Business Daily reported.
Kirinyaga led all counties in auction volume and earnings over the season's first seven months, The Standard reported.
It slipped to fourth, with 4.61 million kg sold for Sh4.31 billion by July 2026.

records.name: Murang'a
records.summary: Lush central-highland county of smallholders: floral, berry and blackcurrant.
records.lede: Murang'a is a lush county in Kenya's central highlands with volcanic soil, where Royal Coffee counts up to 100,000 smallholders and more small farms than estates. Its washed coffees tend toward florals, berries and blackcurrant with balanced acidity.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,900–6,250 ft)
smallholders, by Royal Coffee's 2026 count
rain a year
sold at the Nairobi auction in 2025/26 to July 2026, second among counties

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to December. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

grows.text: Fully washed is the norm, often with a soak after washing, as at Kagumoini, though Gatunyu Kigio's factories skip it. Cooperatives list SL28, SL34, Ruiru 11, Batian and sometimes K7. Most Kenyan lots blend SL28 and SL34 with Ruiru 11 and, more and more, Batian, since farms are too small to keep them apart (Sucafina, 2020); Royal Coffee (2026) calls Batian Kenya's most-planted tree. No county shares are published.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes floral aromas with berry, citrus and blackcurrant, balanced acidity and a medium body, and says washing gives a clean, bright cup.
cup.why: Both 1Zpresso and Royal Coffee point to its fertile volcanic soil.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: InterAmerican's Kaganda factory, of the Kaganda Farmers Cooperative Society in Kahuro, has 1,500 members at 1,800–1,900 m (5,900–6,250 ft). Coffee Hunter lists Kirimahiga (New Kiriti society, 781 growers) and Kanjathi (Kangiri society, 1,300 growers) on the slopes of the Aberdare Range, with the main crop from October and a smaller fly crop from April.

Cafe Imports' Kaguthi factory belongs to the Kandara Coffee Growers Cooperative Society, whose 5,236 members deliver to 11 factories at 1,340–1,950 m (4,400–6,400 ft). Melbourne Coffee Merchants' Kagumoini, one of Kamachiria's four factories, takes cherry from 960 members farming at 1,650–1,750 m (5,400–5,750 ft).

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Melbourne Coffee Merchants describes coffee growing in the foothills on bright red volcanic soil, mostly on smallholdings where it shares the land with avocado, maize, macadamia, banana and vegetables; tea and dairy are other important incomes.

At Kagumoini, cherry is pulped, sorted by density, fermented dry for 16–24 hours, washed with water from the Thuru Thuru River, graded, soaked for about 24 hours and dried on raised beds to 11–12% moisture.

story.text: Most of Murang'a's coffee farms were planted after agricultural reform let smallholders grow cash crops on family land, not only on British-owned estates.
The Kamachiria Farmers' Cooperative Society was formed; it now has over 5,600 members and four active factories.
Kamachiria built its Kagumoini factory at 1,750 m (5,750 ft).
The Gatunyu Kigio Farmers Cooperative Society was registered, based in Gatanga, with factories in Murang'a and Kiambu.
Murang'a ranked second among counties at the Nairobi auction, with 4.96 million kg sold for Sh4.33 billion by July 2026.

records.name: Nyeri
records.summary: Kenya's most famous coffee county: bright citrus and blackcurrant.
records.lede: Nyeri is a county on the southwestern slopes of Mount Kenya, and Royal Coffee calls it Kenya's most famous specialty coffee region. Most of its coffee comes from smallholders, and it tends toward bright citrus acidity and blackcurrant-like fruit.

facts.label: typical altitude (5,250–6,550 ft)
rain a year
which Royal Coffee links to some of Kenya's best cups
sold at the Nairobi auction in 2025/26 to July 2026, third among counties

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to December. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

grows.text: Fully washed is the norm. Naturals are a small, new niche: Royal Coffee says it has only recently been able to buy Kenyan naturals regularly, and Nyeri factories such as Ndiaini and Ichamama now sell natural lots beside their washed coffee. Most Kenyan lots blend SL28 and SL34 with Ruiru 11 and, more and more, Batian, since farms are too small to keep them apart (Sucafina, 2020); Royal Coffee (2026) calls Batian Kenya's most-planted tree. No county shares are published.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes bright citrus acidity and blackcurrant-like fruit with a subtle wine-like edge, complex and well balanced. Royal Coffee says Nyeri's red soil produces some of the best cup quality in Kenya.
cup.why: 1Zpresso points to its 1,600–2,000 m altitude and fertile, well-drained volcanic soil; Royal Coffee singles out the red soil.

sections.title: Selling it
body: In 2013/14 politicians in the Nyeri area stepped into how its coffee was marketed and limited its transport to control where it was sold, saying it was for the farmers; Sweet Maria's notes many questions since about whether farmers gained.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: Importers list Nyeri lots by factory (the Kenyan word for a wet mill) and the cooperative society that runs it. Royal Coffee's Gura factory belongs to the Othaya Farmers Cooperative Society: 500 members at 1,700–1,890 m (5,600–6,200 ft), picking from November to January. StoneX lists Gaturiri, of the Barichu society in Mathira East, and Melbourne Coffee Merchants imports Kiamabara, of the Mugaga society, whose 910 members farm at 1,600–1,900 m (5,250–6,250 ft).

The Othaya society, registered in 1956, runs its factories around Othaya town, between Mount Kenya and the Aberdares, at about 1,720–1,880 m (5,650–6,150 ft): 17 by Cooperative Coffees' count, 19 by Royal Coffee's and Atlas Coffee Importers'. Cooperative Coffees puts the average farm at 0.1 ha. One of them, Ichamama, has begun offering naturals alongside its washed lots.

sections.title: Naturals, a new niche
body: Almost all Kenyan coffee is washed, but Nyeri is one place naturals are appearing. At Ndiaini factory in Mukurweini, run by the small Rumukia society at 1,700–1,950 m (5,600–6,400 ft), a day-lot of ripe cherry was sealed in airtight bags for 24–72 hours and then dried on raised beds for about a month. Royal Coffee tasted it tart and tangy, with rose, mandarin, plum and pomegranate.

In Mathira, farmers from five factories began drying their own cherry as naturals, which the exporter Crowd Farm Africa buys and the New KPCU, a farmers' co-operative union, mills and stores, The Standard reported; natural processing needs no pulping station or water.

story.text: The Othaya Farmers' Co-operative Society was registered with 250 members; it now runs 17 factories by Cooperative Coffees' count, 19 by Royal Coffee's.

Farmers around five Mathira factories, linked to the exporter Crowd Farm Africa after the New Kenya Planters Co-operative Union formed in 2019, began drying their cherry as naturals: 200 farmers delivered 24,000 kg in 2020, and about 600 delivered some 100,000 kg in 2022, The Standard reported.
Nyeri ranked third among counties at the Nairobi auction, with 4.63 million kg sold for Sh4.18 billion by July 2026.
Royal Coffee imported a natural day-lot from Ndiaini factory, saying regular supplies of Kenyan naturals are new.

records.name: Chiapas
records.summary: Mexico’s biggest grower, on the Guatemalan border: full-bodied, chocolatey
records.lede: Mexico’s southernmost coffee state straddles the Guatemalan border and grows more of the country’s coffee than any other state: 36.5%, in shares reported with the 2024/25 harvest figures. Coffee grows here at roughly 800–1,700 m (2,600–5,600 ft), and Indigenous Mayan communities and their cooperatives are at the heart of it.

facts.label: of Mexico’s coffee, reported with the 2024/25 harvest figures; older guides say about 40%
of its coffee farmers grow Robusta; an ICO study finds Robusta mainly in Chiapas
the floor for coffee sold as Café Chiapas (2,600 ft)
the 2019 Cup of Excellence winner, a natural Geisha

harvest.text: Mexico picks from about November to March, with timing shifting by altitude; new-crop beans often reach roasters from spring onward.

grows.text: No published source ranks Chiapas’s varieties. The Café Chiapas rules (2003) name tall Typica, Maragogype, Bourbon and Mundo Novo and short Caturra, Garnica, Catuaí, Catimor and Pacamara. Nationally, an ICO study says traditional Typica, Caturra and Bourbon remain common, and Chapingo University researchers say rust-resistant Colombia, Oro Azteca, Costa Rica 95 and Sarchimors such as Marsellesa have spread since the 2012 rust outbreak. Cup of Excellence lots from Chiapas are mostly Geisha. Almost all washed: the protected-name rules call for washed coffee, and about 95% of farmers in Chiapas do at least some wet processing on the farm (ICO); naturals show up mainly among competition lots.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Chiapas coffee as full-bodied, with chocolatey sweetness and gentle acidity, and Soconusco lots as balanced with a bright, clean finish. Sweet Maria's finds some Chiapas lots resemble those from Guatemala's Huehuetenango, just across the border.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Coffeeness singles out the Soconusco area. Cooperatives named on Chiapas coffees include Majomut and Tzotzilotic Tzobolotic. Coffee had spread here, and to Oaxaca, by the mid-1800s.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Chiapas was requested by the state's coffee commission, COMCAFE. It covers coffee grown above 800 m (2,600 ft), which the declaration puts at about 75% of the state's coffee land, in twelve regions, among them Tapachula, Motozintla, Comitán, San Cristóbal de las Casas and Palenque. The rules name tall varieties (Typica, Maragogype, Bourbon, Mundo Novo) and short ones (Caturra, Garnica, Catuaí, Catimor, Pacamara), call for washed coffee dried at no more than 70 °C (158 °F), and describe high acidity, an intense aroma and a noticeable body. That is livelier than the gentle acidity Coffeeness describes.

sections.title: Robusta and small farms
body: Chiapas is Mexico’s main Robusta state: an ICO study found that 35% of its coffee farmers grow it, against 7.7% in Veracruz and 1.1% in Oaxaca. Its farmers have little coffee land, about 1.7 hectares each on average, and Chiapas has the highest tree density the study found, about 2,913 trees per hectare.

story.text: Café Chiapas becomes a protected name (a denomination of origin) for coffee grown above 800 m (2,600 ft).
A leaf-rust outbreak hits the four main coffee states, Chiapas, Veracruz, Oaxaca and Puebla, hard; afterwards rust-resistant varieties such as Costa Rica 95, Oro Azteca and Marsellesa spread.
Finca Santa Cruz, at 1,680 m (5,500 ft) in the El Triunfo biosphere reserve, wins the Cup of Excellence with a natural Geisha scoring 93.04, from 248 entries.
The same farm wins both the washed category (91.36) and the natural and honey category (90.83).
Its natural Geisha tops the experimental category with 91.33 and draws the year's top bid, $94.70 a pound.

area.note: The whole state is outlined. The Café Chiapas protected name covers only coffee grown above 800 m (2,600 ft), in twelve of the state’s regions.

records.name: Oaxaca
records.summary: Sierra Madre coffee from small farms: bright, citrusy and floral
records.lede: Oaxaca's coffee grows in the Sierra Madre mountains at about 1,200–1,700 m (3,900–5,600 ft), almost all of it on small family farms. Pluma Hidalgo is its best-known area.

facts.label: growing altitude (3,900–5,600 ft)
its prized growing area
Café Pluma becomes a protected name, covering 30 municipalities
growers in 30-plus communities covered by the Pluma name

harvest.text: The Café Pluma rules describe a harvest of about six months, November to April, with altitude shifting when the fruit ripens.

grows.text: Typica leads: the Café Pluma rules name mainly Typica and a local type called Pluma Hidalgo; no source ranks the rest. Mostly washed: the rules call for same-day wet processing, and about 95% of Oaxaca’s coffee farmers do at least some wet processing on the farm (ICO). Dried-cherry (natural) coffee is allowed, and honeys appear among competition lots. Only about 1.1% of farmers grow Robusta.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes bright, citrusy cups with floral aromatics and a light body. Sweet Maria's ranks Oaxaca with Chiapas as Mexico's most interesting regions for quality, and says Oaxaca coffees taste distinct from those of Veracruz and Chiapas.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits Pacific breezes, mountain fog and volcanic, mineral-rich soils.

sections.title: Small farms
body: Almost all farms are small and family-owned, run with traditional, sustainable, organic methods, and the UCIRI cooperative is based here. Coffee had spread to Oaxaca by the mid-1800s.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Pluma, protected since February 2020, covers 30 municipalities in Oaxaca, among them Pluma Hidalgo, Santa Catarina Juquila, Santa María Huatulco and San Pedro Pochutla. Its rules call for shade-grown Arabica, mainly Typica and a local type called Pluma Hidalgo, picked ripe by hand, wet-processed the same day, fermented, washed and dried on patios to 12% moisture; dried-cherry (natural) coffee is also allowed. They describe a cup with pronounced acidity, a good aroma and a light body.

sections.title: Steep, sparse plantings
body: An ICO value-chain study found 38% of Oaxaca’s coffee trees on steep slopes, and about a quarter of its farmers growing fewer than 1,200 trees per hectare, far below the 2,913 it found in Chiapas.

story.text: A leaf-rust outbreak hits the four main coffee states, Chiapas, Veracruz, Oaxaca and Puebla, hard; afterwards rust-resistant varieties such as Costa Rica 95, Oro Azteca and Marsellesa spread.
Café Pluma becomes a protected name for 30 municipalities of Oaxaca's Pluma region, a year after the application.
Tierra Amarilla, an experimental Bourbon and Typica from Heladio García España and Flor Eva Pérez Cueva, places sixth in its Cup of Excellence category.
Two Oaxacan lots place: El Mirador's honey Typica, Bourbon and Geisha (sixth among naturals and honeys) and Finca El Encino's washed Geisha (fourth in the experimental category).

area.note: The whole state is outlined; the Café Pluma protected name covers 30 of its municipalities, among them Pluma Hidalgo.

records.name: Puebla
records.summary: Volcanic highlands that Coffeeness calls Mexico's coffee lab
records.lede: Puebla grows 21.1% of Mexico’s coffee, third after Chiapas and Veracruz, in shares reported with the 2024/25 harvest figures. Its coffee grows at about 1,200–1,800 m (3,900–5,900 ft) in a mild climate, on soils enriched by the region’s volcanic peaks. Coffeeness calls it Mexico’s coffee lab, with younger growers trying honey and natural processing and some experimental Geisha.

facts.label: of Mexico’s coffee, third after Chiapas and Veracruz (reported with the 2024/25 harvest figures)
growing altitude (3,900–5,900 ft)
of coffee on the average farm, against 2.3 ha in Veracruz (ICO study)
El Milagro’s washed Marsellesa and Colombia, 3rd in the washed category at the 2026 Cup of Excellence

harvest.text: Mexico picks from about November to March, with timing shifting by altitude; new-crop beans often reach roasters from spring onward.

grows.text: No published source ranks Puebla’s varieties: Coffeeness names Bourbon and Typica and calls the Geisha experimental, and Cup of Excellence lots from Puebla are mostly Marsellesa, with some Colombia and Typica. About half of Puebla’s coffee farmers wet-process at least some coffee themselves (ICO), and Coffeeness says younger growers are trying honey and natural processing; no figure gives their share.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes crisp acidity, clean citrus notes and a lighter body.

story.text: A leaf-rust outbreak hits the four main coffee states, Chiapas, Veracruz, Oaxaca and Puebla, hard; afterwards rust-resistant varieties such as Costa Rica 95, Oro Azteca and Marsellesa spread.
Los Manantiales' washed Marsellesa places third in the washed category (89.36), and an experimental Typica blend from El Río places second in its category (89.39).
El Milagro's washed Marsellesa and Colombia places third in the washed category (90.25), and Finca Los Naranjos' Marsellesa seventh in the experimental category.

area.note: The whole state is outlined.

records.name: Veracruz
records.summary: Mexico's oldest coffee region, on the Gulf: balanced, sweet, nutty
records.lede: Veracruz, on the Gulf Coast, is Mexico’s oldest coffee region, with plantings documented by 1790; coffee grows here at about 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,200 ft). It grows 24.8% of the country’s coffee, second to Chiapas, in shares reported with the 2024/25 harvest figures, and it now dominates Mexico’s Cup of Excellence, the national competition and auction for top lots. Mexico’s specialty coffee revival began here in the 1990s.

facts.label: of Mexico’s coffee, second to Chiapas (reported with the 2024/25 harvest figures)
first documented coffee plantings in Mexico
growing altitude (3,300–5,200 ft)
the year Café Veracruz became a protected name
2025 Cup of Excellence places, far more than any other state

harvest.text: Mexico picks from about November to March, with timing shifting by altitude; new-crop beans often reach roasters from spring onward.

grows.text: No published source ranks Veracruz’s varieties; Coffeeness names Bourbon, Typica and Mundo Novo. Nationally, an ICO study says traditional Typica, Caturra and Bourbon remain common, and Chapingo University researchers say rust-resistant Colombia, Oro Azteca, Costa Rica 95 and Sarchimors such as Marsellesa have spread since the 2012 rust outbreak. Its Cup of Excellence lots are mostly Geisha, Anacafé 14 and Marsellesa, and about 7.7% of its coffee farmers grow Robusta (ICO). Washed is the tradition: the Café Veracruz declaration cites a deep-rooted habit of fermenting freshly pulped coffee. About half of Veracruz farmers wet-process at least some coffee themselves, mostly on the farm (ICO). Honeys and naturals are common among competition lots: 9 of the 11 places in the 2026 natural and honey category.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes balanced sweetness, gentle acidity and nutty flavors. Sweet Maria's has found some quality lots here and notes that Coatepec coffees are very different from Oaxaca's.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits its humid, subtropical microclimate.

story.text: Mexico's first documented coffee plantings centered on Veracruz.
Veracruz kick-started Mexico's specialty coffee revival.
Café Veracruz is declared a protected name (a denomination of origin) for coffee from the state.
A leaf-rust outbreak hits the four main coffee states, Chiapas, Veracruz, Oaxaca and Puebla, hard; afterwards rust-resistant varieties such as Costa Rica 95, Oro Azteca and Marsellesa spread.
Veracruz takes 23 of the 30 Cup of Excellence places; La Palma's Geisha wins the experimental category.
Huehuetepan's washed Gesha (91.22, $88.70 a pound) and El Izote's honey Gesha (91.03) win their categories, and the state takes 21 of 30 places.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Veracruz was requested by the Consejo Veracruzano del Café and covers green and roasted coffee from the state of Veracruz. The declaration credits volcanic soils, a humid climate, the altitude of the farms and a deep-rooted habit of fermenting freshly pulped coffee, and describes high acidity, an intense aroma, a spicy flavor and a noticeable body. That is a brighter picture than the gentle acidity Coffeeness describes.

sections.title: Farms and mills
body: Veracruz farmers have more coffee land than those in Chiapas and Puebla, about 2.3 hectares each on average against 1.7 and 1.6, an ICO study found. Only about half of its farmers have done any wet processing themselves, mostly on the farm, compared with about 95% in Chiapas and Oaxaca.

names: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
area.note: The whole state is outlined; the Café Veracruz protected name covers coffee from the state of Veracruz.

records.name: Estelí
records.summary: A small, drier coffee department; Miraflor's cooperatives sell washed, sun-dried lots.
records.lede: Estelí is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments, though a small one: the 2011 agricultural census counted about 3,575 manzanas of coffee there (about 2,500 ha), 2% of the national coffee area, grown mainly in the municipalities of Estelí, Condega and Pueblo Nuevo. Much of what reaches importers comes from small farms in cooperatives such as UCA Miraflor, in the Miraflor nature reserve, and is washed and sun-dried.

facts.label: of Nicaragua's coffee area, about 3,575 manzanas (2011 census)
where coffee grows, by Coffeeness (2,600–5,200 ft)
small producers in UCA Miraflor's 12 grassroots cooperatives
year Miraflor was declared a nature reserve

harvest.text: Picked from October to March, peaking in December and January, by Nicaragua's national calendar; the sources give no separate calendar for Estelí.

grows.text: Caturra and Catuaí lead: they made up 72% of the trees PRODECOOP, the cooperative union working in Estelí, Madriz and Nueva Segovia, replanted over four recent seasons, with Catimor lines the other 28%. UCA Miraflor grows Catuaí, Caturra and Catimor and sells its coffee fully washed and sun-dried; Coffeeness also names Bourbon.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Estelí coffee as mellow, with milk chocolate and a subtle fruit sweetness. Grounds for Change sells its Miraflor lot as clean and bright, with caramel apple and roasted nuts.
cup.why: Coffeeness says Estelí is drier than Nicaragua's other coffee regions, with a distinct dry season, and argues that the stress concentrates flavor in the beans.

story.text: UCA Miraflor, a union of small coffee cooperatives, is formed in Miraflor, Estelí.
PRODECOOP, a second-tier cooperative for small producers in Estelí, Madriz and Nueva Segovia, is founded.
Miraflor is declared a nature reserve.
The national agricultural census counts about 3,575 manzanas of coffee in Estelí, 2% of the country's coffee area.
None of the 32 winning lots at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence comes from Estelí, against 23 from Nueva Segovia.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffee grows mainly in the municipalities of Estelí, Condega and Pueblo Nuevo. Wikipedia places the heart of Nicaragua's coffee country in the northern central highlands, north and east of the town of Estelí.

sections.title: Miraflor's cooperatives
body: UCA Miraflor joins 12 grassroots cooperatives and more than 400 small producers in 36 communities of the Miraflor nature reserve, farming at 1,000–1,450 m (3,300–4,750 ft). Fifty-three of its growers hold the Smithsonian's Bird Friendly certification for shade coffee, on 179 ha, and it sells organic and Fair Trade coffee.

sections.title: PRODECOOP
body: PRODECOOP works with about 2,300 small-producer families in 38 cooperatives across Estelí, Madriz and Nueva Segovia, and runs a central dry mill and cupping lab. Grounds for Change's Miraflor lot comes from two of its cooperatives, José Benito Díaz (21 members) and Vicente Talabera (36), whose farm micromills deliver dried parchment to PRODECOOP.

area.note: Coffee is concentrated in the municipalities of Estelí, Condega and Pueblo Nuevo.

records.name: Jinotega
records.summary: Historically top quality; mild acidity, floral and yellow-fruit notes.
records.lede: Jinotega is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments and, with Matagalpa, grows about 78% of the country's coffee, AFP reported in 2019; Coffeeness credits Jinotega alone with about half of the country's beans. Historically it and Matagalpa have produced the country's best coffee, and William Ortiz of the coffee company Caravela says its coffees often show mild acidity, floral notes and yellow-fruit flavors.

facts.label: of Nicaragua's coffee, Jinotega and Matagalpa together (AFP, 2019)
where coffee grows, by Coffeeness (3,900–5,900 ft)
winning lots at the 2025 Cup of Excellence
main coffee departments in Nicaragua

harvest.text: Picked from October to March, peaking in December and January, by Nicaragua's national calendar; the sources give no separate calendar for Jinotega.

cup.text: William Ortiz of Caravela says Jinotega coffees often have mild acidity, floral notes and yellow-fruit flavors. Coffeeness describes citrus (orange, lemon), floral hints and stone fruit such as peach and apricot, with a clean, tea-like finish. Everyday lots can be softer: Burman sells a 2025 Aldea Global lot as a daily coffee with good body, low acidity and malty tones.
cup.watch: Lower farms here face more disease and drying problems, and Nueva Segovia producer Silvio Sanchez finds their coffees generally less complex. Ortiz says good farm management can lift quality, and Caravela is investing in the area.
cup.prized: Pacamara and Maragogype competition lots: its best at the 2025 Cup of Excellence were Los Altiplanos's natural Pacamara (87.64) and Hugo Medina's washed Pacamara (87.59).

grows.text: Caturra leads, as across Nicaragua (72% of plantings nationally in 2021). Coffeeness adds Bourbon and a growing share of rust-resistant Catimor, and a 2025 Aldea Global lot mixes Caturra, Catuaí, Bourbon, Catimor and Maragogype. The importer lots described are washed; Jinotega's recent Cup of Excellence winners were mostly washed Maragogype, Maracaturra and Pacamara.

story.text: COOMAPCOJ, a Jinotega coffee cooperative, is founded by 21 producers from Pavona Central, Monterrey and Loma Alta.
Jinotega and Matagalpa grow about 78% of Nicaragua's coffee, AFP reports.
Caravela says it is investing in Jinotega and Matagalpa, where good farm management can lift quality.
Jinotega farms take 5 of the 32 winning lots at the Cup of Excellence, four of them washed.
San Rafael del Norte, a Jinotega municipality, supplies three winning lots, two of them washed Maragogypes.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffeeness puts Jinotega's coffee at 1,188–1,798 m (3,900–5,900 ft), with cool temperatures and steady rain, and calls the city of Jinotega the 'City of Mists'. Not all farms are that high: Burman's 2025 Aldea Global lot grew at 980–1,400 m (3,200–4,600 ft). San Rafael del Norte is the municipality most often named on recent competition lots.

sections.title: Cooperatives
body: COOMAPCOJ, founded with 21 producers in 2003, had 120 members and 480 manzanas (about 340 ha) of coffee in production by 2018. Aldea Global Jinotega counts more than 500 members, 47% of them women.

records.name: Madriz
records.summary: High cooperative farms around San Juan del Río Coco and Las Sabanas.
records.lede: Madriz is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments, in the north, with Somoto as its capital. The lots sold abroad come mostly from small producers in cooperatives, around towns such as San Juan del Río Coco and Las Sabanas, and are usually washed and dried in the sun. A 2021 guide notes that Madriz coffees generally have different flavor profiles from Nueva Segovia's.

facts.label: where importers' Madriz lots grow (3,600–5,250 ft)
of Nicaragua's coffee from Las Segovias, the northern highlands that include Madriz (AFP, 2019)
De La Finca's natural Maragogype, 7th at the 2025 Cup of Excellence
the department capital

harvest.text: Importers give December to March (Burman) or December to April (InterAmerican) for San Juan del Río Coco coffee, a later start than Nicaragua's national window of October to March.

grows.text: Caturra appears in almost every Madriz lot description, usually with Catuaí; Bourbon, Catimor and Typica also turn up, and PRODECOOP's recent replanting across the Segovias was 72% Caturra and Catuaí. Lots are usually washed and sun-dried on patios; a natural Maragogype placed at the 2025 Cup of Excellence.

cup.text: Importers describe sweet, clean cups. InterAmerican tastes caramel, butterscotch and juicy citrus with a silky body in the Reyna del Café cooperative's lot, and Burman a balanced cup with malty tones and mild acidity from San Juan del Río Coco. Coffeeness hears honey and caramel with mellow acidity.
cup.why: InterAmerican credits the high elevation and cool, dry weather, which let the coffee ripen slowly.

story.text: PRODECOOP, the second-tier cooperative for small producers in Madriz, Estelí and Nueva Segovia, is founded.
Cooperativa 5 de Junio is founded by residents of Las Sabanas.
La Cuesta, Elvis Javier Rodríguez Portillo's Madriz farm, places 13th at the Cup of Excellence with a washed Caturra, Bourbon and Catuaí lot.
Cooperativa 5 de Junio places 24th at the Cup of Excellence; roasters Groundwork, Zoka and Alterra buy its lot.
De La Finca's natural Maragogype scores 88.18, seventh in the natural and honey category and Madriz's only winning lot that year.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Lots sold abroad come from municipalities such as San Juan del Río Coco and Las Sabanas. Cooperativa 5 de Junio's 100 members, all from Las Sabanas, farm at 1,200–1,400 m (3,900–4,600 ft) under extensive shade; the Reyna del Café cooperative's 128 members, mostly on 3.5 ha or less, farm at 1,450–1,600 m (4,750–5,250 ft) around San Juan del Río Coco. Coffeeness says much of the department lies in the protected microclimate of the Tepesomoto–La Patasta range.

sections.title: How it's sold
body: The Madriz lots in importers' catalogs are mostly cooperative coffees, often certified organic and Fair Trade. PRODECOOP, which also works in Estelí and Nueva Segovia, runs a central dry mill and cupping lab, and InterAmerican says Reyna del Café's Fair Trade and organic premiums pay for member training and better milling.

records.name: Matagalpa
records.summary: With Jinotega, historically the home of Nicaragua's best coffee.
records.lede: Matagalpa is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments; with Jinotega it grows about 78% of the country's coffee, AFP reported in 2019, and Coffeeness calls it the second-largest coffee region. Historically it and Jinotega have produced the country's best coffee, and Wikipedia's history says that when most of Nicaragua's coffee grew in Managua department, Matagalpa produced the best beans.

facts.label: of Nicaragua's coffee, Matagalpa and Jinotega together (AFP, 2019)
where coffee grows, by Coffeeness (3,000–4,600 ft)
of the department's coffee from Tuma-La Dalia municipality (2011 census figures)
main coffee departments in Nicaragua

harvest.text: Picked from October to March, peaking in December and January, by Nicaragua's national calendar; the sources give no separate calendar for Matagalpa.

sections.title: Today
body: A 2021 guide groups Matagalpa with Jinotega as lower-altitude areas that face more disease and drying problems, but where, Caravela's William Ortiz says, quality can rise with good farm management; Caravela is investing in both.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffeeness puts Matagalpa's coffee at 914–1,402 m (3,000–4,600 ft), warmer than Jinotega, under cloud-forest shade. A 2021 study from the National Agrarian University reported that Tuma-La Dalia grows 36% of the department's coffee (from 2011 census data) and Matagalpa municipality 23%; San Ramón, with about 5,500 ha of coffee, is another major coffee municipality.

grows.text: On the 25 farms a 2021 National Agrarian University study surveyed in Matagalpa, San Ramón and Tuma-La Dalia, Catimor was the most common variety (on 72% of farms) followed by Marsellesa (52%), both rust-resistant. Caturra leads nationally (72% of plantings in 2021), and Coffeeness names Caturra, Bourbon and Maragogype for Matagalpa. Its recent Cup of Excellence lots were washed Maracaturra (2025 and 2026) and natural Maragogype and Pacamara (2025).

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Matagalpa coffee as chocolatey and caramel-sweet with nutty undertones, sometimes brown sugar or honey, and a smooth, sweet finish.
cup.prized: Solidaridad's washed Maracaturra placed second among washed coffees at the 2025 Cup of Excellence, with 90.50.
cup.watch: A 2021 guide groups Matagalpa with Jinotega as lower-altitude areas with more disease and drying problems.

story.text: Census figures put 36% of the department's coffee in Tuma-La Dalia municipality.
Matagalpa and Jinotega grow about 78% of Nicaragua's coffee, AFP reports.
Caravela says it is investing in Matagalpa and Jinotega, where good farm management can lift quality.
Solidaridad's washed Maracaturra scores 90.50 at the Cup of Excellence, one of three winning Matagalpa lots.

records.name: Nueva Segovia
records.summary: Highlands on the Honduran border; floral naturals, a 90-point lot.
records.lede: Nueva Segovia is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments, in the north on the border with Honduras. Two lots from here show its range: delicate, floral naturals from Finca Santa Teresa de Mogotón, grown above 1,500 m (4,900 ft), and a Centroamericano that scored 90.50 at the 2017 Cup of Excellence competition.

facts.label: winning lots at the 2025 Cup of Excellence
Los Alpes's natural Gesha from Dipilto, top lot in 2026, sold at US$140/lb
Finca Santa Teresa de Mogotón, in La Unión (4,900 ft+)
a Centroamericano's score, second at the 2017 Cup of Excellence

harvest.text: Picked from October to March. No regional calendar has been published, so this is Nicaragua's national window.

grows.text: Caturra leads nationally (72% of plantings in 2021), and Coffeeness names Bourbon, Caturra and Pacamara here. Competition farms grow much more: Gesha, Maracaturra, Maragogype, Pacamara, Parainema and Java among the 2025–26 winners. No source counts ordinary production by process; the department's 23 winning lots in 2025 split 11 washed and 12 natural or honey.

cup.text: Silvio Sanchez of Finca Santa Teresa de Mogotón calls his coffees very delicate and floral, unlike the usual Nicaraguan profile. The 2017 Cup of Excellence jury found cinnamon, peach, cherry and raspberry in Las Promesas de San Blas's Centroamericano, along with notes such as hazelnut, raisin, fig, pineapple and lime. Coffeeness describes the best lots as deep dark chocolate with dried fruit, spice or tobacco and a long, cocoa-heavy finish.
cup.why: Sanchez credits the altitude: farms this high are less affected by weather and heat than lower ones.
cup.prized: Competition Geshas: in 2026 a natural Gesha from Los Alpes, in Dipilto, topped Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence with 92.00 and sold for US$140 a pound.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffeeness puts Nueva Segovia's coffee at 1,005–1,707 m (3,300–5,600 ft), with cooler temperatures and a long growing season that make dense beans. The towns on recent winning lots are Nueva Segovia municipalities: Mozonte, Dipilto, San Fernando and Macuelizo.

sections.title: Naturals and new varieties
body: At Santa Teresa de Mogotón, Sanchez focuses on natural-processed coffee (dried inside the whole cherry), which he says gives a sweet, distinctive profile.

In 2017 Gonzalo Adán Castillo Moreno's farm, Las Promesas de San Blas, placed second at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence with a Centroamericano, an F1 hybrid (the first generation of a cross between two very different parents). Its 90.50 points earned it the Presidential Award, given to coffees scoring 90 or more.

story.text: Las Promesas de San Blas places second at the Cup of Excellence with a Centroamericano, an F1 hybrid, at 90.50 points.
Nueva Segovia takes 23 of the 32 winning lots; La Esperanza's washed Gesha (90.73) and Elite's honey Gesha (91.77) top their categories.
Los Alpes's natural Gesha from Dipilto scores 92.00 and sells for US$140 a pound, and farms in Mozonte (12 lots) and Dipilto (10) take most of the 31 winning places.

records.name: Boquete
records.summary: Misty Barú slopes, home of Esmeralda's record-setting Gesha.
records.lede: Boquete is a highland district on the slopes of Volcán Barú, Panama's highest peak, in Chiriquí province. Its farms sit at about 1,200–1,800 m (3,900–5,900 ft) in a persistent mist off the Pacific, and Gesha is the main variety. The Peterson family's Hacienda La Esmeralda began selling Gesha here as a separate lot in the early 2000s, and its lots still set auction records.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,900–5,900 ft)
of Chiriquí's coffee from Boquete, Volcán and Cerro Punta together (MIDA, 2011)
of rain a year at Los Naranjos, 2006–2014 (96 in)
Esmeralda's washed Gesha at Best of Panama (2025)

harvest.text: Panama picks from about December to March, says Sucafina; Achilles Coffee Roasters gives November–March. Both are Panama-wide dates, not Boquete's own. Rain in Boquete peaks from about May to November.

grows.text: Coffeeness calls Gesha Boquete's dominant variety. The older varieties were far more widespread in 2011, though: in MIDA's survey that year more Boquete farms grew Caturra (79), Catuaí (76) and Typica (60) than Gesha (19). Washed and natural lots both reach the auctions, and Laurina lots appear there too.

cup.text: Ozone Coffee describes Boquete Gesha as intensely jasmine-floral, with a bergamot-like complexity and a tea-like elegance; Coffeeness stresses its clarity and bright acidity.
cup.why: Sucafina credits bajareque, a fine mist carried over the mountains by northerly winds, which cools the farms and slows ripening so the cherries build more sugar.
cup.prized: Clean, floral Gesha: Esmeralda's 2025 washed lot scored 98 points.
cup.watch: Gesha is demanding to grow: it yields about half as much as Catuaí, and its cherries must be processed right after picking.

story.text: European immigrants found coffee farms in Chiriquí, particularly around Boquete.
CATIE, the research centre in Costa Rica, distributes Gesha (accession T2722) across Panama, but most farmers plant only a few trees.
The Peterson family's all-Gesha lot from Hacienda La Esmeralda sells for more than US$20 a pound at Best of Panama, a record at the time.
Esmeralda's washed Gesha scores 98 points and sells for US$30,204 a kilo.
Esmeralda's own auction of 12 nanolots (lots of a few kilos) averages US$5,745 a kilo.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Coffeeness puts the farms at 1,200–1,800 m (3,900–5,900 ft) with mist keeping temperatures around 18–25 °C (64–77 °F); Perfect Daily Grind gives the district's elevation as 1,000–2,800 m (3,300–9,200 ft). MIDA, Panama's agriculture ministry, found the best quality across Chiriquí's highlands at 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft), on well-drained, slightly acidic volcanic soils, and picking done entirely by hand, almost cherry by cherry.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Hacienda La Esmeralda, the Peterson family's estate, is the best-known name. MIDA's 2011 study measured carbon on coffee farms in Jaramillo, Palmira, Bajo Boquete and Los Naranjos, four of the six corregimientos (sub-districts) where Boquete grows coffee.

records.name: Renacimiento
records.summary: Remote district by Costa Rica: mellow, chocolatey and sweet.
records.lede: Renacimiento is a coffee district of Chiriquí near the Costa Rican border, with farms at about 1,100–1,700 m (3,600–5,600 ft) that catch humid Caribbean air. It is the least known of Panama's three main coffee regions because it is remote and short on mills and roads, though Sucafina says its growing conditions match the other two. Many of its producers are small-scale and Indigenous.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,600–5,600 ft)
Río Sereno, the district seat (987 m · 3,238 ft)
Renacimiento farms growing Caturra / Catuaí in MIDA's 2011 survey; 19 grew Gesha

harvest.text: Panama picks from about December to March, says Sucafina; Achilles Coffee Roasters gives November–March. Both are Panama-wide dates, not Renacimiento's own.

grows.text: In MIDA's 2011 survey, 70 of the Renacimiento farms visited grew Caturra and 69 Catuaí, against 21 each with Bourbon and Catimor, 19 with Gesha and 11 with Typica. No source counts processes here; Cafe Imports lists washed and natural for Panama as a whole, and Finca Hartmann sells both.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Renacimiento coffee as more balanced, with mellow acidity, good body, and notes of milk chocolate and brown sugar. Single farms go further: Kudu Coffee's washed Caturra from Finca Hartmann is sold as citrus and red apple with caramel and milk chocolate, and Nomad Coffee's natural Gesha from the same farm, dried about 12 days on raised beds, as lemongrass, blackberry and yogurt.

story.text: MIDA, Panama's agriculture ministry, surveys Chiriquí's highland coffee farms and finds Caturra and Catuaí far more common in Renacimiento than Gesha or Typica.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Coffeeness describes a high share of small-scale and Indigenous producers, and Cafe Imports says Panama's coffee is mainly grown by smallholders from the Ngäbe and Buglé Indigenous peoples. Sucafina links the district's low profile to its remoteness and its thinner processing and transport infrastructure.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Río Sereno is the district seat. Finca Hartmann, in Santa Clara, is one farm name seen on bags: the Hartmann family has grown coffee for more than a century, at 1,300–2,000 m (4,300–6,550 ft) by one roaster's account, keeps more than 100 ha of forest reserve bordering La Amistad International Park, and has its cherries picked by Ngäbe workers.

records.name: Volcán
records.summary: Barú's western side: higher, sunnier, known for naturals and honeys.
records.lede: Volcán is the coffee area on the western side of Volcán Barú, across the mountain from Boquete, and is often grouped with nearby Cerro Punta; since 2017 both lie in the new Tierras Altas district, carved out of Bugaba. Farms climb to about 2,000 m (6,600 ft) and get more direct sun than misty Boquete, and Coffeeness says farms here experiment with natural, honey and fermentation-led processing. The town is a farming hub where coffee grows alongside vegetables, flowers and dairy.

facts.label: top of the coffee lands (6,600 ft)
elevation of Volcán town (4,600 ft)
of rain a year in town, heaviest August–October (115 in)
of dry season, starting around mid-December

harvest.text: Panama picks from about December to March (Sucafina). In Volcán that lines up with the dry season, which starts around December 15 and lasts about four months.

grows.text: In MIDA's 2011 survey of Bugaba district (Volcán and Cerro Punta), the most common varieties were Caturra (27 farms), Typica (24), Catuaí (18) and Gesha (14); Coffeeness adds that Pacamara is spreading. No source counts processes; Cafe Imports lists washed and natural for Panama, and Coffeeness says Volcán farms experiment with natural, honey and fermentation processing.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Volcán coffees as caramel, chocolate and nut with fruit underneath. It hears lemon and florals with a sweet aftertaste in the Typica, and a clear, lemony acidity in the Caturra.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits altitudes up to 2,000 m (6,600 ft), which slow ripening, plus volcanic soil and more direct sun than Boquete gets.

story.text: MIDA studies the coffee of Boquete, Volcán and Cerro Punta, which together grow about 55% of Chiriquí's coffee, to support a planned denomination of origin (a protected place name).
Law 55 creates Tierras Altas district out of Bugaba, with Volcán as its seat.
Tierras Altas district takes effect on 1 July, earlier than first planned.

sections.title: Growing it
body: MIDA's 2011 study measured roughly 2,400–3,600 mm (95–142 in) of rain a year in Volcán and Cerro Punta and found coffee in Chiriquí's highlands from about 1,000 m up to 2,500 m (3,300–8,200 ft), on well-drained volcanic soils. Coffeeness credits cooler temperatures and slower ripening, and notes that farmers here intercrop coffee with other crops.

sections.title: Tierras Altas, not Bugaba
body: Since 1 July 2017 Volcán, Cerro Punta, Paso Ancho, Cuesta de Piedra and Nueva California form Tierras Altas district; older documents, including MIDA's 2011 study, place them in Bugaba.

area.note: Volcán and Cerro Punta have been in Tierras Altas district since 2017, carved out of Bugaba after these 2012 boundaries were drawn. The map uses Bugaba, which contained them; the coffee area is only its highland part, now Tierras Altas.

records.name: Amazonas
records.summary: Peru's northeast: 15% of the crop and prize-winning natural Geishas
records.lede: Amazonas, in Peru's northeast, grows about 15% of the country's coffee, Daily Coffee News reported in 2026, across seven provinces at 900–2,100 m (3,000–6,900 ft). Like most Peruvian coffee it is mainly washed, but in the Cup of Excellence, Peru's national quality competition, it stands out for coffee dried in the fruit: all nine of its winning lots from 2023 to 2025 were naturals, dried inside the whole cherry, or honeys, dried with some of the sticky fruit left on.

facts.label: of Peru's crop (2026)
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,900 ft)
of its Cup of Excellence winners, 2023–25, were naturals or honeys
exporting co-ops, third among regions (2026)

grows.text: Algrano lists Caturra, Typica and Catimor for Amazonas, and nationally most trees are now Catimor (World Coffee Research); no source ranks them for the region. Geisha made up eight of its nine Cup of Excellence winners from 2023 to 2025 (the ninth was a Villa Sarchi), but no source lists it among the region's main varieties. Most coffee is washed; naturals and honeys are the specialty lots that win prizes.

cup.text: Enigma's coffee guide describes bright, fruity Amazonas coffees with balanced acidity. US roaster Colipse lists honey, lemongrass and citrus. Algrano describes a full-bodied, sweet cup with medium-high acidity and notes of chocolate, flowers, stone fruit, nuts and spice.
cup.prized: Natural Geishas: seven of its nine Cup of Excellence winners from 2023 to 2025 were natural Geishas; the others were a natural Villa Sarchi and a honey Geisha.

story.text: Peru's farm census counted 42,744 ha of coffee in Amazonas, 10% of the national total.
Amazonas harvested 53,941 t, up 7.6% on 2021 and the fourth-largest crop among regions.
Three Amazonas naturals won Cup of Excellence places: two Geishas and a Villa Sarchi.
Three more natural Geishas placed, from Santa Teresa, El Gringo and Finca La Florida, which had also placed in 2024.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Colipse's washed lot comes from Yamón district in Utcubamba province, at 1,300–1,800 m (4,300–5,900 ft), grown from Typica, Bourbon and Castillo.

sections.title: Co-ops and new seed
body: In Rodríguez de Mendoza province, organic coffee is sold through groups such as COOPARM, APROCOYCE, La Flor del Café, Monte Verde and Aproexport, and in a 2022 study 73% of the growers surveyed there farmed 1–5 hectares (2.5–12 acres). Algrano works with the AMACOF co-op.
World Coffee Research is setting up seed lots of IPR 107 and Parainema, two rust-resistant varieties that did well in its Peruvian trials, in Amazonas, Cajamarca and San Martín.

harvest.text: Picked mainly from March to August, Algrano says. In 2026 dry weather pushed the start of Peru's harvest from April to May.

records.name: Ayacucho
records.summary: La Mar and Huanta provinces, topping out around 1,600 m
records.lede: Ayacucho grows coffee in the provinces of La Mar and Huanta, at 900–1,600 m (3,000–5,200 ft) by World of Coffee's figures, a lower ceiling than most Peruvian coffee regions. It held about 2.1% of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census. Part of its coffee comes from the VRAEM river valleys, where a Geisha from Santa Rosa district set a local auction record in 2025.

facts.label: of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census
where its coffee grows (3,000–5,200 ft)
record price for a Santa Rosa Geisha, VRAEM auction (2025)

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee names La Mar and Huanta as Ayacucho's coffee provinces. VRAEM coffee news names Santa Rosa district in La Mar and Anchihuay district, home of the Yuraq Yaku co-op.

harvest.text: No published source gives this region's own months. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, with 85% of the coffee picked from April to July (Algrano); in 2026 dry weather pushed the start from April to May.

grows.text: No source ranks varieties for Ayacucho. Nationally most trees are now Catimor (World Coffee Research); a Yuraq Yaku co-op grower in Anchihuay district grows red and yellow Obatã for specialty lots, and a Santa Rosa Geisha topped a 2025 auction. Peru's coffee is mainly washed, and no source describes processing here.

story.text: Peru's farm census counted 8,782 ha of coffee in Ayacucho, 2.1% of the national total.
At the 10th VRAEM Coffee Week auction, a Geisha from Santa Rosa district scored 87.15 points and sold for a record S/110 a kilo.
With support from Devida, a Peruvian government agency, Miguel Lapa Gutiérrez, a Yuraq Yaku co-op grower in Anchihuay district, moved from drying his coffee on the ground to solar dryers.

records.name: Cajamarca
records.summary: Jaén and San Ignacio: Peru's biggest crop and most competition wins
records.lede: Cajamarca, in Peru's north, grows more coffee than any other region by a 2026 count: about 22% of the crop. Its coffee comes from provinces such as Jaén and San Ignacio, at 900–1,950 m (3,000–6,400 ft). Its farmers have won six of the nine Cup of Excellence Peru competitions, the national contest whose top lots sell at online auction, including every one from 2022 to 2025.

facts.label: of Peru's crop, the largest share (2026)
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,400 ft)
Cup of Excellence Peru titles, 2017–2025
exporting co-ops, the most of any region (2026)

harvest.text: Algrano puts the main harvest from April to August; a German roaster lists June to September for its San Ignacio lot. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, starting earlier on lower farms, and in 2026 dry weather pushed the start to May. In 2024 SENAMHI reported the harvest in San Ignacio and Jaén ending in August.

grows.text: No source ranks varieties for Cajamarca: Algrano lists Caturra, Typica and Bourbon, nationally most trees are now Catimor (World Coffee Research), and a German roaster's San Ignacio lot names Catimor alongside Caturra, Typica and Bourbon; Marsellesa appears in two 2024 Cup of Excellence winners. Geisha keeps winning the national competition, but no source lists it among the region's main varieties. Mostly washed; naturals are a small share of its prize lots.

cup.text: Herly Mego, a Cajamarca cupper quoted by PromPerú, Peru's export and tourism promotion agency, says San Ignacio's coffees run fruitier and more floral, with some chocolate and nuts, while warmer Jaén leans citrus. He finds the highest farms the most floral, with lots of honey and vanilla. Algrano describes an elegant body and acidity, with jasmine, honey, caramel and citrus to tropical fruit.
cup.why: Altitude, in Mego's account: low farms tend to give herbal, green-apple cups scoring around 85 points, middle farms chocolate and malt at 86–87, and the highest farms the most floral and intense coffees.
cup.prized: High washed Geishas. The jury's notes for the 2023 national winner, grown at 1,990 m (6,530 ft) in Jaén, include peach, jasmine, bergamot, black tea and honey.

story.text: Juan Heredia won the first Cup of Excellence Peru; his 328 kg lot sold for nearly US$71,000, a Peruvian auction record that still stood in 2024.
Grimanés Morales took the national title for Cajamarca.
Yoniser Mego Silva's washed Geisha from Alto Mirador in Jaén, grown at 1,990 m (6,530 ft), won with 90.74 points and sold for about US$80 a pound.
Miguel Padilla Chinguel won on his first entry, with a washed Caturra, Bourbon and Geisha lot from El Mirador farm in La Coipa, San Ignacio.
Ángel Manosalva Palomino's washed Geisha from La Catarata won with 90.64 points and US$80.10 a pound, in an auction that raised a record US$490,753.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Roasters' bags name Jaén and San Ignacio, the provinces World of Coffee lists for Cajamarca. Recent national winners came from Jaén (2023) and from La Coipa in San Ignacio (2024), and the 2023 winner belongs to the Cenfrocafé cooperative.

sections.title: Co-ops and new seed
body: Cafe Imports calls the northwest, where Cajamarca lies, the source of the bulk of Peru's coffee. Co-ops here include Cenfrocafé, which Cafe Imports says supports nearly 2,000 families; Algrano names El Diamante, La Prosperidad de Chirinos, Coopagro and Aprocassi, and La Coipa and Las Mercedes districts.

Cenfrocafé runs World Coffee Research's trial of 31 varieties, where the rust-resistant IPR 107 and Parainema stood out, and the Chirinos co-op is to run one of the new seed lots spreading them (2025).

records.name: Cusco
records.summary: La Convención: three national titles and many washed Geishas
records.lede: Cusco, in Peru's south, grows its coffee in La Convención province and the Quillabamba area, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft). It won the Cup of Excellence Peru, the national quality competition, in 2018, 2020 and 2021. In 2025 its farms took 14 of the 30 winning places, more than any other region.

facts.label: Cup of Excellence winners in 2025, the most of any region
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,600 ft)
national titles: 2018, 2020 and 2021
harvested in 2022, fifth among regions

grows.text: No source ranks varieties for Cusco. Nationally most trees are now Catimor (World Coffee Research), Typica, Caturra and Bourbon are Peru's long-established varieties (Coffee Review), and Geisha leads the region's competition lots. Mostly washed; naturals and anaerobic ferments are a small competition share.

cup.text: Enigma, a Cusco travel company, describes coffee from Quillabamba and La Convención as high in acidity, with floral aromas and complex flavors. US roaster Colipse lists floral and chocolate notes for Cusco.
cup.prized: Washed lots from its top farms: 12 of Cusco's 14 Cup of Excellence winners in 2025 were washed. Ten of the 14 included Geisha, and three were the variety SL-09.

story.text: Dwight Aguilar Masías's washed Geisha from Nueva Alianza won the second Cup of Excellence Peru with 91.08 points.
Hilda Leguía won the national title for Cusco.
Aguilar won again, Cusco's third title in four years.
Wilfredo Arias Candia's washed Geisha and Bourbon from Campo Verde placed second with 90.21 points and sold for up to US$72 a pound.
Cusco farms took 14 of the 30 winning places; the highest, Gilber Huayllas Huamán's washed SL-09 from Llaqta Pata, placed third.
A Devida program with 1,850 farming families on 1,850 hectares in Calca and La Convención aimed to raise their output 50%, from 14,800 to 22,200 quintals.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Look for La Convención, the province World of Coffee names for Cusco, and Quillabamba, an area Sweet Maria's buyers have visited.
Other coffee districts include Santa Ana, Quellouno, Ocobamba and Vilcabamba in La Convención, and Yanatile in Calca province, home of the Pucamocco Typica growers' association.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Machu Picchu–Huadquiña, granted by Indecopi, Peru's intellectual-property office, in March 2011, is one of Peru's two protected coffee names. It covers green Arabica from the hamlet of Huadquiña, a former hacienda in Santa Teresa district, La Convención. Peruvian press reports credit a microclimate shaped by the nearby Salkantay, Sacsarayoc and Humantay snow peaks, which slows ripening, and describe the coffee by its fragrance, flavor and dense body.

harvest.text: No published source gives this region's own months. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, with 85% of the coffee picked from April to July (Algrano); in 2026 dry weather pushed the start from April to May. In mid-March 2024 Catimor in the Yanatile valley was ripening slowly after on-and-off rain (SENAMHI). In August 2024 higher-altitude Cusco coffee was still ripening (SENAMHI).

records.name: Huánuco
records.summary: Leoncio Prado province and Tingo María, in central Peru
records.lede: Huánuco, in central Peru, grows coffee in Leoncio Prado province, around Tingo María, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft), according to World of Coffee. It held about 4% of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census. In 2025 a washed Geisha from Palma Pampa farm placed 28th in the Cup of Excellence, Peru's national quality competition, the region's only lot in that year's top 30.

facts.label: of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,600 ft)
exporting co-op (2026)

grows.text: No source ranks varieties for Huánuco. The Monzón valley growers' association APROCAF exported Caturra, Catimor, Gran Colombia (the Colombia variety), Catuaí and Costa Rica in 2020, and nationally most trees are now Catimor (World Coffee Research). Mostly washed, as across Peru; its 2025 competition lot was a washed Geisha.

story.text: Peru's farm census counted 16,819 ha of coffee in Huánuco, 4.0% of the national total.
Forty growers from 25 communities in the Monzón, Las Palmas and Marías districts sold 32.4 t of parchment coffee scoring over 82 points to the United States, through the APROCAF association.
Huánuco's regional government was among the backers of that year's Cup of Excellence Peru.
Alcidez Nicki Rodriguez Melgarejo's washed Geisha from Palma Pampa placed 28th with 87.19 points.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee names Leoncio Prado province, with the town of Tingo María, as Huánuco's coffee area. Lots also come from the Monzón valley in Huamalíes province, Las Palmas in Leoncio Prado and Marías in Dos de Mayo; the Monzón valley expected more than 800 t in 2020.

harvest.text: No published source gives this region's own months. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, with 85% of the coffee picked from April to July (Algrano); in 2026 dry weather pushed the start from April to May.

records.name: Junín
records.summary: Chanchamayo and Satipo, about a fifth of Peru's crop
records.lede: Junín, in central Peru, grows about 19% of the country's coffee, by a 2026 count, in the provinces of Chanchamayo and Satipo at 900–1,800 m (3,000–5,900 ft). Coffee took off in the Chanchamayo valley in the second half of the 1800s. USDA's 2022 report put Chanchamayo alone at about 16% of Peru's production, while noting that growth was shifting toward the northern highlands.

facts.label: of Peru's crop (2026)
where its coffee grows (3,000–5,900 ft)
of Peru's coffee from Chanchamayo province alone (USDA, 2022)
exporting co-ops, second to Cajamarca (2026)

grows.text: Algrano lists Caturra, Typica and Catimor, and nationally most trees are now Catimor (World Coffee Research); no source ranks them for Junín. Leading growers' plots also hold Catuaí, Bourbon, Pache, Geisha and Marsellesa. Mostly washed, as across Peru; naturals, honeys and anaerobic ferments are a small specialty share that has done well in competition.

cup.text: Enigma's coffee guide says Junín's cups range from fruity to chocolatey, with a medium body. US roaster Colipse lists tropical fruit and caramel. Algrano describes an elegant body, mild acidity and bold fruit, with caramel, molasses, chocolate and nuts.
cup.prized: Naturals (dried inside the whole cherry) and honeys (dried with some sticky fruit left on) have done well. Two of Junín's three 2023 Cup of Excellence winners were naturals, one a Tupi; the third was a washed Geisha given an anaerobic ferment, in a closed vessel with little oxygen. In 2025 a honey Geisha placed ninth.

story.text: Coffee growing took off in the Chanchamayo valley, where early settlers included Germans, Austrians and Italians.
Guerrilla fighting damaged Chanchamayo's plantations and helped coffee leaf rust spread.
Peru's farm census counted 107,904 ha of coffee in Junín, 25.4% of the national total and more than any other region.
USDA reported Chanchamayo at about 16% of Peru's production, with growth shifting to the northern highlands.
Three Junín lots won Cup of Excellence places; the best, a natural blend of Geisha, Catimor and Caturra from Randu farm, placed fifth.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee lists Chanchamayo and Satipo as Junín's coffee provinces.

sections.title: Growing it
body: A 2019 survey of leading growers' plots in Satipo, Chanchamayo and Oxapampa, at 870–1,638 m (2,850–5,370 ft), identified ten varieties, among them red and yellow Catuaí, red Caturra, red and yellow Bourbon, Geisha, Pache, the hybrid H1 Centroamericano and Marsellesa. Co-ops Algrano works with include CLAC La Florida and groups around Pichanaki.

harvest.text: Picked mainly from March to August, Algrano says. In 2026 dry weather pushed the start of Peru's harvest from April to May.

records.name: Pasco
records.summary: Oxapampa province in central Peru; small in volume
records.lede: Pasco, in central Peru, grows coffee in Oxapampa province, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft) by World of Coffee's figures. It is small by volume: it held about 2.7% of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census. In 2024 a washed Geisha from La Requia II farm scored 86.39 and sold through the Cup of Excellence's National Winner auction, which is for lots scoring 85 or more.

facts.label: of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,600 ft)
exporting co-ops (2026)

grows.text: Algrano lists Caturra, Typica and Catimor for Pasco, and nationally most trees are now Catimor (World Coffee Research); no source ranks them for the region. Mostly washed, as across Peru; its 2024 competition lot was a washed Geisha.

story.text: Indecopi grants Café Villa Rica in August, the first of Peru's two protected coffee names.
Peru's farm census counted 11,429 ha of coffee in Pasco, 2.7% of the national total.
Nancy Tania Andrade Gabancho's washed Geisha from La Requia II sold for US$13.20 a pound in the Cup of Excellence's National Winner auction.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee names Oxapampa as Pasco's coffee province.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Villa Rica covers green Arabica from Villa Rica district in Oxapampa province, and has had a regulatory council since 2014. In 2025 Andina counted 2,600 growers on more than 1,500 ha, and about 49,500 kg exported under the name in 2024 and the first part of 2025. The registration rests on its quality, flavor, aroma and acidity.

sections.title: Growing it
body: A 2019 survey of leading growers' plots in Oxapampa, Chanchamayo and Satipo, at 870–1,638 m (2,850–5,370 ft), identified ten varieties, among them Catuaí, Caturra, Bourbon, Geisha, Pache and Marsellesa. World Coffee Research counts Pasco among the four Peruvian regions where formal seed production is concentrated.

harvest.text: Algrano puts Pasco's main harvest from April to August. In 2026 dry weather pushed the start of Peru's harvest from April to May.
