cup.text: Algrano describes Pasco coffee as sweet and fruity, with dark chocolate, stone fruit, berries and nuts and a medium body and acidity. Café Villa Rica's registration rests on its quality, flavor, aroma and acidity.

records.name: Piura
records.summary: Huancabamba's semitropical valleys; small, with Geishas in the national top ten
records.lede: Piura, in Peru's north, is a small coffee region: it held about 1.1% of the country's coffee land in the 2012 farm census. World of Coffee places its coffee in the semitropical valleys of Huancabamba province, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft). Piura Geishas placed tenth in the Cup of Excellence, Peru's national quality competition, in both 2024 and 2025.

facts.label: of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,600 ft)
Cup of Excellence place in 2024 and again in 2025
exporting co-op (2026)

grows.text: No source ranks varieties for Piura. Norandino, the Piura-based co-op, lists Caturra, Bourbon, Catimor and Typica for its members' coffee, and a Caturra won the 2023 regional contest; Geishas are a small share that has placed in the national competition. Mostly washed, as across Peru.

cup.text: Peruvian newspaper El Tiempo describes Piura's coffee as standing out for bright acidity, fruity notes and balanced sweetness. US roaster Colipse lists nutty, citrus and caramel.

story.text: Piura's regional agriculture office expected more than 64,000 quintals from about 8,000–9,000 ha, at 3–8 quintals a hectare, against 16–20 in Puno and Cusco.
Buyers from the Argentine café chain Café Martínez visited co-ops in Pacaipampa, San Miguel del Faique and Canchaque during the Ficafé 2023 fair.
Natividad de Jesús Abad Arias's Caturra from Montero, in Ayabaca province, won the regional coffee contest with 87.63 points.
Amaro Velasco Herrera's washed Geisha from El Naranjo placed tenth in the Cup of Excellence with 88.64 points.
Café Martínez began selling Piura coffee in its 18 shops and online.
Ronald Alejandro Baca Avila's natural Geisha from Seb placed tenth again for Piura, with 88.28 points.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee names Huancabamba as Piura's coffee province, and its districts of Canchaque, San Miguel del Faique and Lalaquiz grew the most in 2018. In Montero, in Ayabaca province, sugar cane has replaced much of the coffee because it pays better. Café Martínez's buyers visited co-ops in Pacaipampa, San Miguel del Faique and Canchaque.
Norandino, a co-op with about 5,000 coffee growers mostly in Piura, Lambayeque and Cajamarca, runs a plant in Piura that processes about 10% of Peru's coffee (2022).

harvest.text: No published source gives this region's own months. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, with 85% of the coffee picked from April to July (Algrano); in 2026 dry weather pushed the start from April to May.

records.name: Puno
records.summary: Sandia province in the south; home of CECOVASA and Tunki
records.lede: Puno, in southern Peru, grows its coffee in Sandia province at 900–1,800 m (3,000–5,900 ft). The CECOVASA cooperative union, based in Juliaca, groups 10 smallholder cooperatives, eight of them in Sandia, serving about 5,000 families. In 2010 Puno's Tunki coffee was named the best specialty coffee at the SCAA fair in the United States, ahead of more than 120 entries.

facts.label: of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census
where its coffee grows (3,000–5,900 ft)
Cup of Excellence winners in 2023, all washed
families in the CECOVASA co-op union

grows.text: Typica makes up the largest share, followed by Caturra, Bourbon, Catimor and Geisha, which smallholders often grow mixed (Happy Coffee). Mostly washed: all three of its 2023 Cup of Excellence winners were washed.

cup.text: German coffee company Happy Coffee finds chocolate and nutty notes in Puno coffee, with a gently floral acidity, and says light roasts from the south can show papaya and orange. Enigma's coffee guide describes mild acidity, a medium body, and chocolate, caramel and ripe red fruit.
cup.prized: Bourbon: all three of Puno's 2023 Cup of Excellence winners were washed lots with Bourbon in them, and a Bourbon and Caturra blend from Candelaria farm placed fourth in 2018.

story.text: The CECOVASA cooperative union was founded, with its headquarters in Juliaca.
CECOVASA gained Fairtrade certification.
Tunki coffee from Puno was named the best specialty coffee at the SCAA fair in the United States.
Florencia Mamani Calcina's Bourbon and Caturra from Candelaria placed fourth in the Cup of Excellence.
Three Puno lots won Cup of Excellence places, and the awards were announced in Puno at the Ficafé coffee fair.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Look for Sandia, the coffee province, and CECOVASA, most of whose member cooperatives are in Sandia. Tunki is a Puno coffee, blended from smallholders' varieties and traded directly.

Coffee grows in the Tambopata and Inambari valleys and the other valleys of Sandia province, organically, tended by more than 5,000 farmers, mainly Quechua and Aymara, who have registered eight specialty brands, including Tunki, Tambopata, Inambari, Titicaca and Bahuaja. In 2018 CECOVASA produced about 12,000 quintals a year and sold 40% to Europe, 30% to the United States and 30% to Asia. The Tupac Amaru co-op in Alto Inambari district has won international quality awards.

harvest.text: No published source gives this region's own months. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, with 85% of the coffee picked from April to July (Algrano); in 2026 dry weather pushed the start from April to May. In August 2024 ripening and picking in the Tambopata valley were running late, and SENAMHI expected that month's weather to help them finish.

records.name: San Martín
records.summary: Moyobamba to Tocache: neck and neck with Cajamarca for volume
records.lede: San Martín is one of Peru's two biggest coffee regions. USDA puts it at about 20% of the crop, just behind Cajamarca, while ministry figures reported by the National Coffee Board (JNC) had it first in 2020 and 2021. World of Coffee places its coffee at 900–1,200 m (3,000–3,900 ft), the lowest top altitude of any Peruvian region it lists.

facts.label: of Peru's crop, second to Cajamarca (USDA, 2026)
coffee producers (Midagri, 2026)
where its coffee grows (3,000–3,900 ft)
harvested in 2020, the most of any region (JNC)

cup.text: Enigma's coffee guide describes pleasant acidity, a medium body and flavors of citrus, chocolate and nuts. US roaster Colipse lists chocolate, floral and citrus.
cup.watch: Leaf rust on older varieties: in March 2024 SENAMHI reported more rust on susceptible Caturra and Typica in the Alto Mayo valley.

story.text: Peru's farm census counted 93,688 ha of coffee in San Martín, 22% of the national total, second only to Junín.
San Martín harvested about 89,800 t, the most of any region, by ministry figures reported by the JNC.
Its crop fell to 69,950 t, behind Cajamarca's 76,821 t.
Revista Economía reported 81,800 t, ahead of Cajamarca's 76,700 t.

At ExpoCafé San Martín's first business round, buyers signed purchase intentions of about S/13.9 million for 399 t of coffee; the region was then put at 81,000–84,000 t of parchment coffee, 22–23% of Peru's output.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Rioja, Tocache, Bellavista, Lamas and Moyobamba are the main coffee provinces (2026). The regional government's earlier coffee project worked in Moyobamba, Rioja, Lamas, El Dorado and Tocache, and seven of Peru's exporting co-ops are based here (2026).

sections.title: Growing it
body: The Universidad Nacional de San Martín study places the plantations in tropical mountains at 600–1,250 m (2,000–4,100 ft), a wider range than World of Coffee's 900–1,200 m. The regional government estimates that more than 41,000 families depend on coffee, grown on about 64,000 hectares (Agraria.pe, 2026).

harvest.text: No published source gives this region's own months. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, with 85% of the coffee picked from April to July (Algrano); in 2026 dry weather pushed the start from April to May. In mid-March 2024 Catimor in the Alto Mayo valley was already ripening (SENAMHI).

grows.text: Catimor, Caturra and Pache are the most widespread varieties, a 2021 Universidad Nacional de San Martín study says; no source gives shares. Mostly washed, as across Peru.

records.name: Gakenke
records.summary: Rwanda's cool north: Ruli and Coko stations, floral and bright.
records.lede: Gakenke is a district in Rwanda's Northern Province, the country's coolest, whose northern edge is a chain of extinct volcanoes. The Dukunde Kawa cooperative runs washing stations at Ruli and Coko, and northern coffees tend to be floral with pronounced acidity.

facts.label: Dukunde Kawa washing stations: two at Ruli, one at Coko
the Northern Province is Rwanda's coolest all year
where its prize-winning lots grow (4,900–7,200 ft)
Muyongwe station's place in Rwanda's 2015 Cup of Excellence (90.42 points)

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

grows.text: Washed Bourbon is the norm, as at Dukunde Kawa and Muyongwe, whose Cup of Excellence lots are listed as washed Bourbon. Across Rwanda about 80% of coffee is fully washed (KT Press, 2026; World Coffee Research counts about 62% of exports), and naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are roughly 5% of exports. Sucafina puts Bourbon at about 95% of the country's coffee trees.

cup.text: Melbourne Coffee Merchants, which buys its northern coffees in Gakenke, describes them as floral up front with pronounced acidity, often bright tropical fruit and a clean finish. Cup of Excellence jurors described Muyongwe's winning 2015 lot as very sweet and clean, with lemon, cranberry, raspberry, jasmine and apricot.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for Ruli or Coko, the Dukunde Kawa cooperative's station names.

sections.title: Two stations to know
body: In 2015 Dukunde Kawa had about 1,816 members, a third of them women, farming some 1,100 ha in the Ruli, Muhondo and Coko sectors at 1,500–2,000 m (4,900–6,550 ft), and it has been Fairtrade certified since 2004. That 2015 Cup of Excellence listing counts four washing stations; Melbourne Coffee Merchants now lists three, two at Ruli and one at Coko.

Muyongwe sits at 1,644 m (5,400 ft) and processes cherry grown at 1,600–2,000 m (5,250–6,550 ft) by about 1,252 farmers. It has placed in Rwanda's Cup of Excellence many times, including 5th in 2008, 7th in 2013 and 18th in 2018.

area.note: A district of Rwanda's Northern Province.

story.text: The Dukunde Kawa Musasa cooperative was formed, starting with 300 members.
Its Musasa-Ruli washing station opened, the first in Rwanda's Northern Province.
Twelve people set up the Muyongwe washing station; in 2010 its manager bought it from the member farmers to keep it running through the financial crisis.
Muyongwe placed second in Rwanda's Cup of Excellence (90.69 points), then won it the next year (90.42).

records.name: Huye
records.summary: The south, where Maraba opened the first of Rwanda's new washing stations.
records.lede: Huye is a district in Rwanda's Southern Province, the country's rainiest coffee area, with Butare as its capital. In 2001 the Maraba cooperative opened Rwanda's first new washing station here, and southern coffees tend to be jammy and syrupy.

facts.label: Maraba cooperative opens its washing station here
washing stations built across Rwanda since
of Rwanda's coffee provinces: the Southern Province
winners of Rwanda's 2013 Cup of Excellence came from Huye

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

grows.text: Mostly washed Bourbon; Huye Mountain also sells naturals, dried whole on raised tables for 3–4 weeks. Across Rwanda about 80% of coffee is fully washed (KT Press, 2026; World Coffee Research counts about 62% of exports), and naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are roughly 5% of exports. Sucafina puts Bourbon at about 95% of the country's coffee trees.

cup.text: Melbourne Coffee Merchants describes the southern coffees it buys, from Huye, Nyamagabe and Kamonyi, as jammy and juicy with a syrupy body and a long finish of raisin, brown sugar and chocolate. Cup of Excellence jurors found Huye Mountain's 2012 lot floral, creamy and elegant, with honey, peach, rose and a lavender finish.

story.text: Rwanda began reforming its coffee sector, after decades of state-set prices, the price collapse of the early 1990s and the 1994 genocide.
The Maraba cooperative opened its washing station in Huye, the first of more than 200 new stations.
Maraba's coffee was certified Fair Trade, the first Fair Trade single-origin coffee from Rwanda, says the importer Sustainable Harvest.
Huye Mountain's washing station was built, owned and run by 140 growers led by the agronomist David Rubanzangabo.
Six of the 15 winning lots in Rwanda's Cup of Excellence came from Huye, more than from any other district.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Maraba is the best-documented name here; Melbourne Coffee Merchants lists the cooperative's stations as Cyarumbo, Sovu, Kabuye and Kibingo.

sections.title: Maraba and Huye Mountain
body: Abahuzamugambi ba Kawa Maraba, 'those who have common goals', began with 20 growers and has 1,508 members. Its first station, Cyarumbo, built in 2001, was Rwanda's first specialty-focused washing station; its four stations are spread over Huye and Nyamagabe districts, and its offices and dry mill, built in 2006 with support from the USAID-funded PEARL project, are in Huye's Maraba sector. Members' farms sit around 1,700 m (5,600 ft).

Huye Mountain placed second in Rwanda's 2012 Cup of Excellence (89.83 points). The roaster The Barn, which has bought from it since 2013, says Rubanzangabo divided the mountain into seven zones with their own flavor profiles, and grows Red Bourbon at 1,700–2,200 m (5,600–7,200 ft).

area.note: A district of Rwanda's Southern Province.

records.name: Karongi
records.summary: Lake Kivu's eastern shore; home of Gitesi: sweet, black tea, blackcurrant.
records.lede: Karongi is a district on the eastern shore of Lake Kivu in Rwanda's Western Province; its lakeside town, Kibuye, is the province's headquarters. Sweet Maria's has bought washed Bourbon from its Gitesi station for more than a decade.

facts.label: Kibuye, the district's lakeshore town (4,780 ft)
Sweet Maria's has bought from the Gitesi station
Gitesi wins Rwanda's Cup of Excellence (90.19 points)
farms of the Gitesi and Murangara stations (4,900–5,900 ft)

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

grows.text: Washed Bourbon is the norm: Sweet Maria's buys washed Bourbon from Gitesi, and Gitesi's winning 2012 Cup of Excellence lot was a washed Bourbon. Across Rwanda about 80% of coffee is fully washed (KT Press, 2026; World Coffee Research counts about 62% of exports), and naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are roughly 5% of exports. Sucafina puts Bourbon at about 95% of the country's coffee trees.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's describes Gitesi as sweet at its core, with spiced, Darjeeling-like tea, blackcurrant and a hint of lemon: elegant as pour-over, spiced and chocolatey as espresso. Jurors scored Gitesi's 2012 winner well balanced, with hibiscus, peach, pineapple, blackberry and caramel and a bright, lime-like acidity.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Gitesi is the station name to look for; Sweet Maria's visited it in 2014.

sections.title: Gitesi and its growers
body: Gitesi, owned by Alexis Gahizi, stands at 1,750 m (5,750 ft) in Gitesi sector and works with the KOPAKIKA farmers' association, about 200 members, some 80% of them women. Murangara, in Mubuga sector, works with 621 farmers whose coffee grows at 1,500–1,800 m (4,900–5,900 ft), and placed 21st in the 2014 Cup of Excellence.

area.note: A district of Rwanda's Western Province.

story.text: The Kibuye Mont Coffee Cooperative built the Murangara washing station in Mubuga sector; the exporter RWACOF began using it in 2014.
The Gitesi washing station was built; it was fully running by 2010.
Gitesi won Rwanda's Cup of Excellence with 90.19 points.
Sweet Maria's visited Gitesi, which it has bought from for more than a decade.

records.name: Nyamasheke
records.summary: Between Lake Kivu and Nyungwe park: volcanic soil, lake mist, Bourbon.
records.lede: Nyamasheke is a district in Rwanda's Western Province, between Lake Kivu and Nyungwe National Park. Coffee grows on volcanic soil in a warmer, misty lakeside climate, and the lots two importers buy here are washed Bourbon. Sucafina says it has the highest concentration of washing stations in Rwanda.

facts.label: farms supplying the Murundo station (5,600–6,900 ft)
typical plot of Murundo's ~300 small growers, about 300 trees each
Cup of Excellence award for Murundo's Kivu Belt coffee
washing stations in 2017, with seven more due that year (district figures)

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May. Sucafina gives March to June for the Karambi station, a harvest of nearly four months.

grows.text: Mostly washed Bourbon. A few stations experiment: Sucafina sells an anaerobic washed lot from Karambi, whose pulped coffee ferments sealed in plastic bags for 38 hours before washing. Across Rwanda about 80% of coffee is fully washed (KT Press, 2026; World Coffee Research counts about 62% of exports), and naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are roughly 5% of exports. Sucafina puts Bourbon at about 95% of the country's coffee trees.

cup.text: Two importers' lots give a feel for it: Melbourne Coffee Merchants found Murundo's Kivu Belt juicy, with pink cherry, pomegranate, blackcurrant, plum and thyme and a cocoa-powder aftertaste, while Sweet Maria's tasted baking spice, black tea, dried apple and lemon in Gitwe. Cup of Excellence jurors described Mahembe's 2015 lot as syrupy and juicy, with orange marmalade, blackcurrant, grapefruit and jasmine.
cup.why: Melbourne Coffee Merchants credits nutrient-rich volcanic soil and the humid mist that forms over Lake Kivu, in an area hotter than Rwanda's north and south.

sections.title: At one washing station
body: At Murundo, which Melbourne Coffee Merchants buys from, cherries are pulped the same day, fermented dry for 8–12 hours, soaked for 20–26 hours with the water changed every 8 hours, then dried slowly: about 12 days under cover, then about three weeks on raised beds in the sun. Sweet Maria's also buys washed coffee from the Gitwe station in the district.

sections.title: Stations to know
body: Mahembe, at 1,803 m (5,900 ft), works with the Twitezimbere Mahembe association, about 70% women, and won Cup of Excellence places in 2010, 2012, 2014 and 2015. Rwamatamu, also opened in 2010, buys from about 2,000 farmers through collection centres. Karambi sits at 1,893 m (6,200 ft), with farms at 1,700–2,000 m (5,600–6,550 ft) and 755+ smallholders whose farms average under a hectare.

area.note: A district of Rwanda's Western Province.

story.text: The district's coffee trees rose from about 8 million to 13 million, by a 2015 survey.
The Mahembe and Rwamatamu washing stations began working.
The Gishugi station at Shangi won Rwanda's Cup of Excellence with 91.09 points.
Eight Nyamasheke stations finished in the Cup of Excellence top 20; Mahembe was second with 90.13.
RWACOF, Sucafina's Rwandan arm, built the Karambi station beside Nyungwe Forest, the only one it has built from scratch.

records.name: Rulindo
records.summary: Northern Province district; home of Tumba, fruity with black tea.
records.lede: Rulindo is a district in Rwanda's Northern Province, with its capital at Tare. Sweet Maria's buys washed Bourbon from its Tumba station and finds more fruit in it than in the other Rwandan lots it reviewed.

facts.label: the washing station Sweet Maria's buys from
the Northern Province is Rwanda's coolest all year
where its washing stations' farms grow (5,600–7,200 ft)
farmers supplying the Buliza station (2022)

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

grows.text: Washed Bourbon is the norm; Buliza lists Red Bourbon, fully washed. Across Rwanda about 80% of coffee is fully washed (KT Press, 2026; World Coffee Research counts about 62% of exports), and naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots are roughly 5% of exports. Sucafina puts Bourbon at about 95% of the country's coffee trees.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's describes Tumba as very sweet, with pomegranate, berry tea, tamarind and black tea with lemon, turning to bittersweet chocolate when roasted darker. Melbourne Coffee Merchants calls northern Rwandan coffees floral and bright. Cup of Excellence jurors found SACOF's 2014 lot delicate and very clean, with toffee, caramel, hibiscus, honey and tangerine.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Tumba is the station name to look for.

sections.title: Stations to know
body: SACOF sits at 1,794 m (5,900 ft) and processes cherry grown at 1,700–2,100 m (5,600–6,900 ft) by members of two cooperatives, BUCOFA and COFAK; growers who follow good farming practice are rewarded with cows. Buliza, at 1,790 m (5,870 ft), buys from 2,306 farmers at 1,750–2,100 m (5,750–6,900 ft) through the Ucocaru cooperative.

Kinini Village, a 48-member cooperative with its own washing station, farms at 1,800–2,200 m (5,900–7,200 ft). Driftaway Coffee notes that Rulindo is far from Rwanda's main coffee belt in the south, yet its coffee tastes typically Rwandan.

area.note: A district of Rwanda's Northern Province.

story.text: SACOF, a private washing station owned by a woman entrepreneur, Maggy Kagimbanyi Uwimbabazi, was set up in Bushoki sector.
The Buliza washing station was founded in Burega sector.
SACOF won Cup of Excellence places in 2011, 2013 and 2014.
A Rulindo lot grown at 1,750 m (5,750 ft) placed 14th in Rwanda's Cup of Excellence, back after a two-year break.

records.name: Arabica
records.summary: The species behind Typica, Bourbon, Gesha and over half the world's coffee
records.lede: Arabica (Coffea arabica) is a species, not a variety: Typica, Bourbon, Gesha and the dozens of other varieties breeders and farmers have selected all belong to it. So if a bag's variety line just says “Arabica”, nothing is wrong. It tells you the species (so not Robusta), just not which variety.

facts.label: of world coffee: 105.9 of 189.7 million bags (USDA forecast, 2026/27)
years since Robusta and C. eugenioides crossed to form it
chromosomes, twice Robusta's 22
so its varieties grow true from seed

cup.text: Arabica is generally preferred for its sweeter taste. Next to it, Robusta tends toward lower acidity, more bitterness and a fuller, earthier, more woody cup, and Sweet Maria's says Robusta generally makes an inferior-tasting drink.
cup.why: Part of the gap is chemistry: WCR notes that Robusta has more caffeine and less sugar, and links its earthy aroma to compounds called pyrazines.
cup.prized: Within Arabica, WCR associates Ethiopia's landraces with very high cup quality, and Typica and Bourbon with standard to high quality.

story.text: Robusta and the wild C. eugenioides cross in the wild, and the hybrid, carrying a full set of chromosomes from each parent, becomes a new species: Arabica.
The first documented Arabica farming is in Yemen, from around the 1400s, with seed taken from the forests of southwestern Ethiopia.

Seeds that had travelled from southwestern Ethiopia's forests to Yemen, then on to India, are shipped by the Dutch to Java; a Java plant sent to Amsterdam in 1706 starts the Typica line that later reached the Americas.
A natural Arabica × Robusta cross, the Timor Hybrid, appears on East Timor; it later passes Robusta genes, and leaf-rust resistance, to Catimor and Sarchimor varieties.
A study led by Sarada Krishnan of Denver Botanic Gardens, with Kew scientists among its co-authors, confirms South Sudan's Boma Plateau, alongside Ethiopia, as a centre of origin for wild Arabica.
More than 60 scientists from 18 countries publish Arabica's genome, read from 40 wild and cultivated plants, in Nature Genetics.

sections.title: “Arabica” on the bag
body: A species is the broad botanical group; a variety is a named type inside it. WCR describes Arabica's varieties as distinct types that can all breed with one another, and its catalog lists dozens, from Bourbon to Centroamericano.
When a bag says only “Arabica”, it is naming the species rather than the variety. That's fine: you know you're not drinking Robusta, and the roaster simply hasn't said which Arabica variety it is.

sections.title: Why varieties stay true
body: Arabica self-pollinates: a tree's flowers can fertilize themselves. Because of that, Arabica varieties have long been grown from seed, and a stable variety keeps its traits from one generation to the next.

Robusta is the opposite. A Robusta tree can't fertilize its own flowers, so its seed is always a cross and farms are never genetically uniform; growers plant several clones instead. Arabica's own exception is the F1 hybrid, such as Centroamericano, whose seed doesn't breed true, so it is cloned.

sections.title: How it formed
body: Arabica is native to Ethiopia, where most of its genetic diversity is found. The 2024 genome study (Salojärvi and colleagues, Nature Genetics) dates the cross that created it to roughly 350,000–610,000 years ago. The date is uncertain: earlier estimates ranged from 20,000 to 1 million years, and a 2020 study put it at just 10,000–20,000 years.

A 2020 study argued that a single plant gave rise to the whole species, and the 2024 study found Arabica went through several population crashes (bottlenecks). The result is a crop with very low genetic diversity, which leaves it exposed to disease and climate risks.

sections.title: Where it grows and how it sells
body: Arabica wants cooler, higher ground than Robusta. The US International Trade Commission (USITC) says it needs altitudes of about 610–1,830 m (2,000–6,000 ft), milder temperatures and more rain, and a CIRAD summary of Kew's research puts its mean annual temperature at around 19 °C (66 °F), against about 23 °C (73 °F) for Robusta. In the wild it grows in the forests of the Ethiopian Highlands and on South Sudan's Boma Plateau, where wild coffee is mostly found at 1,200–2,200 m (3,950–7,200 ft).

Brazil grows about 45% of the world's Arabica: 47.5 of 105.9 million 60-kg bags in USDA's 2026/27 forecast. Colombia (13.4 million), Ethiopia (12.1 million), Honduras (6.0 million) and Peru (4.8 million) come next. Arabica generally sells for more than Robusta, which the USITC puts down to perceptions of higher quality and a taste consumers prefer.

family.parentsText: Coffea canephora (Robusta) × Coffea eugenioides, a natural cross
family.line: Allotetraploid: it carries a full chromosome set from each parent (2n = 44)

grownIn.text: Brazil grows about 45% of the world's Arabica (47.5 of 105.9 million bags forecast for 2026/27), followed by Colombia, Ethiopia, Honduras, Peru, Mexico, Guatemala and Nicaragua. It is native to Ethiopia and South Sudan's Boma Plateau.

plant.stature: woody evergreen shrub or small tree; height depends on the variety
plant.rust: traditional varieties such as Typica and Bourbon are susceptible; resistant ones mostly carry Robusta genes from the Timor Hybrid. More disease-prone than Robusta overall
plant.altitude: usually 610–1,830 m (2,000–6,000 ft), per the USITC

records.name: Eugenioides
records.summary: Arabica's other parent, alongside Robusta
records.lede: Coffea eugenioides is a wild coffee from the mountains of East Africa and one of Arabica's two parents: hundreds of thousands of years ago it crossed with Robusta (C. canephora). Its beans carry far less caffeine than Robusta's, and since a Colombian farm began growing it for sale it has turned up in barista competitions.

facts.label: years ago it crossed with Robusta to make Arabica
caffeine in wild Kenyan beans, about a fifth of Robusta's 2.64% (2005 study)
where Finca Inmaculada in Colombia grows it (6,250–6,550 ft)
the year a World Barista Champion used it

family.parentsText: Wild species; with Robusta, a parent of Arabica
family.line: Its chromosome set makes up one of Arabica's two genomes

cup.text: Sprudge describes it as inherently sweet, with unusual notes like toasted marshmallow, lemon drops, sesame snaps and cereal milk, and says some feel it doesn't really taste like coffee at all. Competitors quoted by Barista Magazine called it unbelievably sweet, with candied strawberry and guava. Older accounts quoted in a 2023 Kew-led review call the bean mild and agreeable (1944) and the coffee fruity and clean, with a very fine aroma (2000).
cup.prized: Sweetness: one World Brewers Cup champion used it to balance the acidity of a blend.
cup.watch: Yields are lower than Arabica's, and Intelligentsia's Geoff Watts says it has a very niche following.

plant.yield: low: lower than Arabica's, Sprudge says; a 2023 Kew-led review calls it reported to be difficult to grow, though Sprudge says it is not particularly harder to grow than Arabica
plant.altitude: wild in Uganda at 910–1,828 m (2,990–6,000 ft); farmed at 1,900–2,000 m (6,250–6,550 ft) in Colombia

story.text: It crosses naturally with Robusta, and the offspring becomes Arabica.
An early account, quoted by Kew's researchers in 2023, calls the quality of its bean mild and agreeable.
Diego Campos of Colombia wins the World Barista Championship with Finca Las Nubes' Eugenioides, and Andrea Allen places second with it in her blend.

grownIn.text: Wild in East Africa (Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania and DR Congo); grown for sale at Finca Inmaculada in Pichindé, Colombia, the farm that popularized it, and at Finca Las Nubes.

sections.title: Genetics: Arabica's other parent
body: Arabica is an allotetraploid: it carries the full chromosome complement of both its parents, 22 chromosomes from Robusta and 22 from Eugenioides, for 44 in all, so every Arabica tree is part Eugenioides. Eugenioides itself is diploid, with the ordinary two sets (22 chromosomes), and the SCA counts it as one of Arabica's two diploid parents. The 2024 Arabica genome study dates the cross to roughly 350,000–610,000 years ago.
It still crosses with other species in the wild: natural diploid (2n = 22) hybrids between Eugenioides and C. liberica have been found.

sections.title: In the wild
body: It is native to the highlands of East Africa, from DR Congo, Rwanda and Uganda to Kenya and western Tanzania. A 2023 Kew-led review of Uganda's coffees calls it an exclusively forest-dwelling species of the humid evergreen forest understorey, recorded there at 910–1,828 m (2,990–6,000 ft).
The same review notes that its small beans and low yields are the main obstacles to farming it, and that in Uganda children eat its sweet ripe fruit as a snack.

records.name: Excelsa
records.summary: Its own species again since 2025: tart fruit, chocolate and spice
records.lede: Excelsa is Coffea dewevrei, a coffee from Central Africa that botanists folded into Liberica in 2006 and, after a 2025 genomic study led by Kew, recognise again as a species of its own. It copes with heat and long dry spells, out-yields Liberica, and is gaining ground in Uganda, South Sudan and India.

facts.label: a Kew-led study names it a separate species, C. dewevrei
Ugandan farms growing it, mostly switched from Robusta (2023)
where it grows in India's coffee districts (1,650–3,950 ft)
caffeine in wild Excelsa beans, vs 2.64% for Robusta (2005 study)

sections.title: Why the name keeps changing
body: The 2025 study found that what had been called Liberica is three species: C. liberica in upper West Africa, C. dewevrei (Excelsa) in Central Africa, from Cameroon and the Congo to South Sudan and Uganda, and C. klainei in west-central Africa. Kew's Aaron Davis says the wild climates of Liberica and Excelsa are markedly different, and Excelsa has smaller fruits and seeds and thinner parchment than Liberica.

sections.title: “Libex”
body: A 2026 Kew study in Scientific Reports examined 113 samples from three continents and confirmed that many farmed trees mix the two species; in Sarawak, Malaysia, 40 of 45 samples carried Excelsa genes. Libex is reported to out-yield Liberica, with thinner pulp and parchment and smaller beans. Early tasters found it more balanced than Liberica, though the authors say a proper sensory study is still needed.

sections.title: How it's used
body: In Uganda there is no separate market for it yet: most Excelsa is sold as Robusta or mixed with it, and only small lots have gone abroad, to Italy and the UK, a 2023 Kew-led review found. Slow Food has exported it under its local name, kisansa, and Clifton Coffee Roasters in the UK took a dedicated shipment in 2022.

In India, one Kodagu coffee family grew it around their estate's boundaries in place of fences and between blocks of Arabica, and it can serve as a rootstock (the root part of a grafted tree) for Arabica or Robusta. Specialty roasters have begun to show it: Blue Bottle showcased Excelsa from Vietnam and India at an industry event in Peru, and Union in the UK roasted one from Uganda's Luwero District.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Ugandan farmers and published observations say it handles drought better than Robusta, and Kew's Aaron Davis says climate change hitting lowland Robusta farms, at 500–1,000 m (1,650–3,300 ft), is driving its spread in Africa and India. Its thin pulp and parchment dry faster, and it gives a good outturn (green coffee per kilo of fruit): about 1 kg of clean coffee from 7 kg of fresh fruit in Uganda.
It is not trouble-free: India's Coffee Board warned that Excelsa left unharvested is prone to pests such as the coffee berry borer, a beetle that bores into the fruit.

grownIn.text: Farmed in Uganda, South Sudan and India (Kodagu and Hassan), and in Vietnam and Indonesia to supplement Robusta; taking hold in Guinea; grown with Liberica in the Philippines, and Sarawak's trees are often Liberica × Excelsa hybrids. Output figures by country aren't published.

cup.text: Kew's Aaron Davis, writing for the SCA, says Excelsa leans toward tart fruit, chocolate and spice, and is sweet with medium body and acidity. India's South India Coffee Company calls well-processed Excelsa sweet and very fruity, with a fermented-fruit note and little acidity or bitterness, and a 2023 Kew-led review of Uganda's coffees calls it smooth and easy-drinking.
cup.watch: Some lots taste medicinal, and early specialty buyers in India compared it to burnt rubber, so careful processing matters.
cup.prized: A sweet, mild, smooth cup with low acidity and bitterness, as Global Coffee Report's account of Kew's research puts it; one description there calls it the Merlot of the coffee world.

story.text: Excelsa is first recorded in the Congo (today's DR Congo), and in 1901 in the Central African Republic.
Plantations of 10,000–20,000 ha are set up in the Central African Republic; coffee wilt disease ruins them from the early 1940s.
Botanists fold it into Liberica as the variety C. liberica var. dewevrei.
A Kew-led genomic study of 55 plants splits it back out as C. dewevrei.
Kew proposes the name Coffea × libex for Liberica–Excelsa crosses found on farms.

plant.stature: hardy, deep-rooted and quick-growing, and it withstands pruning
plant.yield: distinctly higher than Liberica's; a Ugandan co-author of Kew's research puts it at up to about 8 kg of clean coffee per tree
plant.rust: early-1900s reports praised its resistance to a range of pests and diseases, Global Coffee Report says in its account of Kew's research, and Ugandan farmers find it more tolerant than Robusta; but coffee wilt disease wrecked its Central African plantations from the early 1940s
plant.beanSize: about Arabica's size; smaller fruit and seeds and thinner parchment than Liberica
plant.altitude: wild in Uganda at 680–1,200 m (2,230–3,940 ft)

records.name: Liberica
records.summary: A tall, thick-skinned species, best known as the Philippines' barako
records.lede: Coffea liberica is a tall coffee tree from West Africa that briefly stood second only to Arabica in the coffee trade of the late 1800s, after leaf rust hit Arabica plantations. Today it is a niche crop, best known as kapeng barako in the Philippines. A 2025 genetic study narrowed the species: Excelsa, long lumped in with it, now counts as its own.

facts.label: West African countries where it grows wild, after the 2025 split
estimated world output of Liberica and Excelsa together (2025)
tree height (66 ft); pickers use ladders
when planters took it up as leaf rust ravaged Arabica

cup.text: Kew's Aaron Davis, writing for the SCA, says Liberica tends to be dominated by tropical fruit, and is sweet with medium body and acidity; well processed, it has been praised as sweet and mild with little bitterness. Philippine barako is known for a strong flavor and an aniseed-like fragrance, and the Philippine Coffee Board describes it as smoky and chocolatey with floral and spicy undertones.
cup.watch: It has an old image problem: in the late 1800s drinkers were unsure of its flavor and traders disliked it, and its thick pulp made processing hard.
cup.prized: At its best, a sweet, mild, fruit-driven cup with low to medium acidity and minimal bitterness, as Global Coffee Report's account of Kew's research puts it.

story.text: Spanish friars bring coffee to the Philippines, first planting it around Lipa, Batangas, later the home of barako.
Planters start growing it as leaf rust devastates Arabica in Ceylon; by the late 1800s it is the trade's second species after Arabica.
Leaf rust reaches the Philippines, then one of the world's top four coffee producers, and the industry collapses.
By the turn of the century it has fallen out of favour almost everywhere, as Robusta gains ground.
Liberica is showcased at the World Barista Championship.
A Kew-led genomic study splits it into three species, leaving C. liberica itself to upper West Africa.

grownIn.text: Malaysia grew 2,861 t of coffee in 2024, 87% of it Liberica, mainly in Johor, Sabah and Sarawak. The Philippines (mainly Batangas and Cavite) grows it largely for its own market, as Malaysia and Liberia do, and Indonesia grows it in Java and West Kalimantan and on peatland in Jambi. Published figures by country are scarce.

sections.title: A crop for hot lowlands?
body: Its wild range is now Sierra Leone, Liberia, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Nigeria. Kew's researchers see Liberica and Excelsa as candidates for hot, wet lowlands where Arabica struggles; one Sarawak farm grows Liberica at 500 m (1,650 ft). The second Borneo Coffee Symposium, in Kuching, put both on its cupping tables, and the first Liberica brewing competition has been held.
Many farmed “Liberica” trees carry Excelsa genes too: in a 2026 study, 40 of 45 samples from Sarawak did.

sections.title: How much is grown?
body: You will often read that Liberica is 1–2% of the world's coffee. Kew's 2025 study says that figure dates from the late 1800s, and estimates that Liberica and Excelsa together now come to probably less than 1,000 t a year, about 0.01% of world coffee exports.

National figures don't fit that estimate neatly: Malaysia's agriculture minister reported 2,861 t of coffee for 2024, 87% of it Liberica, which on its own is more than Kew's world estimate. The figures are rough, but either way Liberica is a tiny crop next to Arabica and Robusta.

sections.title: Barako in the Philippines
body: Filipinos call Liberica barako, and most of it is grown in Batangas and Cavite. The Philippine Coffee Board says it is usually dark-roasted and finely ground, drunk black or with muscovado sugar as a breakfast staple, and that the beans give off a strong, durian-like smell while roasting.
It is a small part of the national crop: in 2020 Robusta made up 76.5% of Philippine output and Arabica 16.7%, with Liberica and Excelsa, the country's other two commercial species, sharing the rest.

plant.stature: very tall: up to 20 m (66 ft), harvested from ladders
plant.yield: lower than Excelsa's; its thick pulp means up to twice as much fresh fruit as Arabica for the same weight of green coffee
plant.rust: Kew's researchers say it has useful resistance to some common coffee pests and diseases; in the Philippines its farms held out longer than Arabica and Robusta farms in the late-1800s rust epidemic, though they too eventually succumbed
plant.beanSize: large: leaves, fruit and beans are among the biggest of any coffee
plant.altitude: hot, wet lowlands; one Sarawak farm grows it at 500 m (1,650 ft)

records.name: Racemosa
records.summary: Low-caffeine, drought-hardy wild coffee from southeastern Africa's lowland forests
records.lede: Coffea racemosa is a small-beaned wild coffee from central and southern Mozambique, eastern Zimbabwe and northern KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, where it grows in hot, seasonally dry lowland forest. Herbarium records call it “Inhambane coffee”, and settlers there drank it; one South African farm now grows it for specialty roasters.

facts.label: where it mostly grows wild (2,000 ft), in coastal and lowland forest
mean yearly temperature where it grows (73 °F), with 807 mm (32 in) of rain
caffeine in its beans, vs 2.64% for Robusta (2005 study)
Coffee Review score for a washed South African lot (2020)

cup.text: Kew's 2021 study found its flavor clearly different from Arabica's, with tasting panels noting blackcurrant, spiced wine, star anise and liquorice. Coffee Review found a 2020 lot richly bittersweet, with tangerine zest and quince, and a 2025 lot herbal and spicy, with cedar and cocoa: more subtle than flashy.

feel.body: light to medium (Kew's panels); medium and smooth (Coffee Review)

cup.watch: The tiny beans are hard to roast: all four of Kew's tasting panels struggled. Global Coffee Report says its flavor and scores have varied widely, and Kew's authors count its unusual flavor, with low yields and small beans, among its drawbacks.
cup.prized: Its spice and blackcurrant character and naturally low caffeine: Global Coffee Report notes interest from drinkers avoiding caffeine, and Kew's authors see niche-market potential once plants are selected and processing improves.

plant.stature: shrub-like treelet, about 1–3.5 m (3–11.5 ft) tall, rarely to 5 m; usually drops its leaves in the dry season
plant.yield: very low: about 12 g of green coffee (111 g of fresh fruit) per 7-year-old tree in 2021, from trees not yet fully mature
plant.altitude: under 200 m (650 ft) in coastal forest and bush, and 200–600 m (650–2,000 ft) in riverside forest, occasionally to 780 m (2,560 ft)

story.text: Herbarium specimens record it on farms within about 80 km of Inhambane, Mozambique; one notes trees 35 years old, so farming there goes back to the early 1900s.
Breeders cross it with Arabica, hoping for resistance to the coffee leaf miner; the work leads to the cultivar Siriema.
Coffee Review scores a washed lot from Charles Denison's Elephant Coast Estate 92.
Kew and partners in Mozambique and South Africa publish a study of its climate, farming and flavor.
A London roaster's lot from the same estate scores 89.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Charles Denison farms it at Hluhluwe in KwaZulu-Natal as Cultivar Coffee; bags name Elephant Coast Estate. In 2021 he had about 1,500–2,000 trees, only recently producing, on 1.5 ha. Small farms in southern Mozambique probably still grow it locally. Kew's authors see a niche market for it, held back by low yields and small beans.

Global Coffee Report wrote in 2021 of a small racemosa project on Mozambique's Ibo Island that had likely stalled after cyclones and unrest. Kew's study from the same year, though, identifies the coffee long grown on Ibo and the Quirimbas Islands as its sister species, C. zanguebariae (“Ibo coffee”), and places racemosa's own range in central and southern Mozambique, far to the south of Ibo.

sections.title: Genetics and breeding
body: Kew's 2021 DNA analysis confirms it as a species of its own, the closest relative (sister species) of C. zanguebariae; the two are told apart by racemosa's finely hairy young shoots.

Breeders have crossed it with Arabica, mainly to bring in resistance to the coffee leaf miner (a pest whose larvae tunnel inside the leaves) and also to try to lower caffeine. Crossing the hybrids back to Arabica gave the cultivar Siriema. It has also been crossed with Robusta.

sections.title: In the wild
body: It grows in two kinds of place: low coastal forest and bush on sandy soils below 200 m (650 ft), and seasonal forest along rivers at 200–600 m (650–2,000 ft). The climate is hot with a long dry season, and the shrubs usually drop their leaves while it lasts. Its light pink flowers turn white, each lasting about three days, and the fruit ripens purplish black.
Settlers drank it: a 1962 account says the local settlers used its beans and that the coffee was said to be of excellent quality.

grownIn.text: Native to Mozambique, eastern Zimbabwe and northern KwaZulu-Natal; farmed on a small scale in South Africa and probably on a few farms in southern Mozambique.

records.name: Robusta
records.summary: The hardy, high-caffeine species behind about 44% of the world's coffee
records.lede: Robusta (Coffea canephora) is the world's second big coffee species, native to the forests of central and western Africa. It generally yields more, has fewer pest and disease problems and needs a warmer climate than Arabica, and its share of world coffee has climbed since the early 1990s.

cup.text: WCR says Robusta is often lower in acidity and higher in bitterness, with a fuller body and an earthy aroma. In espresso blends it is used for body and crema. At the fine end, Embrapa describes Brazil's Amazonian Robustas as gently sweet and acidic with a velvety body, with notes of nuts, chocolate and dried fruit, and any bitterness reminiscent of cocoa nibs.
cup.why: WCR links the earthy aroma to compounds called pyrazines, and notes Robusta has more caffeine and less sugar than Arabica.
cup.prized: WCR notes that, handled and processed with care, Robusta can serve specialty markets; Embrapa's research on Rondônia's Robustas backed the world's first protected origin for the species.
cup.watch: Its reputation: CIRAD's summary of Kew's research says Robusta is widely regarded as inferior to Arabica in flavor, and most of it goes into instant coffee.

story.text: The first documented Robusta farming, in Congo, from plants of the Lomami River area.
Botanist Louis Pierre names the species.
Seed from Congo goes via Brussels to Java, where the first systematic Robusta breeding is done.
Robusta reaches Espírito Santo, Brazil, where the subtype “koillou” becomes “conilon”.
Robusta's share of world coffee rises from about 25% to about 40%.
Matas de Rondônia, in Brazil's Amazon, becomes the world's first Denominação de Origem (a protected origin) for canephora coffee, covering 15 municipalities.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Wild Robusta grows in humid forest understory from Guinea to Uganda and Angola, mostly at 50–1,500 m (165–4,920 ft). Today it is farmed in about 20 warm, humid countries, and just six (Vietnam, Brazil, Indonesia, Uganda, India and Côte d'Ivoire) grow 95% of it.
Leaf rust ravaged Arabica in Southeast Asia in the late 1800s, and in the early 1900s Java's growers took Robusta up quickly for its yield and apparent rust resistance.

sections.title: Why farms are never uniform
body: A Robusta tree can't fertilize its own flowers, unlike Arabica, so it needs pollen from a different plant. Farmers plant several clones together, and because some clones can't fertilize each other, matching their flowering times matters.

sections.title: How it's used
body: Most Robusta ends up in instant coffee: the USITC says it is used mainly for soluble (instant) coffee and for blends, and WCR credits the rise of soluble coffee with driving demand for it. Roasters also add it to espresso blends for body and crema, and it carries about twice Arabica's caffeine.

Demand is growing. The USITC expects it to keep rising as Arabica prices climb and hotter, drier weather makes Arabica harder to grow, and notes that Indonesia is developing grades for fine, or specialty, Robusta. In Brazil, Rondônia's Amazonian Robustas won the first protected origin for the species in 2021.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Robusta likes it warm and wet: WCR says it generally needs a lot of rain, and CIRAD's summary of Kew's research puts its mean annual temperature at around 23 °C (73 °F). WCR adds that its tolerance of heat may have been overstated, citing findings that temperatures above 20.5 °C (69 °F) can significantly cut yields.

Yields swing widely by country, from 1.9 bags per hectare in Côte d'Ivoire to 10.4 in Uganda and 47.7 in Vietnam, in figures WCR cites. Disease is not absent either: coffee wilt disease ravaged Uganda's Robusta in the 1990s and remains a problem there, a 2023 Kew-led review says.

family.parentsText: Wild species; two broad groups, Guinean (west-central Africa) and Congolese (central Africa, the most widespread)
family.line: Diploid (22 chromosomes) and cross-pollinating; one of Arabica's two parents

grownIn.text: Vietnam grows about 37% of the world's Robusta (31.4 of 83.8 million bags forecast for 2026/27) and Brazil, where it's called conilon, about 29% (24.4 million); Indonesia (10.0 million), Uganda (6.0 million) and India (4.6 million) follow, and these five grow about 91% of it. World Coffee Research also counts Côte d'Ivoire (1.3 million in USDA's forecast) among the six main growers.

plant.stature: vigorous; trees of the Congolese group grow tall, and in Brazil's Rondônia it is grown as multi-stemmed plants
plant.rust: some varieties resistant; the Congolese group more than the Guinean

records.name: Stenophylla
records.summary: Heat-tolerant West African wild coffee that tastes like Arabica
records.lede: Coffea stenophylla is a wild coffee from Guinea, Sierra Leone and Côte d'Ivoire that was once widely farmed in Upper West Africa and then almost forgotten. A 2021 study found it grows at a mean annual temperature 6.2–6.8 °C warmer than Arabica, yet blind tasters mostly took it for Arabica.

cup.text: Tasters in the 2021 study found natural sweetness, medium-high acidity, fruitiness and good body, with notes including peach, blackcurrant, mandarin, honey, light black tea, jasmine, chocolate and caramel.
cup.why: A 2025 chemistry study found its beans resemble Arabica's in caffeine, sugar and citric acid, though not in every compound, which may help explain why tasters mistake it for Arabica.
cup.prized: An Arabica-like cup from a tree that grows in far hotter conditions: 81% of blind tasters took it for Arabica, and historical reports from 1834 to 1929 praised its taste.
cup.watch: It yields poorly, a main reason it never became a major crop, and its reported drought tolerance and leaf-rust resistance still need testing.

story.text: Named in 1834, it becomes a farmed crop in Upper West Africa, praised for its taste, before falling out of general cultivation in the 1920s.
Stenophylla's last sighting in the wild for more than 60 years.
In December, researchers find a single plant at their main site in Sierra Leone, then a healthy population in another forest.
Davis and colleagues publish its heat tolerance and Arabica-like flavor in Nature Plants; a community nursery is set up in Sierra Leone the same year.
About 5,600 seedlings are planted in eight trial plots, and Sierra Leone's government confirms the plants are growing well.
A Kew study finds theacrine in its beans, the first record of this alkaloid in coffee beans; the first harvest from the trial plots is expected.

sections.title: Bringing it back
body: A five-year project, led by the University of Greenwich and Kew with Coffee Culture Sierra Leone and Welthungerhilfe and supported by Sucafina, aims to restart production in Sierra Leone. About 80% of its young plants survived a 2024 heatwave of 59 straight days at 40 °C (104 °F) or more. More than 5,000 more plants were in production for 2025. As of February 2025, seeds and seedlings weren't being released, and exporting plants would need the government's approval. Kew's stated ambition is production on a scale like that of the late 1800s.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: It grows wild in hot lowlands at about 400 m (1,300 ft); the forests sampled in Sierra Leone's Kenema and Moyamba districts sit at 375–466 m (1,230–1,530 ft). It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. When the 2021 study came out, it was not farmed anywhere, and only a few plants survived in research collections.
CIRAD describes it, and two other wild species tasted in 2020, as apparently resistant to coffee leaf rust, but says that, like its reported drought tolerance, it still has to be proven.

sections.title: The plant
body: In a survey of wild plants in Sierra Leone, almost nine in ten had lance-shaped leaves, long and narrow with a pointed tip. Its fruit ripens mauve and turns black when overripe; CIRAD calls them black cherries. Poor yield is the main reason given for why it never became a major world crop.

grownIn.text: Native to Guinea, Sierra Leone and Côte d'Ivoire; now in eight trial plots in Sierra Leone, where Kew and its partners hope to restart production.

plant.rust: apparently resistant, CIRAD says, but not yet proven
plant.altitude: wild at about 400 m (1,300 ft), in hot lowland forest

records.summary: A 1970s Ethiopian research pick, bred to fight coffee berry disease.
records.lede: One of the first numbered selections from Ethiopia's Jimma Agricultural Research Center (JARC): a single mother tree picked in the Metu-Bishari forest of Illubabor, in the west. It was chosen to resist coffee berry disease, a fungal disease first reported in Ethiopia in 1971, and to yield well, and it was released in 1978/79. Lots named 74110 are common at Ethiopia's Cup of Excellence, often next to its sibling 74112.

cup.text: Coffee Review has scored four 74110 lots at 93–95 (2022–2025), all roasted in Taiwan: a washed lot from Guji with cocoa nib, apricot and narcissus; two Sidama naturals, one with blueberry and baking chocolate, the other with dried mango, cocoa nib and magnolia; and a natural from Dawencho, Arbegona, tasted as espresso, with green apple, dark chocolate and grapefruit zest. Ozone's washed lot of 74110 and 74112 from Gera, in Jimma, listed orange blossom, peach and black tea. In a trial of seven early selections at three research stations in the southwest, 74158 had the top cup score, and 74110, 74112 and 74140 were statistically level with it.
cup.why: Sources don't tie its cup to the selection itself. In the 2015 trial, place and processing moved scores too: washed samples did best at Gera, the highest station at 1,940 m (6,360 ft), while naturals did slightly better at the two lower ones.
cup.prized: Its lots place high at Ethiopia's Cup of Excellence: a natural from Arbegona, Sidama, was second in 2021 with 90.5, and a washed lot from Oromia was third in 2022 with 90.19, when 74110 was named on 10 of the 32 winning lots.
cup.watch: In the 2015 trial its overall cup score was in the top group but its flavor score grouped with the lowest. It was also picked in the southwest, and Ally Coffee says 74110 and 74112 grow well in climates like those where their mother trees grew.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: 74110 often travels with its sibling 74112: Ozone's Gera lot mixed the two, a Sample Coffee lot from Gera combined them with 74140, and one 2024 national-winner lot at Cup of Excellence was listed as “74112/74110”.
Names can blur: Ally Coffee notes that the landrace name Kurume is sometimes put on JARC selections whose trees look alike.

sections.title: Genetics: what DNA tests found
body: A 2021 study using DNA markers on 40 of the 42 commercial varieties developed by JARC found them genetically diverse and mostly distant from one another, and varieties collected in the same area often fell into different groups. So a shared forest of origin, as with 74110, 74112 and 74158, is no guarantee of a close genetic match.

It was the variety named most often among the winning lots at Ethiopia's 2021 Cup of Excellence.

sections.title: In competitions
body: At Ethiopia's 2021 Cup of Excellence, 74158 held 6 of the 30 places, from Bensa and Bura in Sidama to Kokosa in West Arsi, and the only washed lot in the top 30, from Bensa, was a 74158.

In 2022 it had 10 of the 32 winning lots, including the winner, a Sidama natural that sold for $400.50 a pound; the natural Coffee Review later scored 95 placed eighth. sections.title: Growing it
body: Melbourne Coffee Merchants counts 74158, with 74110 and 74112, among the most widely propagated JARC varieties, all descended from the Metu-Bishari forests.
