Unlike compact selections such as 74110 and 74158, it grows as an open, spreading tree. It's named on at least one lot from Gera, in the Jimma zone.

facts.label: released
canopy, unlike the compact 74110 and 74158
(6,470–6,890 ft): altitude of a Gera farm that grows it
bean and cup quality rating in a 1996–2004 research summary

cup.text: Little is written about its own cup. Seid Kemal's washed Gera lot, mixing 75227 with Kurume and Merdacheriko, sold with notes of lemon myrtle, orange peel and mandarin, and a honey-processed Sample Coffee lot from producer Girma Sintayehu that includes 75227 (2025 harvest) listed apricot, mango, coconut and pineapple. In a research-station trial it was in the lower group for cup quality and acidity.
cup.watch: Research cuppings rate it below the best early selections: “fairly average quality” in a 1996–2004 summary, and the lower group for cup quality, acidity and flavor in 2015.

family.parentsText: A JARC selection from Ethiopian forest coffee; its mother tree isn't named in published sources
family.line: Released for resistance to coffee berry disease

grownIn.text: Ethiopia: named on lots from Gera, in the Jimma zone, and from producer Girma Sintayehu, who farms in Kochere, Gedeo

plant.yield: about 1,780 kg/ha on research stations, 800–900 kg/ha on farms (1996–2004 research summary)
plant.altitude: not given for each selection: the 13 early selections (released 1978–81) were recommended for low to high altitudes, with no exact range; in the 2015 trial it grew at 1,550–1,940 m (5,090–6,360 ft)

story.text: Released as a coffee berry disease resistant selection.
Used as a check variety in the southern Awada center's trials, it averages about 2,570 kg/ha in a combined 2003–05 trial.
In a verification trial of local selections from Sidama, all but one outperform it and the other standard check.
A three-site cupping trial puts it in the lower group for cup quality and acidity.
Still a standard check in a JARC trial at Jimma of coffees collected in Horo Guduru Wollega, western Ethiopia, averaging about 1,900 kg/ha.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: Its open, spreading canopy sets it apart from the compact 74110, 74112, 74140, 74158 and 74165; among the seven early selections in the 2015 trial, only 744 shared that open shape.

sections.title: In research trials
body: 75227 is often used as a check variety, the standard that new selections are measured against. Southern researchers at Awada used it in trials from 2003 to 2007, and JARC still used it, alongside 74110, 744 and Dessu, in a 2019–2023 trial at Jimma of coffees collected in Horo Guduru Wollega, where it averaged about 1,898 kg/ha.

records.name: Anacafé 14
records.summary: Guatemala's farmer-found Catimor × Pacamara cross, now winning in Mexico.
records.lede: A rust-resistant variety that grew from a natural cross between a Catimor and Pacamara in Chiquimula, Guatemala, where the farmer Francisco Manchamé noticed it. Anacafé, Guatemala's national coffee association, selected it and released it in 2014; World Coffee Research calls it very high-yielding, with good quality above 1,300 m (4,250 ft). It has since become a regular among the winners of Mexico's Cup of Excellence, the best-known national coffee competition.

facts.label: released by Anacafé
bean size, by WCR's rating
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
points for a honey Anacafé 14 from Veracruz, 2nd in its category at Mexico's 2026 Cup of Excellence

cup.text: The roaster Quantum Coffee Roasters says it often leans toward citrus, chocolate and dried fruit with a hint of spice. Coffee Review's 91-point espresso of 2021, made entirely from Anacafé 14 grown at Finca Santa Augusta in Antigua, Guatemala, tasted of dark chocolate, date, molasses and fresh-cut cedar.

feel.acidity: tart and lively, in a washed lot from El Salvador

cup.prized: Its competition record in Mexico: at the 2026 Cup of Excellence, five lots of pure Anacafé 14 from Veracruz placed, led by a honey from Rancho Viejo at 91.00 points, just behind the 91.03 Gesha that won its category.
cup.watch: It isn't uniform. WCR says plants aren't stable from one generation to the next, and in 2016 Anacafé was already testing a later generation, F5, because it wanted a more even variety.

story.text: On his plot in El Tesoro, Camotán, in Chiquimula, Francisco Manchamé notices a plant that resists rust. WCR dates the natural cross to around 1980; Prensa Libre's 2014 report says the first cross happened in 1984, on the plot where he had planted the parent varieties.
Anacafé starts studying it, and the 2012 rust epidemic speeds the work up.
Anacafé presents it as a rust-resistant variety and releases it commercially, after mass and pedigree selection.
Growers in all eight of Guatemala's coffee regions receive it.
A honey Anacafé 14 from Rancho Viejo, Veracruz, scores 91.00 and places second in its category at Mexico's Cup of Excellence.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR warns it isn't uniform: plants aren't stable from one generation to the next. It ripens late, gives a high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry), first bears in its second year, and is recommended above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator and above 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude. WCR also lists it as drought tolerant but susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms) and to coffee berry disease.

Manuel Quiñónez, Anacafé's coordinator for the Nuevo Oriente region, told Prensa Libre in 2014 that in Camotán, where farms averaged 29 quintales of parchment coffee per manzana, the new variety gave 45–55. By 2016 its discoverers, Francisco Manchamé and Noé Guerra, reported lots of up to 60–70 quintales of parchment per manzana, about 66–77 sixty-kilo bags of parchment per hectare, under the right conditions. Anacafé didn't sell the seed; growers bought it from the discoverers' farms.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Mexico's Cup of Excellence is where it shows up most. In 2024, honey lots of Anacafé 14 from Rancho Viejo (88.08 points) and Santoli (87.68), both in Veracruz, placed in the natural-and-honey category. In 2026 pure Anacafé 14 lots took places in the washed, natural-and-honey and experimental categories, all from Veracruz, with Rancho Viejo's honey on top at 91.00.
In Guatemala, its home, a natural Anacafé 14 from La Cima was among Guatemala's 2026 national winners, a tier below the ranked Cup of Excellence lots, at 86.09 points.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: Francisco Anzueto, a geneticist quoted by Prensa Libre in 2014, described a plant with plenty of side branches and oval fruits that are larger than usual. WCR lists green leaf tips (the new leaves aren't bronze) and very large beans. Prensa Libre named its parents as Maragogipe and Pacas, the two halves of Pacamara, plus a Catimor.

family.parentsText: (Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra) × Pacamara, a natural cross
family.line: Discovered by a farmer around 1980, then selected by Anacafé by mass and pedigree selection.

grownIn.text: Guatemala, where it was found and released; Veracruz in Mexico, whose farms now enter it in the Cup of Excellence; and at least one farm in El Salvador, Finca Plan del Hoyo.

plant.rust: intermediate
plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator; above 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Andungsari
records.summary: ICCRI's dwarf Catimor selection from East Java, released in 1999.
records.lede: A dwarf Catimor-type variety selected in East Java by the Indonesian Coffee and Cocoa Research Institute (ICCRI), from a Catimor of Colombian origin. Selection of Andungsari 1 began in 1982, and after about 17 years of trials Indonesia's agriculture ministry released it: in 1999 according to Royal Coffee, though the ministry's own growing guides give its release decree a number (113/Kpts/TP240/2/01) that points to 2001. It yields well but needs full sun and generous inputs, and sources disagree on how well it resists leaf rust.

facts.label: released by Indonesia's agriculture ministry: 1999 per Royal Coffee; the ministry's decree number points to 2001
(4,100 ft+), where Sucafina says it does best
a compact, high-yielding tree
leaf-rust resistance: susceptible per Royal Coffee, resistant above 1,000 m per Indonesia's 2018 official description

family.parentsText: A Catimor (Caturra × Timor Hybrid) selection; Indonesia's official description says it was picked from a Colombian Catimor of unknown genetic history, possibly descended from CIFC H-440, and some importers name Variedad Colombia or Timor Hybrid 1343 in its background
family.line: Selected by ICCRI in East Java from 1982 and trialled for about 17 years; breeder Surip Mawardi did the selection by hand.

grownIn.text: Indonesia: Java, including its Sunda (western) and central regions and West Java's Java Preanger area, and a little in Aceh, Sumatra.

plant.stature: dwarf: about 1.2 m (4 ft) when fruiting above 1,000 m, 1.75 m (5.7 ft) lower down
plant.yield: high: about 2.8 t/ha on average, 3.5 t/ha potential at 3,300 trees/ha (official description)
plant.rust: disputed: susceptible per Royal Coffee, and susceptible above 1,000 m per the 2010 ministry guide; resistant above 1,000 m and moderately resistant below 900 m per the 2018 official description
plant.altitude: above 1,250 m (4,100 ft) per Sucafina; the official description allows from 700 m (2,300 ft)

cup.text: There's little published tasting detail. Indonesia's official variety description rates its cup 'good'; Sweet Maria's Thompson says it has a nice cup in his experience, Sucafina calls its cup profile delicious, and Single O credits it with sweetness, while saying Sigarar Utang brings more intensity and mouthfeel. One blended example: Coffee Review gave 93 points in 2024 to a washed lot from Riunggunung Estate in Pangalengan, West Java, grown from Andungsari, Borbor, Kartika and Ateng trees: black cherry, hazelnut, tangerine and cedar, with gentle acidity and a full, creamy body. Another blended example: Coffee Review gave 94 points in 2020 to a washed lot from the Koetintji Barokah cooperative in Kerinci, Jambi (Sumatra), grown from Andungsari and Sigarar Utang: jasmine, white peach, almond nougat and sandalwood, with bold, juicy acidity and a silky body.
cup.watch: The agriculture ministry's 2010 growing guide notes that its cherries ripen unevenly.

story.text: ICCRI selected Andungsari 1 in East Java and began about 17 years of trials.
Indonesia's Ministry of Agriculture released it as a commercial variety: in 1999 according to Royal Coffee, though the ministry's own guides give a decree number that points to 2001.
ICCRI released Komasti, an improved Catimor that Sweet Maria's describes as 'Composite Andungsari 3'.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Indonesia's official variety description (IAARD, 2018) describes a dwarf tree with oval leaves, larger than those of the Kartika varieties and with clearly wavy edges, and rather small beans. It averages about 2.8 tonnes per hectare at 3,000 trees, with a potential of 3.5 tonnes at 3,300 trees, and stays productive for 10–15 years, shorter than the 25 years given for S795. Royal Coffee adds that it prefers full sun and needs high inputs.

On rust the national sources split: the 2018 description calls it resistant above 1,000 m (3,300 ft) and moderately resistant below 900 m (2,950 ft), while the agriculture ministry's 2010 growing guide calls it susceptible above 1,000 m. Royal Coffee's 2025 guide lists it as susceptible, and says ICCRI's later Komasti has the resistance the original Andungsari lacks.

sections.title: Not the same as Komasti
body: Royal Coffee lists Komasti as its own ICCRI variety: its name means 'Andungsari Component Three', it is made of six genotypes, and it has leaf rust resistance the original Andungsari lacks. Sweet Maria's records its name as 'Composite Andungsari 3'.

records.name: Arara
records.summary: Brazil's popular yellow-fruited, rust-resistant variety, released by Procafé in 2012.
records.lede: A compact, yellow-fruited Brazilian variety that grew from a natural cross spotted among Obatã trees in Paraná. Fundação Procafé, a Brazilian coffee research foundation, studied it from the late 1990s and released it in 2012. Known for strong rust resistance, high yields and a late harvest, it grew popular through the 2010s; Ozone reports that about 60% of Procafé's seed requests were for Arara.

facts.label: released by Fundação Procafé
more cherry than Catuaí in a 19-farm Procafé test (54 vs 40 bags/ha)
ripening, which spreads out the harvest
(1,950–3,950 ft), the range one Brazilian farm guide recommends

family.parentsText: Obatã (itself a Sarchimor × Catuaí hybrid) × probably Yellow Catuaí or Icatu: a natural cross, and Procafé names both as possible second parents
family.line: Selected from plants that turned up among Obatã trees in Paraná and developed over more than 15 years by Fundação Procafé, with technicians from the former Brazilian Coffee Institute (IBC).

grownIn.text: Brazil, especially Minas Gerais.

plant.yield: high: 56.8 bags/ha over nine harvests at Procafé's Varginha farm, against 35.1 for Catuaí
plant.rust: highly resistant; Procafé adds tolerance to Pseudomonas, a bacterial disease

cup.text: Sucafina describes lots with a classic Brazilian Bourbon pulped-natural profile (skin removed, dried with some fruit on): sweet and chocolatey, with honey and molasses. Ozone describes a sweet cup with good body and restrained acidity, with caramel, nuts and ripe fruit.
cup.prized: Competition scores: Sucafina notes scores in the low 90s; Procafé reported a record 94 points when two organic lots from Fazenda Sertãozinho in Botelhos, Minas Gerais, won the natural and pulped-natural categories of BSCA's Aromas contest (announced in 2017), and Ozone reports a 92.50 that won the 2019 BSCA Aroma contest for the same farm.
cup.watch: Sucafina says farmers sometimes pick it too early, because its signs of ripeness differ from other varieties'.

story.text: First selected in Paraná from a natural cross among Obatã trees.
Fundação Procafé began studying it closely and brought it into its breeding work.
Released commercially.

Procafé reported a record 94 points for two organic Arara lots from Fazenda Sertãozinho, Botelhos, winners in the natural and pulped-natural categories of BSCA's Aromas contest, and called it one of the most recommended and planted varieties of recent years.
An Arara from Fazenda Sertãozinho scored 92.50 to win the BSCA Aroma competition.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Sucafina advises keeping it to 20–30% of a farm's producing area, and notes that newer Brazilian varieties like it often need pruning and renewing sooner. Aegro reports that its cherries cling to the branch, so fewer drop before harvest, and that it does poorly in lowlands.

Procafé describes a short, vigorous, high-yielding tree with large fruits and beans and late ripening; a 2017 Procafé study adds that the late harvest helps farms spread out picking and bring in more quality coffee.

Procafé's analysis of nine harvests on its Varginha experimental farm, published in 2019, gave Arara 56.8 bags per hectare against 35.1 for Catuaí; because it resists the diseases that Catuaí must be sprayed for, it also saved about R$800 per hectare a year in treatments. In 2018 Procafé recommended planting it in separate plots alongside earlier-ripening Yellow Catucaí, so picking can move from one to the other.

sections.title: How popular it is
body: In 2017 Procafé called it one of the most recommended and planted varieties of recent years, and Ozone reports that about 60% of Procafé's seed requests were for Arara (undated). In 2021, nursery owners in the Cerrado Mineiro told Revista Cultivar that Arara had been their most requested seedling in 2020, one of them for three years running, before EPAMIG's MGS Paraíso 2 overtook it.

sections.title: A family of birds
body: Arara leads Fundação Procafé's group of cultivars named after birds; in 2020 Procafé described Arara itself as already widely accepted for its high yields, disease resistance and fruit quality. Its stablemates include Guará, Azulão, Acauã, Asa Branca, Beija-Flor, Saíra and Japy; Procafé recommends some, such as Azulão and Acauã, first for hotter, drier regions.

records.name: Ateng
records.summary: Sumatra's catch-all name for short Catimor trees, from Aceh Tengah.
records.lede: Less a single variety than a local label: on Sumatra and other Indonesian islands, 'Ateng' is the common name for Catimor-type trees (Caturra × Timor Hybrid). The name is short for Aceh Tengah, the Sumatran regency around Lake Takengon, and Sweet Maria's traces the original selection to one productive dwarf tree on an Aceh farm. 'Ateng Super' and 'Ateng Jeluk' (or Jaluk) are usually other names for the same thing.

facts.label: what the name usually means
the Sumatran regency it's named for
picked for low trees that are easy to harvest
where it's usually grown, thanks to its disease resistance

family.parentsText: A Catimor (Caturra × Timor Hybrid) selection
family.line: Sweet Maria's traces it to a single productive dwarf tree on a farm in Silih Nara district, Aceh, whose seed spread among farmers.

grownIn.text: Widely planted on Sumatra, especially the Gayo highlands of Aceh, and on other Indonesian islands; a 2015 agriculture-ministry study lists it among the types grown in West Java too, at Rancabali, Bandung.

plant.yield: high but unstable: Ateng Super gave 1.76 t/ha of green coffee in ICCRI's Gayo trial, the most of five local varieties

cup.text: Little is published about Ateng's cup on its own. Royal Coffee's guide says it isn't considered a high-quality cultivar. Sample Coffee, an Australian roaster, has sold a washed lot from Gayo's Putra mill (May 2024 harvest), grown from Ateng, Bor Bor, Catimor and Timor trees, with notes of blackberry, violet and toffee. Another blended example: Coffee Review gave 93 points in 2024 to a washed lot from Riunggunung Estate in Pangalengan, West Java, grown from Andungsari, Borbor, Kartika and Ateng trees: black cherry, hazelnut, tangerine and cedar, with gentle acidity and a full, creamy body.
cup.watch: Its reputation: farmers plant it for disease resistance and easy picking rather than for the cup.

sections.title: Why the bag names blur
body: Sample Coffee says the various Ateng names usually all mean Catimor plants, so treat 'Ateng' on a bag as an umbrella term, not a precise pedigree. Royal Coffee adds that Ateng is sometimes confused with Sigarar Utang, which genetic testing places close to it, and Sweet Maria's calls Sigarar Utang an improved Ateng selection.

Even the sub-names don't line up. Sweet Maria's equates Ateng Super with Ateng Jeluk, but ICCRI's 2013 Gayo study treats Ateng Super as one of the replacements for 'Catimor Jaluk', and a 2022 review of Gayo coffee lists Ateng 1, Ateng 2, Ateng Super and Ateng Janda as separate local cultivars.

sections.title: Reputation
body: The author of Royal Coffee's guide to Indonesian varieties says Ateng is planted widely for its disease resistance but isn't considered high quality.

sections.title: A farmers' name, not a release
body: Ateng isn't among the varieties described in Indonesia's agriculture ministry 2010 coffee growing guide, which covers released varieties such as S 795 and Andungsari 1. A 2015 ministry study of West Java's Java Preanger coffee lists Ateng among the types farmers there grow, next to released varieties such as Sigarar Utang, S 795 and Andungsari 1.

sections.title: Growing it
body: In ICCRI's 2013 trial of five local Gayo varieties, Ateng Super gave the highest yield, 1.76 tonnes of green coffee per hectare, but its yield wasn't stable, and the researchers picked Timtim Aceh and Borbor, not Ateng Super, as the best candidates for release. All five varieties were more prone to leaf rust below 1,000 m (3,300 ft). Gayo's coffee land sits at about 950–1,450 m (3,100–4,750 ft).

story.text: Ateng and Ateng Super were among a group of local Arabica types introduced in the Gayo highlands of Aceh, according to a 2022 review by Aceh researchers.

A study in ICCRI's research journal reported Gayo farmers planting Ateng Super and other local varieties to replace S-line and 'Catimor Jaluk' trees hit by leaf rust and root disease; Ateng Super yielded most, but unevenly.

records.name: Blue Mountain
records.summary: Jamaica's Typica strain, and separately, a protected Jamaican coffee name.
records.lede: Blue Mountain means two different things. As a variety, it's Jamaica's own strain of Typica, which has been planted in many other countries, including Kenya. As a label, Jamaica Blue Mountain is a protected name: only coffee from Jamaica's Blue Mountains that the country's regulator certifies may carry it.

facts.label: World Coffee Research lists Blue Mountain as another name for it
(3,500–5,000 ft) where Jamaica's farms sit, per Coffee Review
grown in western Kenya, says Coffee Hunter
of Jamaica Blue Mountain coffee goes to Japan (Jamaican embassy figure)

cup.text: Coffee Review's Miguel Meza (2010) found fresh, well-handled Jamaican lots excellent: balanced and sweet, with full body, good acidity and hazelnut and savory notes, though not very bright, fruity or floral.
cup.watch: Meza thought much Jamaica Blue Mountain isn't worth the hype: coffee is pulped in the mountains but dried near sea level in Kingston, problems can arise if it goes down before all the fruit is off, and storage in hot port towns can fade it. Perfect Daily Grind adds that a "Blue Mountain blend" may hold only a little of it, and a "Blue Mountain style" coffee none.
cup.why: Perfect Daily Grind credits the Blue Mountains' steep slopes, soils and cloud cover: mist often shades the high farms, lowering temperatures and slowing the cherries' ripening.
cup.prized: Smoothness and balance. Perfect Daily Grind (2021) describes a silky, well-balanced, full-bodied cup, mild, sweet and creamy with practically no bitterness, and notes of chocolate, sweet herbs and nuts.

story.text: Governor Sir Nicholas Lawes introduces coffee to Jamaica near Castleton, north of Kingston, from a plant given by Martinique's governor.
World Coffee Research gives 1730 as the year the English brought Typica from Martinique to Jamaica.
Blue Mountain is planted in western Kenya, according to Coffee Hunter.
In Papua New Guinea, Carl Wilde buys the government's Wau coffee plantation and renames it Blue Mountain Coffee; Sucafina says most of the country's highland coffee traces to its plants.
On 9 January, 60% of that year's harvest ships to Japan; Japan marked the date as Blue Mountain Coffee Day from 2019.
Hurricane Melissa causes extensive damage to coffee farms in St Andrew, Portland and St Thomas, three of the Blue Mountain parishes.
On Blue Mountain Coffee Day, 9 January, Jamaica's regulator JACRA launches a replanting drive, with 15,000 seedlings already handed to farmers.

sections.title: The region and the label
body: The name covers coffee from the parishes of Saint Andrew, Saint Thomas, Portland and Saint Mary, in the Blue Mountains between Kingston and Port Antonio. Only coffee certified by the Jamaica Agricultural Commodities Regulatory Authority, formerly the Coffee Industry Board, may be called Jamaica Blue Mountain, and the name is a registered trademark in the US, EU and UK.
Jamaican coffee from outside the Blue Mountains is sold as Jamaica High Mountain, grown at 460–910 m (1,500–3,000 ft), or lower down as Jamaica Supreme or Low Mountain.

sections.title: The variety abroad
body: Coffee Review calls Jamaica Blue Mountain Jamaica's own Typica strain and says it has been planted in many parts of the world. Coffee Hunter says it has grown in western Kenya since 1913, resists coffee berry disease (a fungus that attacks the cherries) and copes with high altitude, but can't adapt to every climate. A Blue Mountain-variety coffee from Kenya is a different thing from certified Jamaica Blue Mountain.

Sucafina lists Blue Mountain among Papua New Guinea's common varieties. In Uganda, Royal Coffee says the Bugisu variety (also called Nyasaland), taken there in 1910 and grown almost only on Mount Elgon, is related to Jamaica Blue Mountain Typica.

sections.title: Buying it
body: Certified Jamaica Blue Mountain is washed (the fruit is removed before drying), hand-picked, and exported in handmade wooden barrels, each carrying a certificate of authenticity from JACRA, the regulator, after samples pass checks for size, shape, moisture, color and cup. Perfect Daily Grind warns that a price far below the market is a sign of a fake.

sections.title: Right now (2026)
body: Jamaica's coffee is recovering from Hurricane Melissa (October 2025). In December 2025 some Portland farming areas were still cut off, so farmers couldn't harvest what was left, and the Gleaner reported that JACRA's replanting programme aims to deliver about 1.5 million new trees across 1,720 acres (about 700 ha) over four years. More than 80% of Jamaica Blue Mountain coffee is exported, the Gleaner reported in January 2026.

family.parentsText: A local Typica strain
family.line: Jamaica's Typica line; World Coffee Research treats Blue Mountain as a name for Typica.

grownIn.text: Jamaica, and planted abroad, including western Kenya; Sucafina lists it among Papua New Guinea's common varieties.

records.name: Bourbon Mayaguez 139
records.summary: A tall Bourbon selection that's a Rwandan and Burundian staple.
records.lede: A Bourbon selection made in East Africa from a population probably named for Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, where the US Department of Agriculture kept a coffee collection that had received Bourbon from Central America. The population reached the Mulungu collection in what's now the DR Congo in the 1930s and Rwanda in the early 1950s. It's now common in Rwanda and Burundi.

facts.label: WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
vigorous, productive trees with large beans
where it does best near the equator (5,250 ft)
the population arrived in Rwanda

cup.text: World Coffee Research rates its cup potential very good. Few reviews name BM139 on its own: Coffee Review gave a natural from Kayanza, Burundi, made entirely of it 93 points in 2024, tasting raspberry, narcissus, baking chocolate, salted caramel and pomelo. That's one lot with a yeast fermentation, not a variety-wide profile.

feel.acidity: bright, tart but even (in that lot)

cup.why: Little is published on BM139's own contribution. It's a Bourbon selection, and Perfect Daily Grind credits Rwanda's and Burundi's high altitudes and volcanic, nitrogen-rich soils with bringing out Bourbon's sweet, full-bodied side.
cup.prized: Sweetness and fruit at altitude: WCR rates its cup a step above its sibling BM71 and above Jackson (both rated good).
cup.watch: Disease: like other Bourbons it's susceptible to leaf rust and coffee berry disease.

plant.yield: high: WCR calls it vigorous and highly productive
plant.rust: susceptible, also to coffee berry disease
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: The Bourbon Mayagüez population, believed to have passed through the USDA's coffee collection at Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, enters the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo.
The population is brought to Rwanda; in East Africa, breeders later pick mother trees from it, including those behind BM71 and BM139.
Rwanda releases RAB C15, a variety resistant to rust and coffee berry disease, but it isn't yet widely planted, so traditional Bourbons like BM139 still dominate.
Coffee Review scores a natural made entirely of BM139, from 251 smallholders in Kayanza, Burundi, 93 points.

sections.title: BM139 and BM71
body: Once the Mayagüez population reached East Africa, breeders picked mother trees from it for new releases. World Coffee Research says two of them, Bourbon Mayagüez 71 and 139, perform very similarly in the field. It rates BM71's cup potential good, a step below BM139's very good, and says BM71 suits medium altitudes. The Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) is listed as breeder of both.

sections.title: Growing it
body: It's susceptible to leaf rust and coffee berry disease, and is planted at 2,000–3,000 trees per hectare with several stems per tree.

sections.title: In Rwanda's coffee
body: WCR calls BM139 an important variety in Rwanda, where Melbourne Coffee Merchants puts about 95% of the coffee in long-established Bourbon types. The trees are ageing: WCR estimates about 39% of Rwanda's coffee trees are over 30 years old, and the disease-resistant RAB C15, released in 2015, isn't widely planted yet.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (mother-tree selection)
family.line: Selected in East Africa from the Bourbon Mayagüez population.

grownIn.text: Common in Rwanda and Burundi.

records.name: Bourbon Ají
records.summary: A chili-scented Huila coffee: called Bourbon, reportedly Ethiopian by DNA.
records.lede: A coffee from Huila, Colombia, found around Bruselas when pickers noticed a spicy smell around the trees and a tingling on their skin; importer Sucafina dates the find to about 20 years ago. It's named for ají, chili pepper. Despite the name, genetic analysis reportedly shows it's an Ethiopian landrace rather than a Bourbon, but no details of the tests are given, and one roaster calls the information preliminary.

facts.label: where Sucafina says it was found
chili pepper: Sucafina says the cherry's sticky fruit layer smells and tastes of it
when one Huila grower's Ají first cupped well with an importer
altitude of recent lots from Huila (5,400–5,725 ft)

cup.text: Little has been written about its cup beyond roasters' notes on single lots, which tend toward sweet, fruity and lightly spiced. Ceremony lists wildflower honey, cola, citrus and baking spice; an Algrano seller lists red fruit, jasmine and a gentle peppery twist; one Sample Coffee lot from José Herman Salazar listed orange sherbet, fig and hops.
cup.prized: Sweetness with a floral, spicy edge. José Herman Salazar now makes his best lots from it.
cup.watch: The name oversells the spice: ají describes the smell of the fruit's sticky layer, and Crema says its lot doesn't actually taste of chili. And despite "Bourbon", it isn't one.

family.parentsText: Called a Bourbon, but genetic testing reportedly points to an Ethiopian landrace (no published results)
family.line: A local find in Huila, Colombia; one story says it came up among seedlings grown from Caturra seed

grownIn.text: Colombia, mainly southern Huila around Bruselas

plant.rust: seems resistant to leaf rust, says one roaster's listing; not tested in a published trial
plant.altitude: lots come from about 1,650–1,745 m (5,400–5,725 ft) in Huila

story.text: Sucafina says pickers around Bruselas, Huila, first noticed a spicy smell and a tingling on their skin at harvest.
José Herman Salazar's Ají, from trees that stood out among seedlings he grew from Caturra seed, cups well with the importer Caravela, and he starts to focus on it.
Lots from Huila growers reach roasters abroad, sold as washed, natural and double-fermented coffees.

sections.title: Two discovery stories
body: Sources disagree on how it was found. Sucafina says pickers around Bruselas noticed the spicy smell, and Crema calls it native to Bruselas, where growers in the Guácharos group swap seed: one Bruselas grower, Luz Dary Polo, replanted 7,000 trees with seed from a fellow member, Ildefonso Córdoba. Ceremony instead says José Herman Salazar noticed trees with better traits among seedlings grown from his Caturra seed, and propagated them.
Crema says the ripe cherries turn a chili-red color, and some growers think the fruit is slightly spicy, which gave the name.

sections.title: Genetics: what tests found
body: Every source that mentions testing says the same thing, that Bourbon Ají is not a Bourbon but an Ethiopian landrace, like Pink Bourbon. None names the test or publishes the results; Ceremony says only that the work was done by a lab in France, and Sample Coffee calls the information preliminary. Treat it as likely but unconfirmed.

records.name: Casiopea
records.summary: Caturra × Ethiopian F1 hybrid rated for exceptional quality up high
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of Caturra and an Ethiopian accession, ET41, from CATIE's collection, made by the same consortium of CIRAD, PROMECAFE and CATIE that created Centroamericano. WCR rates its cup potential exceptional at high altitude, but unlike Centroamericano it has little resistance to leaf rust.

facts.label: WCR's rating of its quality at high altitude
where that quality shows (4,265 ft+)
to leaf rust, coffee berry disease and nematodes
its first crop

family.parentsText: Caturra × Ethiopian accession ET41 (CATIE collection)
family.line: F1 cross from the CIRAD–PROMECAFE–CATIE consortium; propagated as clones because its seed won't grow true

plant.rust: low resistance / susceptible
plant.altitude: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator; above 1,300 m (4,265 ft) at 5–15° latitude

cup.text: Little is published about its cup. Sweet Maria's scored a 2025 white-honey lot (a near-washed Costa Rican style) from Zarcero 87.0, with dense body, dark caramel and burnt-sugar sweetness, bittersweet chocolate and a lively orange note; a roaster's listing for an anaerobic natural from Las Lajas names blueberry, dark chocolate, bergamot and panela.

feel.acidity: tea-like, with an orange note at lighter roasts

cup.prized: WCR rates its cup potential exceptional above about 1,300 m (4,265 ft) at Central America's latitudes; Sweet Maria's recommends its Zarcero lot for espresso, where it is creamy and cuts through milk.
cup.watch: It has little resistance to leaf rust and is susceptible to nematodes and coffee berry disease, and because it must be bought as cloned plants, Sweet Maria's notes it is costly for smallholders.

grownIn.text: Published lots come from Costa Rica: Zarcero in the West Valley, at about 1,750 m (5,740 ft), and Las Lajas on Poás volcano, at 1,500 m (4,920 ft). Sweet Maria's says it is becoming more common in Central America.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with bronze young leaves and large beans that yields well, bears its first crop in year three and needs a lot of fertilizer. Its cherries ripen at an average time, it gives a very high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry), and WCR suggests 4,000–5,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning.
WCR lists its breeders as CIRAD and CATIE with the national coffee institutes of Costa Rica (ICAFE), Honduras (IHCAFE), El Salvador (PROCAFE) and Guatemala (Anacafé).

sections.title: Confusions and look-alikes
body: Casiopea and H3 are close cousins: both are Caturra crossed with an Ethiopian accession from CATIE's collection (ET41 for Casiopea, E531 for H3), and both lack rust resistance. Centroamericano, Milenio and Esperanza instead have the rust-resistant Sarchimor T5296 as a parent. Bags also spell the name Cassiopea or Cassiopeia.

records.name: Catiguá
records.summary: EPAMIG's compact, rust-resistant Catuaí × Timor Hybrid, aimed at specialty coffee.
records.lede: A compact Brazilian variety from EPAMIG, Minas Gerais's agricultural research company, crossing Yellow Catuaí with the Timor Hybrid to pair leaf-rust resistance with high cup quality. World Coffee Research recommends it for specialty coffee in Brazil and notes it has out-cupped traditional varieties, Bourbon among them, at lower elevations. In 2021 a Catiguá MG2 won Brazil's Arabica 'Coffee of the Year' prize, announced at the Semana Internacional do Café.

facts.label: to leaf rust, in WCR's rating

copes with moderate water shortages

family.parentsText: Yellow Catuaí IAC 86 × Timor Hybrid UFV 440-10
family.line: An EPAMIG selection from plant 7 of cross H 514.

grownIn.text: Recommended for Brazil, where lots come from the Cerrado Mineiro and Alta Mogiana; also tested at 23 sites in 15 countries in WCR's international trial.

plant.stature: dwarf/compact; height and canopy like Catuaí's
plant.yield: high in WCR's rating; EPAMIG's own 2021 circular calls it medium
plant.rust: highly resistant

cup.text: EPAMIG, its breeder, credits it with excellent cup quality, singling out its sweetness, acidity, body and flavour, and says lots have scored above 94 points on the Specialty Coffee Association of America's 100-point scale; in 2016 it reported that some tasters considered the cup exotic for its distinctive acidity and sweetness. WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude as very good. Published flavour notes come from single lots: La Cabra, a Danish roaster, describes a natural from Alta Mogiana (briefly fermented without oxygen before drying) as strawberry over sweet, creamy milk chocolate.
cup.prized: Competition results: Brazil's 2021 Arabica 'Coffee of the Year', from Fazenda Santiago in Patos de Minas, and a natural from the Cerrado Mineiro that placed 37th (86.91 points) at Brazil's 2018 Cup of Excellence for naturals.

story.text: Sucafina dates the Catuaí × Timor Hybrid cross behind it to 1980, in Minas Gerais.
EPAMIG reported that some tasters considered Catiguá MG2 exotic for its distinctive acidity and sweetness.
A Catiguá natural from the Cerrado Mineiro placed 37th, with 86.91 points, at Brazil's Cup of Excellence for naturals.
EPAMIG reported that Costa Rica had tested it over eight harvests with excellent results, and with larger beans than it gives in Brazil.
A Catiguá MG2 from Fazenda Santiago in Patos de Minas won the Arabica 'Coffee of the Year' prize, announced at the Semana Internacional do Café.
A WCR study across 23 sites rated its rust resistance excellent in some places but less consistent elsewhere.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as late-ripening, with medium fertilizer needs, susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms), and planted at 4,000–5,000 trees per hectare. EPAMIG's own description calls its ripening intermediate and its fruit red, and says it adapts widely to different environments.

WCR adds that it needs less fertilizer and copes with drought better than traditional varieties and other rust-resistant ones, and that it resists red mites. Its cherries hold tightly to the branch: fewer drop on their own, but it is poorly suited to machine harvesting. EPAMIG spaces the trees 0.6–0.8 m (2–2.6 ft) apart in the row.

EPAMIG's 2021 circular adds that its young leaves are light bronze, that it is vigorous and tolerates short dry spells, and that because the cherries cling, harvesting machines must be set carefully and picking timed to the ripe-cherry stage. It suggests rows more than 2.5 m (8 ft) apart.

On nematodes the sources split: Sucafina calls it resistant to root-knot nematodes, while WCR lists it as susceptible. EPAMIG's 2012 study of the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne exigua tested its sister cultivars Catiguá MG1 and MG3, not MG2, and rated both resistant.

sections.title: Beyond Brazil
body: Catiguá MG2 has been tested well outside Minas Gerais. EPAMIG reported in 2018 that Costa Rica had grown it for eight harvests with excellent results. In India's international variety trial, run by the Coffee Board's research institute with World Coffee Research and reported in 2025, it was one of the few Catuaí and Sarchimor types to show high field tolerance to leaf rust. Across WCR's wider trial at 23 sites in 15 countries, reported in 2025, its rust resistance was excellent in some places and less consistent in others; the study put this down to local conditions, since how well a variety resists rust depends on where it is grown.

records.name: Catimor
records.summary: Caturra × Timor Hybrid: high-yielding, rust-resistant, often doubted in the cup.
records.lede: Not one variety but a family of them: short, heavy-bearing trees bred by crossing Caturra with the Timor Hybrid, whose Robusta genes fight leaf rust. Catimors spread from the 1970s across Latin America, Africa and Asia, and in specialty coffee the name came to stand for high yields and ordinary cups.

facts.label: first Catimor lines reach Brazil and Costa Rica
countries growing Catimors, by a 2002 Cenicafé count
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude for T8667, Central America's Catimor
compact trees, from the Caturra side

cup.text: Its reputation is poor. Ozone Coffee says some Catimors have been linked to a heavier body with earthy, woody or herbal notes; Coffee Hunter describes acidity with some bitterness, astringency (a drying feel) and a slightly salty aftertaste; Sweet Maria's says its cup is sometimes inferior.
cup.why: Sweet Maria's puts it down to the Robusta genes from the Timor Hybrid. Ozone adds that careless picking and processing make the earthy notes worse, and Coffee Project New York says big, unshaded commodity farms in Yunnan, China, deepened its image problem. Cenicafé, Colombia's coffee research center, argues that Catimors can cup as well as other Arabicas, but only when breeders rigorously remove the low-quality lines.
cup.prized: Grown and handled well it can surprise: Ozone points to a Peruvian study where Catimors scored 82.5–87.4, with natural and anaerobic lots doing best, and a Brazilian study found a Catimor line, UFV 390-52, cupping at 88.
cup.watch: Bitterness and astringency, or earthy, woody flavors when picking and processing are careless.

story.text: At Portugal's coffee rust center (CIFC), Red Caturra is crossed with Timor Hybrid selections 832/1 and 832/2; sources date the first crosses anywhere from 1959 to the late 1960s.
The CIFC hybrids HW26 and H46 go to Brazil and Costa Rica; in Brazil they get the name Catimor.
CATIE, the research center in Costa Rica, receives fifth-generation seed of the line T8667 from Brazil's Federal University of Viçosa.
T8667 seed spreads across Central America, and national programs pick their own versions: Costa Rica 95, Lempira, Catisic.
National Catimors reach farms: Costa Rica 95 is released in 1995 and Lempira in Honduras in 1998.
Rust starts infecting once-resistant Catimors, notably Lempira and Costa Rica 95.
A new rust race breaks Lempira's resistance in Honduras, where it covered about 45% of the coffee area; Coffee Review later counts as many as four new strains there.

sections.title: One name, many varieties
body: World Coffee Research stresses that Catimor isn't a distinct variety but a group of many with similar parents. The national Catimors of Central America and Mexico, such as Costa Rica 95, Lempira, Catisic, IHCAFE 90 and Oro Azteca, come from Caturra × Timor Hybrid 832/1; Colombia's Variedad Colombia came from Caturra × a different Timor Hybrid line, 1343.

Cenicafé puts it bluntly: the so-called Catimor variety doesn't exist as such; the name covers populations from Caturra × Timor Hybrid crosses, Costa Rica 95 among them. Colombia's own Caturra × Timor Hybrid varieties, Colombia, Castillo and Cenicafé 1, are blends of many lines rather than single selections.
In Africa, Catimor 129 (called Nyika in Malawi) was released in Malawi in 2006 and also resists coffee berry disease; Papua New Guinea selected and released six Catimor lines.
In Sumatra and other Indonesian islands, Catimors are widely planted under the common name Ateng, short for Aceh Tengah, the regency around Lake Takengon, Sweet Maria's reports.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR rates T8667 for the warmest zones and acidic soils at low to medium altitude; in Peru the recommended range is 800–1,400 m (2,600–4,600 ft). Catimors bear heavily and need a lot of fertilizer, and Sweet Maria's says they can wear themselves out in 5 to 10 years.
WCR also lists T8667 with a low ratio of green coffee to cherry and as susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease, and suggests 5,000–6,000 plants per hectare.

family.parentsText: Caturra (Red Caturra CIFC 19/1) × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 or 832/2 (CIFC hybrids HW26 and H46)
family.line: Crossed at CIFC in Portugal, then selected for generations in Brazil, Central America and beyond.

grownIn.text: Central and South America, Asia (including Yunnan, China) and southern Africa.

plant.rust: intermediate (T8667), and can change over time
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator, about 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude, as in Central America

records.name: Catisic
records.summary: El Salvador's Catimor, selected from T8667; WCR rates its cup very low.
records.lede: El Salvador's Catimor, selected from the Central American line T8667 by PROMECAFE and ISIC, the Salvadoran Institute for Coffee Research. It's high-yielding and suited to the warmest zones and acidic soils, but World Coffee Research rates its cup potential very low.

facts.label: WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
rust resistance, by WCR's rating
yield potential

cup.text: Little is published about its cup. World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude very low, as it does for IHCAFE 90.
cup.why: The importer Coffee Hunter puts the weaker cups of Timor Hybrid offspring down to their Robusta genes; Cenicafé says Catimors can match other Arabicas only when breeders rigorously remove poor-cupping lines.
cup.watch: Very low cup potential at high altitude, by WCR's rating.

story.text: CATIE in Costa Rica receives fifth-generation seed of the Catimor line T8667 from Brazil's Federal University of Viçosa.
T8667 seed spreads across Central America, and national programs pick their own versions: Costa Rica 95, Lempira and, in El Salvador, Catisic.
Rust starts infecting once-resistant Catimors from the same line, notably Lempira and Costa Rica 95.

sections.title: Growing it
body: A compact tree with bronze leaf tips that first bears in its third year. WCR recommends it for the warmest zones and acidic soils and lists it as susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease, and to nematodes.

It needs a lot of fertilizer, gives a low ratio of green coffee to cherry, is planted at 5,000–6,000 plants per hectare, and is susceptible to coffee berry disease, which isn't present in Central America, WCR says.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra (selected from T8667)
family.line: Pedigree selection by PROMECAFE and ISIC in El Salvador.

grownIn.text: Selected in El Salvador.

plant.rust: intermediate
plant.altitude: low to medium: about 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude, as in Central America; 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Catuaí
records.summary: Brazil's compact cross of Mundo Novo and yellow Caturra.
records.lede: A cross of Mundo Novo and yellow Caturra made in 1949 at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) in Campinas, first called H-2077 and released in Brazil in 1972. Its compact size lets farms pack in thousands of trees per hectare, and it helped drive Central America's shift to full-sun coffee in the 1970s and 1980s. It comes in red- and yellow-fruited types.

facts.label: compact trees, planted 5,000–6,000 per hectare
of Guatemala's coffee; once nearly half of Honduras's Arabica
WCR's cup rating: good but not great
very highly susceptible to leaf rust

cup.text: World Coffee Research calls its cup good but not great. Coffee Hunter says sweetness is its steadiest trait and depends mostly on how well the plant is fed; on Coffee Review, which lists 164 Catuaí reviews, chocolate and nut notes keep coming up, often with cherry, citrus or flowers in lots from Costa Rica and Panama.
cup.why: Coffee Hunter ties its sweetness to nutrition, and Brazilian researchers note that it bears heavily in its first two harvests and needs careful fertilising, so the cup tends to follow how well the trees are fed.
cup.prized: Steady sweetness that can reach the top: a Catuaí from Los Santos won the experimental category of Costa Rica's 2025 Cup of Excellence (90.47 points), another placed fifth among Nicaragua's 2025 washed coffees (89.36), and the 20 lots on one page of Coffee Review's Catuaí archive (2022–23) scored 88–94.
cup.watch: Coffee Hunter says the common view is that red and yellow Catuaí taste the same, but passes on claims that the yellow cups lower, with a petroleum-like aftertaste as it cools. And in Brazil, where most of it grows, it seldom reaches the top of competitions: in the 2025 Cup of Excellence it appeared only among the national winners below the top ten, at best 87.60.

plant.yield: medium; some Brazilian lines are very productive, but in Honduras and Costa Rica it yielded no more than Caturra, and in Procafé's trials at Varginha, Brazil, it averaged 35.1 bags a hectare over nine harvests against 56.8 for rust-resistant Arara
plant.rust: very susceptible
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: IAC crosses yellow Caturra with Mundo Novo in Campinas.
Introduced to Guatemala.
Released in Brazil after pedigree selection.
Its short trees, easy to plant densely and cheap to harvest, help open coffee farming on Brazil's cerrado, the high savanna.
Reaches Honduras in 1979 (released there in 1983 after IHCAFE trials) and Costa Rica in 1985.
A Catuaí from Costa Rica's Los Santos wins the experimental category of the national Cup of Excellence, at 90.47 points.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Studies in Honduras and Costa Rica found no significant yield difference between Catuaí and Caturra. It needs plenty of fertiliser and is susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms) and coffee berry disease, though that disease isn't present in Central America. Coffee Hunter adds that its cherries hold on in strong wind and rain. Mexico developed a similar variety, Garnica, around 1960–61.
Brazilian breeders have kept using it: Arara is a cross of Obatã and Yellow Catuaí, and Catucaí is a natural cross of Icatu and Catuaí.

sections.title: Red or yellow
body: Catuaí comes in red-fruited (Vermelho) and yellow-fruited (Amarelo) types, both from the same cross, with many selections in different countries, some known only by number. Coffee Hunter says the common view is that the two taste the same, though some sources claim the yellow cups lower and the red keeps a purer taste.

sections.title: Brazil's workhorse
body: A 2012 estimate put Catuaí and Mundo Novo together at about 85% of the coffee planted in Brazil, and Coffee Hunter puts Catuaí alone at about half. It rarely tops Brazil's competitions, though: in the 2025 Cup of Excellence, newer rust-resistant varieties such as Arara and Catucaí took most of the top places, and Catuaí appeared only among the lower-ranked national winners. In Central America it does better on the cupping table, winning a category in Costa Rica in 2025.

family.parentsText: Mundo Novo × Yellow Caturra
family.line: Bred at IAC, Campinas, Brazil, by pedigree selection.

grownIn.text: Brazil's most planted variety; important in Honduras, Guatemala (about 20%) and Costa Rica, and grown in Nicaragua and Panama.

records.name: Catucaí
records.summary: A natural Icatu × Catuaí cross from Brazil, first selected in 1988.
records.lede: A Brazilian variety that grew from a natural cross between Icatu and Catuaí, first selected in 1988 by breeders at the Brazilian Coffee Institute (IBC). Its cherries ripen red or yellow, following the Catuaí parent, and it inherits Robusta genes through Icatu. Barista Hustle says it resists leaf rust and Ascochyta, a fungal leaf disease, well.

facts.label: its first selection
cherries, matching the Catuaí parent
Procafé registered the Catucaí Açu strain
to leaf rust

family.parentsText: Icatu × Catuaí, a natural cross: Yellow Catuaí × Icatu gives Yellow Catucaí, Red Catuaí × Icatu gives Red Catucaí
family.line: A spontaneous cross, selected by IBC breeders in 1988; new strains have kept coming since.

grownIn.text: Brazil, especially Minas Gerais, where Fundação Procafé, a Brazilian coffee research foundation, trialled its lines at Varginha and competition lots come from the Sul de Minas; Ozone describes the Catucaí group as now widely planted; since 2019 Embrapa has also recommended Catucaí Amarelo 2SL for Rondônia, in the Amazon.

plant.yield: high; several lines out-yielded Catuaí in Procafé's trials
plant.rust: resistant (Sucafina, Barista Hustle); Procafé's 2007 trials rated Catucaí lines moderately resistant
plant.altitude: no general range published; Embrapa recommends Catucaí Amarelo 2SL above 300 m (about 1,000 ft) in Rondônia, in the Amazon, where average temperatures are near 26 °C

cup.text: Sucafina describes Yellow Catucaí lots as creamy and sweet with dark chocolate, and calls the Catucaí 2SL strain balanced, much like Caturra and Catuaí. In Procafé's 2009 cupping of rust-resistant lines grown at Varginha, most Catucaí lines scored 80–84 out of 100, rated good, and Red and Yellow Catucaí 20/15 reached 84.5–86, rated very good. Embrapa, recommending Catucaí Amarelo 2SL for Rondônia in 2019, described cups above 80 points with a pronounced body, creamy texture, low acidity and caramel and chocolate notes.
cup.prized: At its best it competes: a Red Catucaí natural from Virgínia, in the Sul de Minas, placed sixth with 89.7 points at Brazil's 2019 Cup of Excellence.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Sucafina describes high yields and even ripening that makes picking easier, but demanding fertilizer and water needs. In 2010–11 trials at São Sebastião do Paraíso and Três Pontas, Minas Gerais, researchers used Catucaí Amarelo 2SL as a rust-resistant benchmark alongside Icatu Precoce.

Procafé's own trials at Varginha, in the south of Minas Gerais, showed several Catucaí lines (Red and Yellow 20/15, Red 24/137, Yellow 2SL) yielding more than Catuaí, and rated the Catucaí lines moderately resistant to rust. Some lines, including Yellow 24/137, Yellow 3SM and Red 785-15, were among those with the highest share of large beans (screen 17 and up).

Ripening varies by line: Procafé groups Yellow Catucaí with its early-to-medium varieties and Catucaí 785-15 with the early ones. In 2018 it recommended planting Yellow Catucaí (2SL, 24/137 or 20/15) in some plots and late-ripening Arara in others on Sul de Minas farms, so the harvest is spread out.

sections.title: On bags
body: Sucafina reported in 2021 that more Catucaí seedlings had started showing up in nurseries three or four years earlier, and that it was the first year several microlots (small lots sold separately) of it were appearing.
Nursery owners in the Cerrado Mineiro told Revista Cultivar in 2021 that Catucaí Amarelo 2SL was among their most requested seedlings.

sections.title: One name, many lines
body: 'Catucaí' covers a family of numbered lines rather than one variety: Procafé's trial reports name Catucaí 785-15, Yellow 2SL, Red and Yellow 20/15, Red and Yellow 24/137, Red 36/6, Yellow 3SM and others, and Coffee Hunter adds Catucaí Açu. A bag that just says 'Catucaí' may hold any of them, with red or yellow cherries.

story.text: Breeders at the Brazilian Coffee Institute (IBC) first selected it from a natural Icatu × Catuaí cross.
Fundação Procafé registered the Catucaí Açu strain, according to Coffee Hunter.
Procafé tested Catucaí lines over six harvests at its Varginha farm in Minas Gerais and recommended several for the region.
A Red Catucaí natural placed sixth, with 89.7 points, at Brazil's Cup of Excellence.
After 13 years of testing 57 Arabica types, Embrapa recommended Catucaí Amarelo 2SL for Rondônia, in the Amazon, where it yielded more than 35 bags per hectare.
Sucafina reported the first year that several Catucaí microlots were appearing on the market.

records.name: Cenicafé 1
records.summary: Cenicafé's 2016 dwarf variety, resistant to rust and coffee berry disease.
records.lede: A short, rust-resistant variety that Cenicafé, Colombia's coffee research center, delivered to growers in December 2016. It comes from Caturra × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343, and Cenicafé bills it as highly productive, resistant to coffee berry disease as well as rust, and better in physical bean quality. By 2020 it was, for the first time, the single variety with the most seed handed out by Cenicafé.

facts.label: delivered to Colombian growers
resists leaf rust and coffee berry disease
Supremo (large) beans in trials, against 79.3% for Castillo and 54.1% for Caturra
of the seed Cenicafé handed out in 2020, the largest share

cup.text: In Cenicafé's release trial, cupped by the Caldas growers' committee on the SCA's 100-point scale, it scored 84.00 with notes of cocoa, honey and hazelnut, level with Castillo and just above Caturra (83.75). Cenicafé calls the cup very good and specialty grade.

feel.acidity: 8.00 of 10 in Cenicafé's release panel, the highest acidity there (Castillo and Caturra 7.75)

cup.prized: Consistency at a good level: in a Cenicafé project in Cesar reported in 2024, Cenicafé 1 had the highest share of cups above 83 SCA points (68.4%), whatever the fermentation temperature.
cup.watch: Not a standout by default: a 2020 Cenicafé panel rated the average Cenicafé 1, Castillo and Tabi sample as standard.

story.text: Cenicafé publishes the release bulletin: eight lines picked from 116 advanced progenies tested at seven experiment stations.
Seed is delivered to Colombian growers.
Cenicafé's variety guide lists it among the only four varieties with seed certified by the ICA, Colombia's farm authority.
It's 41% of the seed Cenicafé hands out, the most of any variety for the first time; the same year Cenicafé finds rust able to grow on all its lines.
In a Cenicafé project in Cesar, it has the highest share of cups above 83 points (68.4%).

sections.title: How it was picked
body: Cenicafé started from 116 advanced progenies of Caturra × Timor Hybrid 1343. Screening for short height, low rust, bean size and yield left six that yielded at least as well as Castillo General; a second test picked six that yielded at least as well as the Colombia variety on shorter trees with more large beans. That gave 11 different progenies, and dropping close relatives, to keep more resistance genes, left eight, all fourth-generation (F4) lines from three first-generation parents. Yield was measured over four harvests at Naranjal and checked at Pueblo Bello, El Rosario, Paraguaicito and El Tambo; rust was scored at Naranjal, La Trinidad, Paraguaicito and La Catalina. DNA markers were used to check resistance to coffee berry disease: one marker is present in all eight lines.

sections.title: Growing it
body: It's short like Caturra (about 140 cm at two years) and yields like Castillo: 17.6 kg of cherry per tree over four harvests, against 17.9 kg for Castillo General, a difference that isn't statistically significant. Cenicafé recommends it for the whole coffee zone, at up to 10,000 plants per hectare in full sun or 5,000–7,000 under shade trees, and reminds growers that other pests and diseases still need watching.

sections.title: Rust pressure
body: In release trials rust stayed at or below 10% of leaf area. By 2020, though, Cenicafé had found rust able to grow, to varying degrees, on all the component lines of Cenicafé 1, Castillo and Tabi, and its 2024 report says rust races have grown more diverse and more virulent (better at getting past resistance) since 2010, especially on Timor Hybrid 1343 lines, the source of Cenicafé 1's resistance.

family.parentsText: Caturra × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343
family.line: Selected by Cenicafé and sold as a blend of eight F4 lines; the older Variedad Colombia came from the same Caturra × Timor Hybrid 1343 cross.

grownIn.text: Bred for Colombia, where its seed is certified.

plant.stature: short (dwarf): about 140 cm at two years, the same as Caturra
plant.yield: high: about 17.6 kg of cherry per tree over four harvests, level with Castillo
plant.rust: resistant (rust at or below 10% of leaf area in trials); also resists coffee berry disease. Since 2020 Cenicafé has found rust able to grow on its lines
plant.beanSize: large: 84.3% Supremo, against 79.3% for Castillo and 54.1% for Caturra
plant.altitude: recommended for all of Colombia's coffee zone

records.name: Centroamericano
records.summary: Rust-resistant F1 hybrid that hit 90.5 points at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid, meaning the seed comes straight from crossing two unrelated parents: the rust-resistant Sarchimor line T5296 and Rume Sudan, an old landrace collected in South Sudan in the 1940s that WCR groups with Ethiopian landraces. It was released to Central American farmers in 2010, and in 2017 a Nicaraguan lot placed second at the Cup of Excellence with 90.5 points.

facts.label: coffee than standard varieties in breeding trials
released to Central American farmers
where WCR says its quality is best (4,265 ft+)
its own seed won't grow true, so nurseries clone it

cup.text: The 2017 Cup of Excellence jury in Nicaragua called its prize lot balanced, with cinnamon, peach, cherry and hazelnut. Ozone Coffee says the variety can make clean, sweet cups with bright acidity, and that floral and fruity notes are possible alongside more familiar chocolate and citrus.
cup.why: In Nicaraguan trials it out-scored Caturra on the SCA scale (the industry's 100-point cupping score), 80.4 to 76.3. WCR's history of the variety says it has shown exceptional cup potential when grown high and managed well; its rating chart puts that potential at very good.
cup.prized: WCR rates its cup potential at high altitude very good (its history of the variety says exceptional when well managed), on top of very high yields and strong rust resistance.
cup.watch: It needs very heavy feeding, can struggle to root in its first two years, and is susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms).

story.text: CATIE, CIRAD and PROMECAFE, a network of Central America's national coffee institutes, start the breeding program behind the region's F1 hybrids.
Centroamericano is released to Central American farmers; about 1,000 hectares were planted by 2017.
CIRAD reports that, at nine trial sites in Central America, it out-yielded the best traditional variety at every one, by 37% on average.
A frost on the night of February 6 kills or badly injures most trees in a trial plot in Laos; Centroamericano is one of the few survivors.
Gonzalo Castillo's lot from Las Promesas de San Blas in Nueva Segovia places second at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence with 90.50 points.
Castillo's honey-processed Centroamericano places second again, with 90.42, one of four F1 hybrids in the top eleven.
CATIE begins supplying Centroamericano, Milenio and Esperanza plants to about 200 coffee-growing families in the Trifinio region of Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with large beans and very high yields that bears its first crop in year two. It is highly resistant to leaf rust and tolerates coffee berry disease, but nematodes can harm it, and it should not get too much nitrogen.
In a Nicaraguan trial of nine F1 hybrids, it showed no rust lesions and was among the two most promising for yield and stability.

WCR also rates it well suited to agroforestry (coffee grown under shade trees), gives it a very high outturn, meaning a lot of green coffee per kilo of cherry, and suggests 3,000–4,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning. A 2020 Costa Rican study recommends it for 800–1,500 m (2,600–4,900 ft) and notes it has been one of the hardest of the hybrids to clone in the lab.

sections.title: In trials
body: In CIRAD's trials across Central America, published in 2011 under the name Centroamerica, it beat the best traditional variety at each of nine sites by 14% to 243%, 37% on average. It also started early, giving about 10% of its first-cycle crop in its first year, against 4% for the traditional line.

Across all the hybrids in those trials the gain over traditional varieties was 58% under shade trees and 34% in full sun, and the authors say earlier tastings found the hybrids as good as or better than the traditional lines.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Its best-known results are back-to-back second places at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence for Gonzalo Castillo's Las Promesas de San Blas: 90.50 in 2017 and 90.42 for a honey lot in 2018, when, by Daily Coffee News's count, four of the top eleven coffees were F1 hybrids (the 2018 results list the variety only as "Hybrid"). No lot listing it was among the winners of Nicaragua's 2025 or 2026 competitions, where Geisha won every category and Maracaturra and Maragogype were the most common varieties among the winners.

Elsewhere, a natural from Aquiares Estate in Turrialba was a national winner at Costa Rica's 2024 competition with 87.42 points (national winners are listed apart from the ranked Cup of Excellence lots). In Guatemala in 2026, a washed lot from Finca Vinaros in Alta Verapaz placed 7th in the One of a Kind category at 87.05, and a honey blend of Catuaí and Centroamericano from Sacatepéquez was a national winner at 85.68. A year earlier, El Nazareno in Huehuetenango won that category at 89.26 with a natural blend that lists H1 among six varieties.

sections.title: How it reaches farms
body: Seed from an F1 plant doesn't breed true, so the hybrids from this program are multiplied as clones, first in labs by somatic embryogenesis (growing whole plants from leaf tissue). Commercial production began in 2008; by 2010 nearly 2 million hybrid plants had gone to growers, mainly in Nicaragua, and by 2018 the CIRAD–ECOM partnership was producing 2 to 3 million a year there.

That makes the plants dearer: a 2018 review by CIRAD scientists puts a six-month-old cloned F1 plant at about US$0.8–1.0, against US$0.3–0.5 for a seedling, or an extra US$2,000–3,600 per hectare. CATIE's 2023 Trifinio project uses rooted cuttings instead.

family.parentsText: T5296 (a Sarchimor) × Rume Sudan
family.line: F1 cross by CIRAD, CATIE and Central America's national coffee institutes; propagated as clones

grownIn.text: No source ranks the countries. Prize lots come from Nicaragua's Nueva Segovia, Costa Rica's Turrialba and Guatemala's Alta Verapaz and Huehuetenango; a grower in Cartago (Costa Rica) has planted it, a grower near Xalapa in Veracruz (Mexico) sells it, and CATIE has supplied plants to farmers in the Trifinio region since 2023.

plant.rust: highly resistant
plant.altitude: best quality above 1,300 m (4,265 ft)

records.name: Chandragiri
records.summary: India's semi-dwarf Sarchimor, released in 2007 by its coffee research institute.
records.lede: A semi-dwarf Sarchimor (Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid) released by India's Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI) in 2007, after the cross came to India through a coffee research centre in Portugal. Counter Culture Coffee calls it fairly rust-resistant and, with Selection 9, one of the two most popular varieties in Indian cultivation.

facts.label: released by CCRI at the third (F3) generation
its number in India's 'Selection' series
a Sarchimor-type tree
to leaf rust, per Counter Culture

family.parentsText: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid (a Sarchimor)
family.line: Introduced to India through a research centre in Portugal; CCRI selected it and released it at the F3 generation. Cafe Imports dates the hybrid work to 1975–1981. A 2021 CCRI paper identifies Chandragiri as selection S.4202, a plant picked from a base population that stayed tolerant to all the rust races then present in India.

grownIn.text: India: estates in Karnataka's Chikmagalur district sell it as a single variety, and it is grown in Tamil Nadu, where it was trialled in the Pulney hills and an estate at Yercaud placed with it at India's 2013 Flavour of India competition.

plant.yield: about 1,000 kg/ha in CCRI's early trials; 887–1,303 kg/ha a year over 2017–21 at CCRI's Balehonnur farm
plant.rust: fairly resistant (Counter Culture); high field tolerance in CCRI trials, with resistance genes from both Arabica and Robusta
plant.beanSize: 70–75% of beans in the top (A) grade in CCRI's early trials

cup.text: Little is published about Chandragiri's cup as a variety; what exists is roasters' notes on single-estate lots. George Howell Coffee describes a washed lot from Kerehaklu Estate in Chikmagalur (fermented with a starter culture) with milk chocolate, black tea and plum, and Naivo Coffee calls a washed Balanoor Plantations lot floral and almond-like, with clean, bright acidity.
cup.prized: At India's 2013 Flavour of India cupping competition, a pulped, sun-dried Chandragiri from Moon Estate at Yercaud placed fourth among specialty Arabicas.

story.text: Cafe Imports dates the Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid work behind it to these years; a 2000 report on CCRI's Sarchimor trials says the seed came from Portugal in 1975 and a selfed generation was planted in 1980.
CCRI released it at the F3 generation as Selection 13, Chandragiri.
A Chandragiri from Moon Estate, Yercaud, placed fourth among specialty Arabicas at India's Flavour of India competition.
A CCRI paper identified Chandragiri as selection S.4202 and traced its rust resistance to SH genes from Arabica (SH1, 2, 4 and 5) and from Robusta (SH6 to SH9).
After touring CCRI in March 2024, Counter Culture wrote that Chandragiri and Selection 9 are the most popular of the institute's 13 releases.

CCRI and World Coffee Research reported that in India's international variety trial of 28 Arabicas, planted in 2015–16, Chandragiri was among the few Sarchimor and Catuaí types with high field tolerance to rust, doing better than Parainema and IPR 107.

sections.title: India's Selection series
body: CCRI, the research arm of the Coffee Board of India, numbers its Arabica releases. Chandragiri is Selection 13; earlier ones include S795 (Selection 3) and Selection 9, which Counter Culture names with Chandragiri as India's two most popular varieties.

Counter Culture adds that of the 13 varieties CCRI has released, only these two have kept their popularity; most of the others were dropped because they performed poorly in the field or fell to disease.

sections.title: Growing it
body: In a four-season study in Tamil Nadu's Pulney hills, published in 2016, researchers at the Regional Coffee Research Station in Thandigudi compared Chandragiri with three other Indian selections. Chandragiri had the most cropping nodes and flower buds per branch, a fruit set of 95%, and the lowest fruit drop (29%, against 32–43% for the others). The authors concluded that it and the tall Sln.5B were the more physiologically efficient choices for that region.
George Howell Coffee reports that Kerehaklu Estate in Chikmagalur, at about 3,940 ft (1,200 m), grows its Chandragiri under shade and native forest.

sections.title: Rust resistance and pedigree
body: A 2000 report on CCRI's Sarchimor work, from seed received from Portugal in 1975, describes 19 years of trials in which one progeny, S4202, stood out as vigorous, dwarf and rust-resistant, averaging about 1,000 kg per hectare with 70–75% of beans in the top (A) grade. A 2021 CCRI paper names S.4202 as Chandragiri.

That paper traces its resistance to two sets of genes: SH1, SH2, SH4 and SH5, which come from Arabica itself, and SH6 to SH9, which entered Arabica from Robusta. At CCRI's Balehonnur farm, rust incidence on Chandragiri ranged from 2.8% to 30% over 2017–21, and in two of those seasons the infections stayed as non-sporulating spots (spots that release no spores), which the authors read as high tolerance. Its yield there ranged from 887 to 1,303 kg per hectare a year.

In India's international variety trial, run by CCRI with World Coffee Research and reported in 2025, Chandragiri was one of the few Sarchimor and Catuaí types to show high field tolerance to rust; Parainema and IPR 107, two other Sarchimors, were badly affected (about 80% of plants).

records.name: Costa Rica 95
records.summary: Costa Rica's Catimor: high-yielding, now catching rust, low cup rating.
records.lede: Costa Rica's own Catimor, selected from T8667, the Caturra × Timor Hybrid line that spread through Central America, and released in 1995. It was bred for high yields in warm zones and acidic soils, but World Coffee Research now lists it as susceptible to leaf rust in Costa Rica and rates its cup potential low.

facts.label: released in Costa Rica
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
to leaf rust in Costa Rica now, WCR says
yield potential

cup.text: Its reputation is poor: Sweet Maria's calls its cup quality medium to low, with harsh, unbalanced flavors, and World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude low. In a small trial in Peru at 1,250 m (4,100 ft), published in 2018, it scored 80.89 on the SCA's 100-point scale, between the Colombia variety (82.05) and a Catimor (79.93).
cup.why: The importer Coffee Hunter puts the weaker cups of Timor Hybrid offspring down to their Robusta genes; Cenicafé says Catimors can match other Arabicas only when breeders rigorously remove poor-cupping lines, and notes that Costa Rica 95 comes from a single line.
cup.watch: Harsh, unbalanced flavors, says Sweet Maria's; Costa Rica's small producers and micromills later moved to varieties with more cup potential.

story.text: CATIE in Costa Rica receives the Catimor line T8667, which Costa Rica 95 was later selected from.
Costa Rica releases it as a short, rust-resistant variety.
Rust begins infecting it; WCR names it, with Lempira, as a notable case of resistance breaking down.
Cenicafé reports that Costa Rica 95 planted in parts of Colombia has already lost its resistance, and advises growers to plant Castillo instead.
A Peruvian study confirms it growing in the Perené valley of Junín, where it out-yields the Colombia variety and a Catimor.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR recommends it for the warmest zones and for acidic, aluminium-rich soils, and lists it as susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease. It's a compact tree with bronze leaf tips that first bears in its third year.

Cenicafé says it can yield 25–35% more than Caturra or Catuaí, but needs heavy fertilizing and may decline by its third year of production. Sweet Maria's adds that it needs a lot of inputs, often chemical fertilizer, and that early plantings in full sun, without shade trees, made it controversial. WCR suggests 5,000–6,000 plants per hectare and lists it as susceptible to nematodes (root worms) and coffee berry disease, which isn't present in Central America.

sections.title: Outside Costa Rica
body: It travelled. Cenicafé's 2012 question-and-answer bulletin on Castillo shows Costa Rica 95 with rust in Andes, Antioquia, says it has lost its resistance in some Colombian zones, and notes that neither the growers' federation nor Cenicafé produces its seed.

In Peru, a trial at 1,250 m (4,100 ft) in the Perené valley, published in 2018 and run without a formal statistical design, found it the highest-yielding of three rust-resistant cultivars, at 2.20 t of parchment per hectare.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra (a selection from T8667)
family.line: Pedigree selection from T8667. WCR's catalog credits ICAFE, Costa Rica's coffee institute, on the variety's page and CATIE on the T8667 page.

grownIn.text: Selected in Costa Rica; also planted in parts of Colombia and in Peru's Junín region.

plant.rust: low resistance/susceptible: recently confirmed susceptible in Costa Rica
plant.altitude: low to medium: about 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude, as in Central America; 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Cuscatleco
records.summary: El Salvador's Sarchimor from T5296, released by PROCAFÉ in 2007.
records.lede: A Sarchimor that PROCAFÉ, El Salvador's coffee research foundation, selected from the line T5296 and released in February 2007. World Coffee Research describes it as well-adapted to medium altitudes and resistant to leaf rust and some nematodes, though its rating for rust resistance is only intermediate; it has large beans and a good rating for cup potential. Two cuppers interviewed by Perfect Daily Grind describe a balanced, pleasant cup rather than a striking one, and the article recommends it up to 1,300 m (4,250 ft) and for high-volume markets.

facts.label: released by PROCAFÉ, in February
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
bean size
