cup.text: Francis López, a cupper at El Salvador's Cuzcachapa cooperative, told Perfect Daily Grind in 2023 that it tends toward a balanced cup with medium acidity and sweetness, a round body, a short aftertaste and an herbal note he doesn't find very pleasant. Rafael Castillo, an agronomist and cupper, calls it pleasant but not complex, with low to medium acidity and good body.
cup.prized: Processing can lift it: López says honey, natural or fermented lots can give fruitier cups of about 84–85 points.
cup.watch: In general López puts it at roughly 77–82 points on the SCA cupping scale, and Perfect Daily Grind notes that some people in the trade speak badly of its cup; very few specialty farms higher up grow it, preferring Pacamara or Pacas.

story.text: At CIFC, Portugal's coffee rust research centre, work begins on crossing the Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 with the compact Villa Sarchi: the Sarchimor cross.
CIFC sends the hybrid out for field trials; the population studied at CATIE in Costa Rica is named T5296 and passed on to national breeding programs in the region.
After further generations of selection, PROCAFÉ releases Cuscatleco in February.
A Salvadoran government renewal program buys 167,000 Cuscatleco plants as part of 1.5 million new coffee plants, 90% of them rust-resistant.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR rates its yield medium and its rust resistance intermediate, with a high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry). It isn't resistant to Pratylenchus, another group of root nematodes.

López says it can be grown from 600 to 1,200 m (1,950–3,950 ft), and the article recommends it up to 1,300 m (4,250 ft) and for high-volume coffee markets; López sees good technical support as growers' biggest challenge with it. Castillo notes that a few isolated producers have reported rust and other diseases on Catimors and Sarchimors, so their resistance has been questioned in recent years.

sections.title: Planted in El Salvador
body: A 2016 renewal project run by El Salvador's agriculture ministry and its research centre CENTA bought about 1.5 million coffee plants, 90% of them rust-resistant. Its Sarchimor group was specified as Cuscatleco, Parainema or Sarchimor, and the purchases included 167,000 Cuscatleco plants; most of the rest were the Catimor Costa Rica 95, with smaller lots of Catisic, Pacamara, Icatu and plants sold simply as Sarchimor.

Perfect Daily Grind says it is grown mainly in El Salvador and also in neighbouring Guatemala and Honduras. Rafael Castillo says its Salvadoran area has shrunk over the years as towns spread and farmland goes to other businesses.

family.parentsText: Selection of T5296 (Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10 × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2)
family.line: Pedigree selection by PROCAFÉ in El Salvador.

grownIn.text: Mostly El Salvador, with some in Guatemala and Honduras.

plant.rust: intermediate
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Dawairi
records.summary: A Yemeni name meaning rounded; most sampled trees were Yemenia types.
records.lede: Dawairi means rounded in Arabic, probably a nod to the tree's bushy shape. It was the second most-cited coffee name in a 2022 survey of 148 farms. Most Dawairi trees sampled (86%) were in the New-Yemen (Yemenia) group, but the same study found that Yemeni names overall aren't a reliable guide to genetics.

facts.label: of names farmers cited in the 2022 survey
of sampled Dawairi trees were New-Yemen (Yemenia) types
how farmers in some regions describe it; in others they call it tall

cup.text: Lots that name Dawairi usually list Tufahi with it. Two Dragonfly Coffee naturals from Sanaa governorate sold as Dawairi and Tufahi scored 94 and 93 with Coffee Review in 2021: one with green grape, a rum-barrel sweetness, cocoa nib and oak, the other with macadamia, baking chocolate, magnolia, blackberry and cedar.

story.text: Coffee Review rates two Dawairi-and-Tufahi naturals from Sanaa governorate at 94 (July) and 93 (October).
A survey of 148 farms finds Dawairi the second most-cited name (16%), with 86% of sampled trees in the New-Yemen group.

sections.title: Where the name points
body: In the 2022 survey Dawairi was absent in Ibb and rarely cited in Al Mahwit. Genetically it was more consistent than Udaini (67% New-Yemen) or Tufahi (56%), but the study found no significant link between names and genetics overall.
Its look isn't fixed either: the scarce written descriptions make Dawairi a dwarf or more compact tree, and farmers in some regions call it compact, but in others they say it's tall.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Spellings vary: Dawairi, Dawaeri and Dwairi all appear in Coffee Review's 2021 listings, usually next to Tufahi, and on Haraaz lots next to Tuffahi and Jaadi too.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name; most sampled trees were New-Yemen types

grownIn.text: Grown in Yemen; the 2022 survey found no Dawairi in Ibb.

plant.stature: dwarf or compact by the scarce descriptions; tall in some regions, farmers say

records.name: Esperanza
records.summary: Rain-tolerant F1 hybrid that Costa Rican farmers asked for
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of the rust-resistant Sarchimor T5296 and an Ethiopian accession, ET25, from CATIE's collection. It was tested alongside Centroamericano and Milenio but not chosen at first; then plants left on a farm in Costa Rica did well in heavy rain and humidity, farmers asked for it, and it became one of the country's most requested F1 hybrids.

facts.label: yield potential
WCR's rating of its quality at high altitude
climates it handles well
its first crop

story.text: Tested for years alongside Centroamericano and Milenio, into the early 2000s, but not picked for release; plants left on a farm in Costa Rica later did well in heavy rain and humidity, and local farmers asked for it.
A Costa Rican study calls it a very vigorous hybrid that does very well around Turrialba and recommends it for 800–1,500 m (2,600–4,900 ft).
CATIE starts supplying Esperanza, with Centroamericano and Milenio, to about 200 coffee-growing families in the Trifinio region.
An Aquiares Esperanza natural reaches the second round of Costa Rica's Cup of Excellence, its roaster reports.

family.parentsText: T5296 (a Sarchimor) × Ethiopian accession ET25 (CATIE collection)
family.line: F1 cross from the CIRAD–PROMECAFE–CATIE consortium; propagated as clones (CATIE uses rooted cuttings)

grownIn.text: Mostly Costa Rica, where nearly every published lot comes from Aquiares Estate in Turrialba; since 2023 CATIE has been bringing it, with Centroamericano and Milenio, to farms in the Trifinio region where Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador meet.

plant.rust: tolerant
plant.altitude: 800–1,500 m (2,600–4,900 ft) recommended in Costa Rica

cup.text: Little is published beyond roasters' notes on lots from Aquiares Estate in Turrialba. Fulcrum Coffee lists a washed lot from 1,400 m (4,600 ft) with watermelon, white wine, strawberry, green apple and cocoa; Prolog Coffee describes a natural with banana, apricot and chocolate mousse.

feel.acidity: soft and balanced when washed; bright and juicy in a natural

cup.prized: WCR rates its quality very good at high altitude, and CATIE says a visiting Korean coffee taster rated it even higher than Milenio.
cup.watch: Almost all published lots come from one estate, Aquiares, so little is known about how it tastes elsewhere.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with green young leaves and large beans, very high yields, tolerance to leaf rust and a first crop in year two. It needs a lot of fertilizer, ripens at an average time, gives a very high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and suits 3,000–4,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning. Its standout trait is how well it handles humid, rainy places.

A 2020 Costa Rican study recommends it for 800–1,500 m (2,600–4,900 ft). Like other F1s it has to be cloned: in that study 90% of its mini-cuttings rooted within 12 weeks, and CATIE propagates it from rooted cuttings.

sections.title: The hybrid that farmers picked
body: Breeders tested Esperanza for years alongside Centroamericano and Milenio, which share its Sarchimor parent T5296, and left it out of the first releases. It survived because a few plants stayed on a Costa Rican farm, where they did well in heavy rain and humidity. Growers nearby asked for it, and WCR now calls it one of the most requested F1 hybrids in Costa Rica. Today nearly every lot sold comes from Aquiares, a large estate on the slopes of Turrialba volcano, and one roaster that sells them says it was developed there.
Its Ethiopian parent, ET25, was collected in Ethiopia by a French ORSTOM/IRD expedition and kept in CATIE's gene bank.

records.name: Evaluna
records.summary: Catimor × Ethiopian F1 hybrid bred for big yields at altitude
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of Naryelis, a Catimor-type line, and an Ethiopian landrace accession, ET06, from CATIE's collection, bred by CIRAD with the coffee trader ECOM. WCR says it was selected and released in 2010 and yields very well at high elevations.

facts.label: selected and released
its best altitude at Central America's latitudes (4,265 ft+)
seed from it won't grow true

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with light bronze young leaves and large beans that may struggle to root in its first two years, so it needs careful feeding without too much nitrogen. It ripens at an average time, gives a very high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and suits 4,000–5,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning.

In the Nicaraguan trial it grew the biggest bush of all, with a canopy of 1.02 m³ against Caturra's 0.54 m³, and ranked third on the researchers' combined score for yield and stability across sites. It showed some rust lesions with little spore production, which the researchers read as weak susceptibility.

sections.title: Good to know
body: WCR's catalog credits the breeding to CIRAD and ECOM, while its history note names the CIRAD–PROMECAFE–CATIE consortium. Its codes are EC18 and H18, and its Catimor-type parent, Naryelis, is also a parent of Nayarita.

family.parentsText: Naryelis (a Catimor) × Ethiopian accession ET06 (CATIE collection)
family.line: F1 cross bred by CIRAD and ECOM; propagated as clones

grownIn.text: Trialled on farms in Nicaragua; no published source names lots or plantings elsewhere.

plant.rust: some lesions, low spore production in trials
plant.altitude: high: above 1,300 m (4,265 ft) at 5–15° latitude

story.text: Evaluna is selected and released, WCR says.
It is tested at seven Nicaraguan sites from 710 to 1,250 m (2,330–4,100 ft) against Caturra, Marsellesa and other hybrids.
The researchers rank it third on a combined score for yield and stability and call it a serious candidate for low-input smallholder farms, pending tasting work.

records.name: French Mission
records.summary: Bourbon brought to Kenya by French Spiritan missionaries in 1893.
records.lede: French Mission is the name for the Bourbon coffee that Spiritan missionaries planted in Kenya. In 1893 they sowed Bourbon seed from La Réunion at their mission at Bura in the Taita Hills, and in 1899 moved seedlings to the St Austin mission near Nairobi, which handed seed out to settlers. Kenya's K7 was selected from it.

facts.label: Bourbon from La Réunion planted at Bura, Taita Hills
seedlings moved to St Austin's mission near Nairobi
was selected from French Mission coffee
Rwanda's old variety was probably mixed with it

cup.text: Little is published on French Mission's cup on its own. The Grounds, an Australian coffee seller offering a coffee from Kenya's Chania and Oreti estates, calls it an old Bourbon that gives a balanced cup with bright acidity, medium body and fruity sweetness; that's one seller's description, not a measured profile.

story.text: French Spiritan missionaries set up a mission at Bura in Kenya's Taita Hills and plant Bourbon seed from La Réunion.
Seedlings from Bura go to the St Austin mission near Nairobi, which hands seed out to settlers.
K7 is picked from French Mission trees on a Kenyan estate and released.
Scott Labs selects SL34 from a tree labelled "French Mission" on Loresho Estate in Kabete; DNA tests later tie SL34 to Typica instead.

sections.title: A name to read carefully
body: Because the seed came straight from La Réunion, French Mission is widely treated as another name for Bourbon. But SL34, long said to come from a French Mission tree on Loresho Estate in Kabete, tests as Typica-related, so World Coffee Research says that account may be wrong. Sweet Maria's goes further and calls "French Mission" mostly a marketing term.

Even the arrival story has versions. Sweet Maria's credits a Scottish mission with bringing coffee to Kibwezi in 1893, and says French Mission coffee came into Kenya from Tanzania a few years later, in 1897, while World Coffee Research has the Spiritans planting Bourbon from La Réunion at Bura, in the Taita Hills, in 1893.

sections.title: On Kenyan estates
body: You'll still see the name on some Kenyan estate coffees. Chania and Oreti estates in Thika, founded in 1904 and farmed at 1,600–1,800 m (5,250–5,900 ft), list French Mission among their varieties, alongside SL28, SL34, SL14, Ruiru 11 and Batian.

family.parentsText: Bourbon from La Réunion
family.line: Mission-grown Bourbon, spread to Kenyan settlers from 1899.

grownIn.text: Kenya, where missions handed its seed to settlers; French Mission plants were also taken from Kenya to Rwanda, where they were very likely mixed with the old Mibirizi coffee.

records.name: Gesha 1931
records.summary: Gesha Village's Panama-like selection from Ethiopia's wild Gori Gesha forest
records.lede: Gesha 1931 is a name Gesha Village, a farm in southwestern Ethiopia's Bench Maji zone, uses for one of its own Gesha selections. The farm picked it out of the varied wild coffee from around the Gori Gesha forest, keeping the plants whose shape, beans and cup came closest to Panama's Geisha. Roasters say the number is the year a British expedition first collected Gesha there.

facts.label: the year roasters say Gesha was first collected in the area
the altitude band Gesha Village chose for its land (6,250–6,900 ft)
Coffee Review score for a natural Gesha 1931 from the Oma plot (2024)
when the farm's founders leased its 471 ha

cup.text: Roasters tend to describe it as floral and tea-like. La Cabra found jasmine, stone fruit and a black-tea finish in a natural from the Oma plot; Sey called a washed Oma lot intensely floral and tea-like in clarity; and a natural that Coffee Review scored 96 in 2024 (No. 29 on its Top 30 of the year) showed wisteria, pink peppercorn, dried mango, bergamot and cocoa nib. April Coffee Roasters, which buys from the farm, sums up the selection as honeysuckle, ripe yellow fruit and lime.
cup.prized: Its likeness to Panama's Geisha, which is what the farm selected for.
cup.watch: The "1931" is a story, not a test result: World Coffee Research dates Gesha's collection only to the 1930s, and no published genetic test compares Gesha 1931 with the Panama line.

family.parentsText: A selection from the wild Gesha coffee of Ethiopia's Gori Gesha forest
family.line: Gesha Village kept the plants whose shape, bean size and shape, and cup came closest to Panama's Geisha

grownIn.text: Grown at Gesha Village, near the town of Gesha in Bench Maji zone; some bags give the zone as West Omo.

plant.beanSize: picked to match Panama Gesha's seed shape and size
plant.altitude: high: about 2,000–2,100 m (6,560–6,890 ft) on the Oma plot; Sey lists 2,100 m, La Cabra up to 2,040 m

story.text: Roasters date the first collection of Gesha in this area, by British researchers, to 1931, and the selection is named for that year.
Adam Overton and Rachel Samuel lease 471 ha in Bench Maji; seed they gathered with Willem Boot from the Gori Gesha forest's wild trees is planted there.
Coffee Review scores two natural Gesha 1931 lots from the farm 94 and 95.
A natural Gesha 1931 from the Oma plot scores 96 and is No. 29 on Coffee Review's Top 30 of the year.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Gesha Village sells by plot and by selection. Roasters list three selections from the farm: Gesha 1931, Gori Gesha, and Illubabor Forest 1974, a disease-resistant selection named for the 1974 expedition that collected it. Plot names such as Oma, Surma and Gaylee are among the farm's eight blocks, named after nearby villages and sites.

sections.title: Gesha 1931 or Gori Gesha?
body: Both come from the same wild population. Sey says research and genetic testing point to the Gori Gesha forest as where Panama's Gesha was first collected, and that two groups were identified there: Gori Gesha and Gesha 1931, the plants most like Panama's Geisha. Roasters disagree on how Gesha 1931 relates to the Panama line: Intelligentsia calls it the original Gesha and the Panama line's forebear, while Rosso calls it a descendant of the Panamanian strain. No published genetic test comparing them was found.

records.name: Gori Gesha
records.summary: Seed from the Ethiopian forest that likely gave Gesha its name.
records.lede: Coffee selected from wild trees in the Gori Gesha forest of southwestern Ethiopia, the forest Gesha's name is thought to come from. Gesha Village, an estate about 20 km away in the Bench Maji zone, gathered seed there with Gesha specialist Willem Boot and planted it on the farm it leased in 2011. Unlike the farm's Gesha 1931, it wasn't picked to look like Panama's Gesha: it keeps the forest's mix of types.

sections.title: Gori Gesha and Panama Gesha
body: The famous Panama Gesha comes from one accession: seed collected in Ethiopia's forests in the 1930s, grown at the Lyamungu research station in Tanzania, and logged at CATIE in Costa Rica as T2722 in 1953. World Coffee Research found that line distinct and uniform, and notes that several genetically different coffees have been called Gesha.
Gesha Village's Gori Gesha is a separate selection, taken straight from wild trees in the forest.

sections.title: At Gesha Village
body: Gesha Village grows three main selections. April Coffee Roasters says about 40% of its trees are Gori Gesha; Gesha 1931 was picked from the same forest population for its likeness to Panama's Gesha; and Illubabor Forest 1974, a disease-resistant coffee from an Ethiopian research center, covers about a third of the estate. The farm is split into eight blocks, and coffee is planted at about 2,000 trees a hectare among more than 30,000 native shade trees.

family.parentsText: Selected from wild trees in the Gori Gesha forest; an Ethiopian landrace, separate from the Panama line (T2722)
family.line: Seed harvested from forest trees and planted at Gesha Village; April says it replicates the forest's genetic diversity

grownIn.text: Ethiopia: Gesha Village, Bench Maji zone, in the southwest

cup.text: April Coffee Roasters describes rose, strawberry, ripe red fruit and blueberry. Coffee Review scored a 2023 natural 94, with pomegranate, lilac, pink grapefruit zest, hazelnut and a woody note.
cup.prized: Complex flavour with intense floral notes, says The Roasters Pack, from seed gathered in the forest Gesha is thought to come from.
cup.watch: It's a mix of the forest's types, not the uniform Panama line, so don't expect a Panama Gesha; for the selection made to resemble Panama's, look for Gesha 1931.

story.text: Gesha seed is collected from Ethiopia's coffee forests, the start of the line that later made Panama famous.
Adam Overton and Rachel Samuel lease 471 ha in Bench Maji; with Willem Boot they trek into the Gori Gesha forest and harvest seed from its wild trees.
Gesha Village holds its first auction, with 21 lots.
A natural Gori Gesha from the farm scores 94 at Coffee Review.

records.name: H3
records.summary: Caturra × Ethiopian F1 hybrid dropped for rust, kept for flavor
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of Caturra and an Ethiopian landrace accession, E531, from CATIE's collection, from the first wave of Central American F1s. Breeders dropped it after 2000 because it catches leaf rust, but WCR says some farmers kept growing it for its cup quality.

facts.label: for very good quality, says WCR (4,265 ft+)
why it was dropped from release

family.parentsText: Caturra × Ethiopian accession E531 (CATIE collection)
family.line: F1 cross from the CIRAD–PROMECAFE–CATIE consortium; propagated as clones

plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: very good quality above 1,300 m (4,265 ft)

cup.text: Little is published about its cup beyond a few Costa Rican lots. Ozone Coffee lists an anaerobic honey from Sumava de Lourdes in Naranjo with orange blossom, lime zest and honey; a Stillers Coffee listing for a yellow honey from Volcán Azul names peach, caramelized sugar, vanilla and milk chocolate.
cup.prized: Its cup: WCR says breeders rated its quality exceptional, which is why some farmers in the early trials kept it even after it was dropped.
cup.watch: Leaf rust. WCR rates it susceptible to rust, nematodes and coffee berry disease, so it needs careful disease control.

story.text: The CIRAD–PROMECAFE–CATIE breeding program begins; H3 is one of its first wave of F1 hybrids.
Breeders drop it from the final round of selection because it catches leaf rust, but some farmers in the early trials keep growing it for its cup.
Francisco Mena harvests an anaerobic honey H3 at Sumava de Lourdes in Naranjo, Costa Rica, which Ozone Coffee sells in 2023.

grownIn.text: Published lots come from Costa Rica's West Valley: Naranjo at 1,670–1,780 m (5,480–5,840 ft) and Volcán Azul at 1,600 m (5,250 ft). Ozone calls it rare.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a plant between compact and tall, with green young leaves and large beans, that yields well and bears its first crop in year three. It needs a lot of fertilizer, ripens at an average time, gives a very high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and suits 3,000–4,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning.
WCR rates it susceptible to leaf rust, nematodes and coffee berry disease. Breeders left it out of the final round of selection after 2000 because it showed some susceptibility to rust.

sections.title: Confusions and look-alikes
body: H3 and Casiopea are close cousins: both are Caturra crossed with an Ethiopian accession from CATIE's collection (E531 for H3, ET41 for Casiopea), and neither resists rust. Don't confuse it with H1, another name for Centroamericano, which has a rust-resistant Sarchimor parent.

records.name: IAPAR 59
records.summary: A Sarchimor from Paraná's IAPAR, resistant to rust and some nematodes.
records.lede: A compact Sarchimor selected by IAPAR, the agronomy institute of Paraná state in Brazil, from a Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi cross, and recommended for planting from 1992. It was made for densely planted farms, ripens fairly early, and resists leaf rust and the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne exigua. World Coffee Research rates its cup potential low, though IAPAR itself compares its cup to Red Bourbon's.

facts.label: recommended for planting by IAPAR
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
to the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne exigua
IAPAR varieties drawn from its Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid line: IAPAR 59 and IPR 98, 99, 104, 107 and 108

cup.text: IAPAR's leaflet says that, grown well, it cups like Red Bourbon and the Catuaí group: sweet, with pleasant acidity and good body. In a trial at Fundação Procafé's farm in Varginha, Minas Gerais, at about 1,000 m (3,300 ft), naturals from the 2009 and 2010 harvests scored 82.0 and were described as balanced with medium acidity, against 81.5 for Yellow Bourbon and 78.5 for Red Catuaí IAC 144.
cup.watch: Expectations: World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude as low, well below its breeders' description.

story.text: At CIFC, Portugal's coffee rust research centre, work begins on crossing Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10 with the Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2; the hybrid is called H361 there.
Brazil's IAC registers the hybrid as IAC 1669, the same line that later gives Obatã and Tupi.
IAPAR brings in the third generation as IAPAR 75163; one of its progenies, 75163-22, becomes IAPAR 59.
IAPAR recommends it for planting.
It is formally registered as a cultivar.
INIFAP names IAPAR 59 among the varieties used to replant 150,000 ha of Mexican coffee since 2015.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR rates its yield medium and its rust resistance intermediate, with a high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry). It's a compact tree with light bronze leaf tips that first bears in its third year, and it isn't resistant to Pratylenchus, another group of root nematodes.

IAPAR built it for dense planting: its canopy is about three-quarters the volume of Catuaí's, and the leaflet recommends 0.5 m (1.6 ft) between plants in the row. At 8,000 trees per hectare it averaged 4,736 kg per hectare a year over six years in IAPAR's trials, against 3,860 kg for Catuaí and 3,333 kg for Mundo Novo at their usual, wider spacings. It ripens earlier and more evenly than Catuaí (in Londrina, picking can start at the end of June), which lets growers harvest before frost reaches unripe fruit.
It suits cooler, rainier areas with clay or organic-rich soils. Below 500 m (1,650 ft), IAPAR says, it is only viable with irrigation and careful soil-water management.

sections.title: Rust and other diseases
body: IAPAR's leaflet claims complete, lasting rust resistance: 94% of its plants fall in physiological group A, which resists 29 of the 30 rust races then known, and it kept that resistance as 15 newer races were identified. WCR, on its own scale, rates its rust resistance intermediate, and a trial in Viçosa, Minas Gerais, reported in 2011, placed it among the most rust-resistant of 32 cultivars.

The leaflet lists it as susceptible to Cercospora (brown eye spot), to bacterial halo blight (worse with too much nitrogen) and to the leaf miner, a moth larva, though it tolerates the leaf miner better. A 2006 IAPAR study in Londrina, though, found enough halo-blight resistance in it to reduce damage, and noted its beans were among the largest tested, bigger than Catuaí's.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid 832/2 × Villa Sarchi
family.line: Bred by IAPAR in Paraná, Brazil; IAPAR's Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid line also gave several IPR varieties, including IPR 107.

grownIn.text: Paraná, Brazil, where IAPAR recommends it around Londrina, Cornélio Procópio, Bandeirantes, Apucarana, Ivaiporã and Campo Mourão, among other areas; INIFAP lists it among Mexico's replanting varieties.

plant.rust: intermediate
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Icatu
records.summary: Brazil's tall Arabica with Robusta genes, bred at IAC from 1950.
records.lede: A tall, productive Brazilian variety from the Instituto Agronômico de Campinas (IAC) that carries genes from Robusta. Breeders crossed a Robusta with doubled chromosomes (which made a fertile cross with Arabica possible) with Bourbon, then crossed the offspring back to Mundo Novo over several generations; Daily Coffee News calls it the world's first artificial, commercial Arabica × Robusta hybrid. So its Robusta genes came from a deliberate cross, not from the Timor Hybrid, the natural Arabica × Robusta hybrid widely used in Arabica breeding.

facts.label: when IAC began the Robusta × Bourbon cross

and vigorous, with lots of side branches

family.parentsText: Robusta (chromosome-doubled) × Bourbon, then backcrossed to Mundo Novo
family.line: IAC used a Robusta with doubled chromosomes, which allowed a fertile cross with Bourbon, then backcrossed to Mundo Novo for generations, selecting for disease resistance and Arabica traits.

grownIn.text: Widely grown in Brazil (Minas Gerais, São Paulo, Paraná, Espírito Santo); much smaller plantings elsewhere, such as Finca Argentina in El Salvador's Apaneca-Ilamatepec range, at about 1,300 m (4,250 ft).

plant.yield: high; Sweet Maria's puts it at 30–50% more cherry than Mundo Novo
plant.rust: moderate resistance or tolerance, which can weaken as new rust races appear

cup.text: Ozone Coffee describes Icatu as often sweet and rounded, with chocolate, caramel, nuts and dried fruit, moderate rather than bright acidity and a substantial body, and says it works well as espresso.
cup.why: Ozone finds that naturals lean further into dried fruit and sweetness, while washed lots show more clarity and structure.
cup.prized: Ozone says a well-grown, well-processed Icatu can be properly satisfying, with a profile that works very well as espresso and sits comfortably with milk. In competition, a Yellow Icatu natural from the Cerrado Mineiro placed 34th (87.41 points) at Brazil's 2018 Cup of Excellence for naturals. In a trial of Bourbon types at four Minas Gerais sites, published by Embrapa Café in 2021, Yellow Icatu IAC 3282, grown as a comparison, scored 83–87 points everywhere, above the 80-point line for specialty coffee.
cup.watch: Results vary by line and place: in a 2002 laboratory study of beans from EPAMIG's farm at Lavras, Red Icatu IAC 2942 tested in the 'hard' range of Brazil's traditional cup grades (bebida dura, below the 'soft' grades), while Yellow Icatu IAC 3282 tested 'soft'. The grades came from an enzyme test, not tasting.

story.text: IAC began crossing a chromosome-doubled Robusta with Bourbon.
IAC released Red and Yellow Icatu, by Ozone's dates (Cafe Imports and Sweet Maria's say 1993).
Icatu Precoce, selected to ripen earlier, followed.
A Yellow Icatu natural from the Cerrado Mineiro placed 34th, with 87.41 points, at Brazil's Cup of Excellence for naturals.

sections.title: Its children
body: Icatu is a parent of later Brazilian varieties: Catucaí came from a natural cross of Icatu and Catuaí, and EPAMIG's MGS Aranãs crosses a Catimor with Icatu IAC H3851-2. Ozone describes the Catucaí group as now widely planted.

sections.title: Growing it
body: In a 1995–2004 Embrapa trial in Acre state, the Icatu lines showed no rust while Mundo Novo did. A 2008 paper on the trial notes, citing earlier Brazilian work, that Icatu doesn't handle dry spells the way Robusta does, even with a good root system.

Its height has a cost: Ozone notes that tall Icatu trees are harder to manage by hand and don't suit the dense planting used for dwarf varieties, so rows are commonly 3.5–4 m (11.5–13 ft) apart with 0.8–1 m (2.6–3.3 ft) between plants. Ozone also warns that its rust resistance can weaken as new races of the fungus appear.

Ripening depends on the line: Fundação Procafé puts Icatu 3282 (Icatu Precoce, selected for early bearing) among its early-ripening varieties. In a trial in Espírito Santo's mountains, at Venda Nova do Imigrante (750 m, 2,460 ft), planted in 1995, Yellow Icatu LC 328-2 averaged 50.2 bags of green coffee per hectare over two harvests (1997–99), the most of the IAC and IAPAR entries, though its cherries ripened early and unevenly.

records.name: IHCAFE 90
records.summary: A Honduran Catimor for low farms; WCR rates its cup very low.
records.lede: A Caturra × Timor Hybrid variety from IHCAFE, Honduras's coffee institute, made in the 1990s for high yields at low altitudes with heavy fertilizing. World Coffee Research rates its cup potential very low and says it's now susceptible to rust in Honduras, yet IHCAFE 90 lots have placed in the country's Cup of Excellence, in 2017 and again in 2026.

first harvest

cup.text: On paper it's one of the weakest: World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude very low, and Perfect Daily Grind says it gives low cup quality at high altitudes. Competitions disagree, at least for single lots: IHCAFE 90 was among the varieties of the 2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winners, and a washed lot scored 87.96 in 2026.
cup.why: Coffee Review groups IHCAFE 90 and Lempira as rust-resistant hybrids carrying Robusta genes, and the importer Coffee Hunter blames those genes for the weaker cups of Timor Hybrid offspring.
cup.prized: A washed IHCAFE 90 from El Cutal, in Lempira department, placed sixth in the Traditional category of Honduras's 2026 Cup of Excellence at 87.96 points and sold for $23.60 a pound.
cup.watch: Very low cup potential at high altitude, by WCR's rating.

story.text: IHCAFE creates two new varieties, IHCAFE 90 and Lempira, Perfect Daily Grind says.
A new rust race breaks Lempira's resistance; in IHCAFE's tests IHCAFE 90 shows 20% susceptibility to it.
IHCAFE 90 is among the varieties of the winning lots at Honduras's Cup of Excellence.
A washed IHCAFE 90 from El Cutal, in Lempira department, places sixth in the Traditional category of Honduras's Cup of Excellence.

sections.title: Its reputation
body: WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude very low. Competitions cut the other way: IHCAFE 90 was among the varieties of the 2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winners, and in 2026 a washed IHCAFE 90 from El Cutal, in Lempira, placed sixth in the Traditional category at 87.96 points and sold for $23.60 a pound.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR says it needs very high fertilization, suits the lowest altitudes and is planted at 4,000–5,000 plants per hectare. It's highly susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease, and is now confirmed susceptible to leaf rust in Honduras. Coffeeness lists it in Copán, Comayagua, Agalta and El Paraíso.
It's a compact tree with dark bronze leaf tips, a low ratio of green coffee to cherry, and susceptibility to nematodes (root worms) and coffee berry disease, by WCR's catalog.

sections.title: Rust: better than Lempira, not immune
body: When a new rust race got through Lempira, IHCAFE 90 held up better. IHCAFE researcher Yonis Morales Reyes found it, like Brazil's Obatá, about 20% susceptible to the new race, and IHCAFE staff told La Prensa in 2017 that it kept 80% resistance to the new strain, while Lempira proved not immune and Parainema kept 100%. WCR now lists it as confirmed susceptible in Honduras.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra
family.line: Bred by IHCAFE in Honduras; WCR calls it highly similar to the line T5175.

grownIn.text: Honduras: Copán, Comayagua, Agalta, El Paraíso and Lempira.

plant.rust: low resistance/susceptible
plant.altitude: the lowest altitudes: about 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude, as in Central America; 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: IPR 107
records.summary: Paraná's dwarf, rust-resistant Sarchimor bred for dense, machine-picked farms.
records.lede: A dwarf Brazilian variety bred in Paraná by IAPAR (now IDR-Paraná) from IAPAR 59 and Mundo Novo, and released in 2010. It was made to pair strong leaf-rust resistance with a small tree that suits tightly packed rows and harvesting machines. In World Coffee Research's trial across 23 sites in 15 countries, it was one of three varieties singled out for fairly strong, stable rust resistance.

about the size of Catuaí, for dense planting

family.parentsText: IAPAR 59 × Mundo Novo IAC 376-4
family.line: Crossed at IAPAR in Paraná and selected over generations (F3 progenies planted in 1998, F5 in 2006) for complete rust resistance.

grownIn.text: Bred for and recommended in Paraná, Brazil; also tested at 23 sites in 15 countries in WCR's international trial.

plant.rust: highly resistant
plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator; above 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude; above 700 m (2,300 ft) beyond 15°

story.text: IAPAR began the crossing program that led to IPR 107.
The selected third-generation (F3) progenies were planted out for testing.
Released to Brazilian farmers.
A WCR study of 29 varieties at 23 sites named it among the top performers for stable rust resistance.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Its breeders recommend it for semi-dense to super-dense plantings in Paraná, with plants 0.5–0.7 m apart in rows 2.5–3 m apart. Over four harvests in Paraná it out-yielded both IAPAR 59 and Catuaí Vermelho IAC 81.

World Coffee Research lists it as needing a lot of fertilizer and as susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms). Its mother parent, IAPAR 59, is itself a Sarchimor: Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10 × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2.

A 2016 Revista Cultivar report on IAPAR's varieties says it was bred to join a short tree and complete, lasting rust resistance with Mundo Novo's hardiness, ripens semi-early, and averaged 53 bags per hectare over its first four harvests in rain-fed fields in Paraná; it recommends it for clay and medium-textured soils where the mean annual temperature is 19–22 °C (66–72 °F). The same report dates its entry in Brazil's national cultivar register to 2001, well before the 2010 release its breeders and WCR give.

In an irrigated trial of 22 cultivars at Monte Carmelo, in the Cerrado Mineiro, written up as a 2023 undergraduate thesis at the Federal University of Uberlândia, it averaged 42.77 sixty-kilo bags per hectare over the 2019–2022 harvests, against 34.29 for Red Catuaí IAC 144. Both swung hard from year to year: IPR 107 from 90.22 bags in 2021 to 12.92 in 2022, Catuaí from 64.58 to 3.62.

cup.text: Its breeders rated its cup equal to or better than Mundo Novo's, and World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude as very good. In an irrigated trial of 22 cultivars at 1,050 m (3,450 ft) in Monte Carmelo, Cerrado Mineiro, written up as a 2023 undergraduate thesis at the Federal University of Uberlândia, Q-graders scored IPR 107 at 84.45 points on average over the 2019–2022 harvests, against 82.73 for Red Catuaí IAC 144. No roaster tasting notes for it are given here.

records.name: Ja'adi
records.summary: A Haraaz name for curly-leaved, tightly clustered Yemeni trees.
records.lede: Ja'adi comes from the Arabic ja'd, curly or rough; farmers link it to wavy leaf edges or to cherries packed in tight clusters. In a 2022 survey it was specific to Sanaa governorate, especially Haraaz, and most sampled trees (83%) were in the New-Yemen (Yemenia) group. Like other Yemeni names, it's a local label rather than a defined variety.

facts.label: of sampled Ja'adi trees (15 of 18) were New-Yemen types
of names cited in Haraaz, the most there
(5,600–8,550 ft) where Ozone Coffee says Haraaz coffee grows
Coffee Review score for a lot of only Ja'adi from Manakhah (2022)

cup.text: Ozone Coffee, which sells a single-farm Ja'adi from East Haraaz, describes dried fruit like dates, figs and raisins, warm spices such as cardamom and clove, and a dark-chocolate and molasses base. Coffee Review's blind tasters found a similar picture in a 95-point natural made only from Ja'adi in Manakhah (2022): black currant, clove, dark chocolate, tangerine zest and cedar. Because the name covers mixed genetics, lots can differ.
cup.why: Ozone credits Haraaz's big swing between hot days and cold nights, which slows the cherry's development and, it says, builds much of the bean's density and sugar.
cup.prized: Spice and dried fruit with clarity. Ozone says that where cherry selection and drying are tight, red fruit such as raspberry and redcurrant comes through on top.
cup.watch: Ozone warns that dark roasting tends to burn off its spice first, and that as espresso it can turn boozy if you push the ratio; it says filter shows it best.

story.text: Coffee Review rates a Haraaz natural listing Tuffahi, Dawairi and Jaadi at 94; a similar Haraaz lot scores 97 in 2022.
A survey of 148 Yemeni farms finds Ja'adi only in Sanaa governorate, where it is the top name in Haraaz (32%); 15 of 18 sampled trees are New-Yemen types.
A natural made only from Ja'adi trees in Manakhah, roasted by Taiwan's Kakalove Café, scores 95 with Coffee Review.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Ozone Coffee describes Haraaz farms on hand-built stone terraces with under 400 mm of rain a year, fed with manure and ground stone rather than chemical fertiliser. Almost all Yemeni coffee, Ja'adi included, is natural-processed: whole cherries dried in the husk, on rooftops and, more and more, on raised beds.
The beans tend to be small, hard and often irregular, and there is no working seed sector, so verified Ja'adi seedlings are hard to get.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: Ozone describes leaves with a wavy, crimped edge, unlike the flat, elongated leaves linked with Udaini, and small cherries pressed in dense clusters against the branch. In the 2022 survey some farmers said the name refers to curly leaves, others to rough cherry clusters that are hard to pick.

Two of the 18 sampled Ja'adi trees were Typica/Bourbon types and one an SL34 type, so the name is a good hint, not proof. The study didn't test whether the curly leaves or tight clusters go with the genetics.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name; most sampled trees were New-Yemen types, with a few Typica/Bourbon and SL34

grownIn.text: Sanaa governorate, concentrated in Haraaz.

records.name: Jackson
records.summary: An Indian rust-tolerant selection that became common in Rwanda and Burundi.
records.lede: Jackson traces to trees a Mr. Jackson found resisting leaf rust on his farm in Mysore, India, in the early 1900s. In the 1920s seedlings went to research stations in Kenya and Tanzania, and today it's common in Rwanda and Burundi. Its rust tolerance has since been lost, and genetic tests place it in the Bourbon group.

facts.label: from very vigorous, tall trees
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
where it does best near the equator (3,950 ft)
the genetic group tests place it in

cup.text: Sample Coffee's Burundi lots featuring Jackson have been described with strawberry and orange, or with rich chocolate, green grape and soft florals. Those are notes on single lots, not a variety-wide profile.
cup.why: Little is published on Jackson's own cup. It's Bourbon-related, and Perfect Daily Grind credits Rwanda's and Burundi's high altitudes and volcanic, nitrogen-rich soils with bringing out Bourbon's sweet, full-bodied side.
cup.prized: Mostly its harvest: WCR calls it very vigorous and highly productive. Its cup potential is rated good, a step below BM139's very good.
cup.watch: The rust tolerance its original trees were picked for is gone; WCR and Sweet Maria's now class it as susceptible to leaf rust.

plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator

story.text: Baba Budan brings coffee seeds from Yemen to India; Jackson is most likely a late descendant of them.
Mr. Jackson spots rust-tolerant trees on his farm in Mysore, India.
Seedlings go to research stations in Kenya and Tanzania.
It reaches Rwanda, possibly through the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo (set up in the 1930s) or with Kenyan settler farmers in the 1940s.

sections.title: The family
body: Jackson, Kent, Coorg and Mysore all come from the same part of India and are likely late descendants of the seeds Baba Budan brought from Yemen to India in 1670. The Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) is listed as the breeder of today's Jackson 2/1257.

sections.title: Growing it
body: A tall, very vigorous tree with bronze young leaves and large beans, planted at about 1,000–2,000 trees per hectare on a single stem. It bears its first crop in year 3 and does best above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator, 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude and 700 m (2,300 ft) farther out.
It was once valued for rust tolerance, but that tolerance has been lost, and it's now susceptible to leaf rust.

sections.title: Jackson, BM139 and the other Rwandan Bourbons
body: Sweet Maria's files Jackson as a Bourbon variant of Rwanda and Burundi, and the region's other old varieties came by different routes: Jackson from India via Kenya and Tanzania, BM139 from a Bourbon population that probably passed through Puerto Rico and then the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo, and Mibirizi, a Typica-related coffee a Belgian historian says Germany's colonial administration brought from Guatemala in the 1910s.
WCR describes both Jackson and BM139 as highly productive, but rates BM139's cup potential higher: very good, against Jackson's good.

family.parentsText: Farmer selection from rust-tolerant trees in Mysore, India (Bourbon-related)

grownIn.text: Common in Rwanda and Burundi.

records.name: Java
records.summary: An Ethiopian landrace once mistaken for Typica, later brought to Central America.
records.lede: Named for the Indonesian island, but World Coffee Research says DNA fingerprinting indicates it's a selection from an Ethiopian landrace population called Abyssinia, not the Typica it was once taken for. The Dutch took it from Ethiopia to Java in the early 1800s; it was later selected in Cameroon for tolerance of coffee berry disease and brought to Central America in 1991.

facts.label: CIRAD breeder Benoit Bertrand brought it to Costa Rica
Panama recognized it officially, first in Central America
of coffee berry disease, but susceptible to leaf rust
fertilizer needs, a fit for smallholders

story.text: The Dutch take it from Ethiopia to the island of Java.
It reaches Cameroon through the seed company Vilmorin, where breeder Pierre Bouharmont notes partial tolerance of coffee berry disease.
Released in Cameroon after about 20 years of selection.
CIRAD brings it to Costa Rica for smallholders; seed goes to other Central American countries but isn't released there.
Panama becomes the first Central American country to recognize it officially.

sections.title: Growing it
body: A tall tree with bronze new leaves and large beans, first cropping in its third year. World Coffee Research rates its quality potential very good at high altitude, above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, and presents it as a hardier alternative to Gesha for small farmers.

sections.title: Java and AB3
body: World Coffee Research lists another Ethiopian selection grown on Java separately: AB3, picked in Ethiopia by P. J. S. Cramer and brought to Indonesia in 1928, released in 1995 and grown on a small scale on Java's state plantations.

sections.title: Not the same as coffee from Java
body: Java the variety is named for the island it passed through, but genetic fingerprinting places it in an Ethiopian landrace population called Abyssinia. Sweet Maria's notes it's distinct from the Typica types grown on Java, such as Bergendal and BLP, so coffee from the island of Java is not necessarily this variety.

Sweet Maria's first found it on the Mierisch family's farms in Nicaragua, which got it from a defunct nursery; in Nicaragua's Dipilto it grows mixed in among Caturra on Finca Buenos Aires at about 1,500 m (4,920 ft).

family.parentsText: A selection from the Ethiopian landrace population Abyssinia, by DNA fingerprinting; once thought to be a Typica
family.line: Taken from Ethiopia to Java, later selected in Cameroon

grownIn.text: Central America: CIRAD brought it to Costa Rica in 1991, Panama recognized it officially in 2016, and it grows on farms in Nicaragua. Also Cameroon, where it was selected and released in 1980–90, and a few farms elsewhere, such as Bolivia. It was taken to the island of Java in the early 1800s, but no source on this page says it's grown there now.

plant.rust: susceptible, though Sweet Maria's says it's vigorous enough to recover; tolerant of coffee berry disease
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

cup.text: Tends toward tea-like, sometimes floral cups with soft sweetness. Sweet Maria's says it shares some of Gesha's tea-like and floral character; its Nicaraguan lot showed raw sugar, black tea, apricot and candied lemon, and Sey's Bolivian lot grown at 1,710 m (5,610 ft) had passion-fruit acidity, a matcha-like herbal, floral side and chocolate sweetness.
cup.why: Altitude and care: World Coffee Research rates its quality very good when grown high, and Sweet Maria's says altitude, plant care and processing decide how good it gets.
cup.prized: Gesha-like tea and floral notes from a hardier plant that needs less fertilizer; Sucafina says it can rival Gesha while being easier to grow.
cup.watch: Quality swings with where and how it's grown, so Central American lots vary. And "Java" on a bag may mean coffee from the island, not this variety.

records.name: K7
records.summary: A 1930s Kenyan selection that tolerates coffee berry disease.
records.lede: K7 is a Kenyan selection from French Mission coffee. World Coffee Research credits it to R.H. Walker and says it was released in 1936 after five generations of selection by Scott Agricultural Laboratories. It tolerates coffee berry disease (CBD), a fungal disease of the cherries, and is found mainly in Kenya and Tanzania, where breeders have used it widely.

facts.label: released in Kenya
WCR's rating for coffee berry disease
(3,300–5,250 ft) where it does best near the equator
beans on tall trees with medium yield

cup.text: 1Zpresso's Kenya guide describes K7's cup as floral, with citrus and berry flavors, delicate sweetness, bright acidity and a full mouthfeel. Coffee Review gave a washed K7 from Kona, Hawaii, 95 points in 2023, tasting toffee, hazelnut, magnolia and green grape with bright, juicy-sweet acidity.
cup.why: Little is published on why it tastes as it does. Like SL28 and SL34 it was selected in the 1930s for yield, bean size and cup quality, but 1Zpresso says it suits mid and lower altitudes, and Paradise Roasters finds it does best lower down.
cup.prized: A sound, sweet cup on a tree that partly resists coffee berry disease. Grown with care it can go far: that 95-point Kona lot was entirely K7.
cup.watch: It isn't a high-altitude specialist: Paradise Roasters says K7 seems better suited to lower elevations, where it's very productive, so its harvest on Noelani Farm, high for Kona at about 2,500 ft (760 m), is very limited.

plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: K7 is selected in Kenya; a 1950s Kenyan agricultural officer wrote that it came from one of two trees picked that year from French Mission trees on a Kenyan estate. WCR dates its release to 1936.
A severe coffee berry disease outbreak in Kenya cuts yields by up to 50%; Ruiru 11 is bred in response.
Kenya releases Ruiru 11, a hybrid whose complex male parent includes K7.
Batian is released; K7 is one of the varieties built into it.
Noelani Farm in Holualoa, Kona, Hawaii, plants an acre of K7.
Coffee Review scores Paradise Roasters' washed Kona K7 from Noelani Farm 95 points.

sections.title: Rust and berry disease
body: World Coffee Research rates it susceptible to leaf rust, but a 2014 review of Kenyan varieties says K7 resists some rust races and partly resists CBD, and 1Zpresso calls its rust resistance moderate. 1Zpresso suits it to mid and lower altitudes.
You can spot it by its spreading young side branches, while older main branches tend to droop.

sections.title: A parent of Kenya's resistant varieties
body: K7, SL28 and SL34 were Kenya's first released varieties, all from the 1930s. K7's partial resistance made it useful to breeders: it's in the ancestry of Ruiru 11 (1985) and part of Batian (2010), Kenya's disease-resistant varieties, and WCR says it has been widely used in breeding in both Kenya and Tanzania.

sections.title: Beyond East Africa
body: K7 is grown mainly in Kenya and Tanzania, but Noelani Farm in Holualoa, Kona, on Hawaii's Big Island, planted an acre in 2020. Its washed K7 scored 95 with Coffee Review in 2023, and a yeast-fermented anaerobic lot placed 15th in the 2021 Isla PCA auction, says its roaster.

family.parentsText: Selection from French Mission (Bourbon-like)
family.line: Credited to R.H. Walker; refined over five generations at Scott Labs. By DNA it sits in the Bourbon group.

grownIn.text: Mainly Kenya and Tanzania; a small planting in Kona, Hawaii.

records.name: Kent
records.summary: India's early rust-tolerant selection, parent of S795 and KP423.
records.lede: Kent is an old Indian Arabica that World Coffee Research traces to a single tree Mr. L.P. Kent selected on his Doddengooda Estate in Mysore in 1911. It's known as the first coffee selected for tolerance to leaf rust, a tolerance that has since broken down. Its descendants, such as S795 in India and Indonesia and KP423 in Tanzania and Uganda, are now more common than Kent itself.

facts.label: selection date per WCR; India's Coffee Board says the 1920s
taken to Tanzania and other parts of East Africa
Indian planters favoured it for being less prone to rust
the most popular Indian Arabica selection of the 1940s, developed from Kents

cup.text: Homegrounds describes a mild, naturally sweet cup with low acidity and medium body, often with nutty or spicy notes, and My Coffee Explorer says Indian Kents tend toward chocolate, nuts and mild fruit. India's Coffee Board still credits it with exceptional cup quality.
cup.prized: A good cup: Sweet Maria's says Kents was used in later crosses to improve the taste of newer disease-resistant hybrids, such as the Coffee Board of India's SLN9.

story.text: Kent is believed to descend from the first Bourbon-type seeds Baba Budan brought from Yemen to India.
L.P. Kent selects a single tree on Doddengooda Estate in Mysore, the start of Kent and the varieties bred from it.
Kent reaches Tanzania, where Lyamungu Research Station starts a selection program on it.
India releases S795 (S.288 × Kents) in 1945–46, and Tanzania releases the Kent selection KP423.

sections.title: Which family?
body: Sources disagree. World Coffee Research calls Kent a Bourbon-related population and puts its offspring KP423 in the Bourbon group, and Royal Coffee's 2026 Uganda review calls it genetically similar to Bourbon. Royal Coffee's Kenya review, Homegrounds, Sweet Maria's and Cafe Imports' glossary call it a Typica selection, and Coffee Review's Miguel Meza (2009) listed Kents among Typica's mutations and selections. Cafe Imports dates the selection on the Kent family estate to 1920. WCR also says Jackson, Kent, Coorg and Mysore all come from the same part of India and likely descend from Baba Budan's seeds.

sections.title: Where it's grown
body: India's Coffee Board says Kent is now grown in only a few areas, listing it among the main varieties of the Nilgiris. Royal Coffee calls it an older variety still sometimes found in Kenya, and Tanzania's Acacia Hills farm, at 1,750–1,950 m (5,750–6,400 ft), still grows some Kent.
In Uganda it is still common: Royal Coffee's 2026 review lists Typica, Kent, SL14 and SL28 as the country's most common Arabica varieties.

family.parentsText: A single-tree selection from Mysore, India
family.line: A planter's selection; WCR and Royal Coffee's Uganda review call it Bourbon-related, others call it Typica.

grownIn.text: One of Uganda's most common Arabicas (Royal Coffee, 2026); in India now grown in only a few areas; an older variety in Kenya and Tanzania.

plant.yield: modest: Counter Culture says Kent, Jackson and Mysore gained popularity for rust resistance but struggled to meet the global market's productivity demands
plant.rust: once resistant (the first useful rust-resistant cultivar, per Sweet Maria's), until new rust strains overcame it

records.name: Kurume
records.summary: A small-cherried local Ethiopian landrace from around Yirgacheffe.
records.lede: A regional Ethiopian landrace (a local type farmers have kept, not a research release) from the Yirgacheffe area. It's named after a native tree with small fruit, and is known for small cherries and a generous crop. It's common in the Gedeo and Guji zones, often grown alongside other local types such as Wolisho and Dega.

facts.label: and a big crop most years
the zones where it's commonly grown
in the top 30 at Cup of Excellence Ethiopia 2021, both from Guji, in Oromia
the name is sometimes used for research selections whose trees look similar

family.parentsText: A landrace kept by farmers; no known parents
family.line: From Ethiopia's wild coffee, with seed selected locally by farmers; named after a native tree

grownIn.text: Ethiopia: Gedeo (around Yirgacheffe) and Guji; also named on lots from Gera, in Jimma

plant.yield: good, regular crops of small cherries

cup.text: The Roasters Pack says Kurume and Dega are known for floral, citric cups. Single lots vary: Coffee Review scored a natural Kurume 93 in 2024, with cocoa nib, dried pineapple and magnolia over a plush, syrupy body, and Sample Coffee's washed Kurume from Kochere, Gedeo, listed apricot, lemon myrtle and honeydew melon.
cup.why: Melbourne Coffee Merchants says the local landraces of Gedeo, Kurume among them, are widely believed to play a major role in the floral character of the area's coffee, though little is documented about them.
cup.prized: It can reach competition level: two Guji lots, a natural from Hambela Wamena and an anaerobic lot from Odo Shakiso, placed 13th and 24th at Cup of Excellence Ethiopia 2021.
cup.watch: The name is loose: Ally Coffee says it's sometimes put on JARC selections whose trees look similar (Melbourne Coffee Merchants says the same of landrace names generally), and mixed planting makes pure lots hard to guarantee.

story.text: Surveys help identify Ethiopia's local landraces by name.
Two Kurume lots from Guji place in the top 30 at Ethiopia's Cup of Excellence.
Coffee Review scores a natural Kurume 93.

sections.title: How to tell it from Wolisho
body: Kurume bears small cherries and a good crop most years; Wolisho, often in the same plots, has larger cherries, long leaves and crops that vary from year to year. Melbourne Coffee Merchants lists both among six landraces common across Gedeo, Guji and Sidama, with Bedessa, Dega, Mique and Sawe.
They usually reach the cup together: a washed Yirgacheffe lot Coffee Review scored 93 in 2022 came from trees of Kurume, Wolisho, Dega and other local selections.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Around Yirgacheffe, Melbourne Coffee Merchants describes smallholders growing coffee under native shade trees such as birbira, wanza and acacia, alongside false banana, maize and other food crops, usually organically.

Lots named for Kurume come from about 1,800–1,950 m (5,910–6,400 ft) in Kochere, Gedeo, and from around 1,950 m (6,400 ft) at the Hadeso station in Shakisso, Guji, where it's mixed with Wolisho and JARC selections.

records.name: Laurina
records.summary: A dwarf, low-caffeine Bourbon mutant from La Réunion.
records.lede: Laurina, also called Bourbon Pointu, is a dwarf mutant of Bourbon generally thought to have been selected from a field on La Réunion, then called Bourbon island, in the early 1800s; its trees grow in a pyramid, like a Christmas tree. It's best known for its caffeine, about half that of ordinary Arabica in a 1963 Brazilian study. A 2009 scientific review says its beans are known for excellent cup quality, but calls the exact story of its origin ambiguous and debated.

facts.label: selected on La Réunion, by the usual account
and pyramid-shaped, like a Christmas tree
the caffeine of a standard Arabica, in a 1963 Brazilian study
cup quality, per a 2009 review in Euphytica

cup.text: Gabriel Agrelli of Daterra, a Brazilian farm that grows it, describes it as bright, sweet and delicate, with citrus, a mild body and very little bitterness. Coffee Review scored three Laurina lots at 91–95 and found flowers in all of them (rose, gardenia, magnolia) and dark chocolate in two.
cup.why: It's a natural mutation of Bourbon, nearly identical to it genetically, and Coffee Review describes its cup as fruity and Bourbon-like.
cup.prized: A rare, naturally low-caffeine coffee that can still taste complex: Coffee Review gave a natural from Kona, Hawaii, 95 points, and Emi Fukahori won the 2018 World Brewers Cup with Daterra's anaerobically fermented Laurina.
cup.watch: Roasting: Daterra says its small, dense beans leave a fine line between under- and over-developed, and Costa Rican grower James Evans finds light roasts taste underdeveloped and sour while medium roasts bring out the sweetness.

plant.beanSize: small, tapering to a point at each end (the 'pointu')

story.text: Farmers on Réunion notice smaller Bourbon-type trees with pointed cherries and seeds, according to the island's museum; a 2009 review puts its selection in the early 1800s.
Sugarcane, which pays better, replaces coffee on Réunion, and Bourbon Pointu nearly dies out, surviving mostly as wild trees.
Réunion's government relaunches its coffee with CIRAD and IRD, two French research institutes; seedlings raised from 30 rediscovered trees go to 105 farmers from 2002.
Réunion's harvest reaches 800 kg of green coffee; about 200 kg is exported and sells out within a week at US$70 per 100 g.
Emi Fukahori wins the World Brewers Cup with an anaerobically fermented Laurina from Daterra in Brazil.

sections.title: The shape
body: A CIRAD study found that Bourbon and Bourbon Pointu branch off the trunk at about the same angle, around 50°. The Christmas-tree shape comes instead from the Laurina mutation changing how the top of the main stem grows compared with the side branches.

sections.title: How low is the caffeine?
body: Lower than other Arabica, but not caffeine-free. A 1963 Brazilian study of 16 Arabica varieties found Laurina had about half the caffeine of the standard variety it was compared with, and traced the Laurina traits to a single recessive gene, called lr. A 1998 study in Phytochemistry measured single Laurina beans at 0.36–1.08% caffeine, with the parent line averaging about 0.7% of dry weight, and found the gene slows how much caffeine the plant makes.
A decaf-focused newsletter puts it at 0.2–0.8% caffeine by weight, against 1.2–1.8% for most Arabica, but it cites no study, and its low end sits below what the 1998 study measured.

sections.title: Growing it
body: It's a fussy plant. Daterra, a Brazilian farm that has grown it for about 20 years with illycaffè and Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC), says roughly 30% of plants in a new field die in their first year, far more than with other Arabica, which it blames mainly on the low caffeine, a natural pest deterrent. Daterra traps pests around the trees and keeps most of them in shade, where they grow better. The cherries are delicate and can drop early in heavy rain, and Daterra expects the crop to stay small because it needs so much care.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural dwarf mutant)
family.line: Selected on La Réunion; the details of its origin are debated. Its traits come from one recessive gene, lr.

grownIn.text: First selected on La Réunion, the former Bourbon island, where it was revived from 2002. Now also grown in small amounts in Brazil (notably Daterra), Hawaii's Kona district, Guatemala and Costa Rica.

records.name: Lempira
records.summary: Honduras's Catimor, once rust-resistant, now confirmed susceptible there.
records.lede: A Catimor that IHCAFE, Honduras's national coffee institute, selected from the Central American line T8667 and released in 1998. Farmers planted it for higher yields and rust resistance, and it came to cover about 45% of the country's coffee area by an IHCAFE estimate, but a new rust race has since got through, and World Coffee Research now lists it as confirmed susceptible in Honduras.

facts.label: released in Honduras, rated fully resistant to rust races I and II
of Honduras's cultivated coffee area, by an IHCAFE researcher's count (c. 2018)
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
to leaf rust in Honduras, confirmed by scientific evaluation

cup.text: Little is published on its cup. World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude low and calls it highly similar to Costa Rica 95. Competition results are kinder: Lempira was among the varieties of the 2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winners.
cup.why: Coffee Review groups Lempira and IHCAFE 90 as rust-resistant hybrids carrying Robusta genes, and the importer Coffee Hunter blames those genes for the weaker cups of Timor Hybrid offspring.
cup.prized: At its best it can be competition coffee: in 2017 it was among the varieties of Honduras's Cup of Excellence winners, a year when every winning lot scored at least 86.
cup.watch: Low cup potential at high altitude, by WCR's rating.

story.text: CATIE in Costa Rica receives the Catimor line T8667, which IHCAFE later selected Lempira from.
IHCAFE releases Lempira, rated 100% resistant to rust races I and II.
Rust starts infecting Lempira, one of the cases WCR singles out of resistance breaking down.
A rust epidemic reported in April 2016 affects 210 ha, in an IHCAFE study of the new race attacking Lempira.
IHCAFE says Lempira isn't immune to a newly found rust strain; Coffee Review later counts as many as four new strains in Honduras.
Lempira is among the varieties of the winning lots at Honduras's Cup of Excellence, where every winning lot scored at least 86.

sections.title: Its reputation
body: WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude as low and calls it highly similar to Costa Rica 95. Competition results are kinder: Lempira was among the varieties of the 2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winners, a year when winning lots scored 86 to 91.81.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffeeness names Lempira among the varieties of El Paraíso, Montecillos and Agalta. WCR recommends it for the warmest zones and for acidic, aluminium-rich soils.

WCR lists it as susceptible to nematodes (root worms), coffee berry disease and ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease, with a high fertilizer need, a low ratio of green coffee to cherry, and 5,000–6,000 plants per hectare.

sections.title: Why its resistance broke
body: An IHCAFE study found the rust attacking Lempira carries seven virulence genes. Varieties such as Parainema held out because they carry a resistance gene, SH8, that Lempira lacks, while IHCAFE 90 and Obatá showed 20% susceptibility. IHCAFE staff told La Prensa in 2017 that IHCAFE 90 kept 80% resistance to the new strain and Parainema 100%, and that 60% of the country's coffee area was improved, rust-resistant plants.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra (selected from T8667)
family.line: Pedigree selection by PROMECAFE and IHCAFE in Honduras.

grownIn.text: Honduras, including El Paraíso, Montecillos and Agalta.

plant.rust: rated intermediate, but now confirmed susceptible in Honduras
plant.altitude: low to medium: about 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude, as in Central America; 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Limani
records.summary: Puerto Rico's compact, rust-resistant Sarchimor, released to farmers in 1994.
records.lede: A compact, rust-resistant variety grown in Puerto Rico, from a cross of the Timor Hybrid and Villa Sarchi. Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas sent the seed to the island's Agricultural Experiment Station in 1982, and after trials it went to farmers in 1994. World Coffee Research warns that plants sold as Limani often don't match the original.

facts.label: released to Puerto Rican farmers
a dwarf tree, planted 5,000–6,000 to the hectare
(3,300 ft+), where WCR says true Limani does well
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude

cup.text: WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude as good. Tasting notes come from blends: Coffee Review's 93-point natural of 2026 from Hacienda Tierra Viva in Utuado, a mix of Limani, Frontón, Bourbon and Typica, tasted of dark chocolate, toasted walnut, dried cherry, cedar and orange zest, with a gentle, bright acidity and a very full, syrupy body.

story.text: Brazil's IAC supplied Limani, along with another variety, Fronton, to Puerto Rico's Agricultural Experiment Station.
After trials showed rust resistance and high yield potential, it was released to farmers.
The University of Puerto Rico's coffee production guide names Limaní and Frontón as the island's rust-resistant semi-dwarf varieties.
A University of Puerto Rico study confirms that the Limaní line resists rust in leaf-disc tests and in the field at the Adjuntas substation, where Caturra was heavily infected.

sections.title: The name problem
body: WCR calls true Limani elusive: because the seed has been hard to trace, plants sold under the name often don't match the original reference material.

On the island it has proved itself. A 2021 University of Puerto Rico thesis notes that the experiment station found it outperformed Bourbon, Caturra and Pacas there, and that it remains important to Puerto Rican production for its performance and rust resistance.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as needing a lot of fertilizer, ripening at an average pace, and giving a high outturn, meaning a lot of green coffee from each kilo of cherry.

The University of Puerto Rico's 1999 guide groups it with Caturra, Pacas and Frontón as semi-dwarf trees: easy to pick by hand but awkward to harvest with nets, planted about 6 ft (1.8 m) between rows and 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) apart, quicker to start bearing, and, the guide says of the group, late to ripen.

sections.title: Rust tests in Puerto Rico
body: Limaní is the name later given to LC-1668, a sixth-generation Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid line from the collection Puerto Rico received from IAC (a 2021 University of Puerto Rico thesis gives its code as LC-1665). Frontón came from a separate, Catimor-type line of Caturra × Timor Hybrid. In a 2020 University of Puerto Rico study, LC-1668 showed no rust in leaf-disc tests or under natural infection at the Adjuntas substation, 594 m (1,950 ft) up, matching the resistant Timor Hybrid check, while Caturra was badly infected (7 on the study's 0–9 field scale, against 0).

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid 832/2 × Villa Sarchi
family.line: A pedigree selection made by Puerto Rico's Agricultural Experiment Station from a Brazilian population of this Sarchimor cross: the IAC introduction LC-1668 (given as LC-1665 in a 2021 thesis).

grownIn.text: Released in Puerto Rico, where it is still important to the island's coffee.

plant.rust: resistant (WCR's scale: intermediate resistance)
plant.altitude: above 1,000 m (3,300 ft)

records.name: Maragogipe
records.summary: A Typica mutation with giant beans, found in Brazil in 1870.
records.lede: A natural mutation of Typica found near the town of Maragogipe, Brazil, in 1870, caused by a single dominant gene. It's known for its very large beans, sometimes called elephant beans, and it's one of the two parents of Pacamara.

facts.label: beans, WCR's yardstick for the biggest size
from tall trees with big leaves and long gaps between leaf pairs
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
where it does best near the equator (5,250 ft)

cup.text: Coffee Hunter describes a mild, smooth cup with gentle, sweet acidity, a fresh oaky note and a dark, syrupy body. World Coffee Research rates its cup good to very good in Central America. Ozone Coffee quotes researcher Gerson Silva Giomo calling it naturally very sweet and low in acidity, with floral, honey and sometimes spicy notes, and roaster Brandon von Damitz finding peach and chocolate with herbal hints.
cup.why: Coffee Review says its porous beans are hard to roast and tend to taste woody and flat, which is why it never took off as a single-origin coffee. Processing shifts it too: researcher Gerson Silva Giomo, quoted by Ozone, finds naturals (dried in the fruit) get more sweetness, body and complexity, and washed lots a lighter, less sweet cup with more acidity and floral aroma.
cup.prized: Novelty and sweetness. Coffee Review says the giant "elephant beans" are the draw, and carefully grown, processed and roasted lots can taste subtly unusual, leaning sweet-savory; Sweet Maria's notes Europe once prized it for its bean size.
cup.watch: Yields are so low that World Coffee Research calls Pacamara, its big-bean offspring, the better option for farmers. Ozone adds that lots sold as Maragogipe may contain other varieties.

plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

sections.title: Growing it
body: Besides leaf rust, it's susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms). It needs little fertiliser and turns a high share of cherry weight into green coffee. Coffee Hunter says it matures slowly and names Brazil, Guatemala and Mexico as where it's most common, but Ozone says Brazil now grows little of it, and Coffee Review that it's grown most widely in Central America, in small amounts.

sections.title: Roasting and grinding it
body: Sweet Maria's says the giant beans are hard to roast and can even be awkward to feed into grinder burrs, but can be excellent when roasted well, with a gentle warm-up and a long, gentle roast. Coffee Review (2018) says its porous beans are difficult to roast and tend to taste woody and flat, which kept it from catching on as a single-origin coffee.

sections.title: Offspring: Pacamara and Maracaturra
body: Pacamara comes from a cross of Pacas, a Bourbon mutation, with Maragogipe, selected by El Salvador's coffee research institute, ISIC. It keeps the big bean, and Coffee Review says it typically gives a deeper, more complex cup than Maragogipe.

Maracaturra is Maragogipe crossed with Caturra. Coffee Review credits Byron Corrales of Finca Los Pinos in Nicaragua, while Ozone says it likely began as a natural cross there. Perfect Daily Grind describes a short, wind-resistant, productive plant with large beans that is susceptible to leaf rust, and a cup with tropical fruit and bright acidity.

family.parentsText: Typica (natural mutation)
family.line: A single dominant gene mutation found near Maragogipe, Brazil.

grownIn.text: Now mostly Central America and Mexico, in small amounts; Ozone also names Colombia and Hawaii, and says Brazil, where it was found, grows little of it.

story.text: The mutation is found near the town of Maragogipe in Bahia, Brazil.
Coffee writer William Ukers calls it "generally disagreeable in the cup".
El Salvador's coffee research institute, ISIC, releases Pacamara, a cross of Pacas and Maragogipe that keeps the giant bean.
Coffee Review's big-bean report scores a Guatemalan La Providencia Maragogype 94, though Pacamaras do best overall.

records.name: Marsellesa
records.summary: A high-yielding Nicaraguan Sarchimor that WCR notes for high acidity.
records.lede: A Sarchimor selected in Nicaragua for rust resistance by CIRAD and ECOM and released in 2009. World Coffee Research describes a high-yielding plant adapted to medium altitudes, with notably high acidity in the cup. It has since become a regular among the winners of Mexico's Cup of Excellence, especially from Puebla and Chiapas.

facts.label: released, after selection in Nicaragua
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
acidity in the cup, WCR notes
points for a washed Marsellesa from Puebla, 3rd in the experimental category at Mexico's 2024 Cup of Excellence

cup.text: WCR notes notably high acidity. The importer Coffee Hunter describes a fruity, floral fragrance, a medium, balanced acidity and a medium body, like Caturra but sweeter. PT's Coffee found its honey-processed lot from northwestern Nicaragua light-bodied, sweet-tart and lightly floral, with Swiss chocolate, honeycomb and rose hip.
cup.prized: The Costa Rican consultant Jorge Ramírez Rojas told Perfect Daily Grind that Marsellesa and Obatã cup even better than Caturra and Catuaí.
cup.watch: Its prominent acidity: PT's Coffee says the honey process (drying the seed with some of the sticky fruit left on) softens it.

story.text: Breeding of these hybrids in Central America begins in the late 1990s, PT's Coffee reports; in 2002 the coffee trader ECOM approaches CIRAD, France's agricultural research centre, about the partnership that now sells Marsellesa.
Marsellesa is released after pedigree selection for rust resistance in Nicaragua.
About 2,000 Nicaraguan growers are replanting with Marsellesa and the hybrid H1, using plants from the exporter Exportadora Atlantic's lab in Sébaco, Matagalpa.
Seed and plants are sent to Peru through Camsa–Ecom, working with Concytec, Peru's national science council.
Marsellesa appears in six of the top ten washed places at Mexico's Cup of Excellence, and a pure Marsellesa takes 3rd in the experimental category with 90.26.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as susceptible to nematodes and tolerant of coffee berry disease, with a high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and heavy feeding needs. Coffee Hunter says it matures and grows faster than Caturra and Catuaí, holds its cherries in heavy rain, and does best up to 1,300 m (4,250 ft).

La Prensa reported from Nicaragua in 2014 that Marsellesa and H1 gave 30–40 quintales per manzana in their third year and more than 50 from the fourth, against a national average of 11, and that the two cupped at 83–87 points; the figures came from Reynaldo Soza of Exportadora Atlantic, whose lab produces the plants. One grower, Gonzalo Castillo, said rust wiped out his Caturra in 2012 while his Marsellesa survived.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Mexico's Cup of Excellence is where it shines. In 2019 a washed Marsellesa from Ocoteno in Huitzilan de Serdán, Puebla, placed 11th with 88.36. In 2024 pure Marsellesa lots took 4th, 5th and 6th among washed coffees (Peña Blanca in Chiapas, 89.03; Ocoteno and Tapula in Puebla), and Las Barrancas in Puebla took 3rd in the experimental category with 90.26. In 2026 a Marsellesa–Colombia lot from El Milagro in Puebla was 3rd among washed coffees at 90.25, and a natural from Fatima in Veracruz placed 7th in the natural-and-honey category.

sections.title: Name and parentage
body: CIRAD sells it under a registered name, Marsellesa®, and lists it with CentroAmerica® as the two CIRAD-ECOM varieties now sold on a large scale. WCR gives its parents as Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10; Coffee Hunter instead calls it a Sarchimor × Caturra hybrid. Competition lists sometimes spell it Marcellesa.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10
family.line: Pedigree selection for rust resistance in Nicaragua by CIRAD-ECOM.

grownIn.text: Selected in Nicaragua, where about 2,000 growers were replanting with it and H1 by 2014. In Mexico it is among the varieties of the national replanting program and a frequent Cup of Excellence winner from Puebla, Chiapas and Veracruz; seed went to Peru in 2015. It has spread beyond Latin America too: Mount Sunzu Coffee in Zambia sells a washed Marsellesa grown at 1,550–1,650 m (5,100–5,400 ft).

plant.rust: intermediate
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Mibirizi
records.summary: Probably Rwanda's oldest coffee, a Typica type with top cup ratings.
records.lede: Probably the oldest coffee variety in Rwanda, and still important to smallholders there and in Burundi. A Belgian coffee historian wrote that Germany's colonial administration brought it from Guatemala in the 1910s, and in the 1920s it went to Catholic missions, including one at Mibirizi in western Rwanda. Genetic tests tie it to the Typica group.

facts.label: WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
and copes with little care and harsh conditions
highly susceptible to the major coffee diseases
