plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: Germany's colonial administration brings coffee from Guatemala to Rwanda, where it's called "Guatemala"; it was probably Typica, since Guatemala then grew only Typica.
The coffee is handed out to Rwanda's Catholic missions, including the one at Mibirizi, whose well-kept trees later supplied seed to the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo.
Several Mibirizi lines are compared at the Rubona research station near Huye; it's unclear whether any reached farmers.

sections.title: The family
body: Its history is poorly documented. World Coffee Research says Mibirizi plants were probably mixed with French Mission plants from Kenya, which are Bourbon-type, but recent genetic tests confirm a link to the Typica group.
Cafe Imports' variety glossary likewise dates its arrival from Guatemala to the 1910s and calls it a possible Typica-Bourbon cross.

sections.title: On the bag
body: “Mibirizi” on a Rwandan bag may name a place rather than the variety. A washed lot from the NCMC Mibirizi washing station, grown at 1,750 m (5,740 ft), placed fifth in Rwanda's 2012 Cup of Excellence, and its variety was listed as Bourbon.

Coffee Review's 2009 reviews of Burundian lots called Mibirizi a Bourbon derivative. WCR says genetic tests now tie it to the Typica group, though Mibirizi plants were probably mixed with French Mission (Bourbon) plants.

family.parentsText: Typica-like, possibly mixed with French Mission (Bourbon)
family.line: Probably Typica from Guatemala, kept at Rwandan missions.

grownIn.text: Smallholder farms in Rwanda and Burundi; rare lots elsewhere, such as Costa Rica's Chirripó.

cup.text: Little is published about Mibirizi's cup on its own: in Rwanda and Burundi it usually goes into lots alongside Bourbon and Jackson. Two such lots from Kayanza, Burundi, scored 93 and 95 at Coffee Review in 2009, praised for lively, floral acidity, and WCR rates the variety's quality potential at high altitude as exceptional. A rare single-variety lot, a slow-dried natural from Finca Los Alpes in Costa Rica's Chirripó at 1,750 m (5,740 ft), was described by London roaster Scenery Coffee as brown sugar, baked peach, berry and spiced plum jam.

records.name: Milenio
records.summary: F1 hybrid that placed third at Costa Rica's 2022 Cup of Excellence
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid from the same parents as Centroamericano: the rust-resistant Sarchimor T5296 and Rume Sudan, an old landrace from South Sudan. It came from the first wave of Central American hybrids, and WCR rates it very high-yielding and rust-resistant, though its plants are not uniform.

facts.label: third place at Costa Rica's 2022 Cup of Excellence
Coffee Review score for a Costa Rican lot in 2023
where WCR says its quality is good (4,265 ft+)
plants can vary, WCR warns

cup.text: Coffee Review scored a Finca Las Lajas lot from Costa Rica's Central Valley 93 in 2023, calling it sweetly tart and citrusy, with bergamot, cedar, persimmon, cocoa and macadamia nut. A 2020 Costa Rican study says its cup is similar to or better than Caturra's and Catuaí's when they grow in the same conditions.
cup.prized: Competition-level cups: an anaerobic lot from Pérez Zeledón placed third at Costa Rica's 2022 Cup of Excellence with 90 points.
cup.watch: WCR warns that its plants are not uniform, so a field can vary.

story.text: The PROMECAFE–CATIE–CIRAD breeding program that produced Milenio begins.
John Alvarado Abarca's anaerobic Milenio from Los Toños, in Pérez Zeledón, places third at Costa Rica's Cup of Excellence with 90 points.
Coffee Review scores a 100% Milenio lot from Finca Las Lajas 93 points.
CATIE starts supplying Milenio, with Centroamericano and Esperanza, to smallholders in the Trifinio region.

family.parentsText: T5296 (a Sarchimor) × Rume Sudan
family.line: F1 cross from the CIRAD–PROMECAFE–CATIE consortium; propagated as clones

grownIn.text: Its best-known lots come from Costa Rica: competition lots from Pérez Zeledón and the West Valley, and a lot from Finca Las Lajas in the Central Valley that Coffee Review scored 93. Since 2023 CATIE has supplied plants to the Trifinio region of Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

plant.rust: resistant
plant.altitude: good quality above 1,300 m (4,265 ft)

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with green young leaves and large beans that yields very well, resists leaf rust and bears its first crop in year two. It gives a very high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry), and WCR suggests 4,000–5,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning.

A 2020 Costa Rican study says it has adapted and yielded very well at 800–1,500 m (2,600–4,900 ft) and stood out in many field trials. In the same study its mini-cuttings had the highest rooting rate of the three hybrids tested (about 94% after 12 weeks, against about 90% for Esperanza and 84% for Centroamericano), though the study found no significant difference between the hybrids. Rooting matters because, like other F1s, it has to be multiplied as clones.

sections.title: In competitions
body: At Costa Rica's 2022 Cup of Excellence, two lots of Milenio (listed as "Milenium") from Los Toños in Pérez Zeledón shared third place at 90 points, behind only Gesha lots, and a natural from San Cristóbal in the West Valley placed 18th at 87.41. CATIE says a Korean coffee taster rated it a high-quality coffee.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: Milenio and Centroamericano have the same parents, T5296 and Rume Sudan. Coffee Review's 2016 review of a Tarrazú natural (92 points) names only "an F1 hybrid" of Sarchimor and Sudan Rume, so it may be one of the two, but the review doesn't say which. WCR lists Milenio as H10, a 2020 Costa Rican study calls it L12A28, and Costa Rica's 2022 competition results spell it Milenium.

records.name: Monte Claro
records.summary: Venezuela's rust-tolerant Sarchimor, bred by INIA in Táchira.
records.lede: A Sarchimor (Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid) selected in Venezuela over about 40 years by the coffee breeding program of INIA, the national agricultural research institute, in Táchira state; its name was registered with the national seed commission in 2013. It's a compact, heavy-bearing Arabica that tolerates leaf rust, and in 2023 a natural Monte Claro from Trujillo state took first place among 186 samples at a Caracas coffee show, scoring 90.11 points.

facts.label: points, first of 186 samples at a Caracas show (reported in 2023)
registered with Venezuela's national seed commission
it also tolerates other diseases
paid in 2023 for about 46 kg (100 lb), vs about $180 for an ordinary variety

cup.text: Venezuelan growers and roasters describe fruit and flowers together: Alfredo Rojas of Caracas Coffee Roasters, who processed it as a natural, says that combination is what's remarkable about it. Bilal El Ayoubi, the researcher who released it, describes herbal aromas, a silky body, juicy acidity and a long aftertaste.
cup.prized: Its 2023 win: a natural Monte Claro from finca El Caotal in Trujillo scored 90.11 and took the top prize, the Taza de Oro, at EICEV, Venezuela's international specialty coffee meeting. The grower Víctor Montilla called it a record for Venezuelan coffee; Reuters reported that the judges came from Colombia, Nicaragua, the United States and Peru.

story.text: At CIFC, Portugal's coffee rust research centre, Villa Sarchi is crossed with the Timor Hybrid, the Sarchimor cross that Monte Claro comes from.
The material reaches Venezuela through CIFC, and generations of INIA researchers in Táchira select from it for more than 40 years.
Bilal El Ayoubi, a former coordinator of INIA's coffee breeding program, registers the variety and its name with Venezuela's national seed commission, and it is officially released.
A Monte Claro won first place among 186 samples at a Caracas exhibition, scoring 90.11, enough to count as specialty coffee.

sections.title: Growing it
body: El Ayoubi describes a low tree with compact branching, like Caturra, and cherries with a pointed tip; its beans are large, above screen size 17 (17/64 inch). He says that well managed it can give up to 120 quintales per hectare, against a Venezuelan average of only 8–10.

Besides tolerating rust, he says, it resists some nematodes (root worms), aluminium-rich soils and the coffee berry borer, which the pointed cherry makes harder to bore into. It is about as susceptible as Caturra and Catuaí to ojo de gallo and mancha de hierro, two leaf and cherry diseases.

sections.title: Selling it
body: El Ayoubi says Japanese buyers take most of the crop and that interest is growing in France and the United States. Víctor Montilla, who began growing it on his Trujillo farm around 2019, started exporting small lots of 5–6 kg in 2020 to Colombia, Panama and Spain, Reuters reported, and in 2023 sold about 46 kg for $600.

sections.title: On the record
body: World Coffee Research lists Monte Claro among the varieties on its 2023 poster of its variety catalog. Reuters reported in 2023 that coffee experts praise its flavor and yield.

family.parentsText: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid (a Sarchimor)
family.line: Bred by the coffee program of Venezuela's INIA in Táchira; published sources don't give its cross.

grownIn.text: Venezuela: bred in Táchira and now grown in several regions, including Trujillo and Táchira states.

plant.yield: high: up to 120 quintales per hectare when well managed, says its breeder
plant.rust: tolerant

records.name: Mundo Maya
records.summary: ECOM–CIRAD F1 hybrid with the top yields in Nicaraguan trials
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of the rust-resistant Sarchimor T5296 and a wild Ethiopian accession, ET01, selected in Nicaragua by the coffee trader ECOM and the French research institute CIRAD. In a multi-site Nicaraguan trial it gave the highest yield of eleven coffees, more than 56% above Marsellesa, with no rust lesions.

facts.label: yield over Marsellesa in Nicaraguan trials
lesions seen on it in those trials
testing it, according to CIRAD
for very good quality, says WCR (4,265 ft+)

cup.text: In a Nicaraguan trial it scored 79.5 on the SCA scale (the industry's 100-point cupping score), between Caturra at 76.3 and Starmaya and Centroamericano at about 80.5, and not clearly different from the rest. WCR rates its quality very good above 1,300 m. Monogram Coffee describes an anaerobic natural from producer Carlos Cadena in Mexico as juicy, with blood orange, soft melon and cherry.
cup.prized: Yield first: it out-produced every other coffee in the Nicaraguan trial whatever the site, with no rust, and the researchers called it promising.
cup.watch: Its cup has been studied far less than its yield, and WCR says it has no resistance to Pratylenchus root nematodes.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with large beans that yields very well if planted in healthy soil and suits agroforestry (coffee grown under trees). It resists some root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne) but not Pratylenchus, another root worm, and should be propagated only as clones.

In the Nicaraguan trial its canopy was only about 20% bigger than Caturra's or Marsellesa's, yet it produced about 50% more, and its beans had the fewest defects of the group (2.6%), though the differences in defects were not significant.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: Bags and papers call it Mundo Maya, MundoMaya or the codes EC16 and H16. It shares its Sarchimor parent, T5296, with Centroamericano, Milenio and Esperanza, but its Ethiopian parent, ET01, is different; MundoMex (EC15) is a separate hybrid with a Catimor parent.

family.parentsText: T5296 (a Sarchimor) × wild Ethiopian accession ET01 (CATIE collection)
family.line: Selected by ECOM and CIRAD in Nicaragua; propagated as clones

grownIn.text: Selected and trialled in Nicaragua; at least one lot has been sold from Mexico (a single roaster listing, with no region given), and CIRAD says it is being tested in more than 15 countries.

plant.rust: no lesions in Nicaraguan trials
plant.altitude: very good quality above 1,300 m (4,265 ft)

story.text: The coffee trader ECOM approaches CIRAD; the partnership that will select Mundo Maya sets up a lab to clone hybrids by somatic embryogenesis (growing plants from leaf tissue).
In trials at seven Nicaraguan sites from 710 to 1,250 m (2,330–4,100 ft) it gives the highest yield of eleven coffees, more than 56% above Marsellesa.
ECOM and CIRAD sign a 15-year cooperation agreement; CIRAD later reports Mundo Maya on test in more than 15 countries.

records.name: Mundo Novo
records.summary: Brazil's tall, vigorous natural cross of Bourbon and Typica.
records.lede: A natural cross of Bourbon and Typica found in Brazil's São Paulo state, discovered in 1943 and handed to Brazilian farmers from 1952. It's tall, vigorous and productive, can be harvested by machine, and is important in Brazil and elsewhere in South America, though rare in Central America. Crossed with Caturra, it gave Catuaí.

facts.label: discovered; given to farmers from 1952
why it never caught on in Costa Rica, where it arrived in 1952
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
of Brazil's planted coffee is Mundo Novo or Catuaí (2012 estimate)

cup.text: Coffee Hunter's notes are mixed: some describe it as sweet and full-bodied with low acidity, while others say it often lacks sweetness and can turn a little bitter, and that rich fertilising may help. Coffee Review has rated it in Brazilian naturals blended with Catuaí; one, from southern Minas Gerais, showed dark chocolate, hazelnut and raisin.
cup.watch: It can taste short on sweetness or bitter, says Coffee Hunter.
cup.why: It's a big, heavy-bearing tree that needs a lot of fertiliser, and Coffee Hunter says rich fertilising and added nutrients might improve a cup that can otherwise lack sweetness or turn a little bitter.
cup.prized: Body and chocolate-and-nut sweetness in Brazilian naturals. Two Coffee Review lots blending Mundo Novo with Catuaí scored 91 and 92: a 2018 natural from southern Minas Gerais (dark chocolate, hazelnut, raisin, silky body) and a 2008 natural from Coromandel, Minas Gerais, with lavender, fruit and white-wine-like florals.

plant.yield: medium in World Coffee Research's rating; Coffee Hunter says about 30% more than Bourbon, and IAC breeder Luiz Carlos Fazuoli says up to 200% more than Typica
plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator; 1,500 m (4,900 ft) and up is recommended in Peru, while Coffee Hunter puts its best range at 1,050–1,670 m (3,450–5,500 ft)

story.text: The natural cross is found at Mineiros do Tietê, São Paulo; selection from seed sown at Novo Mundo, today Urupês, gives rise to the variety.
Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) crosses it with yellow Caturra, the start of Catuaí.
Brazilian farmers start receiving it, and it begins replacing Bourbon on their farms; it reaches Costa Rica the same year but isn't widely planted there.
Introduced to Guatemala, and to Honduras by CATIE in 1974.
Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) starts releasing new selections.
Mundo Novo and Catuaí together are estimated to make up about 85% of the coffee planted in Brazil.

sections.title: Growing it
body: It's very vigorous, responds well to pruning and needs plenty of fertiliser. World Coffee Research rates its ripening as average, while Coffee Hunter says its cherries ripen a bit later than average. It's susceptible to the major coffee diseases. Being tall, it's planted wider apart than compact varieties, at 3,000–4,000 trees per hectare, and World Coffee Research says it can be harvested by machine. Coffee Hunter says the Typica parent was the Sumatra type, and IAC's Fazuoli calls a Red Bourbon × Sumatra cross the probable origin.

sections.title: In Brazil today
body: Mundo Novo and Catuaí were the backbone of Brazil's coffee: a 2012 estimate put them together at about 85% of the trees planted. Mundo Novo also helped open coffee farming on the cerrado, Brazil's high savanna.

They rarely shine in competitions, though. In Brazil's 2025 Cup of Excellence, Mundo Novo appeared in just one of 39 ranked lots, a natural blended with Arara and Catucaí that placed ninth (87.66), while newer rust-resistant varieties led by Arara took most of the places.

family.parentsText: Bourbon × Typica (natural cross)
family.line: Found in São Paulo state; selected by IAC.

grownIn.text: Mainly Brazil and elsewhere in South America, including Peru; also Malawi.

records.name: MundoMex
records.summary: Catimor × wild Ethiopian F1 hybrid made in Nicaragua
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of Catimor line 17931, selected in Nicaragua in the 1990s, and a wild Ethiopian accession, ET26. Both parents reached La Cumplida farm in Matagalpa in 1991; CIRAD developed the hybrid in Nicaragua with the ECOM Group, and the plants are cloned in a tissue-culture lab in Sébaco.

facts.label: WCR's rating of its quality potential
suits coffee grown under shade trees
its first crop

story.text: Both parents arrive at La Cumplida farm in Matagalpa, Nicaragua, with help from CODOCAFÉ, a member of the PROMECAFE network.
CIRAD starts its breeding program in Nicaragua, which produced MundoMex with ECOM.
It is tested at seven Nicaraguan sites from 710 to 1,250 m (2,330–4,100 ft) and shows stable yields with little rust.
The researchers call it a serious candidate for low-input smallholder farms, pending tasting work.

family.parentsText: Catimor line 17931 × wild Ethiopian accession ET26
family.line: F1 cross by CIRAD and ECOM; cloned by somatic embryogenesis, a lab method that grows plants from tissue

grownIn.text: Developed and trialled in Nicaragua.

plant.rust: WCR rates its resistance low; it showed little rust in Nicaragua's 2013–18 trials, and WCR notes results may vary with local rust races

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with bronze young leaves and large beans that yields well, bears its first crop in year two and suits agroforestry (coffee grown under shade trees). It needs a lot of fertilizer, ripens at an average time, has an average outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and suits 3,000–4,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning.

In the Nicaraguan trial it grew a big canopy, 0.98 m³ against Caturra's 0.54 m³, and combined stable yields with a low rust reaction. WCR has also tested it at 23 sites in 15 countries in its International Multilocation Variety Trial, and warns that its rust performance may vary with the rust races present locally.

sections.title: Good to know
body: Its Catimor parent, line 17931, was selected in Nicaragua in the 1990s from Colombian lines bred from Timor Hybrid × Caturra. Its Ethiopian parent, ET26, was collected by an ORSTOM/IRD mission and is also a parent of Nayarita.
Don't confuse it with Mundo Maya (EC16), a different ECOM–CIRAD hybrid with a Sarchimor parent.

records.name: Nayarita
records.summary: ECOM–CIRAD F1 hybrid for high altitudes with very good cups
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of Naryelis, a Catimor-type line, and a wild Ethiopian accession, ET26, from CATIE's collection, selected in Nicaragua by ECOM and CIRAD. WCR describes it as high-yielding at high altitudes with very good cup quality.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with dark bronze young leaves and large beans that yields well at high altitudes. It ripens at an average time, needs a lot of fertilizer, gives a very high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and suits 3,000–4,000 plants per hectare with single-stem pruning.

In the Nicaraguan trial it had the steadiest high yields of all the coffees tested and a big canopy, 0.98 m³ against Caturra's 0.54 m³. It showed some rust lesions with little spore production, which the researchers read as weak susceptibility; its tasting quality still needs study.

sections.title: Good to know
body: Its Ethiopian parent, ET26, was collected in Ethiopia by an ORSTOM/IRD mission. It shares its Catimor-type parent, Naryelis, with Evaluna, and ET26 with MundoMex; its codes are EC19 and H19.

family.parentsText: Naryelis (a Catimor) × wild Ethiopian accession ET26 (CATIE collection)
family.line: Selected by ECOM and CIRAD in Nicaragua; propagated as clones

grownIn.text: Selected and trialled in Nicaragua; no published source names lots or plantings elsewhere.

plant.rust: some lesions, low spore production in trials
plant.altitude: high: above 1,300 m (4,265 ft) at 5–15° latitude

story.text: Nayarita is tested at seven Nicaraguan sites from 710 to 1,250 m (2,330–4,100 ft) against Caturra, Marsellesa and other hybrids.
The researchers rank it first of all the coffees for stable yields across sites and call it a serious candidate for low-input farms.

records.name: Obatã
records.summary: Brazil's rust-resistant Sarchimor, released in 2000 and now grown in Costa Rica.
records.lede: A high-yielding Sarchimor bred by Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) in Campinas and released in 2000; Costa Rica's coffee institute brought it in for commercial release in 2014. It has large beans and a good rating for cup potential from World Coffee Research, and some lots have impressed: one from Sítio Novo Canaã scored 94 points in a cupping at Brazil's Fazenda Ambiental Fortaleza, the farm's highest score to that point.

facts.label: released in Brazil by IAC
released for farmers in Costa Rica
bean size
its full IAC code

cup.text: Felipe Croce of Fazenda Ambiental Fortaleza describes an Obatã lot with high acidity, a big body, strong sweetness and a floral side, and says that at a blind cupping it gave off a burst of floral aroma when ground. The Danish roaster Stillers lists chocolate, caramel and honey, among other notes, for a red-honey Obatã from Costa Rica's Central Valley. In a Procafé trial in Varginha, Minas Gerais, its naturals from the 2009 and 2010 harvests scored 84.0, described as excellent with a caramel flavor.
cup.prized: Obatã reached the final rounds of Brazil's BSCA quality contest in 2004 and 2006, Revista Cultivar reported.
cup.watch: Croce found only 18–22 Brix (a sugar reading) at visual ripeness in Obatã and similar hybrids, against 26–35 for pure Arabica.

story.text: IAC registers IAC 1669, the first-generation hybrid of a 1967 Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 cross made in Portugal; Obatã's code, IAC 1669-20, carries that number.
IAC releases Obatã in Brazil.
It reaches the final rounds of the BSCA quality contest in both years.
Costa Rica's coffee institute (ICAFE) releases it for commercial planting.
A washed lot of Obatã and Garnica from Ahuateno in Puebla places 7th among washed coffees at Mexico's Cup of Excellence, with 87.58.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR rates it high-yielding with intermediate rust resistance, late ripening and heavy feeding needs. Five Elephant's story describes it as disease-resistant and well suited to São Paulo and southern Minas Gerais.
It's also a parent: Arara, a newer Brazilian variety, is Yellow Catuaí × Obatã.

sections.title: In trials
body: In a Procafé cupping of 30 cultivars at Varginha, about 1,000 m (3,300 ft) up, scored by two tasters, Obatã's 84.0 beat Yellow Bourbon (81.5) and Red Catuaí IAC 144 (78.5), though several newer cultivars scored higher (IPR 104 topped the trial at 89.0). In a trial in Viçosa, Minas Gerais, reported in 2011, it was among the five highest-yielding of 32 cultivars.

IAC's description, cited in a 2007 study, gives a short tree with green young leaves, red cherries that ripen medium to late, and beans of about screen 17 (17/64 inch), best planted densely. IAC also selected a yellow-fruited sister, IAC Obatã Amarelo; WCR's catalog entry is for the red.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10
family.line: Pedigree selection by IAC in Campinas, Brazil.

grownIn.text: Brazil, and Costa Rica since 2014, including the Central Valley; in Mexico it shows up in Cup of Excellence lots from Puebla and Chiapas, blended with other varieties.

plant.rust: intermediate
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Orange Bourbon
records.summary: Sold as an orange-cherried Bourbon; one DNA test found Pink Bourbon.
records.lede: A name for Bourbon-type trees whose ripe cherries are orange. The trade usually calls it a natural colour mutation of Red Bourbon and strongly associates it with El Salvador; importer Sucafina gives it Bourbon's general traits: excellent cup quality, good performance at high altitude and susceptibility to the major diseases. Its genetics are barely published: in 2023 an importer had one 'Orange Bourbon' DNA-tested alongside four Pink Bourbons, and it carried Pink Bourbon's markers, which point to an Ethiopian landrace.

facts.label: ripe cherries
the country it's most associated with, says Ozone Coffee
samples in a 2023 DNA test; it carried Pink Bourbon markers
Coffee Review score for a washed lot from the Santa Ana volcano, El Salvador (2021)

cup.text: A washed Orange Bourbon from the Santa Ana volcano in El Salvador (93 points with Coffee Review, 2021) showed toffee, orange zest, oak, magnolia and vanilla. Coffee Review has also rated at least five of Wilton Benítez's lots from Cauca, Colombia, made with thermal-shock or double-anaerobic fermentation (94 to 97 points, 2023–2026), with citrus such as blood orange or kumquat, tropical fruit and candy-like sweetness.
cup.why: Ozone Coffee cautions that cherry colour doesn't reliably predict flavour: genetics, altitude, climate, harvesting and processing matter more. At Finca La Huella in Nicaragua, it says, trees that ripen solid orange and trees that ripen striped make noticeably different coffees from the same land and the same washed process.
cup.prized: Sucafina's entry for it repeats what it says of Bourbon in general: excellent cup quality and good performance at high altitude.
cup.watch: Like other Bourbons it is susceptible to the major coffee diseases, which makes it hard to grow, says Sucafina. And the name on the bag doesn't guarantee what's inside (see below).

story.text: Cuvée Coffee sells an Orange Bourbon from José Antonio's El Molino farm in El Salvador and describes it as a natural cross of red and yellow Bourbon.
Coffee Review rates a washed Orange Bourbon from Malacara B, on the Santa Ana volcano in El Salvador, at 93.
Wilton Benítez's fermented Orange Bourbon from Piendamó, Cauca, in Colombia scores 96 with Coffee Review; his later lots score 94 to 97 through 2026.
Cafe Imports has one Orange Bourbon tested with four Pink Bourbons by geneticist Christophe Montagnon of RD2 Vision; it carries Pink Bourbon's markers.
A Hawaiian "Orange Bourbon Natural" made from red and yellow Bourbon trees ("Red + Yellow = Orange") makes No. 12 on Coffee Review's Top 30 of 2024.

sections.title: One name, several meanings
body: Ozone says the trade usually calls Orange Bourbon a natural colour mutation of Red Bourbon, but that it isn't settled whether the same colour factor as Yellow Bourbon's is involved. Cuvée described its El Salvador lot in 2016 as a natural red × yellow Bourbon hybrid, and a Hawaiian farm uses the name for a coffee made from red and yellow Bourbon trees together.

Pink Bourbon blurs the line too. Intelligentsia notes that Pink Bourbon's cherries are closer to orange than pink, so some people call it Orange Bourbon, and the one Orange Bourbon that Cafe Imports had tested carried Pink Bourbon DNA. A bag that says Orange Bourbon could hold a Bourbon colour form, a red-and-yellow mix, or Pink Bourbon.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Ozone ties it most strongly to El Salvador, and the washed lot Coffee Review rated in 2021 came from the Santa Ana volcano there. In Colombia, Wilton Benítez grows it at Granja Paraíso 92 in Piendamó, Cauca. Ozone describes orange and striped trees at Finca La Huella in Nicaragua, and the 2023 DNA sample came from a producer in Colombia or Costa Rica. No published source says how much is planted anywhere.

family.parentsText: Unsettled: usually called a colour mutation of Red Bourbon; also sold as a red × yellow Bourbon cross or mix; the one sample DNA-tested (2023) carried the markers of Pink Bourbon, an Ethiopian landrace
family.line: Unclear; may overlap with Pink Bourbon

grownIn.text: The tested sample came from a producer in Colombia or Costa Rica; published sources don't say where else it's grown

plant.rust: susceptible to major diseases, like other Bourbons (Sucafina)
plant.altitude: does well at high altitude, like Bourbon in general, says Sucafina

records.name: Oro Azteca
records.summary: Mexico's Catimor, released in 1995 for warm zones and acidic soils.
records.lede: A Catimor that INIFAP, Mexico's national agricultural research institute, released in 1995 after pedigree selection from a Caturra × Timor Hybrid cross. It's high-yielding and suited to warm zones and acidic soils, and World Coffee Research rates its cup potential at high altitude as good, where it rates T8667, a key Catimor line in Central American breeding, low. It is one of the rust-resistant varieties Mexico has used to replant its coffee farms since 2015.

facts.label: released in Mexico by INIFAP
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
(2,000–4,250 ft) where Coffee Hunter says it does best in Mexico
(about 370,000 acres) of Mexican coffee replanted by 2022 under a program whose varieties include Oro Azteca

cup.text: The importer Coffee Hunter describes a pleasant fragrance, medium intensity, a long aftertaste and a lean toward high acidity.
cup.prized: At its best it comes close to Cup of Excellence level: an Oro Azteca from Los Pinos in Zihuateutla, Puebla, was among the national winners at Mexico's 2019 Cup of Excellence, the tier just below the ranked lots, with 86.88 points.
cup.watch: Its reputation: a 2024 review of Geisha in Mexico, citing a 2019 source, says new rust-resistant hybrids such as Oro Azteca, Costa Rica and Marsellesa are considered lower in bean and cup quality than the original varieties.

story.text: INIFAP releases Oro Azteca, a pedigree selection from Timor Hybrid 832/1 × Caturra; Coffee Hunter says it took about 15 years of research.
Mexico starts a national program to renew its coffee farms; by 2022 it has replanted 150,000 ha with 550 million new trees, and INIFAP names Oro Azteca among the varieties.
A washed Oro Azteca from Julia Ortega Carballo's Los Pinos farm in Puebla is a national winner at Mexico's Cup of Excellence, with 86.88 points.
A Los Pinos lot blending Oro Azteca, Costa Rica 95 and Anacafé 14 places 9th among washed coffees at Mexico's Cup of Excellence, with 87.26.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Coffee Hunter says it suits Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla and Veracruz and that it came out of about 15 years of research. WCR recommends it for the warmest zones and for acidic, aluminium-rich soils, and lists it as susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease.

Coffee Hunter gives a best temperature range of 18–24 °C (64–75 °F). WCR suggests 5,000–6,000 trees per hectare with single-stem pruning, rates its outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) as average, and notes that its yield and rust resistance were tested at 23 sites in 15 countries in its international variety trial; how well it resists rust locally depends on which rust races are present.

sections.title: In competitions
body: It turns up rarely and usually in blends. At Mexico's 2024 Cup of Excellence, lots containing Oro Azteca placed 9th among washed coffees (Los Pinos, with Costa Rica 95 and Anacafé 14, 87.26) and among the national winners (Capolcuahutitan, with Costa Rica 95, 87.05), both from Puebla. No Oro Azteca lot was among the ranked 2026 lots.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra
family.line: Pedigree selection by INIFAP in Mexico.

grownIn.text: Mexico: Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla and Veracruz. A 2024 review, citing a 2017 study, puts it with Geisha and Caturra at under 20% in Veracruz, behind Typica, Garnica and Costa Rica at about 20–33%.

plant.rust: intermediate
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Pacas
records.summary: El Salvador's dwarf Bourbon mutant, found on a Pacas farm in 1949.
records.lede: A natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon found in 1949 on a farm owned by the Pacas family in El Salvador's Santa Ana region. Like Caturra and Villa Sarchi, it carries a single-gene change that keeps the plant compact, so farms can plant it closer together and harvest more fruit per hectare. It's about a quarter of El Salvador's coffee and one parent of Pacamara.

facts.label: of El Salvador's coffee, per WCR
compact trees, planted 5,000–6,000 per hectare
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
very highly susceptible to leaf rust

cup.text: Coffee Hunter describes a cup much like Bourbon's but slightly less sweet, with good body, and World Coffee Research calls its quality standard in Central America. Ozone Coffee describes well-made Pacas as sweet, balanced and clean, sometimes with chocolate, caramel, nut or fruit notes; Coffee Review hears the same quiet flowers, stone fruit, berry and gentle citrus in Salvadoran Pacas as in Bourbon.
cup.why: It's Bourbon with one dwarfing gene, so it cups much like Bourbon. Ozone says the exact profile depends heavily on the farm, the altitude and the processing: washed lots lean toward clarity and defined acidity, while honeys and naturals add sweetness, body and fruit.
cup.prized: Sweet, clean, balanced cups that can win: in Honduras's 2025 Cup of Excellence, Pacas took 6 of the 11 places in the traditional-varieties category, including second place at 89.41 points.
cup.watch: It can come across a little less sweet or expressive than Bourbon. Coffee Review calls it usually less distinctive-tasting, and Ozone, tasting both from the same farms, often found the Bourbon slightly more expressive, though some of its most memorable coffees were Pacas.

plant.stature: dwarf/compact, with dense foliage and short internodes
plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, or above 1,300 m (4,250 ft) at El Salvador's latitude

story.text: Found on the Pacas family's farm in Santa Ana, El Salvador.
El Salvador's coffee research institute, ISIC, begins selecting the best plants generation by generation.
ISIC crosses Pacas with Red Maragogipe, a big-bean Typica, beginning Pacamara.
Honduras's coffee institute, IHCAFE, introduces it to Honduras.
Pacas lots take 6 of the 11 traditional-variety places in Honduras's Cup of Excellence, all from Santa Bárbara.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Besides leaf rust, it's susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms). Coffee Hunter adds that it handles wind, sun and drought. Seed is available from Procafé in El Salvador.

sections.title: On the bag
body: In El Salvador, Bourbon is often sold mixed with Pacas, Coffee Review notes, so a Salvadoran bag that says 'Bourbon' or 'Bourbon and Pacas' may hold both. Pacas also gave El Salvador its best-known variety, Pacamara (Pacas × Maragogipe), which is a different plant with very large beans.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Pacas does better in Honduras's Cup of Excellence than at home. In Honduras in 2025, six of the 11 ranked lots in the traditional-varieties category were Pacas, all from Santa Bárbara, with the best at 89.41 points. In El Salvador's 2025 competition, by contrast, only one of 32 ranked lots was Pacas (an anaerobic natural at 87.98), while its offspring Pacamara took 15.

sections.title: The name
body: It's named after the Pacas family, on whose San Rafael farm, in the Santa Ana area of the Apaneca-Ilamatepec mountains, it turned up. In the family's telling, relayed by the importer Coffee Hunter, they first took the high-yielding, oddly sized trees for the famous San Ramón Bourbon hybrid, until observations by Dr. William Cowgill of the University of Florida showed they were a new variety, which was then named Pacas. Coffee Hunter's article dates the find to the 1930s in one place and the 1960s in another; World Coffee Research gives 1949.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural dwarf mutation)

grownIn.text: Mainly El Salvador, where it's about a quarter of the coffee; also Honduras, where IHCAFE brought it in 1974 and where Santa Bárbara's Pacas lots now do well in competition.

records.name: Pache
records.summary: A compact Typica mutation from Guatemalan farms.
records.lede: Pache is a natural single-gene mutation of Typica with a short, compact habit. World Coffee Research says it was found in 1949 on the Brito farm in Santa Cruz Naranjo, Santa Rosa, Guatemala, the farm Sample Coffee also names. It's grown mainly in Guatemala, with some in El Salvador and Honduras.

facts.label: natural mutation, found in Guatemala
found on the Brito farm, Santa Rosa, Guatemala
(3,450–5,500 ft) where Coffee Hunter says it grows well
Sample Coffee calls it highly susceptible to rust and berry disease

cup.text: Usually described as gentle. Coffee Hunter calls it mild or even plain, and Achilles Coffee Roasters describes a balanced, delicate cup that can lean sweet, nutty, fruity or floral. Sample Coffee's Guatemalan lots featuring Pache have listed green apple, pear and plum.
cup.prized: A gentle, balanced cup from a plant that fits more trees per hectare: World Coffee Research sums it up as compact, with medium yield and good quality.
cup.watch: Coffee Hunter's word is "plain": it's subtle rather than vivid.

plant.rust: highly susceptible to the major coffee diseases (WCR); Sample Coffee names leaf rust and coffee berry disease
plant.altitude: high: WCR says it's best above 1,200 m (3,940 ft) where yearly rain is under 2,500 mm, and recommends above 1,400 m (4,590 ft) in Peru

story.text: Pache is found on the Brito farm in Santa Cruz Naranjo, in Guatemala's Santa Rosa department.
Private farms in Guatemala improve it by mass selection (saving seed from the best plants), and it spreads to other regions and countries.
Achilles Coffee Roasters describes it as grown mainly in Guatemala, with some in El Salvador and Honduras.

sections.title: Pache Colis and Pache Enano
body: Coffee Hunter describes Pache Colis, found in Mataquescuintla, Guatemala, where Caturra and Pache grew side by side: a short plant, 0.8–1.25 m (2.6–4.1 ft) tall, with very large berries, sturdy leaves and partial resistance to phoma, a fungal disease. Pache Enano is an especially small Guatemalan plant.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Its short habit lets farms plant densely, about 5,000–6,000 plants per hectare in WCR's guide, and get more coffee per hectare. It bears its first crop in year 4, but WCR calls it highly susceptible to the major coffee diseases, and Sample Coffee names leaf rust and coffee berry disease.

sections.title: Typica or Bourbon?
body: Cafe Imports' variety glossary describes Pache as a dwarf mutation of Bourbon found on a single Guatemalan farm in 1949, though the same entry files it as Typica-related. World Coffee Research, a 2022 genetic study of Yemeni coffee, Sample Coffee and Coffee Hunter all call it a Typica mutation, and WCR's catalog puts it in the Typica-related group.

family.parentsText: Typica (natural mutation)
family.line: A single-gene mutation with a compact habit, found in Guatemala in 1949.

grownIn.text: Mainly Guatemala, also El Salvador and Honduras.

records.name: Papayo
records.summary: A long-cherried Huila coffee whose roots are still disputed.
records.lede: A rare coffee from Huila, Colombia, named because its long, pointed cherries reminded growers of papaya. It was first taken for a Caturra mutation. Importer Sucafina says World Coffee Research testing shows a close relationship to Ethiopian landraces, but a 2025 test by Cenicafé, Colombia's coffee research center, found it 80–97% similar to part of Castillo, so its origin is still open.

facts.label: (4,600–6,550 ft) where most reported lots grow
its DNA match to a component of Castillo in Cenicafé's 2025 test
Jack Simpson won the World Barista Championship with a Papayo in his milk course

cup.text: Ozone, a London roaster, sums up Papayo lots as tropical (mango, pineapple, papaya) and stone-fruity, with jasmine or hibiscus and black tea; some washed ones lean to chocolate and caramel. Sam Klein of Partners Coffee describes intense sweetness and a silky mouthfeel, and Sucafina's Juan Andrés Gutiérrez finds chocolate, dulce de leche and caramel in washed lots, with naturals adding cherry-like fruit.
cup.prized: High-scoring microlots: Gutiérrez says plants at 1,400–2,000 m (4,600–6,550 ft) produce them, and a Papayo was in the milk course of the 2025 world barista champion.
cup.watch: Its large, dense beans take heat slowly: Ozone warns that an aggressive roast leaves the outside and the middle out of step, and Gutiérrez advises a longer development stage, the part of the roast after first crack.

story.text: Miller Bustos of Finca El Mirador in Huila starts planting Papayo on another producer's word about its quality; in 2024 he said that was more than 20 years earlier.
Coffee Review rates an anaerobic Papayo from Finca Lord Baltimore in Pitalito at 94; the listing already calls it an "Ethiopia landrace Papayo variety".
A national survey, later cited by Cenicafé, finds 68 varieties in Colombia, with Geisha, Pink Bourbon and Papayo the ones seen most in competitions and auctions.
Cenicafé compares Papayo with 92 accessions of the Colombian coffee collection using 41 genetic markers and finds 80–97% similarity to a component of Castillo.
Jack Simpson of Australia wins the World Barista Championship in Milan with 643 points, using a Papayo from Finca Zarza in Bruselas, Huila, in his milk course.

sections.title: What the DNA says
body: Sucafina reports that World Coffee Research testing shows a close relationship to Ethiopian landrace material, without a date or details. Some sellers already label it that way: a 2020 Coffee Review listing called it an "Ethiopia landrace Papayo variety".

Ozone reports that Cenicafé's 2025 annual report compared Papayo with 92 accessions in the Colombian coffee collection using 41 genetic markers and found 80–97% similarity to a component of Castillo; Ozone notes that's not a full lineage. The report's summary says DNA sequencing of the main varietals grown in Colombia found several widely planted ones highly similar to components of varieties Cenicafé itself bred.

sections.title: Confusions and look-alikes
body: Papayo is often linked with Ombligón, another Huila coffee, named for its navel-shaped seed: both come from the same area and look alike. World Coffee Research has said it is unlikely they are the same variety and that there is no evidence to confirm a link; it calls for genetic tests of more samples and more field research. Sam Klein of Partners Coffee suggests both could be similar mutations of Pink Bourbon, or of varieties with the same unclear origins; Ozone calls these theories, not established relationships.

How Papayo reached Huila is unknown. Sucafina's Juan Andrés Gutiérrez relays a rumour of an abandoned coffee research farm in Huila, near Acevedo by Ozone's account, that once grew varieties from around the world and left its plants behind. Sucafina's glossary says Ombligón may come from an abandoned Cenicafé research centre in Huila, or be another name for Pacamara.

sections.title: In competitions and reviews
body: Jack Simpson used Ombligón at the 2023 World Barista Championship and won the 2025 title with a Papayo from Jhonatan Gasca's Finca Zarza in his milk course and a Panamanian Geisha from Finca Deborah in his espresso.

Coffee Review has rated Papayo lots at 94 to 95: a washed lot from Finca Villa Betulia in Huila (2024) with white peach, pink grapefruit zest and lilac and a very silky body, and a koji-fermented lot from Wilton Benítez in Cauca (2023) with lychee, passion fruit, bergamot and jasmine. Ozone says Papayo works across a broad range of processes: washed lots can be clean and sweet with clear fruit and florals, while naturals add body and fruit.

family.parentsText: Unresolved: once thought a Caturra mutation; tests point to Ethiopian landrace material or to part of Castillo
family.line: Found on farms in Huila; origin unconfirmed

grownIn.text: Mainly Huila, especially around Acevedo and Pitalito; smaller plantings in Cauca, Tolima and Quindío

plant.altitude: 1,400–2,000 m (4,600–6,550 ft) for the high-scoring lots, says Sucafina's Juan Andrés Gutiérrez

records.name: Parainema
records.summary: Honduras's Sarchimor that set a Cup of Excellence price record.
records.lede: A Sarchimor selected in Honduras by IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, from the line T5296 and released in 2004. World Coffee Research rates it very high-yielding and highly rust-resistant, and it has done well in competition: Parainemas won Honduras's Cup of Excellence in 2015 and 2017, and the 2017 winner sold for a then-record $124.50 a pound.

facts.label: released by IHCAFE
2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winner, then a record for any CoE coffee
points for that lot
winning lots in the 2026 Honduras Cup of Excellence's own Parainema category

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind reported the 2017 Honduran winner as vibrant and lingering with a velvety mouthfeel, and its acidity as refined, crisp and citric; the jury's flavor list ran from green apple, jasmine and bergamot to lemon peel, peach and blueberry. That's one lot, though; WCR rates the variety's quality potential at high altitude as good.

feel.acidity: refined, crisp, citric, in the 2017 winner

cup.prized: Its competition record: Cup of Excellence wins in Honduras in 2015 and 2017, and since at least 2025 a Honduran category of its own; the 2026 one was topped by a natural from La Loma in Santa Bárbara at 89.14 points.
cup.watch: Not every farm suits it: a grower in Chiapas told Perfect Daily Grind it didn't adapt to his farm's excess humidity.

story.text: IHCAFE starts developing it.
IHCAFE releases Parainema, a pedigree selection of T5296.
Oscar Daniel Ramírez Valerio's washed Parainema from Finca El Laurel, El Paraíso, wins the Honduras Cup of Excellence and sells for $124.50 a pound.
As a new rust strain breaks Lempira's resistance, La Prensa reports that Parainema shows 100% resistance to it, against 80% for IHCAFE 90.
The Honduras Cup of Excellence runs a separate Parainema category, won by a washed lot from El Rubí in Santa Bárbara (89.65) in 2025; in 2026, as Parainema Catracha, it has ten winning lots.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as resistant to some root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne, worms that attack roots) but not to Pratylenchus, another nematode group, and tolerant of coffee berry disease. It suits low to medium altitudes and needs plenty of fertilizer.

IHCAFE technicians caution that rust resistance in improved varieties isn't permanent, Bloomberg Línea reported in 2022; the same report said producers in Matagalpa, Nicaragua, had started planting it.

sections.title: In competitions
body: In Honduras it now competes mostly against itself. The 2025 Parainema category had six ranked lots, washed and natural, from Santa Bárbara and El Paraíso, led by El Rubí at 89.65; seven of the ten 2026 winners came from Santa Bárbara, with others from El Paraíso, La Paz and Comayagua. The 2017 winner, grown at 1,400 m (4,600 ft), scored 91.81.

Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence has had Parainema naturals as well: Las Neblinas in Nueva Segovia placed 6th in the natural-and-honey category in 2025 (88.18), and Los Suyates in Dipilto 3rd in 2026 (89.19).

family.parentsText: Selection of T5296 (Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2)
family.line: Pedigree selection by IHCAFE in Honduras.

grownIn.text: Honduras, where 7 of the 10 winners in the 2026 Cup of Excellence's Parainema category came from Santa Bárbara; in Nicaragua, Matagalpa farmers had begun planting it by late 2022, and naturals from Nueva Segovia have placed in the national Cup of Excellence.

plant.rust: highly resistant
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Paraíso
records.summary: EPAMIG's yellow-fruited, rust-resistant dwarf for Brazil's mountain coffee farms.
records.lede: A short, yellow-fruited Brazilian variety, Paraíso MG H 419-1, from a cross of Yellow Catuaí and the Timor Hybrid. Work on it began at the Federal University of Viçosa and continued at the São Sebastião do Paraíso research station of EPAMIG, Minas Gerais's agricultural research company. EPAMIG recommends it for mountain coffee farming, and its lots have won top places at the Cerrado Mineiro region's coffee awards.

facts.label: ripe cherries
average (60 kg bags) over 106 farm harvests, statistically level with Catuaí
points, winning the natural category of the 8th Cerrado coffee awards
a short tree, planted 0.5–0.6 m apart in the row

family.parentsText: Yellow Catuaí IAC 30 × Timor Hybrid UFV 445-46
family.line: From plant 3 of cross H 419, begun at the Federal University of Viçosa and selected at EPAMIG's São Sebastião do Paraíso station.

grownIn.text: Minas Gerais, Brazil: a 2021 study interviewed growers in 12 municipalities, from Capitólio to Sacramento, and estimated about 600 ha (1,480 acres) planted in the state, with the largest areas around São Sebastião do Paraíso; its lots win awards in the Cerrado Mineiro. A Berlin roaster has also sold a lot from São Paulo state.

plant.rust: resistant; also resistant to the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne exigua
plant.altitude: recommended for mountain coffee farms; no metre range published

cup.text: Little is published about Paraíso's cup beyond competition results. The Barn, a Berlin roaster, describes a natural lot from a small São Paulo estate as malty and creamy, like almond butter, turning to orange marmalade and lemon zest as it cools, with low acidity and a full texture.
cup.prized: Competition form: Paraíso lots have won the natural category (90.33 points) and taken first and third in the pulped-natural category of the Cerrado Mineiro's coffee awards, and Minas Gerais's state news agency calls it a reference for cup quality.

story.text: At the Federal University of Viçosa, breeders crossed Yellow Catuaí IAC 30 with Timor Hybrid UFV 445-46, the cross EPAMIG gives for its MGS Paraíso 2; Paraíso MG H 419-1 has the same two parents.
An EPAMIG technical circular rated Paraíso MG H 419-1 resistant to the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne exigua: the worms multiplied far less in its roots than in Mundo Novo's.
A study of 25 commercial farms, covering 106 harvests, showed it yields level with Catuaí and noted farmers' complaints about cherries that cling to the branch.
At the 9th Prêmio de Cafés do Cerrado, announced in November, Paraíso lots took first and third place in the pulped-natural category.

A lot of its sister cultivar MGS Paraíso 2, from Guima Café in the Cerrado Mineiro, won the 8th Ernesto Illy International Coffee Award; Guima Café's technician said it was the first Brazilian coffee to take first place there.

sections.title: On the farm
body: In a study of commercial fields published in 2021, farmers named rust resistance and vigour as its strengths. Their main complaint (44% of farmers) was that ripe cherries cling hard to the branch at picking; some also reported slow early growth and plants toppling over, and 28% still preferred traditional varieties for new plantings. Ripening was intermediate to late, and most farmers still sprayed fungicides.

EPAMIG notes that its short side branches allow trees to be planted closely in the row, 0.5–0.6 m (1.6–2 ft) apart. Minas Gerais's state news agency has reported that it isn't adapted to machine harvesting, though it is a reference for cup quality. A 2013 Revista Cultivar article on EPAMIG's releases also lists it as resistant to root-knot nematodes (tiny worms that make galls on roots), and an EPAMIG circular from 2012 reports the same for Meloidogyne exigua, one of these worms; its authors think the resistance comes from the Timor Hybrid.

sections.title: Awards
body: A Paraíso from Fazenda Londrina in Coromandel won the natural category of the 8th Prêmio de Cafés do Cerrado with 90.33 points. At the 9th edition, announced in November 2021, Paraíso lots from Fazenda Cinco Estrelas in Patrocínio and Fazenda M&F Coffee Bioma Café in Campos Altos placed first and third in the pulped-natural category (skin removed, dried with some fruit left on), with EPAMIG's MGS Paraíso 2 in second.

sections.title: Paraíso or Paraíso 2?
body: EPAMIG sells two cultivars with the name, and a bag that just says 'Paraíso' could hold either. Paraíso MG H 419-1, this page's variety, is the one Minas Gerais's state news agency describes as suited to mountain coffee farming. MGS Paraíso 2 comes from the same two parents but is aimed at mechanized farms: a short, yellow-fruited, rust-resistant tree whose cherries ripen semi-early and evenly, with over 80% of its beans on screen 16 or larger (6.4 mm).

In EPAMIG's 2019–2020 trials in the Sul de Minas, MGS Paraíso 2 averaged 37.0 bags per hectare against 31.1 for Catuaí Vermelho IAC 99, and its cups averaged 83.2 points with lively acidity, a dense, creamy body and high sweetness. Cerrado Mineiro nursery owners told Revista Cultivar in 2021 that it had become their most requested seedling, and when Guima Café asked EPAMIG which Paraíso best suits the Cerrado, the answer was Paraíso 2.

records.name: Ruiru 11
records.summary: Kenya's compact, disease-resistant hybrid of 1985, made by hand-pollination
records.lede: Kenya's answer to the 1968 coffee berry disease (CBD) epidemic, which cost the country about half its crop. Released in 1985, it is not one plant line but a composite: a mix of sibling first-generation (F1) hybrids from Catimor mother trees hand-pollinated by a complex male parent bred from K7, SL28, N39, Rume Sudan and others.

facts.label: released by Kenya's coffee research station at Ruiru
a mix of F1 hybrid siblings, not one line
so it can be planted far more densely than SL trees
WCR's rating of its quality at high altitude

cup.text: Royal Coffee says it has a poor reputation with specialty cuppers, who expect the flavor and sweetness of Kenya's SL varieties. In 2008 Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids said several Kenyan samples showed the signs of a well-constructed modern hybrid: sturdy but simple, with good acidity, body and balance but less aromatic nuance. He added that he had never cupped Ruiru 11 side by side with SL28 and couldn't generalize. Single-variety lots exist: an estate in Meru that sells a washed Ruiru 11 on its own lists blackberry, honey, vanilla, blackcurrant and lemon, with an apricot and sugar-cane aftertaste.

feel.acidity: good; fruity and juicy in a light-roasted Meru lot

cup.why: Breeders bred cup quality into its male parent from N39, SL28, SL34 and Bourbon, and coffee berry disease resistance from Rume Sudan, Timor Hybrid lines and K7; the Catimor mother adds compactness and more rust and coffee berry disease resistance. A 2013 Kenyan study of 34 sibling families of Ruiru 11 by Bernard Gichimu and colleagues found that most cup-quality traits had either no link or a negative link with resistance to coffee berry disease.
cup.prized: Growers value it for its productivity and its resistance to coffee berry disease and leaf rust. In Guatemala, naturals of Ruiru 11 from Finca Pampojila on Lake Atitlán placed 7th in the Cup of Excellence's exotic natural and honey category in 2025 (88.46) and 2026 (87.36).
cup.watch: Sucafina's Kenyan team says it must be picked at a near-purple ripeness to do well in the cup. Some in the trade wonder whether Kenya's blackcurrant character has faded as farms moved from SL trees to Ruiru 11; Sucafina doesn't confirm it.

story.text: A coffee berry disease epidemic costs Kenya about half its production.
The Ruiru research station starts breeding for CBD resistance in a compact tree.
Ruiru 11 is released; it stays Kenya's most widely distributed variety into the early 2020s.
Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids writes that specialty buyers have long feared Ruiru 11 as a "shadowy threat", and finds Kenyan samples with signs of a modern hybrid sturdy but simple.
Batian, a tall variety drawn from lines behind Ruiru 11's male parent, is released.
A natural Ruiru 11 from Finca Pampojila in San Lucas Tolimán places 7th in its category at Guatemala's Cup of Excellence two years running.
Royal Coffee reports that Batian has overtaken it as the most-planted tree in Kenya.

sections.title: How the seed is made
body: Breeders hand-pollinate the Catimor mother trees with pollen from the male-parent lines, then hand farmers the resulting F1 seed as one mixed variety. Hand pollination is slow, and WCR says it has made it hard to grow enough seed to meet demand.
Some Kenyan farmers graft it onto SL rootstock, so the SL trees' wide root system makes up for Ruiru 11's shallower roots.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with large beans, very high yields and an average outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) that needs a lot of fertilizer and bears its first crop in year two. It suggests 2,000–3,000 plants per hectare with multiple-stem pruning (several stems per tree). Gichimu gives Kenya's spacing for it as 2 m × 2 m, against 2.75 m × 2.75 m for the traditional varieties.

Sucafina says it copes less well with drought than the SL trees and needs more intensive feeding. Kenya's Coffee Research Institute director, Elijah Gichuru, has urged farmers to graft Ruiru 11 or Batian onto old stems rather than replant, which takes almost three years, and says the disease resistance saves around 30% of production costs by cutting spraying.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: On a Kenyan bag, Ruiru 11 is usually one name in a list: Sucafina says most lots blend SL trees, Ruiru 11 and sometimes Batian, because most farms are too small to keep varieties apart. Lots of Ruiru 11 alone do exist, such as one from an estate in Meru. Guatemala's competition lists spell it Ruiru-11 or Rui-11.
Batian is its closest relative: a tall variety selected from the lines behind Ruiru 11's male parent and released in 2010, which Royal Coffee calls a reformulation of Ruiru 11.

family.parentsText: Catimor (mother) × multi-cross male parent from K7, SL28, N39, Rume Sudan and others
family.line: Hand-pollinated F1 seed released as a composite by the Coffee Research Foundation, now part of KALRO

grownIn.text: Mainly Kenya. Royal Coffee, which gives no figures, said in 2026 that it was the country's most widely distributed variety from the 1980s to the early 2020s and that Batian is now the most-planted tree; Sucafina reported in 2020 that most Kenyan farms still keep SL trees alongside Ruiru 11 and, increasingly, Batian. It is also grown in Guatemala, where naturals from Lake Atitlán placed in the 2025 and 2026 Cup of Excellence and a washed lot from Santa Rosa was a 2026 national winner.

plant.rust: tolerant to leaf rust; resistant to coffee berry disease
plant.altitude: wide range: above 1,000 m (3,300 ft) near the equator

records.name: Rume Sudan
records.summary: An old South Sudanese landrace prized by breeders and baristas.
records.lede: An old landrace collected in 1941 from relict trees at Rume, on South Sudan's Boma Plateau near the Ethiopian border. It yields too little for most farms, but breeders have used it for disease resistance: World Coffee Research credits it, with other parents, for the coffee berry disease resistance in Kenya's Ruiru 11, and it's in Batian's family tree too. Saša Šestić won the 2015 World Barista Championship with a Sudan Rume from Colombia.

facts.label: A. S. Thomas collects its seed on South Sudan's Boma Plateau
a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume from Colombia won the World Barista Championship
why few farms grow it commercially
of Kenya's disease-resistant Ruiru 11 and Batian

family.parentsText: Wild South Sudanese Arabica from the Boma Plateau; no known parents
family.line: Seed collected by A. S. Thomas in 1941 at Rume and sent to research stations in Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda, then on to CATIE in Costa Rica
family.type: South Sudan landrace (the wild Boma coffee it was collected from is a genetic group distinct from Ethiopian landraces; gene-bank Rume Sudan only partly matches it)

grownIn.text: Today mostly a handful of specialty farms in Colombia, notably Café Granja La Esperanza in Valle del Cauca. Rume itself has lost its forest: a 2021 study reports none left there on a 2012 visit, though wild Arabica, in poor health, survives nearby at Barbuk.

plant.stature: fairly compact, around 2 m (6.6 ft) or more
plant.rust: reports differ: Sucafina says it resists leaf rust and coffee berry disease better than Bourbon or Typica; Ozone says it resists coffee berry disease strongly but is susceptible to leaf rust
plant.beanSize: elongated, says Ozone (its collector, A. S. Thomas, noted 'bold beans' at nearby Barbuk)
plant.altitude: high: about 1,700–1,800 m (5,600–5,900 ft), says Ozone

cup.text: Sweet, bright and aromatic, often with florals and spice. Two washed Sudan Rumes that Coffee Review rated highly, both from Café Granja La Esperanza in Valle del Cauca, Colombia, showed cardamom, black tea, bergamot and honeysuckle (94, 2020) and lychee, marjoram, pink peppercorn and cocoa nib (95, 2025). Šestić's carbonic-macerated lot gave raspberry and white chocolate in milk.
cup.why: Ozone says processing moves it a long way: washed lots are transparent, letting acidity and aromatics show; naturals add weight and fruit; carbonic maceration pushes it to raspberry and candy-like notes.
cup.prized: Its sweetness and layered spice and florals, and its rarity.
cup.watch: Low yields keep it scarce and pricey, and gene-bank "Rume Sudan" may not be the original wild coffee: in a 2021 study only one of three of Thomas's accessions at CATIE carried South Sudan's marker allele.

story.text: Botanist Auguste Chevalier makes the first recorded find of wild Arabica on the Boma Plateau.

In December, A. S. Thomas of Uganda's agriculture department collects seed at Rume, from coffee left standing in maize fields, and at Barbuk; it goes to breeding stations in Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda.
Rume Sudan reaches CATIE, the research center in Costa Rica, which still holds two accessions of it.
Centroamericano, an F1 hybrid of the Sarchimor T5296 with Rume Sudan, is released to Central American farmers; Batian, with Rume Sudan in its ancestry, is released in Kenya.
Saša Šestić wins the World Barista Championship with a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume from Camilo Merizalde's Finca Las Nubes in Colombia.
A DNA study finds Boma's wild coffee is its own genetic group, separate from Ethiopia's, and reports that Rume's forest was already gone on a 2012 visit.

sections.title: Genetics: what DNA tests found
body: In April 2012 Sarada Krishnan, Aaron Davis and Tim Schilling collected wild coffee on the Boma Plateau. Its DNA was read at the Denver Botanic Gardens and Nevada Genomics in the US and by the ADNiD lab of Qualtech in France; Krishnan analysed the South Sudan samples, and Solène Pruvot-Woehl and Christophe Montagnon compared them with Ethiopian landraces held at CATIE and with Yemeni coffees. In 2021 they reported that Boma's coffee forms a South Sudan group distinct from Ethiopian landraces, Yemen's coffees and the world's cultivars, and concluded that, in addition to Ethiopia, the Boma Plateau is a center of origin of Arabica. So 'Ethiopian Sudan Rume', as Perfect Daily Grind wrote, is not quite right.

They also tested the three accessions from Thomas's collection kept at CATIE. Only one, Rume Sudan T.02724, carried one of the two alleles specific to South Sudan's wild trees, and the authors think even it was cross-pollinated before it reached CATIE. The other two, a second Rume Sudan and a Barbuk Sudan, carried neither, which they put down to more cross-pollination or mislabelling.

sections.title: In breeding
body: Breeders prize it for resistance to coffee berry disease, a fungus that rots green cherries, and Kenyan programmes used it heavily. World Coffee Research lists it among the parents behind Ruiru 11's resistance and in Batian's family tree, and it is one parent of Centroamericano, an F1 hybrid released in Central America in 2010.

Sucafina calls SL28 one of its best-known descendants, but that can't be right: World Coffee Research says SL28 was selected in Kenya in 1935, from a Tanzanian population, six years before Thomas collected Rume Sudan. The two meet only in later Kenyan crosses such as Ruiru 11 and Batian.

records.name: S795
records.summary: India's 1940s Arabica with Liberica genes, also Indonesia's 'Jember'.
records.lede: One of India's most widely grown Arabicas, released in 1945–46 by the Coffee Board of India's research station at Balehonnur and later spread across Indonesia, where it is often called 'Jember' or 'Lini S'. Its rust resistance comes from Liberica genes and from Kent, not from the Timor Hybrid: its parent S288 was selected from a natural Arabica × Liberica hybrid, and its other parent, Kent, was prized for rust tolerance.

facts.label: released in India as Selection 3
top lots at Indonesia's first Cup of Excellence, in 2021, contained it
of coffee in a 2009-harvest survey on Flores, the most of any variety
a vigorous tree with bronze young leaves

family.parentsText: S288 × Kent; S288 is an Indian line selected from S26, a natural Arabica × Liberica hybrid
family.line: Bred by R.L. Narasimhaswamy at the Balehonnur Coffee Research Station, then improved by mass selection for yield, rust tolerance, and bean and cup quality. Indonesia's official description calls it a selection from fifth-generation offspring of line S 288-23 backcrossed to Kent, introduced from India.

grownIn.text: Widely grown in India and Indonesia; Sweet Maria's calls it one of the main varieties on Sulawesi, it led a 2009 variety survey on Flores, and it is among the varieties farmers use in West Java's Java Preanger area; in India, the Coffee Board's 2017 geographical-indication application for Bababudangiri Arabica lists it first among that area's main varieties, with Sln.9 and Cauvery.

plant.stature: tall and spreading, about 3 m (10 ft) unpruned
plant.yield: high (WCR); 700–1,200 kg/ha in India per Tamil Nadu Agricultural University's crop guide; 1–1.5 t/ha in Indonesia's official description
plant.rust: susceptible in India, where the Coffee Board says it lost its resistance after 30–35 years; highly resistant in WCR's 15-country trial; moderately resistant in Indonesia's official description
plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator; above 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude; in Indonesia, from 700 m (2,300 ft)

cup.text: In a 2009-harvest study on Flores, tasters most often ranked S795 their favourite, describing a balanced cup with strong sweet tones. Single O tastes maple syrup, caramel and brown sugar in it.
cup.prized: Sweetness and balance, and it keeps turning up in winning lots: 12 of the 26 top coffees at Indonesia's first Cup of Excellence, in 2021, contained it, and an S.795/Catimor lot from Tata Coffee's Gorghully Estate placed fifth among specialty Arabicas at India's 2013 Flavour of India competition.
cup.watch: In Coffee Review's 2001 tasting of Indian coffees, three washed S795 samples scored 77–81: mostly sweet but plain, and two went flat as they cooled.

story.text: India released S288, the Liberica-carrying parent line, as Selection 1.
S795 was released as Selection 3.
Its introduction to Indonesia began through the Jember research station in East Java.

The Coffee Board of India told the International Coffee Organization that S.795, the main planting stock of India's small growers, had become very susceptible to leaf rust after 30–35 years in the field.
Twelve of the top 26 coffees at Indonesia's first Cup of Excellence contained S795.

sections.title: The rust story
body: WCR rates S795 susceptible to rust in India, where most of it grows, yet highly resistant across its trial at 23 sites in 15 countries. The difference is the fungus: India has the world's largest concentration of rust races (strains), and a variety that resists rust in one place may not in another. Sweet Maria's likewise reports that it had some rust resistance but has widely lost it.

India's own experience shows the decline. In a 2006 proposal to the International Coffee Organization, the Coffee Board of India said S.795, the planting stock of the small growers who make up 98% of India's coffee growers, had become very susceptible to leaf rust after 30–35 years of doing well in the field, with attacks that can strip the plants of all their leaves. A 1994 review of India's coffee germplasm gives S795 the resistance factors SH2, SH3 and SH5.
Its resistance genes still matter: Oil Slick Coffee notes that researchers have used the SH3 gene from S795 to pass on highly effective rust resistance.

sections.title: Many names
body: In Indonesia it is called Jember, after the research station that supplied it, or Lini S. Sweet Maria's notes that some say 'Jember' really refers to its parent S288, which has turned up on Sulawesi but not Sumatra.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University's crop guide gives Indian yields of 700–1,200 kg per hectare, with bold beans, 75% of them in the top (A) grade.

Indonesia's official variety description (IAARD, 2018) calls it a tall, spreading tree, about 3 m (10 ft) if unpruned, with brown young leaves, cherries that ripen unevenly to a deep red, and a 'fairly good' cup. It yields 1–1.5 tonnes per hectare at 2,000–2,500 trees, grows from 700 m (2,300 ft) up, somewhat tolerates light shade and poor soils, and stays productive for about 25 years. The agriculture ministry's 2010 growing guide adds that it resists rust above 1,000 m (3,300 ft) but only moderately below 900 m (2,950 ft), and that its large beans are not always even in size.

records.name: Sarchimor
records.summary: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid: the rust-resistant family behind Parainema.
records.lede: The other big Timor Hybrid family: compact Villa Sarchi crossed with the Timor Hybrid in Portugal in 1967. Like Catimor it's a group, not one variety, and its offspring include Honduras's Parainema, Nicaragua's Marsellesa and Brazil's Obatã.

facts.label: first cross, the hybrid H361, made at CIFC in Portugal
the name its population got at CATIE in Turrialba, Costa Rica
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude for T5296

cup.text: Opinions split. Sweet Maria's finds the cup can show green or herbal flavors, while the Costa Rican consultant Jorge Ramírez Rojas told Perfect Daily Grind that its base is similar to Caturra and Catuaí, and Coffee Hunter says it cups well at low and medium altitudes.
cup.why: Perfect Daily Grind notes that cup quality depends heavily on altitude and conditions, and that in poorer settings the Timor Hybrid side shows more.
cup.prized: Some newer Sarchimors have won quality awards, says the Chiapas grower Tomás Edelmann; a Parainema set a Cup of Excellence price record in Honduras in 2017. Honduras's 2026 Cup of Excellence ran a separate Parainema category, whose top lot, a natural from La Loma in Santa Bárbara, scored 89.14.
cup.watch: Green or herbal flavors.

story.text: CIFC crosses Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 with compact Villa Sarchi; the hybrid, H361, is nicknamed Sarchimor.
H361 goes into field trials, and Brazil's IAC registers the first-generation hybrid of the same 1967 cross as IAC 1669.
PROMECAFE, a Central American research cooperative, forms to fight leaf rust.
National selections arrive: Obatã in Brazil (2000), Parainema in Honduras (2004) and Marsellesa in Nicaragua (2009).
A washed Parainema wins Honduras's Cup of Excellence and sells for a record $124.50 a pound.
Honduras's Cup of Excellence holds a separate Parainema category; ten Parainema lots place, scoring 87.50 to 89.14.

sections.title: The family
body: Selections from T5296 include Parainema (Honduras), Cuscatleco (El Salvador), Limani (Puerto Rico), and Obatã, Tupi and IAPAR 59 (Brazil). Marsellesa, picked in Nicaragua, comes from the same Timor Hybrid 832/2 × Villa Sarchi cross. CATIE in Costa Rica handed the material on to breeding programs across Latin America.
It also feeds the newer F1 hybrids (first-generation crosses) made with Ethiopian landraces: Centroamericano is Rume Sudan × T5296.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes T5296 as well-adapted to medium altitudes but not uniform: its plants aren't stable from one generation to the next, so it isn't recommended to farmers as is. A grower and a consultant interviewed by Perfect Daily Grind say Sarchimors are vigorous, with big leaves and beans, but need a lot of fertilizer.

sections.title: Rust: holding up, with doubts
body: In Honduras, the rust race that broke Lempira, a Catimor, in 2016–17 didn't break Parainema: an IHCAFE study found varieties such as Parainema carry a resistance gene, SH8, that Lempira lacks, and IHCAFE staff put Parainema's resistance to the new strain at 100% in 2017.

Doubts are growing all the same. In a 2023 Perfect Daily Grind article on El Salvador's Cuscatleco, the agronomist and cupper Rafael Castillo said the resistance of Catimors and Sarchimors has been questioned in recent years, with isolated producers reporting rust and other diseases.

family.parentsText: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 (CIFC hybrid H361)
family.line: Crossed at CIFC in Portugal in 1967, then selected by national programs across the Americas.

grownIn.text: Selected and grown across Central America, Mexico, Brazil and Puerto Rico.

plant.rust: intermediate (T5296)
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Sidra
records.summary: Ecuador's competition favorite: sold as Typica × Bourbon, possibly Ethiopian.
records.lede: A coffee from Pichincha, in northern Ecuador, long described as a cross of Typica and Bourbon. Reported DNA tests point instead to Ethiopian landrace roots, though that evidence is second-hand and unpublished. It became a competition star after Jooyeon Jeon won the 2019 World Barista Championship with a Sidra from La Palma y El Tucán in Colombia.

facts.label: Jooyeon Jeon won the World Barista Championship with Sidra
(5,400–5,900 ft) where it's usually grown
La Palma y El Tucán in Colombia planted its first Sidra trees, about 1,800 of them
and highly susceptible to coffee berry disease, say growers

cup.text: Importer Cole Torode describes ripe stone fruit, citrus, orange blossom and white grape; a former La Palma y El Tucán producer finds honey, malt and red apple with mild citrus acidity. Jonathan Ramírez, Ecuador's 2018 barista champion, points to an unusual menthol note.
cup.why: Ozone says processing drives most of the range: washed lots give the cleanest read (jasmine, white grape, orange blossom), naturals add peach and red berry, and long anaerobic ferments push toward cherry and red wine. Sweetness is the trait that survives every process.
cup.prized: Its sweetness and florals, and a strong competition record: World Barista and World Brewers Cup winners have used it since 2019.
cup.watch: The label: what's sold as Sidra may be a different plant. And long anaerobic ferments push it toward cherry and red wine, away from the florals of a washed lot.

sections.title: What the DNA says
body: Sidra was first reported as a Typica × Bourbon cross, and importers still describe it that way, but no test is cited for it. Some farmers and roasters had samples tested and were told it resembles Ethiopian heirloom coffees; other tests reportedly gave different parents. None of these results has been published in detail.

Perfect Daily Grind's Spanish edition reports that World Coffee Research found Sidra to be fully landrace; its English edition quotes World Coffee Research as saying Sidra may lack a clear identity and could be several varieties sold under one name. One unproven story traces it to a since-closed Nestlé breeding station in Pichincha that worked with Ethiopian and Bourbon coffees.

Ozone Coffee reports a 2026 peer-reviewed study in Frontiers in Plant Science of plants bought as Sidra on one Ecuadorian farm: two matched Sidra reference material inside a "Core Ethiopia" genetic group, and a third matched Batian, a Kenyan variety. One farm can't settle what every Sidra is, but it shows how loose the name is.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Sidra's fame comes from the world championships. Cole Torode placed fifth at the 2018 World Barista Championship with a natural Sidra from La Palma y El Tucán, then third in 2019, the year Jooyeon Jeon won with Sidra from the same farm. Anthony Douglas won the 2022 World Barista Championship with a Sidra from El Diviso fermented without oxygen for 80 hours before drying, and Carlos Medina won the 2023 World Brewers Cup with a natural Sidra.
Several of these lots were fermented hard; Ozone calls a washed lot the cleanest read on the variety itself.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Growers say it does best in shade; Pepe Jijón of Finca Soledad in Imbabura says it needs shade and that some think it first grew in forest. It bears well but has no resistance to leaf rust, and La Palma y El Tucán reports trouble with coffee berry disease and Ceratocystis. The best-known plantings are specialist farms.

In Ecuador it's grown in Pichincha, Loja, Imbabura, Napo, Azuay and Chimborazo, with new plantings in Morona Santiago, El Oro and Zamora; Finca Soledad grows it at 1,515 m (4,970 ft), below the usual range.

family.parentsText: Sold as Typica × Bourbon; reported DNA tests point to Ethiopian landrace roots (second-hand, unpublished)
family.line: Origin unconfirmed; possibly a former Nestlé research station in Pichincha

grownIn.text: Mainly Ecuador (Pichincha, Loja, Imbabura and others) and Colombia; also planted in Honduras, Peru and Panama

plant.stature: tall, up to about 4 m (13 ft), with thick trunks
plant.rust: not resistant; La Palma y El Tucán also reports high susceptibility to coffee berry disease and to Ceratocystis, a canker fungus

story.text: Sidra reportedly comes out of a Nestlé breeding station in Pichincha, Ecuador, that never released its varieties; seed spreads to farms, and Ecuadorian growers credit Olger Rogel with introducing it.
La Palma y El Tucán in Cundinamarca, Colombia, plants about 1,800 Sidra trees, one of the first commercial plantings; it adds about 4,300 more in 2015.
Jooyeon Jeon of South Korea wins the World Barista Championship with a Sidra from La Palma y El Tucán; Cole Torode places third with Sidra from the same farm.
Anthony Douglas wins the World Barista Championship with an anaerobic natural Sidra from Néstor Lasso's El Diviso in Huila, Colombia.
Carlos Medina of Chile wins the World Brewers Cup with a natural Sidra from Café Granja La Esperanza's Finca Potosí, in Valle del Cauca.

records.name: Sigarar Utang
records.summary: North Sumatra's fast-cropping farm selection; the name means 'repay the debt'.
records.lede: A Timor Hybrid-based variety from North Sumatra whose Batak name means 'repay the debt', a nod to how quickly and heavily it crops. Local accounts trace it to a farm at Batu Gajah village in Humbang Hasundutan regency in 1988, and Indonesia's agriculture ministry endorsed it in 2005.
