Its exact parentage is murky: Royal Coffee says the information around it is full of misinformation.

facts.label: when farmers say it first turned up, in North Sumatra
endorsed by Indonesia's agriculture ministry
to mature, and high-yielding
fruiting, says Single O

family.parentsText: Arabica × Timor Hybrid selection 831, as usually reported; genetic testing suggests the Arabica was a Typica (Blawan Pasumah), and Indonesia's official description suspects a natural cross of a Typica of that type with a Catimor
family.line: A farmer's field selection, not a breeding-program cross; other accounts name Caturra or Bourbon as the Arabica parent.

grownIn.text: Indonesia: selected in Humbang Hasundutan, North Sumatra, where a 2017 Antara news report calls it the district farmers' mainstay crop, and grown across Sumatra and Java, per Single O; West Java has an official seed garden for it at Pangalengan.

plant.stature: semi-dwarf, with very active side branching
plant.yield: high; crops quickly, and year-round per Single O; the official description gives about 1.5 t/ha on average (0.8–2.3) at 1,600 trees/ha
plant.rust: moderately resistant (official description); also moderately susceptible to the coffee berry borer and susceptible to the burrowing nematode R. similis
plant.altitude: above 1,000 m (3,300 ft)

cup.text: Little tasting detail is published for it on its own. Indonesia's official variety description rates its cup 'good', the head of Humbang Hasundutan's agriculture office said in 2017 that its quality is better than other types, and Single O finds it more intense, with more mouthfeel, than Andungsari. One blended example: Coffee Review gave 94 points in 2020 to a washed lot from the Koetintji Barokah cooperative in Kerinci, Jambi (Sumatra), grown from Andungsari and Sigarar Utang: jasmine, white peach, almond nougat and sandalwood, with bold, juicy acidity and a silky body.

story.text: Spotted among the coffee of Opung Sopan Boru Siregar (Sweet Maria's records 'Opung Opan') at Batu Gajah village, Humbang Hasundutan, about 1,400 m (4,600 ft) up; the official description and Royal Coffee place the village in Paranginan, in the Lintong area, and the district agriculture office names Paranginan district.
ICCRI reportedly introduced it more widely.
Indonesia's Ministry of Agriculture endorsed it, by a decree dated 12 April 2005.
A 2-hectare mother garden for its seed at Margamulya, Pangalengan, in West Java (1,510–1,550 m, 4,950–5,090 ft) was designated by ministry decree; it yields about 3.1 million seeds a year.

An Antara news report called it the mainstay crop of Humbang Hasundutan's farmers, and the head of the district agriculture office, Junter Marbun, said its quality is better and it suits the export market.

sections.title: A tangled pedigree
body: Royal Coffee gives it as Arabica × Timor Hybrid selection 831, but notes genetic testing suggests a Typica called Blawan Pasumah crossed with the Timor Hybrid, and that it clusters closely with Ateng. Single O lists Caturra × Timor Hybrid 831, and Sweet Maria's records it as an improved Ateng selection with Bourbon in it, while doubting such details for a farmer's selection.

Indonesia's official variety description (IAARD, 2018) suspects a natural cross between a Typica of the BLP (Blawan Pasumah) type and a Catimor, and says only three of the original trees are still alive.

sections.title: Growing it
body: The official description calls it a semi-dwarf tree with very active side branching, dark green older leaves and reddish-brown young ones, and bright red ripe cherries with large beans. It averages about 1.5 tonnes per hectare (0.8–2.3) at 1,600 trees, suits sites above 1,000 m (3,300 ft) with evenly spread rainfall, and stays productive for about 20 years. It is rated moderately resistant to leaf rust, moderately susceptible to the coffee berry borer and susceptible to the burrowing nematode Radopholus similis.
A 2023 profile of the Indonesian coffee breeder Surip Mawardi credits him with developing it as an early-bearing, short-stemmed variety.

sections.title: On bags
body: It turns up blended with Andungsari, for example in a washed lot from the Frinsa collective in West Java and a lot from Kerinci in Sumatra. Single O finds it more intense, with more mouthfeel, than Andungsari.

records.name: SL14
records.summary: A late-1930s Kenyan selection from a drought-resistant tree.
records.lede: SL14 is one of the selections Kenya's Scott Agricultural Laboratories made in the late 1930s, taken from a single tree labelled "Drought Resistant II". Royal Coffee says it matters in both Kenya and Uganda, and that genetic tests place it in the Typica group, unlike the Bourbon-related SL28.

facts.label: selected by Scott Agricultural Laboratories
the genetic group tests place it in
where Royal Coffee says it's important
it tolerates both, says World Coffee Research

cup.text: Little is published about SL14's cup on its own, because it usually reaches buyers mixed with SL28 and other varieties. One such lot, an anaerobic natural (fermented without air, then dried in the fruit) of SL14 and SL28 from Sipi Falls in Uganda's Bugisu region, scored 93 at Coffee Review in 2023, with tangerine zest, cocoa nib and brown sugar.

plant.stature: tall, with light bronze young leaf tips
plant.rust: susceptible; also coffee berry disease and nematodes
plant.altitude: medium to high: above 1,200 m (3,940 ft) near the equator

story.text: Seedlings of a tree labelled Drought Resistant II (D.R. II) are planted at Kabete, and later spread widely east of Kenya's Rift Valley.
Scott Labs gives the SL prefix to the single trees it selects in these years.
SL14 is selected from one D.R. II tree, chosen for drought tolerance.
Royal Coffee counts SL14 among Uganda's most common Arabica varieties, with Typica, Kent and SL28.

sections.title: Scott Labs
body: Selections made at Scott Labs from 1935 to 1939 got the SL prefix, and Sweet Maria's says 42 trees of various origins were studied for yield, quality, drought and disease resistance. The lab's founding date varies by source: Sweet Maria's says 1903, named after Dr Henry Scott of the Church of Scotland mission at Kikuyu, while World Coffee Research says 1922.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a tall, good-yielding tree that tolerates drought and cold and needs little fertiliser. It bears its first crop in year 3, has average-sized beans, and is susceptible to leaf rust, coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms). WCR suggests 1,000–2,000 plants per hectare.

sections.title: In Uganda
body: Royal Coffee (2026) lists Typica, Kent, SL14 and SL28 as Uganda's most common Arabicas; the country's Arabica regions include Mount Elgon in the east, the Rwenzori Mountains in the southwest and West Nile in the northwest. Sweet Maria's names SL-14 among the varieties farmers deliver to the Bugoye washing station in the Rwenzoris, from hillside farms at about 1,500–1,800 m (4,900–5,900 ft).

family.parentsText: Single-tree selection from a tree labelled "Drought Resistant II"
family.line: Picked at Scott Labs in 1936; the tree's own origin is unrecorded, and DNA ties it to the Typica group.

grownIn.text: Kenya and Uganda; Royal Coffee (2026) counts it among Uganda's most common Arabicas.

records.name: Selection 9
records.summary: India's Tafarikela × Timor Hybrid, known for its cup but rust-prone.
records.lede: An Indian variety from the Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI) that crosses Tafarikela, an Ethiopian Arabica, with the Timor Hybrid. Counter Culture calls it known for its cup quality but susceptible to rust, and names it, with Chandragiri, one of India's two most popular varieties in cultivation. A Selection 9 lot won the Fine Cup Award at the Flavour of India competition in 2002.

facts.label: its Ethiopian parent, credited with the cup
won the Fine Cup Award at Flavour of India
with drooping branches
and suited to different coffee zones

family.parentsText: Tafarikela × Timor Hybrid (via Selection 8, India's pure-line Timor Hybrid selection)
family.line: Developed by CCRI in the 1970s, using a Timor Hybrid introduced to India in 1961.

grownIn.text: India, where Counter Culture names it, with Chandragiri, one of the two most popular varieties in cultivation, and Tamil Nadu Agricultural University calls it suited to different coffee zones; prize-winning lots have come from Kerala (Poabs Estates, Palakkad), and it has been trialled in Tamil Nadu's Pulney hills. The Coffee Board's 2017 geographical-indication application for Bababudangiri Arabica, in Karnataka, names it as one of that area's three main varieties, with S.795 and Cauvery.

plant.rust: susceptible

cup.text: Coffee Review notes that Indian coffees from Selection 9 can show more floral and fruity delicacy than India's usual clean, straightforward cup, with more emphasis on flowers and clean fruit.
cup.why: Sucafina credits its Ethiopian parent, Tafarikela, for the cup quality.
cup.prized: Its cup is the reason it's grown: a Selection 9 lot won the Fine Cup Award at Flavour of India in 2002, and Poabs Estates' organic Selection 9 was named Best Specialty Arabica at the 2013 edition.
cup.watch: Counter Culture calls it susceptible to leaf rust, a real handicap in India, where World Coffee Research says farmers face more disease pressure than anywhere else.

story.text: The Timor Hybrid was introduced to India; a pure-line selection of it became Selection 8, Selection 9's parent.
CCRI developed the Tafarikela × Timor Hybrid cross.
A Selection 9 lot won the Fine Cup Award at the Flavour of India competition.
Poabs Estates' organic SLN-9 won Best Specialty Arabica at the 12th Flavour of India awards.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University's crop guide describes Selection 9 as drought-hardy and suited to different coffee zones, and Sucafina describes a tall tree with drooping branches. Its Timor Hybrid parent, Selection 8, has the highest leaf-rust resistance in that guide's list, but Counter Culture reports that Selection 9 itself is susceptible.

In a four-season study in the Pulney hills of Tamil Nadu, published in 2016, Selection 9 dropped the most fruit of the four Indian selections compared: about 43% on average, against 29% for Chandragiri.

sections.title: In competitions
body: At India's 2013 Flavour of India cupping competition (the Fine Cup Award), whose winners list the Coffee Board of India publishes, Poabs Estates of Palakkad, Kerala, took Best Specialty Arabica and first place in the specialty Arabica ranking with an organic Selection 9; the same list shows a Chandragiri in fourth and an S.795/Catimor lot in fifth.

records.name: Starmaya
records.summary: The first F1 coffee hybrid that can be grown from seed
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of the rust-resistant Marsellesa and a male-sterile plant (one that makes no pollen) found among Ethiopian coffees in CATIE's gene bank in Costa Rica. Because the mother can't pollinate itself, the seed it sets is hybrid seed, so Starmaya can be grown from seed instead of costly lab clones.

facts.label: the only F1 coffee hybrid seed growers can multiply this way
cost per seed, about half a lab-made hybrid plantlet
green coffee per plant vs Caturra and Marsellesa in trials
of trees can come out off-type

cup.text: WCR notes notably high acidity. PT's Coffee described a red-honey lot from Costa Rica as fruit-forward, with marmalade, grape and semi-sweet chocolate and a creamy body. In a 2013–18 Nicaraguan trial it had the best average cupping score of the coffees tasted, 80.5 against 76.3 for Caturra. A washed AA lot from Zambia's Mount Sunzu, scored 84.5 by its seller in 2025, is described as clean and balanced, with caramel, nuts, a touch of brown spice, a silky body and soft acidity.

feel.body: fuller than Caturra in trial cuppings

cup.why: In Nicaraguan trials from 710 to 1,250 m (2,330–4,100 ft) it out-scored Caturra at every site, 79.2–83.1 points against 72.5–78.9, and did best at the highest site; the breeders note that both the plant and the place shape the cup.
cup.watch: It resists rust less well than its Marsellesa parent: in one commercial field 8% of Starmaya plants showed rust spores, against 1% of Marsellesa.
cup.prized: A rare mix of traits: it yields well above Marsellesa, cupped about as well as Centroamericano in the 2013–18 Nicaraguan trial, and can be grown from cheap seed. The 2020 trial's authors called it the most interesting variety for low-intensity farms in terms of yield for the size of the bush.

story.text: CIRAD researchers spot a male-sterile plant while screening Ethiopian coffees in CATIE's gene bank in Costa Rica.
The first half-hectare seed garden goes in, in Nicaragua: 1,600 sterile mother trees and 400 Marsellesa pollen donors.
ECOM names the variety and starts farm trials; World Coffee Research calls it a major breakthrough.
CIRAD announces Starmaya can now be supplied as seed, at about half the cost of lab propagation.

sections.title: Why seed matters
body: Most F1 coffee hybrids lose their traits if grown from their own seed, so they are cloned in labs, which WCR says can cost double what seed-grown plants do. A Starmaya seed garden yields about half a million seeds per hectare, at roughly half the price of a lab-made hybrid plantlet.

The trade-off is uniformity: WCR says about 15% of planted trees may come out different from the standard, the breeders counted 16% off-types in Starmaya fields, and CIRAD's 2019 announcement puts it at about 10%.

sections.title: In trials
body: In a five-year trial at seven Nicaraguan sites from 710 to 1,250 m (2,330–4,100 ft), Starmaya gave about 32% more coffee than Marsellesa from a canopy 43% larger, ranked second of all the coffees for stable yields, and, with Centroamericano, had the heaviest beans and the biggest share of large (screen 16–20) beans.

Its cupping score, 80.5, was the trial's best, though not significantly above Centroamericano's 80.4 or Mundo Maya's 79.5; Caturra scored 76.3. All three hybrids cupped best at the highest site. Chemically it had more d-limonene and 3-methylbutanoic acid, two aroma compounds, than Caturra, but the researchers found no link between such compounds and the final score.

family.parentsText: Male-sterile Ethiopian plant CIR-SM01 (mother) × Marsellesa (pollen)
family.line: Hybrid seed from a seed garden where sterile mothers are pollinated by Marsellesa; bred by CIRAD with ECOM

grownIn.text: Bred and trialled at ECOM's La Cumplida farm in Nicaragua; lots also come from Costa Rica's Naranjo area and from Mount Sunzu in Zambia, at 1,550–1,650 m (5,090–5,410 ft), and trial plants went to Vietnam and Cameroon. No source ranks the countries.

plant.rust: resistant, but less so than Marsellesa
plant.altitude: medium: 900–1,300 m (2,950–4,265 ft) at Central America's latitudes

records.name: Tabi
records.summary: Colombia's tall rust-resistant variety, from Typica, Bourbon and Timor Hybrid.
records.lede: A rust-resistant variety that Cenicafé, Colombia's coffee research center, released in 2002, aimed at small, low-tech farms in regions with long dry spells and strong sun. Unlike the short Castillo and Colombia varieties, Tabi is a tall tree with long branches, like the Typica and Bourbon in its family. Its name means "good" in the Guambiano language.

facts.label: released by Cenicafé
a tall tree with long branches
the Timor Hybrid line in its parents
its SCA scores in a 2023 Cenicafé study, best of the three varieties tested

cup.text: In a 2023 Cenicafé fermentation study, Tabi out-cupped Castillo and Colombia, scoring 82.7–83.2 on the SCA's 100-point scale. The importer Coffee Hunter says it normally gives very good cups. Cenicafé's breeder found its cup indistinguishable from the varieties it was tested against, and in farm samples from the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, 27.3% of Tabi samples rated excellent, level with Colombia and above red Caturra (18.2%).
cup.why: The retailer Japanese Coffee Co. credits its Typica and Bourbon genes.
cup.prized: Balance: in Cenicafé's panel tests, some of the lines that became Tabi formed their own group as the most balanced, with the highest overall-impression scores, and in the Sierra Nevada samples Tabi stood out for aroma, bitterness, acidity and overall impression.
cup.watch: Like any variety it depends on the farm: a 2020 Cenicafé panel rated the average Tabi, Cenicafé 1 and Castillo sample as standard.

story.text: Cenicafé begins crossing the Timor Hybrid with tall Typica and Bourbon, starting about 25 years of selection.
Field trials are planted in Huila, Santander, Valle and Cesar, some under shade trees and some in full sun.
During a rust epidemic, the candidate lines keep low levels of attack.
Cenicafé releases Tabi as a tall, rust-resistant variety.
Cenicafé's variety guide lists Tabi as one of only four varieties with seed certified by Colombia's farm authority (ICA), with Castillo, the regional Castillos and Cenicafé 1.
Cenicafé finds rust able to grow, to varying degrees, on all of Tabi's component lines, as on Castillo's and Cenicafé 1's.
A Tabi from Buena Vista places 22nd among 25 winning lots in Colombia's Cup of Excellence.

sections.title: Who it was bred for
body: Cenicafé built Tabi for small farms with little technology in regions with long dry periods, uneven rain and strong sunshine, about 240,000 ha or 30% of Colombia's coffee area in 2002. Yields there were traditionally 40–50 arrobas (12.5 kg each) of dry parchment per hectare a year, about half the national average.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Tabi is planted like Typica and Bourbon, usually at no more than 3,000 plants per hectare. In Cenicafé's trials its Bourbon-cross lines, the most vigorous, reached 2.0–2.4 m (6.7–8.0 ft) at two years, and its lines yielded 169–272 arrobas of parchment per hectare a year, beating the comparison varieties at all four sites, two of them under guamo (Inga) shade trees and two in full sun.
Its resistance comes from the Timor Hybrid, which carries at least five rust-resistance genes: complete where rust race II is the only race present, partial where newer races have appeared.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Tabi is rare among Cup of Excellence winners, but it does appear: a Tabi from Buena Vista placed 22nd in Colombia's 2021 competition, one of 25 winning lots, of which one was Castillo and none were listed as Colombia or Cenicafé 1.

family.parentsText: Typica × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343 and Bourbon × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343
family.line: Bred by Cenicafé from crosses of tall Typica and Bourbon with the Timor Hybrid, plus tall offspring of Caturra and Villa Sarchi crosses with the Timor Hybrid, selected to the F5–F6 generation and sold as a blend of lines.
family.type: Neither Catimor nor Sarchimor: Timor Hybrid crossed with tall Typica and Bourbon

grownIn.text: Bred for Colombia's small farms in drier, sunnier regions; its seed is certified there.

plant.stature: tall: a little taller and wider than Typica in Cenicafé's trials; its Bourbon-cross lines, the most vigorous, reached 2.0–2.4 m (6.7–8.0 ft) at two years
plant.yield: high for a tall variety: 169–272 arrobas of dry parchment per hectare a year in trials, against 40–50 on traditional farms in its target regions
plant.rust: resistant: complete where only rust race II is present, partial where newer races appear; since 2020 Cenicafé has found rust able to grow on its lines
plant.beanSize: large: over 80% Supremo (held on a 17/64-inch screen), more than Typica

records.name: Tekisic
records.summary: El Salvador's improved Bourbon, selected over nearly 30 years.
records.lede: Tekisic is a Bourbon selection made by El Salvador's coffee research institute, ISIC, which started selecting in 1949 and released it in 1977. The name joins tekiti, a Nahuatl word for "work", with ISIC. It ripens early, rates very good for cup quality at high altitude, and out-yields unselected Bourbon between 900 and 1,500 m (2,950–4,900 ft).

facts.label: released after nearly 30 years of selection
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
of El Salvador's coffee is Tekisic or unselected Bourbon
ripening, on tall trees

plant.stature: tall; planted at 3,000–4,000 trees per hectare
plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, or above 1,300 m (4,250 ft) at El Salvador's latitude; out-yields unselected Bourbon at 900–1,500 m (2,950–4,900 ft)

sections.title: How it was made
body: ISIC used mass selection: it picked the best plants, pooled their seed to grow the next generation, and repeated. Tekisic isn't resistant to the major coffee diseases, leaf rust included. It's widespread in El Salvador and economically important in Guatemala.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Tekisic is a tall tree, planted at 3,000–4,000 per hectare against 5,000–6,000 for compact Pacas, and it gives its first crop in year 4. It ripens early and needs a medium amount of fertiliser. In World Coffee Research's account it out-yielded unselected Bourbon between 900 and 1,500 m (2,950–4,900 ft), but like Bourbon it's susceptible to leaf rust, coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms).

sections.title: On the bag
body: Bags sometimes call it Bourbon Tekisic or Bourbon Mejorado, "improved Bourbon". It rarely shows up by name in competitions: none of the 32 ranked lots in El Salvador's 2025 Cup of Excellence was listed as Tekisic.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (mass selection)
family.line: Selected by ISIC, El Salvador, 1949–1977.

grownIn.text: Widespread in El Salvador; important in Guatemala.

cup.text: Little is published about Tekisic's cup on its own. World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude as very good, a notch above its rating for Pacas, Caturra or Catuaí. Coffee Review describes Salvadoran coffee, about 70% of it from Bourbon-type trees such as Tekisic before 2012–13, as generally sweet, smooth and clean.

story.text: El Salvador's coffee research institute, ISIC, starts selecting the best Bourbon plants and pooling their seed, generation after generation.
After nearly 30 years, ISIC releases the selection as Tekisic, from tekiti, Nahuatl for "work", and ISIC.
A leaf-rust epidemic hits El Salvador, where about 70% of the coffee came from Bourbon-type trees, including the widely planted Tekisic.

records.name: Timor Hybrid
records.summary: A natural Arabica × Robusta cross that gave coffee rust resistance.
records.lede: A coffee tree that appeared on the island of Timor in the 1920s from a natural cross of Arabica and Robusta. Its Robusta genes let it resist leaf rust, a fungus that strips coffee leaves, so breeders spent much of the 20th century crossing it into new varieties, including the Catimors and Sarchimors.

facts.label: first rust-resistant tree found, in a Typica plantation
Timor farmers start planting it
the two selections behind the Catimor and Sarchimor families
the line Colombia's breeders used, received in 1960

cup.text: Its offspring carry a poor reputation: World Coffee Research says varieties carrying Robusta genes, as its offspring do, have traditionally been linked with lower cup quality. Slow Food, by contrast, says the original tree has Robusta's disease resistance but quality closer to Arabica's. A 2015 Brazilian study was kinder too: its trial, mostly Timor Hybrid plants and their offspring, averaged about 82 points, above the 80-point specialty line, and one Timor Hybrid plant was described as chocolatey, full-bodied and sweet, with medium acidity.
cup.why: The importer Coffee Hunter blames its Robusta (Coffea canephora) genes for the weaker cups of its offspring. Cenicafé counters that Catimors, its Caturra-cross offspring, can cup like other Arabicas when breeders rigorously remove the poor-cupping lines.
cup.prized: New flavors, say the Brazilian researchers behind the 2015 study, who found that the Timor Hybrid and its offspring offer nuance rarely found on the market; in that trial a Catimor line, UFV 390-52, scored 88. A 2008 Embrapa Café report, carried by Revista Cultivar, described Timor Hybrid-derived cultivars from EPAMIG and UFV, Catiguá MG2 among them, scoring above 90 by the Brazil Specialty Coffee Association's method.
cup.watch: Lower cup quality in poorly selected offspring, the traditional complaint about varieties with Robusta genes.

story.text: A rust-resistant tree turns up in a Typica plantation on Timor that had been planted in 1917; it's taken to be a natural Arabica × Robusta cross.
Seeds from that tree start small plantations on the island.

Portugal's coffee rust center (CIFC) receives Timor Hybrid seed in 1958 or 1959 and shares its selections with breeding programs; through the 1960s seeds also go to other research centers and Indonesian islands.
Colombia releases its first variety bred from Timor Hybrid line 1343, the Colombia variety; Castillo, Tabi and Cenicafé 1 follow.
Indonesia brings in TimTim selections in at least two waves, and its coffee research institute, ICCRI, releases a more stable, productive type in the 1990s.
World Coffee Research warns that the Timor Hybrid's rust resistance is showing signs of breaking down.
Researchers report new rust races in Timor-Leste that infect both key selections, CIFC 832/1 and 832/2.

sections.title: Why breeders wanted it
body: Besides leaf rust, breeders have used it to add resistance to coffee berry disease, root-knot nematodes (tiny worms that attack roots) and bacterial blight.

That resistance is wearing thin. Some once-resistant varieties, notably Lempira in Honduras and Costa Rica 95, began catching rust in the early 2000s, and because most rust-resistant varieties share this one parent, World Coffee Research says most experts expect them to lose their resistance in the near to medium term.

sections.title: Three lines, three families
body: Breeders drew on three seed collections of the Timor Hybrid, which Cenicafé says carry at least five rust-resistance genes between them. Line 832/1 crossed with Caturra gave most Catimors, among them Costa Rica 95, Lempira, Catisic and IHCAFE 90. Line 832/2 crossed with Villa Sarchi gave the Sarchimors, such as Parainema and Obatã. Line 1343, which also resists coffee berry disease, gave Colombia's varieties: Colombia, Castillo and Cenicafé 1 with Caturra, and the tall Tabi mainly with Typica and Bourbon. The lines don't split neatly by family: Catimor 129, grown in Malawi, comes from a Colombian Caturra × 1343 line.

sections.title: In Timor-Leste today
body: Many of the farms where the original type grows were abandoned after Indonesia's 1975 invasion and now grow semi-wild, says Slow Food, which places it in the Ermera area. Most of Timor-Leste's plantations today are Timor Hybrid offspring crossed back to traditional Arabica.

sections.title: When was it found?
body: Sources disagree. Slow Food says the first tree was found in 1927 in a Typica plantation set up in 1917, and a 2025 ASIC poster also gives 1927; a 2015 Brazilian paper says it was found in 1917; World Coffee Research says it appeared in the 1920s; and Cenicafé's 2017 variety guide and Sweet Maria's place the find in the 1940s, when, by Slow Food's account, Timor farmers began planting it.

family.parentsText: Arabica × Robusta (Coffea canephora), a spontaneous cross found in a Typica plantation
family.line: Not bred: a natural cross on Timor. Breeders later picked lines such as CIFC 832/1, 832/2 and 1343 and crossed them into Arabica varieties.
family.type: Founder of both the Catimor and Sarchimor families

grownIn.text: Found in what is now Timor-Leste; seeds also went to other Indonesian islands from the late 1950s. In Sumatra, where it's called TimTim, pure Timor Hybrid is also widely planted in many sub-types, Sweet Maria's reported in 2019.

records.name: Tufahi
records.summary: A Yemeni name meaning apple, for apple-shaped cherries.
records.lede: Tufahi comes from the Arabic word for apple, and Yemeni farmers use it for trees with apple-shaped cherries. It was the third most-cited coffee name in a 2022 survey of 148 Yemeni farms. Like Udaini, it covers trees from all three of Yemen's genetic groups, so it's a local name rather than a defined variety.

facts.label: of names farmers cited in the 2022 survey
of sampled Tufahi trees were New-Yemen (Yemenia) types
the rest were Typica/Bourbon (23%) or SL34 (21%) types

cup.text: Lots that name Tufahi usually list other names too. Three such naturals from Haraaz and Al Hayma, listing Tufahi alongside Dawairi, Jaadi or Udaini, scored 94, 95 and 97 with Coffee Review in 2021–2022, with dried fruit such as plum, black cherry or goji berry, baking chocolate, and woody notes like sandalwood or oak.
cup.prized: A Haraaz natural listing Tuffahi, Dawairi and Jaadi scored 97 with Coffee Review in 2022.

story.text: Coffee Review rates a Haraaz natural listing Tuffahi, Dawairi and Jaadi at 94, and an Al Hayma lot listing Udaini, Tufahi and Dwairi at 95.
PT's Coffee's Haraaz natural listing Tuffahi, Dawairi and Jaadi scores 97 with Coffee Review.

A survey of 148 farms finds Tufahi the third most-cited name (14%), with trees in all three of Yemen's genetic groups; Qima's Faris Sheibani warns that selling such names as varieties risks misleading buyers.

sections.title: Where the name points
body: With Udaini, Tufahi was the main name in Ibb, Dhamar and Raymah, and it made up 17% of names cited in Haraaz. Tufahi trees from Al Mahwit and Sanaa were mainly New-Yemen, while those from Ibb and Dhamar were mainly SL34 and Typica/Bourbon types.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for Tuffahi as well as Tufahi. Most reviewed lots that name it list it with Dawairi, Jaadi or Udaini. In the 2022 survey, 80% of farmers in Sanaa and Al Mahwit said they grow two or more varieties, while in Ibb 80% said they grow only one.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name, not a genetic line: New-Yemen, Typica/Bourbon and SL34 trees all go by it

grownIn.text: Named across Yemen, especially Ibb, Dhamar and Raymah.

plant.stature: tall, by the few written descriptions; the study's authors say it isn't clear-cut

records.name: Tupi
records.summary: An early-ripening, rust-resistant Brazilian Sarchimor from IAC.
records.lede: A Sarchimor from Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC), one of the selections Brazil made from the Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid cross. A 2012 article on IAC's history describes it as rust-resistant and early-ripening, and IAC describes a short tree with short internodes (the gaps between leaf pairs) suited to dense planting.

facts.label: its full IAC code
ripening
to leaf rust
points in a Procafé cupping of 2009–2010 naturals, vs 81.5 for Yellow Bourbon

cup.text: Felipe Croce of Brazil's Fazenda Ambiental Fortaleza says Tupi has a distinctive taste that often recalls bell pepper. A grower in Chiapas, Mexico, told Perfect Daily Grind it does well there, especially as a natural (dried inside the whole cherry) or honey (dried with some of the sticky fruit left on the seed). In a trial at Fundação Procafé's farm in Varginha, Minas Gerais, at about 1,000 m (3,300 ft), its naturals scored 83.5 and were described as excellent, with a citrus sweetness.
cup.prized: In that Procafé trial, scored by two tasters, its 83.5 beat both Yellow Bourbon (81.5) and Red Catuaí IAC 144 (78.5), though it sat mid-table among the 30 cultivars tested.
cup.watch: A bell-pepper note, says Croce.

story.text: At CIFC, Portugal's coffee rust research centre, work begins on crossing the Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 with Villa Sarchi.
IAC registers the first-generation hybrid as IAC 1669; Tupi's code, IAC 1669-33, carries that number.
A Revista Cultivar piece on IAC's 125th anniversary lists Tupi among six IAC cultivars whose selection Brazil's coffee research consortium funded.
Finca Hamburgo in Chiapas, Mexico, reports success with it in heavy rain, especially as a natural or honey.

sections.title: Growing it
body: IAC's description, as cited in a 2007 study, gives a short tree with short internodes, bronze young leaves, red cherries that ripen early and beans averaging about screen 17 (17/64 inch), best suited to dense planting. In a trial in Viçosa, Minas Gerais, reported in 2011, it was among the shortest and most rust-resistant of 32 cultivars.

It isn't for every site: in a trial begun in 1998 at Selvíria, Mato Grosso do Sul, a hot, low region once zoned unsuitable for Arabica, it grew the weakest of the short cultivars, and the 2007 study listed it among the least recommended there. In Chiapas, by contrast, Tomás Edelmann Blass of Finca Hamburgo told Perfect Daily Grind it does very well because the area gets so much rain.

sections.title: Not the same as IAC 125 RN
body: IAC 125 RN, once called Tupi RN IAC 1669-13 and also known as IBC 12 or Uva, is a separate selection from the same IAC 1669 hybrid. It was registered in 2012 and bred for resistance to the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne exigua as well as rust, and a 2012 Revista Cultivar piece on IAC's history lists Tupi IAC 1669-33 and IAC 125 RN as separate cultivars.

family.parentsText: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 (IAC's hybrid 1669)
family.line: Selected by IAC in Brazil from its Sarchimor population.

grownIn.text: Brazil, and farms such as Finca Hamburgo in Chiapas, Mexico.

plant.rust: resistant

records.name: Typica Mejorado
records.summary: Ecuador's “improved Typica”, which DNA tests say isn't a Typica.
records.lede: Its name is Spanish for “improved Typica”, but DNA testing reportedly done by World Coffee Research, and public comments by geneticist Christophe Montagnon, point to a cross of Bourbon and an Ethiopian landrace instead. It's one of Ecuador's newer specialty varieties, grown alongside Gesha and Sidra, and Olger Rogel is reported to have introduced it, as he did Sidra. A washed Typica Mejorado won Ecuador's first Cup of Excellence in 2021.

facts.label: at Ecuador's first Cup of Excellence, 2021 (washed, 90.39 points)
winning places there went to Typica Mejorado lots (one mixed with Bourbon)
by DNA fingerprinting; reported as Bourbon × Ethiopian landrace
(5,250–7,200 ft) where most Ecuadorian plantings sit

cup.text: Ozone Coffee describes jasmine, peach or apricot and citric acidity over a syrupy, honeyed body, with a long sweet finish; washed lots lean to tangerine, caramel and soft florals, naturals to plum, cherry cordial and honeysuckle. SEY's washed 2023 lot from Arashi, the farm that won the 2021 Cup of Excellence, showed soft florals, peach and lemon.
cup.prized: Clean, elegant florals and fruit that people compare with Gesha: Ecuadorian producer Pepe Jijón calls Gesha its closest reference, and says the trees are hard to tell apart.
cup.watch: Bean size is uneven within a lot, some long like Gesha's and others small: Juan Peña sorts his coffee by density again and again, and Jijón adjusts roast development to the spread of sizes; Ozone advises roasting light to medium-light because heat dulls the aromatics.

story.text: The industry story places Typica Mejorado and Sidra at a reported Nestlé-linked breeding station in Pichincha, Ecuador, where field technician Olger Rogel picked out both seed lines; the Nestlé link is unconfirmed.
Juan Peña plants it as the first variety at Hacienda La Papaya in Loja, with seed from an experimental farm in northern Ecuador.
Pepe Jijón plants it at Finca Soledad, from seed Olger Rogel supplied to his cooperative.
A washed Typica Mejorado from Abel Salinas Pacheco's farm Arashi, in Loja, wins Ecuador's first Cup of Excellence with 90.39 points and sells for US$97.10 a pound.
Thirteen years after planting, Jijón reports that his trees resist some pests and diseases better; Ozone calls this unverified.

sections.title: Genetics: what DNA tests found
body: Ozone reports that The Coffee Quest sent Ecuadorian leaf samples to World Coffee Research for DNA fingerprinting, and the results showed Typica Mejorado is not a Typica. Christophe Montagnon has said publicly that testing points to a cross of Bourbon and an Ethiopian landrace, and that the link to a breeding program is unconfirmed. Roasters SEY and Sample Coffee also cite WCR testing for a Bourbon × Ethiopian landrace parentage.

No published source gives these results in detail, and WCR's variety catalog has no entry for it. Material from Juan Peña's export partners gives conflicting parents: Bourbon × Ethiopian heirloom on one page, probably Typica × Ethiopian landrace on another.

sections.title: In competitions
body: At Ecuador's first Cup of Excellence in 2021, lots of Typica Mejorado took 10 of the 23 winning places, one of them mixed with Bourbon, including first (Arashi, 90.39) and third (Alaska del Sur, 90.07), both washed lots from Loja. Sidra, listed as Sydra, took seven places, including second. The winning lot sold for US$97.10 a pound to a Taiwanese buyer.

Hong Kong's Dawn Chan took a Typica Mejorado from Jijón's Finca Soledad, processed with his "tyoxidator" method (an open-air ferment of whole cherries, then an anaerobic ferment in the mucilage), to fifth place at the 2023 World Barista Championship. Perfect Daily Grind (2026) lists Typica Mejorado among the lesser-known varieties that competition finalists used in the early 2020s.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Ozone describes a tall, upright tree with slim vertical branches and bronze-tipped new leaves. Growers report a poor root system, trouble with heavy rain and too much direct sun, and low yields: low enough, Ozone says, that planting it is a commitment rather than a hedge.

Loja province has produced many of its best-known lots, with plantings in Pichincha too; SEY's Arashi lot grew at 1,900 m (6,250 ft) in Saraguro, Loja. Small plantings exist in Colombia and Costa Rica.

family.parentsText: Parentage not documented in published sources; the Typica link rests on the name
family.line: Reportedly picked out in Ecuador in the 1990s, possibly at a Nestlé-linked breeding station in Pichincha; origin unconfirmed

grownIn.text: Mainly Ecuador, especially Loja and Pichincha (Cup of Excellence lots also came from Zamora); small plantings in Colombia and Costa Rica

plant.stature: tall, upright, with slim vertical branches
plant.rust: no formal rating; one grower reports better pest and disease resistance (unverified)
plant.beanSize: uneven: some long like Gesha's, some small
plant.altitude: 1,600–2,200 m (5,250–7,200 ft) in Ecuador; no formal recommendation

records.name: Udaini
records.summary: Yemen's most common coffee name, but not one genetic variety.
records.lede: Udaini is the name Yemeni farmers use most for their coffee trees: a third of all names cited in a 2022 survey of 148 farms. The study says it's named after a region, Al Udaini. DNA tests found Udaini trees in all three of Yemen's genetic groups, so the name tells you about local tradition more than about the plant.

facts.label: of names farmers cited in the 2022 survey, the most of any
of sampled Udaini trees were New-Yemen (Yemenia) types
the rest were Typica/Bourbon (19%) or SL34 (14%) types
Coffee Review score for Port of Mokha's Udaini Lot 106 (2021)

cup.text: Coffee Review rated at least three naturals sold as only Udaini in October 2021. Port of Mokha's Lot 106 from Al Hayma (96 points) showed dried black currant, dark chocolate, sandalwood and tangerine zest; Port of Mokha's Al Wadi (94) showed date, orange blossom, dark chocolate and cedar; and a 92-point Al Hayma lot showed dark chocolate, fresh-cut pine, magnolia and golden raisin. A few lots can't define a name that spans three genetic groups.
cup.prized: Lot 106 was No. 13 on Coffee Review's Top 30 Coffees of 2021.
cup.watch: The name doesn't tell you the tree: in the 2022 survey a third of Udaini trees were SL34 or Typica/Bourbon types, and two-thirds of the trees in the SL34 group were called Udaini.

story.text: Port of Mokha's Lot 106, a natural sold as Udaini from Bait Alal smallholders in Al Hayma, scores 96 with Coffee Review and makes No. 13 on its Top 30 of 2021.
A survey of 148 Yemeni farms finds Udaini the most-cited name (34%), with trees under it in all three of Yemen's genetic groups.
Qima's Faris Sheibani warns that selling names like Udaini or Tufahi as varieties risks misleading marketing, and calls for nurseries with genetically verified seed.

sections.title: Where the name points
body: Region says more than the name. Udaini trees from Al Mahwit and Sanaa were mainly New-Yemen, while those from Ibb and Dhamar were mainly SL34 and Typica/Bourbon types. In Ibb, farmers named only Udaini and Tufahi. Of the trees that tested as SL34 types, 67% were called Udaini.
The few written descriptions make Udaini a tall tree, and Ozone Coffee says farmers link it with flat, elongated leaves, but the study's authors say the tall-versus-compact split isn't clear-cut.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Udaini often shares a bag with other names. Coffee Review's 2021 reviews include an Al Hayma lot listed as Udaini, Tufahi and Dwairi, and a Sanaa lot spelled "Audaini, Dawaeri and Tuffahi".
Labels also depend on the seller: Bait Alal smallholders supplied Port of Mokha's Lot 106, sold as Udaini, and a Qima lot sold as Yemenia, both reviewed in October 2021.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name, not a genetic line: New-Yemen, Typica/Bourbon and SL34 trees all go by it

grownIn.text: Named across Yemen's coffee governorates, including Ibb, Dhamar, Raymah, Sanaa and Al Mahwit.

plant.stature: tall, by the few written descriptions; the study's authors say it isn't clear-cut

records.name: Villa Sarchi
records.summary: Costa Rica's wind-tolerant dwarf Bourbon, a parent of Sarchimor.
records.lede: A natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon found in the northwest of Costa Rica's Alajuela province in the 1950s or 1960s, then improved by local growers through selection. It's suited to the very highest farms and tolerates strong winds. Crossed with Timor Hybrid in Portugal from 1967, it gave the Sarchimor group of rust-resistant varieties.

facts.label: compact trees, planted 5,000–6,000 per hectare
and suited to the highest-altitude farms
bean size, a notch under Caturra's
its cross with Timor Hybrid (hybrid H361)

cup.text: Coffee Hunter describes elegant acidity, intense berry notes and a lot of sweetness. World Coffee Research rates its cup potential up high as good, and Coffee Review's tasters found chocolate in both of two Villa Sarchi lots from Costa Rica's West Valley, with orange, honey and almond in one (a honey-processed lot) and apricot and flowers in the other.

feel.body: light and silky in Costa Rican lots; one Guatemalan lot was full and syrupy

cup.why: It's Bourbon with a single dwarfing gene, like Caturra and Pacas, so it starts from Bourbon's sweetness. World Coffee Research says it's suited to the very highest farms, and Coffee Hunter says it's most productive high up under shade trees.
cup.prized: Sweetness with elegant, berry-like acidity. Coffee Review scored two West Valley lots at 91 points (2012 and 2013), and a West Valley Villa Sarchi placed 7th in the experimental category of Costa Rica's 2025 Cup of Excellence, at 88.13.

plant.rust: susceptible
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: Found as a dwarf Bourbon mutation in northwestern Alajuela, Costa Rica.
Portugal's coffee rust research center (CIFC) starts crossing compact plants with rust-resistant Timor Hybrid; Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi becomes hybrid H361, Sarchimor.
Honduras's coffee institute, IHCAFE, introduces it to Honduras.
Brazil registers IAC 125 RN, a Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid cross selected at IAC.
A West Valley Villa Sarchi places 7th in the experimental category of Costa Rica's Cup of Excellence (88.13 points).

sections.title: Names
body: World Coffee Research lists La Luisa and Villalobos Bourbon as other names for it. Cafe Imports, though, lists Villalobos as a separate Costa Rican variety, so a bag that says Villalobos may or may not be this plant. Coffee Hunter says the name comes from the town of Sarchí, in the area where it was found. It's rarely grown outside Costa Rica; Cafe Imports says the West Valley grows a lot of it.

sections.title: Growing it
body: World Coffee Research says it's well adapted to the highest altitudes and tolerates strong winds, but it's susceptible to leaf rust, nematodes (tiny root worms) and coffee berry disease, and needs a lot of fertiliser. Coffee Hunter says it's most productive at altitude under shade trees with light chemical fertilising, and describes branches growing at about 45° from the trunk and bronzy leaves; World Coffee Research, though, lists its leaf tips as green.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural dwarf mutation)
family.line: Improved by Costa Rican growers through pedigree selection.

grownIn.text: Mainly Costa Rica, especially the West Valley; introduced to Honduras in 1974, and also grown in small amounts elsewhere, such as Antigua in Guatemala.

records.name: Villalobos
records.summary: A compact Costa Rican Typica mutation, with a disputed identity.
records.lede: Villalobos is a coffee found mostly in Costa Rica. Most sources describe it as a dwarf (compact) mutation of Typica: Costa Rica's coffee institute, ICAFE, calls it a subtype of Typica, and Cafe Imports' variety glossary and Sweet Maria's a naturally occurring dwarf Typica mutation. World Coffee Research, though, lists "Villalobos Bourbon" as another name for Villa Sarchi, a dwarf Bourbon mutation, so the name may cover more than one plant. Importer Cafe Imports says Costa Rica's West Valley grows a lot of it.

facts.label: Costa Rica's coffee institute calls it a subtype of Typica
where Cafe Imports says much of it grows
a compact Typica mutation, say Cafe Imports and Sweet Maria's
WCR treats "Villalobos Bourbon" as another name for it

cup.text: Sweet Maria's says it often shows interesting flavors and pronounced acidity. A semi-washed Villalobos (fruit removed by machine) from El Ciprés in Naranjo placed 20th in Costa Rica's 2012 Cup of Excellence, with jurors noting rose, pear, lychee and brown sugar and crisp, lime-like acidity; a red-honey lot from Tarrazú that Sweet Maria's sold in 2025 showed honey, brown sugar and hibiscus tea.
cup.prized: Lively acidity: Sweet Maria's notes pronounced acidity, and the Cup of Excellence jury called the 2012 El Ciprés lot delicate, with complex, crisp acidity.

story.text: Coffee Review's Miguel Meza lists Villalobos among the mutations and selections of Typica.
A Villalobos lot from El Ciprés, in Barranco de Naranjo in the West Valley, scores 86.10 and places 20th in Costa Rica's Cup of Excellence.
Sweet Maria's sells a red-honey Villalobos from Canet, Tarrazú, grown above 2,000 m (6,560 ft) alongside Catuaí.

sections.title: Typica or Bourbon?
body: ICAFE, Cafe Imports, Sweet Maria's and Coffee Review's Miguel Meza all put Villalobos on the Typica side. WCR's catalog instead lists "Villalobos Bourbon" (also called La Luisa) among the other names for Villa Sarchi, a compact Bourbon mutation found in the northwest of Costa Rica's Alajuela province in the 1950s or 1960s. None of these sources reports a DNA test of Villalobos.

sections.title: Where it's grown
body: Cafe Imports says the West Valley grows an abundance of Villa Sarchi and Villa Lobos, both Costa Rica-specific varieties, and the 2012 Cup of Excellence lot came from Naranjo there, at about 1,645–1,685 m (5,400–5,530 ft). It also turns up in Tarrazú: the farm behind Sweet Maria's 2025 lot plants it with Catuaí on plots above 2,000 m (6,560 ft).
1Zpresso notes that it's on ICAFE's list of recognized Arabica varieties, alongside Caturra, Catuaí, Typica and others.

family.parentsText: Typica (natural dwarf mutation), by most accounts; WCR files "Villalobos Bourbon" under Villa Sarchi, a Bourbon mutation

grownIn.text: Costa Rica, especially the West Valley; also Tarrazú.

records.name: Wolisho
records.summary: A big-cherried, shade-loving local landrace from Ethiopia's Gedeo zone.
records.lede: A regional Ethiopian landrace (a local type farmers have kept for generations) named after a tree native to Gedeo, the zone around Yirgacheffe. It's a large tree with long leaves and big cherries, usually grown under semi-forest shade, and often on the same farms as Kurume and Dega.

facts.label: that ripen slowly and are easy to pick by hand
crop from year to year
drought-tolerant and at home in shade

family.parentsText: A landrace kept by farmers; no known parents
family.line: Grown for centuries in Ethiopia's highlands, especially Gedeo

grownIn.text: Ethiopia: Yirgacheffe (Gedeo), Sidama and Guji, including Shakisso

plant.stature: large canopy, long branches and leaves

cup.text: Wolisho is almost always grown and sold mixed with other local types, so there's no published cup of it alone. Sample Coffee and Melbourne Coffee Merchants say the local landraces it belongs to are widely credited with the floral character of Sidama and Gedeo coffee. Coffee Review scored a washed Yirgacheffe lot of Kurume, Wolisho, Dega and other local selections 93 in 2022, with cocoa nib, bergamot, red plum and jasmine and apple-like acidity; Melbourne Coffee Merchants' Hadeso natural from Guji, largely Kurume and Wolisho, listed candied fruit, strawberry and peach with pink grapefruit acidity.
cup.watch: Its crop is uneven from year to year, and mixed planting makes pure Wolisho lots hard to guarantee.

sections.title: How to tell it from Kurume
body: Wolisho has large cherries, long leaves and crops that vary from year to year; Kurume, often grown beside it, bears smaller cherries and a good crop most years.

sections.title: One of several tree-named landraces
body: Wolisho is one of a handful of local types named after native, non-coffee trees. Sample Coffee lists it among five popular in Sidama (Bedessa, Kudhumi, Mique, Sawe and Wolisho); Melbourne Coffee Merchants lists six across Gedeo, Guji and Sidama (Bedessa, Dega, Kurume, Mique, Sawe and Wolisho).
Both say little is documented about their history, and that it's unclear whether each name is a single type or a wider group.

records.name: Wush Wush
records.summary: A southwest Ethiopian landrace that found a second home in Colombia.
records.lede: An Ethiopian landrace named for Wushwush, a town a few kilometres from the Bonga forest in Kafa, southwest Ethiopia, where it was isolated on a farm. It reached South America in the early 1990s and is now grown mostly in Colombia and Panama, where it's valued for sweet, tea-like, aromatic cups. A 2013 study also lists a cultivar named Wushwush among 23 that Ethiopia's agricultural research institute released to resist coffee berry disease.

facts.label: when it reached South America
where it's most grown today
bean sizes (screen) in one crop: they vary a lot
Ethiopian research cultivars released, late 1970s–1990s, to resist coffee berry disease; one is named Wushwush

family.parentsText: An Ethiopian landrace from the Wushwush area of Kafa; no known parents
family.line: A regional landrace propagated by local farmers and isolated on a farm at Wushwush

grownIn.text: Mostly Colombia (recent lots from Santander and Cauca) and Panama; it comes from the Wushwush area near Bonga, in Kafa, southwest Ethiopia.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's says it's prized for delicate, aromatic, tea-like flavors and strong sweetness. Coffee Review scored a honey-process lot from Santander 94 (bergamot, lilac, pink peppercorn, caramel, plum) and an anaerobic natural from Caldono, Cauca, 95 (guava, jasmine, blood orange, raw honey).
cup.prized: Delicate florals and tea-like aromatics over a lot of sweetness.
cup.watch: It costs more to grow: Sweet Maria's says it yields less than Caturra or Bourbon and resists disease less well than common hybrids, which is why it sells at a premium.

plant.rust: less disease resistance than many common hybrid varieties

story.text: Ethiopia's agricultural research institute releases 23 cultivars selected from forest coffee for coffee berry disease resistance; one is named Wushwush.
Wush Wush is brought to South America; today it's most common in Colombia and Panama.
Coffee Review scores a honey-process Wush Wush from Hacienda La Pradera in Santander, Colombia, 94.
An anaerobic natural Wush Wush from Paola Trujillo in Caldono, Cauca, scores 95.

sections.title: One name, maybe two coffees
body: The Wush Wush sold from Colombia is described as a landrace that farmers around Wushwush propagated, with weaker disease resistance than common hybrids. Ethiopia's research institute also released a cultivar called Wushwush, developed from forest coffee to resist coffee berry disease. No source says whether the two are the same plant, so treat the name as a place, not a guarantee of one genotype.

records.name: Yellow Bourbon
records.summary: Yellow-fruited Bourbon that turned up in São Paulo around 1930.
records.lede: Bourbon whose ripe cherries are yellow instead of red. It turned up around 1930 on a Red Bourbon farm near Pederneiras, in Brazil's São Paulo state, and Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) has studied and selected it since the 1940s. It ripens early and yields less than Mundo Novo and Catuaí, but IAC researchers describe its cup as sweet and floral with balanced citric acidity, which keeps it on Brazilian specialty farms.

facts.label: first seen near Pederneiras, São Paulo
xanthocarpa, controls the yellow fruit (IAC, 1942)
ripening, and fairly even, which makes it easier to pick ripe cherries
(3,300 ft) where Brazilian researchers recommend growing it

cup.text: IAC researchers say it's known for floral aroma, balanced citric acidity and sweetness, and in their cuppings of Yellow Bourbon lines tasters kept writing chocolate, caramel, honey, citrus and floral. Treat that as a tendency: the lines differ, and farm and processing shape the cup too.
cup.why: The yellow colour itself isn't the reason: the yellow pigment, luteolin, has no established link with cup quality. Research cited by Daily Coffee News links cup quality to sugar (sucrose) and certain fatty and organic acids in the bean, and since 2005 IAC has been choosing lines specifically for the cup; early, even ripening also makes it easier to pick only ripe cherries.
cup.prized: Sweetness and clean, lively acidity at competition level. A Yellow Bourbon from Carmo de Minas scored 88.47 in Brazil's 2012 Cup of Excellence (pulped natural), with jurors writing plum, milk chocolate, honey and a syrupy mouthfeel, and in 2017 a Brazilian Yellow Bourbon scored 92.33 and sold for US$126 a pound.
cup.watch: Quality varies from line to line: in one IAC trial on a single farm (2012/13 harvest), lines ranged from 80.1 to 83.6 points, and in another, published in 2022 from the 2019 harvest, from just above 80 to 90.6. It also needs altitude and careful picking and drying to show its best.

plant.yield: low to medium: about 25 bags a hectare expected; less than Mundo Novo and Catuaí, though early IAC trials found it out-yielded Red Bourbon
plant.rust: highly susceptible to leaf rust, and to nematodes (tiny root worms)
plant.beanSize: large in tested lines (most beans on screen 16 and up)
plant.altitude: above 1,000 m (3,300 ft) in Brazil

story.text: A yellow-fruited Typica, later called Amarelo de Botucatu, appears at Botucatu in São Paulo state.
Yellow Bourbon turns up on a Red Bourbon farm near Pederneiras, São Paulo.
Carlos Arnaldo Krug and colleagues at IAC in Campinas show that a single genetic factor, xanthocarpa, controls the yellow fruit.
IAC picks 30 mother trees on a farm in Jaú, grows their seed at five research stations and records eight harvests; seed from the best trees goes to farmers.
IAC restarts its Yellow Bourbon selection, this time aiming at cup quality.
An IAC study of 14 lines, published in 2022 from the trial's first harvest (2019), picks IAC J3-1, J9-16 and J19-18 as the best mix of yield and cup.

sections.title: Where it came from
body: Two explanations are still open: it may be a mutation of Red Bourbon, or a natural cross between Red Bourbon and Amarelo de Botucatu, a yellow-fruited Typica. The 1942 work at Campinas was led by Carlos Arnaldo Krug.
The yellow comes from the recessive form of one gene (xanthocarpa): a tree needs two copies to bear yellow fruit, while trees with one copy bear light-red or orange-ish fruit.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Brazilian researchers describe tall trees with early-ripening yellow fruit that are highly susceptible to leaf rust and nematodes, and they recommend planting it above about 1,000 m (3,300 ft). Its early, even ripening is a practical plus, because more of the crop can be picked ripe at once.

Yield is the weak point. A 33-year study in Campinas (Fazuoli and colleagues, 2005), cited in a 2013 Embrapa journal paper, found Mundo Novo progenies out-yielded Yellow Bourbon ones by 38.7%. More intensive farming narrows the gap: in that 2013 paper's trial, over four harvests (2007/08 to 2010/11) at five Minas Gerais sites, Yellow Bourbon selections averaged about 25 to 33 bags a hectare, against 32.6 for Catuaí Vermelho IAC 144 and 35.1 for Mundo Novo, so the best of them matched Catuaí but none reached Mundo Novo.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Yellow Bourbon has placed well in Brazil's Cup of Excellence, the national competition whose winners are sold at auction. In 2012 Fazenda São Pedro in Carmo de Minas placed 8th with a pulped-natural Yellow Bourbon at 88.47 points, and in 2017 a Brazilian Yellow Bourbon scored 92.33 and sold for US$126 a pound, about 100 times the commodity price then, says Daily Coffee News.

Other varieties now crowd it out at the top. In the 2025 competition Arara was in 17 of the 30 top-ten lots (16 on its own, one in a blend), and the only Yellow Bourbon among the top ten of the three categories was Sítio Córrego Frio's pulped natural from Mantiqueira de Minas, 8th in Washed + Honey with 87.71.

sections.title: The IAC lines
body: IAC released Yellow Bourbon to farmers as numbered lines named after the mother trees it chose in Jaú in 1945, with codes like IAC J10 or J9. The best of the original progenies were J3, J8, J10, J11, J24 and J30, and IAC has registered seven lines.

The lines really do differ. In an IAC trial at 1,100 m (3,600 ft) in São Sebastião da Grama, São Paulo, published in 2022 from its first harvest (2019), 12 of 14 lines averaged above 85 points, and J3-1, J9-16 and J19-18 stood out for yield and cup, J9-16 with floral notes and J19-18 with honey. With only one harvest, the authors call the results, especially for yield, preliminary.

family.parentsText: Red Bourbon (mutation), or Red Bourbon × Amarelo de Botucatu
family.line: Origin unresolved; selected by IAC from 1945 into numbered IAC J lines.

grownIn.text: Associated above all with Brazil: São Paulo, where it was found and selected, and Minas Gerais, including the Cerrado and Carmo de Minas in Mantiqueira de Minas.

records.name: Yemenia
records.summary: A genetic group of Arabica found so far only in Yemen.
records.lede: Yemenia is the name Qima Coffee and plant scientist Christophe Montagnon of RD2 Vision gave in 2020 to a group of Yemeni coffee trees whose DNA matched no known cultivated variety and no sampled Ethiopian coffee. Scientists call it the New-Yemen group, and Qima says the name means "the Yemeni mother" in Arabic. It's a genetic group, not one defined variety: trees in it go by several local names.

facts.label: no cultivated variety or sampled Ethiopian coffee belongs to it
announced by Qima Coffee and RD2 Vision
winning lots at Qima's 2020 auction were Yemenia
points for several Yemenia lots in a blind 2020 jury cupping

cup.text: Early descriptions came from the blind jury that cupped lots for Qima's 2020 auction: German roaster Raphael Braune heard berry notes like SL28, the sweetness of a Yellow Bourbon and aromatic complexity like Gesha's. Coffee Review's later reviews of lots sold as Yemenia include a 93 (2021) and two 95s (2023, 2025), with red currant, chocolate and woody notes such as cedar, oak or sandalwood. These are tastings of particular lots, not a side-by-side trial of the group.
cup.why: No study has tied Yemenia's genes to its flavor. Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids offers Yemen's ancient tree varieties as one possible reason for the complexity of its best coffees, alongside high elevation and the way the fruit is dried.
cup.prized: Clean, sweet, layered naturals: a Yemenia from Hayma Kharijiya, helped by a 2021 Qima program to improve farmers' drying, was No. 30 on Coffee Review's Top 30 Coffees of 2023.
cup.watch: Drying makes or breaks it: Coffee Review notes that Yemen's top naturals use only ripe fruit and controlled drying to avoid flat or woody flavors. And not every Yemenia is a plain natural: Qima's 2021 Bait Alal lot went through a three-stage fermentation, partly in sealed pressurized tanks.

story.text: A genetic study by World Coffee Research and partners, published in Scientific Reports, finds Yemen's coffee is a sub-group of Ethiopian Arabica and, as a whole, less diverse.
Qima Coffee and RD2 Vision announce Yemenia after DNA fingerprinting 137 Arabica samples; 15 of the 20 winning lots at that September's auction are Yemenia.
A paper in Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution describes the New-Yemen cluster as found only in Yemen and unrelated to any known cultivated variety or Ethiopian sample.
A follow-up survey of 148 Yemeni farms, funded by the Lavazza and Qima foundations, finds that local variety names don't reliably match the trees' genetics.
The Qima and Lavazza foundations build Yemen's first genetically verified coffee nursery, able to raise 150,000 seedlings a year to sell to farmers at cost.

sections.title: A group, not a name on a bag
body: In the 2022 survey, most trees farmers called Dawairi (86%), Jaadi (83%) and Udaini (67%) tested as New-Yemen. But some trees under those same names were Typica/Bourbon or SL34 types, and overall the names showed no significant link to genetics. A bag that says Udaini doesn't guarantee Yemenia.

Region was a better clue than the name: Udaini and Tufahi trees from Al Mahwit and Sanaa were mainly New-Yemen, while those from Ibb and Dhamar were mainly SL34 and Typica/Bourbon types. The study's authors recommend collecting Yemen's trees in controlled collections and describing both their genes and their looks.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Qima's Faris Sheibani said in 2021 that the Yemenia name is free for any Yemeni trader, exporter, cooperative or farmer to use. In scientific papers the same group is called New-Yemen.

Labels depend on the seller. In October 2021 Coffee Review rated a Qima lot from the Bait Alal community in Al Hayma sold as Yemenia, and Port of Mokha's Lot 106, also from Bait Alal smallholders, sold as Udaini.

sections.title: Why breeders care
body: Yemen's coffee has grown for centuries in hot, dry, full sun, unlike Ethiopia's shaded forests, and World Coffee Research asks whether Yemeni trees could help scientists learn more about heat and drought tolerance. Global Coffee Report (2025) puts rainfall in Yemen's coffee regions at about 200–350 mm a year, against the roughly 1,000 mm coffee usually needs.

The 2022 paper's authors see "little doubt" that centuries of growing in Yemen favored drought-resistant trees. In 2025 Qima's Faris Sheibani named the next step: assessing the quality, climate resilience, and pest and disease tolerance of Yemen's native trees.

family.parentsText: A genetic group (the New-Yemen cluster), not a bred variety
family.line: Found by DNA fingerprinting; it may still overlap with Ethiopian coffee that hasn't been collected or tested yet.

grownIn.text: Found only in Yemen so far.

family.parentsText: Not one variety: Ethiopia's own Arabica, from local types farmers kept and selected to numbered research selections picked from forest mother trees
family.line: Farmers chose healthy, productive mother trees for seedlings over generations; since the 1970s Ethiopia's research center has picked and numbered its own selections

grownIn.text: Ethiopia, across the south and west, from Sidama, Gedeo (Yirgacheffe) and Guji to Jimma, Kaffa and Wollega, and in Harar in the east

plant.stature: varies: from big landrace trees with long leaves, like Wolisho, to compact research selections like 74110
plant.yield: low on farms: about 500 kg/ha for local landraces in southern Ethiopia, against about 800 kg/ha for the released disease-resistant selections
plant.altitude: varies: the 13 early selections (released 1978–81) were recommended for low to high altitudes, with no exact range; Angefa, a southern landrace selection, for 1,700–2,000 m (5,580–6,560 ft)

cup.text: Because most lots mix many types, the cup is usually described by region and process. Where single-selection lots exist, as with 74158, roasters and reviewers have started naming them.

feel.acidity: bright and citric in washed lots

cup.why: Sweet Maria's says the shrubs' greater genetic diversity is likely part of why Ethiopian coffees are counted among the world's best, but that processing has perhaps the most influence on the cup in the end.
cup.prized: Coffee Review says Ethiopia's native varieties can show such complex aroma and flavor that SL28 and Bourbon seem limited beside them, and calls Gesha the only cultivated variety that competes with the finest of them.
cup.watch: “Heirloom” on a bag tells you little about what's inside: Melbourne Coffee Merchants notes that traditional mixed planting makes single-variety lots hard to guarantee, and Sweet Maria's finds Yirgacheffe can seem inconsistent in quality.

story.text: Coffee berry disease, a fungus that attacks the cherries, is first reported in Sidama, Illubabor and Kaffa; by 1978 it has reached almost every coffee region.
Ethiopia releases 13 disease-resistant pure-line selections; Melbourne Coffee Merchants says the search found 13 mother trees in Gera, Wush Wush, Washi and Metu-Bishari.
Surveys help identify the local landraces farmers grow by name.
Ethiopia releases 12 landrace-based varieties in 2006 and 2010. In the south, the Awada research center releases Angefa (2006) for Sidama and Gedeo, then Odicha, Fayate and Koti (2010).
Getu Bekele, a longtime JARC coffee breeder, and Counter Culture's Tim Hill publish A Reference Guide to Ethiopian Coffee Varieties, aiming to correct misconceptions about them.
Every one of the 29 winning lots at Ethiopia's Cup of Excellence names a numbered research selection; 21 are 74158.

sections.title: Why “heirloom” is a loose word
body: Getu Bekele, a longtime breeder at JARC, points out that “heirloom” was borrowed from other crops, where it means open-pollinated varieties; coffee pollinates itself, so the word never quite fit. Australia's trade says “heritage variety” instead.

Royal Coffee's Chris Kornman wrote in 2019 that the blanket label does a disservice to Ethiopia's genetic range, since many so-called heirloom coffees are in fact selected cultivars, and that “landrace” is catching on as the more precise word. Ally Coffee, drawing on Bekele and Hill's guide, goes further: most coffee grown for export today is some form of selected or bred variety.

sections.title: Landrace selections for the south
body: The first disease-resistant selections came from the southwest and often adapted poorly in the south and east, so researchers turned to local landraces. By 2006, a national landrace program had set up seven coffee research centers and collected about 3,000 local coffees from Harerge, Sidamo, West Wollega and Limmu to select from.

Awada, the southern coffee research center near Yirgalem, released Angefa in 2006 for Sidama and Gedeo at 1,700–2,000 m (5,580–6,560 ft), then Odicha, Fayate and Koti in 2010. Its researchers put average farm yields in the south at about 500 kg/ha for local landraces and 800 kg/ha for the released disease-resistant selections.

sections.title: In competitions
body: At Ethiopia's 2021 Cup of Excellence, 26 of the 33 winning lots named a numbered JARC selection (74112, 74110, 74158 or 74165); the rest were Kurume, Typica, Gesha or plain “heirloom”.
In 2022 all 32 winning lots named a JARC number: 74158, 74112 and 74110 had ten lots each, plus one 74165 and one 744. In 2024 all 29 did again, and 21 of them were 74158.

sections.title: What DNA tests found in the research varieties
body: A 2021 study using DNA markers on 40 of the 42 commercial varieties developed by JARC found them genetically diverse and mostly distant from one another, and varieties collected in the same area often fell into different groups.

records.name: Gesha
records.summary: An Ethiopian coffee that became the star of Panama's auctions.
records.lede: An Ethiopian forest coffee that spent decades in research gardens and on a few Panamanian farms before a 2004–05 competition win started its run of auction records. Grown high and handled well, it is known for jasmine-like florals and a light, tea-like body.

facts.label: first crop after planting, the same year as Bourbon
World Brewers Cup champions, 2011–2019, who used Gesha
a kilo: the top lot at Best of Panama 2026, Elida Geisha Torre

cup.text: Roasters and judges tend to describe strong jasmine-like florals with peach, citrus and bergamot. Ozone Coffee adds a long, clean finish, and the Cup of Excellence jury described Taiwan's 2025 runner-up, a washed Gesha, as jasmine, black tea, peach, apricot and bergamot.
cup.why: World Coffee Research ties its top cup quality to high altitude and good farm management. Ozone stresses there is no single Gesha flavor: altitude, climate, soil, picking, fermentation, drying and roasting all change it, so neighbouring farms can taste different.
cup.prized: Its intense florals and clarity. 2018 World Barista Champion Agnieszka Rojewska called it the champagne of coffee.
cup.watch: The name: in World Coffee Research's 2020 DNA study only 39% of 88 samples sold as Gesha were true Gesha. Competitors also worry that rising production in Colombia and Ethiopia will bring more ordinary Geshas to market. Process changes it too: Ozone says washed lots lean floral and citrus, while naturals and honeys add fruit, sweetness and fermented notes.

family.parentsText: An Ethiopian landrace; the Panama line descends from one accession, T2722
family.line: Collected from Ethiopia's coffee forests in the 1930s, kept at research stations in Tanzania and Costa Rica, then planted in Panama in the 1960s

grownIn.text: Panama is its best-known home. World Coffee Research says it's also grown widely in Malawi; Ozone adds Colombia, Guatemala, and China and Thailand from 2015 on, and Ethiopia is growing its own Gesha selections again. It has placed at Cup of Excellence in Mexico and Taiwan.

plant.rust: intermediate resistance
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, above 1,300 m (4,270 ft) at 5–15° latitude, above 1,000 m (3,280 ft) farther out

story.text: Seed is collected from Ethiopia's coffee forests and sent to the Lyamungu research station in Tanzania.
It reaches CATIE, the research center in Costa Rica, and is logged as accession T2722.
It is handed out in Panama for its tolerance of leaf rust; Francisco Serracín plants it in Boquete, but most farmers pass on its brittle branches.
Hacienda La Esmeralda's Gesha wins Best of Panama and sells for a then-record of about $21 a pound; Perfect Daily Grind and Ozone date it to 2004, World Coffee Research to 2005.
Seven of the nine World Brewers Cup champions in these years compete with a Gesha.
A washed Gesha from La Esmeralda scores 98 at Best of Panama and sells for a record $30,204 a kilo ($13,705 a pound).
At the 2026 Best of Panama, the year the competition marked 30 years, all 40 Gesha lots topped $1,500 a kilo and the highest, Lamastus Family Estates' Elida Geisha Torre, sold for $18,004 a kilo.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Gesha became the default competition coffee after its Panama auction wins: Perfect Daily Grind counts seven of the nine World Brewers Cup champions from 2011 to 2019 using it, including Chad Wang's natural Gesha in 2017. At national Cup of Excellence contests it has set marks outside Panama too, such as a natural Geisha from Finca Santa Cruz in Chiapas that scored 93.04 in 2019, the highest in Mexico's Cup of Excellence history at the time.
Competitors have also looked elsewhere to stand out: Saša Šestić won the 2015 World Barista Championship with a Sudan Rume, and in 2021 several finalists used the separate species Coffea eugenioides.

sections.title: Prices and auctions
body: Best of Panama, run by the Specialty Coffee Association of Panama, sets Gesha's price records. The top price went from about $21 a pound in 2004–05 to $1,300.50 a pound in 2020 and $2,560 a pound in 2021, and in 2025 a 20 kg lot from La Esmeralda sold for $30,204 a kilo. In 2026 the top lot fetched $18,004 a kilo, and buyers from China, Japan, the United Arab Emirates and South Korea took most of the value.
Ozone points out that these are tiny lots that say little about the price of a normal bag, and that scarcity, scores, the farm's name and auction bidding drive them as much as the cup.

sections.title: Beyond Panama
body: Gesha now grows far from Boquete. World Coffee Research notes it is grown widely in Malawi; Ozone points to Colombia's high Andes, Guatemala's volcanic soils, and Thailand and China since about 2015. Sweet Maria's buys a washed Gesha grown at 1,600–1,700 m (5,250–5,600 ft) on Volcán Acatenango in Guatemala, and a washed Gesha from Alishan placed second at Taiwan's 2025 Cup of Excellence.

In Ethiopia, farms such as Gesha Village grow their own selections from the forests where Gesha was first collected, sold under names like Gesha 1931 and Gori Gesha. These are separate selections from the Panama line, not the same seed. Ethiopia's agricultural research institute has also released a cultivar called Gesha, one of 23 bred from forest coffee for coffee berry disease resistance between the late 1970s and the 1990s, another reason the name alone says little.

records.name: Pink Bourbon
records.summary: Sold as a Bourbon, but DNA points to an Ethiopian landrace.
records.lede: A tall, pink-cherried coffee that a Cafe Imports buyer spotted in Colombia in 2014, growing among Bourbon trees; Sucafina says it was first identified in and around Huila. Its producer took it for a Red × Yellow Bourbon cross, but DNA tests ordered by importer Cafe Imports in 2017 and 2023 point to an Ethiopian landrace. It has spread fast because buyers keep paying for its floral, juicy cups.

facts.label: Coffee Review scores for washed Pink Bourbons from San Adolfo, Huila (2016 and 2017)
samples pure Pink Bourbon in the 2023 tests; the rest were mixed
when a Cafe Imports buyer first spotted its pink cherries

cup.text: Coffee Review's two 94-point washed lots from San Adolfo showed violet-like florals, pink peppercorn, peach, date and maple. Recent washed lots from Huila that Sey sells list hibiscus, blueberry and citrus.
cup.prized: Florals with a spicy, sweet edge, and a cup reputation Cafe Imports' Ian Fretheim calls established and undeniable.
cup.watch: What's in the bag may be part something else: in the 2023 tests four of five samples were Pink Bourbon mixed with Bourbon or with Catimor-type genes (as in Castillo). Cherry color doesn't settle it either, since the one Orange Bourbon tested carried Pink Bourbon DNA.

family.parentsText: An Ethiopian landrace by DNA; not related to Bourbon, despite the name
family.line: Found growing among Bourbon on a Colombian farm and long believed to be a natural Red × Yellow Bourbon cross

grownIn.text: Mostly in and around Huila, Colombia, with lots now also from Cauca and Quindío; some of the 2023 test samples came from Costa Rica.

plant.stature: tall and scraggly; a shorter form also grows
plant.rust: some resistance, growers report; not tested in a published trial

story.text: In November, Cafe Imports buyer Luis Arocha spots pink cherries in Colombia and traces them to a farm where the trees grow among Bourbon.
Coffee Review scores a washed Pink Bourbon from several San Adolfo farms 94, still describing it as a Red × Yellow Bourbon hybrid.
Cafe Imports has a tall and a short plant tested by DNA Analytica: the results resemble wild Ethiopian coffee, but no reference matches closely, unlike the 95–100% matches other coffees gave.
A farm in Quindío that switched from avocados to 10 ha of Pink Bourbon brings in its first crop.
Geneticist Christophe Montagnon of RD2 Vision tests five samples from Colombia and Costa Rica for Cafe Imports and calls it an Ethiopian landrace, not a Bourbon mutation.

sections.title: Look-alikes and mix-ups
body: Its cherries are closer to orange than pink, Intelligentsia notes, so some people call it Orange Bourbon; the one Orange Bourbon sample Cafe Imports tested in 2023 carried Pink Bourbon DNA. Coffee Review's 2016 and 2017 reviews still called it a Red × Yellow Bourbon hybrid, the belief that came from its first farm.

Sources disagree on its nearest relatives. Sucafina calls Gesha a sibling; Cafe Imports, after the 2023 tests, says it is distinct from other Ethiopian landraces such as Gesha. Intelligentsia reports a story in Colombia that it came out of unfinished breeding work at Cenicafé, the national coffee research center, but no source confirms it.

sections.title: Where it's grown
body: Most Pink Bourbon still comes from in and around Huila. The early lots came from San Adolfo, in Acevedo municipality, and Sey's recent lots come from San Adolfo and El Tabor at around 1,600–1,730 m (5,250–5,680 ft).

It has spread as buyers asked for it: Intelligentsia says exporters, including all three of its main Colombian partners, help growers get seed. Banexport grows it on an experimental farm in Sotará, Cauca, and a 10 ha farm near Armenia, Quindío, grows it at 1,480 m (4,860 ft).

records.name: Chiroso
records.summary: A Colombian variety from Urrao, once taken for a Caturra or Bourbon.
records.lede: A local coffee of Urrao, a high valley in Antioquia, first valued there for its yield. A Cup of Excellence win in 2014 made buyers notice its floral, tea-like cups, and a Chiroso won Colombia's competition outright in 2020. Researchers now describe it as an Ethiopian landrace rather than a Caturra.

facts.label: the washed Chiroso that won Colombia's 2020 Cup of Excellence
an Urrao grower's Cup of Excellence win that spread it beyond the valley
where Urrao's Chiroso farms sit (6,230–7,220 ft)

cup.text: Tea-like, sweet and often floral. Sweet Maria's tasted Earl Grey, chamomile, raw sugar and grape in an Urrao lot; the Cup of Excellence jury found florals, berry, plum, honey and lime in a 2023 lot from Santa Bárbara, Antioquia.
cup.why: Growers and importers credit Urrao itself: Partners Coffee says the high valley's climate ripens fruit slowly and keeps fermentation and drying slow, and Sweet Maria's says cold spring water lets farmers ferment for several days.
cup.prized: Floral, tea-like aromatics with strong sweetness; Sucafina likens it to Gesha, with more herbal notes.
cup.watch: Sucafina says it is susceptible to leaf rust. Its name also misleads: coverage of the 2020 Cup of Excellence still called it a Caturra mutation, which the 2024 genetic study rejects for Caturra Chiroso.

family.parentsText: Described as an Ethiopian landrace; long taken for a Caturra mutation or a Bourbon
family.line: A local variety of Urrao whose origin is unknown. Chica-Acosta and colleagues (2024) write that Christophe Montagnon and colleagues identified it as an Ethiopian landrace in 2021; their own chloroplast DNA work placed it nearest eastern Ethiopian coffees.
