grownIn.text: Mostly Urrao, Antioquia; also elsewhere in Antioquia, such as Santa Bárbara, and a few farms abroad: a Panamanian Chiroso sold at Best of Panama in 2024.

plant.stature: tall (Bourbon Chiroso) or short and compact (Caturra Chiroso)
plant.yield: high; more productive than Caturra, says Partners Coffee
plant.rust: susceptible
plant.beanSize: long, narrow beans, shaped like Typica's
plant.altitude: high: grown at about 1,900–2,200 m (6,230–7,220 ft) in Urrao, where Sucafina says it does better than Castillo or Variedad Colombia

story.text: Carmen Montoya, an Urrao grower, wins the Cup of Excellence with a Chiroso, and the variety starts to spread beyond Urrao.
Felipe Henao Triana's washed Chiroso from Los Tres Mosqueteros wins Colombia's Cup of Excellence with 90.03.
Christophe Montagnon and colleagues identify Chiroso as an Ethiopian landrace, according to a 2024 study that cites their work.
A washed Chiroso from Santa Bárbara, outside Urrao, places 8th at Colombia's Cup of Excellence with 89.39.
A chloroplast DNA study of Urrao's three Chiroso types finds them closest to eastern Ethiopian coffees, and a Panamanian Chiroso sells for $1,630 a kilo at Best of Panama.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Chiroso's reputation comes from competitions. Sey says Carmen Montoya's 2014 Cup of Excellence win, with a Chiroso nobody knew, made it look at Urrao when most buyers were focused on Huila and Tolima, and Sweet Maria's says the win spread the variety beyond the valley. In 2020 a washed Chiroso from Felipe Henao Triana won Colombia's Cup of Excellence with 90.03; Partners Coffee, which buys from him, his brother Leonardo and their farm manager Jorge Cuellar, says it was the only lot that year to earn the 90-point Presidential Award, and that Leonardo placed again in 2021 with another Chiroso.
In 2023 a Chiroso from La Palma in Santa Bárbara, Antioquia, placed 8th, and in 2024 Black Moon Farm's Chiroso sold for $1,630 a kilo in the Varietals category at Best of Panama.

sections.title: Urrao and beyond
body: Urrao is a remote Andean valley about four and a half hours' drive from Medellín, with a valley floor above 1,800 m (5,900 ft) and coffee farms from about 1,900 to 2,200 m (6,230–7,220 ft). Locals named the variety and first grew it for its high yield; the 2024 study's plants came from the Bellavista farm in San Carlos, Urrao.
It is still rare outside Colombia, Sucafina says, but demand is growing: Sey says it is building a buying program in Urrao around Chiroso.

family.parentsText: Arabica from southwestern Ethiopia, cultivated in Yemen
family.line: One of the two lines that left Yemen; it spread from a few seeds via India and Java, then through a single plant in Amsterdam.

plant.stature: tall, with bronze young leaf tips
plant.rust: susceptible; also susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms)
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, above 1,300 m (4,270 ft) at 5–15° latitude, above 1,000 m (3,300 ft) farther out

grownIn.text: Still widely planted in Peru, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica (WCR); also Kona's heirloom trees in Hawaii. Sucafina lists it among Papua New Guinea's common varieties, and single-variety lots come from places such as Laos.

feel.acidity: clean; brighter when grown high, softer lower down

cup.why: 1Zpresso puts its clarity down mostly to altitude: cooler temperatures slow the cherries' ripening. It adds that washing (removing the fruit before drying) brings out clarity, while natural processing (drying in the fruit) brings out sweetness.
cup.prized: Balance and sweetness. Miguel Meza of Coffee Review wrote in 2009 that high-grown Typicas often show a very balanced profile with well-developed sweetness and hints of nuts and citrus, and that quality-minded growers were going back to it for quality rather than quantity.
cup.watch: It's a quiet cup rather than a loud one. Kenneth Davids of Coffee Review wrote in 2010 that Kona and Jamaica, both Typica growers, tend to grow traditional, respected varieties that aren't especially distinctive in flavor. Its low yields also make good Typica scarce.

story.text: Arabica, which WCR thinks came from southwestern Ethiopia, reaches Yemen, where it is cultivated.
Seeds from India's Malabar coast go to Java and found the Typica line.
A plant goes from Java to Amsterdam's botanical garden; its descendants spread through European colonies to the Caribbean and the Americas.
Leaf rust devastates Typica farms; Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) never recovers and switches to tea.

Until the 1940s most coffee farms in Central and South America grow Typica; from then on it is gradually replaced across much of the Americas, because it yields little and is highly susceptible to the major coffee diseases.
A genome study confirms how narrow cultivated Arabica is: each new growing area started from a very small number of plants, or even just a few seeds.

sections.title: Typica or Bourbon?
body: The two left Yemen separately. Typica went by way of India and Java; WCR says French missionaries took Bourbon from Yemen to Bourbon Island (now La Réunion) in the early 1700s. Some writers call Bourbon a Typica mutation, but WCR's history gives it its own route out of Yemen.

In the field, WCR lists Typica with bronze young leaves, large beans and low yields, and Bourbon with green young leaves, average beans and medium yields. 1Zpresso sums up the cup difference as Typica clean and silky, Bourbon sweeter and fuller.

sections.title: Where you'll still find it
body: WCR says Typica is still widely planted in Peru, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica, where it's called Jamaica Blue Mountain. Hawaii's Kona Coffee Farmers Association credits its heirloom Kona Typica with the region's balanced, smooth cup, grown at about 800–2,500 ft (240–760 m).

Sucafina lists Typica among Papua New Guinea's common varieties, and Sweet Maria's sells washed Typica from Laos's Bolaven Plateau, where farms average about 1,200 m (3,940 ft). In 2009 Coffee Review's Miguel Meza also named Panama, Mexico, Colombia, India and Indonesia as places it could be found, with some searching.

sections.title: Relatives, and names that mislead
body: Several varieties with other names test as Typica-group by DNA in WCR's catalog: Kenya's SL34 and SL14, and Rwanda's Mibirizi. Others are Typica mutations or selections: Maragogipe (giant beans) and Pache (a compact plant), and Meza also lists Kents, Villalobos, Mokka (tiny beans) and Golden Drops (yellow fruit).
The name Java misleads: WCR says that variety was once thought to be a Typica selection but is actually from an Ethiopian landrace population called Abysinia.

family.parentsText: Single-tree selection from a tree labelled “French Mission” on Loresho Estate, Kabete; DNA places it in the Typica group
family.line: Picked by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in the late 1930s.

plant.stature: tall, with long side branches that droop as they age
plant.yield: medium, by Ozone Coffee's rating (a 2014 Kenyan research paper calls SL28, SL34 and K7 high-yielding as a group)
plant.rust: susceptible; highly susceptible to coffee berry disease, and to nematodes
plant.altitude: medium to high: above 1,200 m (3,940 ft) near the equator, where rain is good

grownIn.text: Mostly Kenya, usually alongside SL28; Ozone says other East African countries grow some too, and single-variety lots turn up farther away, such as Taiwan's Alishan.

cup.text: Coffee Review's Kim Westerman (2020) finds SL34 “not as dynamic as SL28”, typically with citrusy acidity and a full body. Ozone Coffee describes blackcurrant, red fruit and citrus with wine-like acidity and a long finish, and good examples as juicy and full-bodied.
cup.why: Place and processing count as much as the tree: Ozone says 'altitude, soil, rainfall, crop conditions and especially processing' all shape the cup, and Coffee Review describes Kenya's usual washing: 12–24 hours of fermentation after pulping, a rinse, then an overnight soak in fresh water.
cup.prized: Its cup. WCR gives its quality potential at high altitude its top rating, exceptional, and Ozone says growers keep planting it for the cups despite its disease and yield trade-offs.
cup.watch: It's hard to taste on its own: Sucafina says most Kenyan lots are blends of SL trees, Ruiru 11 and sometimes Batian, because farms are too small to separate varieties.

story.text: Spiritan missionaries plant Bourbon seed from La Réunion at Bura in Kenya's Taita Hills, the start of the “French Mission” coffee that SL34's mother tree was labelled as.
Scott Agricultural Laboratories selects trees given the SL prefix; SL34 comes from a single tree on Loresho Estate in Kabete.
SL28, SL34 and K7 are released as Kenya's first varieties.
Kenya releases Ruiru 11, whose male parent draws its cup quality partly from SL34.
Kenya releases Batian, a disease-resistant variety with SL34 among its parents.

A genetic survey of Yemen's coffee uses “SL34” as the name of one of the country's three genetic groups; most trees in it were called Udaini or Tufahi by farmers, though the study found no real link between local names and genetic groups.

sections.title: SL34 or SL28?
body: Coffee Review links SL28 with dark berries such as blackcurrant and strikingly bright, juicy acidity, and SL34 with citrusy acidity and a fuller body. WCR adds that SL34 suits high, rainy areas, and its DNA puts it in the Typica group while SL28 tests as Bourbon.
Since most Kenyan lots mix the two, Ozone suggests tasting single-variety lots from the same producer side by side if you want to learn the difference.

sections.title: On the bag
body: “SL28, SL34” on a Kenyan bag usually describes a farm's mix rather than a pure lot. Sucafina says most Kenyan lots blend SL trees with Ruiru 11 and sometimes Batian, because most farms are too small to separate lots by variety, and Kenyan researcher Bernard Gichimu wrote in a 2014 conference paper that improved varieties are replacing the traditional ones on a large scale.

sections.title: Genetics: what DNA tests found
body: WCR says recent tests tie SL34 to the Typica group, so the story that it was picked from a French Mission (Bourbon) population may be wrong. A 2022 study of Yemen's coffee uses “SL34” as the name of one of Yemen's three genetic groups, more common in Ibb and Dhamar; most trees in it were called Udaini or Tufahi, though local names didn't reliably match genetic groups.

cup.text: Ozone Coffee ties Bourbon to sweetness, balance and a rounded structure, with caramel and chocolate and, when it's grown high, stone fruit, citrus or flowers. Sweet Maria's says Rwanda's all-Bourbon tree stock gives its coffees a high potential for sweetness.
cup.why: Much of it is altitude and care: WCR rates its quality potential very good specifically at high altitude, and Ozone says altitude, climate, harvest and processing shape the cup more than the variety name or cherry colour. In Rwanda and Burundi, Perfect Daily Grind credits high altitude and volcanic, nitrogen-rich soils with bringing out its sweet, full-bodied side.
cup.prized: Sweetness and balance from high farms. It's the base of Rwanda's coffee, about 95% of which is long-established Bourbon types, and Melbourne Coffee Merchants describes Rwandan cups as floral and sweet with dried fruit, stewed fruit and chocolate.
cup.watch: The name is no promise. Bourbons from different places, and different colour forms, can taste very different, and East Africa's Bourbon-like trees don't exactly match Latin America's; some coffees sold as Bourbon, like Pink Bourbon, turn out to be other plants entirely.

plant.rust: susceptible, also to coffee berry disease and nematodes
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, 1,300 m (4,270 ft) at 5–15° latitude, 1,000 m (3,300 ft) farther out

family.parentsText: Yemeni Arabica grown on Bourbon Island (La Réunion)
family.line: Grew from the few Yemeni plants that survived on Réunion in the early 1700s; that narrow start helps explain why Bourbon-type varieties have little genetic diversity.

grownIn.text: World Coffee Research names El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Peru in Latin America; about 95% of Rwanda's coffee is Bourbon types, Burundi grows it widely, and Brazil keeps Red and Yellow Bourbon on specialty farms.

story.text: The French make three attempts, in 1708, 1715 and 1718, to bring coffee from Yemen to Bourbon Island; plants from the second and third survive.
Laurina, a dwarf Bourbon mutant also called Bourbon Pointu, is generally thought to have been selected from a field on the island.
Bourbon reaches Brazil, near Campinas, and spreads north through South and Central America.
French Spiritan missionaries plant Bourbon seed from La Réunion in Kenya's Taita Hills, the start of East Africa's "French Mission" coffee.
Caturra, a dwarf mutation of Bourbon, is found in Brazil.
Mundo Novo, a natural Bourbon × Typica cross, is found in Brazil; crossed later with Caturra it gives Catuaí.
Pacas, another dwarf Bourbon mutation, is found in El Salvador.

sections.title: Red, yellow, orange, pink
body: Classic Bourbon ripens red. Yellow Bourbon is the best-studied colour form: it turned up in Brazil around 1930, and Brazil's coffee institute (IAC) showed a single gene controls the yellow. Orange Bourbon is linked above all to El Salvador, but its genetics are thinly published, and "striped" Bourbon is a description rather than a variety.

Ozone Coffee's point is that cherry colour doesn't reliably predict flavour: genetics, altitude, climate, harvest and processing matter more. Pink Bourbon is the cautionary tale; DNA tests point to an Ethiopian landrace, not Bourbon.

sections.title: Bourbon in East Africa
body: East Africa's Bourbon arrived by several routes. Spiritan missionaries brought seed from La Réunion to Kenya in 1893 (the "French Mission" coffee), and Kenya's SL28 tests as Bourbon-related. In Rwanda and Burundi the common Bourbons include Bourbon Mayagüez 139, from a population that probably came via Puerto Rico, and Jackson, which came from India.
World Coffee Research says none of East Africa's many Bourbon-like varieties exactly matches Latin America's Bourbon, so an African "Bourbon" and a Salvadoran one aren't necessarily the same plant.

sections.title: In competitions today
body: Bourbon's descendants now win more than Bourbon itself. In El Salvador's 2025 Cup of Excellence, a national competition whose winners sell at auction, 15 of the 32 ranked lots were Pacamara (bred from Pacas, a Bourbon mutation, crossed with Maragogipe) and 10 were Geisha; the only Bourbon was a half-Bourbon, half-Typica lot in 5th place in its category. In Brazil's 2025 competition the only Bourbon in the top tens was a Yellow Bourbon.

World Coffee Research's Hanna Neuschwander told Perfect Daily Grind in 2020 that Bourbon may become rarer as new varieties ask farmers for fewer trade-offs, but will likely persist with growers who can sell it to specialty buyers.

cup.text: Ozone Coffee calls SL28 famous for its acidity and says the best examples show intense blackcurrant and dark berry with citrus, red fruit and a wine-like quality, and notes that World Coffee Research rates its quality potential at high altitude very highly.

feel.body: full and juicy, with a long finish

cup.why: Place and processing do a lot: most Kenyan coffee is fully washed, which Ozone says tends to bring out clarity and acidity, and coffees from different Kenyan counties taste different even with the same variety and washing.
cup.prized: That intense, juicy acidity and dark fruit at altitude. It's the reason farmers keep a low-yielding, disease-prone tree, and Finca Las Brumas in El Salvador, whose SL28 won the 2017 World Barista Championship, grows its competition lots at about 1,750–1,850 m (5,750–6,070 ft).
cup.watch: It doesn't always win side by side: in KALRO's trial of 31 varieties at two Kenyan sites, Batian scored highest overall and SL28 stood out mainly at one site. A lot sold as Kenya SL28 may also hold other varieties.

plant.stature: tall, with long branches that droop after several crops
plant.yield: low (but trees last: 60–80-year-old trees still bear in Kenya)
plant.rust: susceptible, also to coffee berry disease, bacterial blight and nematodes
plant.beanSize: large, with high green-coffee outturn per cherry
plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,940 ft) near the equator, 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude, 700 m (2,300 ft) farther out

family.parentsText: Single-tree selection from the "Tanganyika Drought Resistant" population (Bourbon-related by DNA)
family.line: Selected at Scott Agricultural Laboratories, Kenya, in 1935 from seed collected in Monduli, Tanganyika, in 1931.

grownIn.text: Above all Kenya; also Uganda, Malawi and Zimbabwe, and small plantings in Latin America, notably El Salvador.

story.text: Kenya's British colonial government sets up Scott Agricultural Laboratories at Kabete.
Coffee officer A.D. Trench collects seed in Tanganyika's Monduli district from trees that seem to shrug off drought, pests and disease.
SL28 is picked from a single tree of that population, one of 42 trees Scott Labs evaluated from 1935 to 1939.
Kenya releases Ruiru 11, a disease-resistant hybrid whose male parent has SL28 in its ancestry.
Batian, a tall, disease-resistant variety built partly from SL28, is released.
Dale Harris wins the World Barista Championship in Seoul with a washed SL28 from Finca Las Brumas, El Salvador.
Las Brumas returns to El Salvador's Cup of Excellence and places first in the Experimental category.

sections.title: Variety or place?
body: Kenya's coffee research institute (KALRO) grew 31 varieties, SL28 among them, at two research sites, Koru and Ruiru, and cupped them over the 2021 and 2022 harvests. Batian had the highest cupping score across both sites and years; SL28 stood out at Ruiru, above all in 2021, and Geisha at Koru.

The researchers concluded that you need site-specific best performers to get the best cup. In other words, how well SL28 cups changes with where and in which year it's grown; the trial didn't look at processing, but Ozone Coffee says Kenya's full washing tends to bring out clarity and acidity too.

sections.title: Outside Kenya
body: World Coffee Research lists SL28 as common in Malawi, Uganda and Zimbabwe as well as Kenya, and says it has spread to Latin America.

El Salvador is where it's best known outside Africa: Finca Las Brumas, between three volcanoes, grew the SL28 that won the 2017 World Barista Championship, and in El Salvador's 2025 Cup of Excellence a natural anaerobic "Kenya SL 28" from Finca Ethiopia placed 7th in the Experimental category with 87.96.

sections.title: Why Kenya plants other trees now
body: SL28, SL34 and K7 were Kenya's first varieties, released in the 1930s after selection for yield, bean size and cup quality. SL28 and SL34 fall to coffee berry disease, leaf rust and bacterial blight, and a 2014 conference paper by B.M. Gichimu says spraying susceptible trees can take up to 30% of production costs.

That is why Kenya bred Ruiru 11 (1985) and Batian, which resist the main diseases and are, in that paper's words, "largely replacing" the traditional varieties. Farmers still keep SL28 next to them, mainly for its cup.

records.name: Caturra
records.summary: A compact mutation of Bourbon found in Brazil.
records.lede: A natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon found in Brazil's Minas Gerais state between 1915 and 1918. Its short stature let farms plant more trees per hectare than with Bourbon or Typica; it became the benchmark for testing new varieties in Central America and a large part of Colombia's coffee, until leaf rust pushed growers toward resistant varieties bred from it.

facts.label: Brazil's IAC starts selecting it, but never officially releases it there
trees per hectare, the dense planting its size allows
first crop

cup.text: Sweet Maria's finds a little more citric acidity and a lighter body than Bourbon. Coffee Hunter says Caturra tends toward pronounced acidity, with lemony citrus when it's grown high, and less sweetness than Typica or Bourbon; on Coffee Review, chocolate and nut notes come up again and again in Caturra lots.

feel.body: light to medium, a bit lighter than Bourbon

cup.why: Only one dwarfing gene separates it from Bourbon, so the cup starts close to Bourbon's. Altitude does much of the rest: Sweet Maria's and Coffee Hunter both say its quality rises the higher it's grown, while its yield falls.
cup.prized: Clean, lively, citric acidity in high-grown lots. Sweet Maria's counts it among the best varieties for cup quality in Colombia, and the 20 lots on one page of Coffee Review's Caturra listings (2024–25), from Colombia, Guatemala, Costa Rica and Panama, all scored 90–95.
cup.watch: It can taste less sweet than Bourbon or Typica, and grown low it loses quality. Several of the top-scoring Caturra lots on Coffee Review are co-ferments or anaerobic lots, where the processing shapes the flavor as much as the variety does.

plant.stature: dwarf/compact, with short internodes (the stem segments between pairs of leaves)
plant.rust: very susceptible to leaf rust; also to nematodes (tiny root worms) and coffee berry disease
plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, or above 1,300 m (4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude, as in Central America; Coffee Hunter puts its best range at 1,200–2,000 m (3,950–6,550 ft)

story.text: Found on a plantation in Minas Gerais, Brazil, as a single-gene dwarf mutation of Bourbon.

Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) begins mass selection (choosing the best plants and pooling their seed, generation after generation), but never officially releases it in Brazil, where Sweet Maria's says it set too much fruit and wasn't hardy enough.
Reaches Guatemala, though wide commercial planting takes about three more decades; it then spreads to Costa Rica, Honduras and Panama.
IAC crosses yellow Caturra with Mundo Novo, the start of Catuaí.
Colombia starts a program that replaces more than three billion trees, many of them Caturra, with rust-resistant Castillo, itself bred from Caturra.

sections.title: How to spot it
body: In the field, Caturra is short, with short internodes (the stretches of stem between pairs of leaves), and its new leaves are green. Green tips alone don't prove it's Caturra: Sweet Maria's notes that many other varieties have them too, and Cenicafé's identification guide shows lots of Castillo, a Caturra descendant, with both bronze and green shoots.

sections.title: Red and yellow Caturra
body: Caturra comes with red or yellow ripe cherries, which is why bags say Caturra Rojo or Caturra Amarillo. Both carry the same dwarfing mutation of Bourbon; Coffee Hunter says the yellow colour comes from a separate recessive gene, that the yellow form may ripen faster and drop its ripe fruit earlier, and that its taste is considered a bit weaker than the red's. It was a yellow Caturra that Brazil's IAC crossed with Mundo Novo to make Catuaí.

sections.title: On the cupping table
body: Caturra still turns up in a lot of high-scoring coffee. The 20 lots on one page of Coffee Review's Caturra listings, reviewed in 2024–25, all scored 90–95; half came from Colombia, the rest from Guatemala, Costa Rica and Panama. Several were co-ferments (coffee fermented with added fruit) or anaerobic lots, so a high score on a Caturra bag says as much about the processing as about the tree.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural single-gene dwarf mutation)
family.line: Found in Minas Gerais, Brazil; selected by IAC from 1937 by mass selection. A parent of Catuaí, the Catimors and Castillo.

grownIn.text: Long a mainstay of Central America (Guatemala, then Costa Rica, Honduras and Panama) and once thought to be nearly half of Colombia's coffee, before Colombia replanted more than three billion trees with Castillo from 2008.

records.name: Pacamara
records.summary: El Salvador's big-bean cross of Pacas and Maragogipe.
records.lede: A cross of Pacas, a dwarf Bourbon, and Red Maragogipe, a Typica mutant with huge beans, made in 1958 by El Salvador's coffee research institute (ISIC) and released in 1980. It became El Salvador's signature coffee and a regular Cup of Excellence winner, though its seedlings never became fully uniform.

facts.label: crossed by ISIC; released 1980, widely planted from 1992
ranked lots in El Salvador's 2025 Cup of Excellence
of seedlings revert toward a parent, by Coffee Review's count

cup.text: Coffee Review describes all-Pacamara lots as deep, savory-sweet and resonant, often with floral top notes. Coffee Hunter finds spice, balance, citrus and flowers, and Ozone Coffee says the best lots bring tropical fruit, citrus, florals and spice with strong sweetness and a creamy texture.
cup.why: Its parents come from Arabica's two classic lines: Bourbon, through Pacas, and Typica, through the giant-bean mutant Maragogipe. The cross was never fully stabilised, so plants differ and so do cups; in one side-by-side tasting, Ozone found a red-fruited Pacamara more citrus-led and a yellow one more peach and apricot.
cup.prized: Big, layered, sweet cups that win: El Salvador's coffee institute counts 10 Cup of Excellence first places for it, and in the 2025 edition Pacamara took 15 of the 32 ranked lots, including the top washed-and-honey lot at 90.93 points.
cup.watch: Ozone says weak lots can taste vegetal, muddy, mushroomy or flat, and heavy fermentation can push it savory. The very large beans are also easy to roast unevenly (see Roasting it).

plant.stature: dwarf/compact (Ozone says up to medium-tall), with very large leaves
plant.yield: low in World Coffee Research's rating, moderate in Ozone's; Coffee Hunter says it's more productive than Maragogipe
plant.rust: very susceptible to leaf rust; highly susceptible to Ojo de Gallo, a leaf-spot fungus; also susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes
plant.altitude: high: above 1,300 m (4,250 ft) at El Salvador's latitude, or above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: Pacas, a dwarf Bourbon mutation, turns up on the Pacas family's farm in Santa Ana, El Salvador.
The genetics department of ISIC, El Salvador's coffee research institute, crosses Pacas with Red Maragogipe.
After several generations of selection, the fifth generation (F5) goes out to farmers, though the selection is never completed.
Wide distribution begins, and Pacamara is promoted through the 1990s.
A security guard at Finca Limoncillo in Nicaragua notices trees with yellow fruit; the Mierisch family builds them up into Yellow Pacamara.
El Salvador celebrates March 23 as National Pacamara Day, declared by its Legislative Assembly.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Pacamara is El Salvador's competition coffee. In the 2025 Cup of Excellence it took 15 of the 32 ranked lots, among them the top washed-and-honey lot (a honey from Santa Rosa at 90.93) and the first five places in the experimental category; Geisha took most of the rest. El Salvador's coffee institute, ISC, says it has won first place 10 times.

It does well beyond El Salvador too: in Nicaragua's 2025 competition five of 32 lots were Pacamara, including a natural that placed second at 90.59, and in Honduras a Pacamara natural ranked seventh among the exotic varieties.

sections.title: Why seedlings vary
body: Because ISIC never finished selecting it, Pacamara doesn't breed true. Ozone says 10–15% of seedlings commonly revert toward one parent, and Coffee Review puts it at 10% to 40%, so nurseries have to weed out off-types. When El Salvador's agriculture ministry reported on the trees it had handed out to renew farms, by early 2024, it described its 29,750 Pacamara plants as more than 80% genetically pure.

sections.title: Roasting it
body: The very large beans take longer for heat to reach the centre, so an aggressive roast can develop the outside and leave the middle underdone. Ozone suggests slower, more controlled profiles, and warns that Pacamara can look lighter than it tastes, so color alone is a poor guide.

family.parentsText: Pacas × Red Maragogipe
family.line: Crossed by ISIC, El Salvador, in 1958; selected to the fifth generation but never fully stabilised. Its cousin Maracaturra, probably a Caturra × Maragogipe cross from Nicaragua, has never been stabilised either.

grownIn.text: Mainly El Salvador, where Perfect Daily Grind singles out Chalatenango's microclimate for it; also Guatemala, where six Pacamara lots placed in the 2025 Cup of Excellence, Nicaragua, home of Yellow Pacamara, and Honduras.

records.name: Castillo
records.summary: Colombia's main rust-resistant variety, a blend of Caturra × Timor Hybrid lines.
records.lede: The variety Colombia replanted with after its leaf-rust epidemics. Colombia's growers' federation released it in May 2005, from a Cenicafé breeding program begun in 1968, and by 2012 more than 90% of the 234,000 hectares of renewed coffee had gone to Castillo. It's a blend of many short, large-beaned lines from Caturra × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343, and Cenicafé's tasting panels have kept finding its cup in line with Colombia's traditional varieties.

facts.label: start of the rust-breeding program it came out of
of the 234,000 ha of coffee renewed by 2012 went to Castillo
regional versions, each picked at a Cenicafé station for its zone

cup.text: Cenicafé's tasting panel describes the cup at a medium roast as mild in body and bitterness, with pronounced aroma and acidity, and found no significant difference from Típica, Bourbon, Caturra and Colombia. In a 2016 Cenicafé trial cupped by the Caldas growers' committee on the SCA's 100-point scale, Castillo scored 84.00 with notes of panela (unrefined cane sugar), chocolate, almond and caramel; Caturra scored 83.75.
cup.why: Cenicafé's view is that Timor Hybrid offspring can cup like any other Arabica if breeders throw out the poor-cupping lines, and that its cup tests on Colombia and Castillo lines have shown no difference from Caturra. A 2009 Cenicafé study of all the lines in Castillo and its regional versions could not tell them apart from the traditional varieties on cup attributes.
cup.prized: Clean, sweet cups with chocolate and nut tones, and sometimes more: a natural Castillo from El Zafiro, in Cauca, placed third in Colombia's 2021 Cup of Excellence at 89.46 points.
cup.watch: Results swing with the farm. Of 12 young Castillo farms studied in Nariño, in southern Colombia, half scored below 80, the specialty line (range 76.5–85.5), and the score didn't follow altitude. The best-scoring group, in La Unión, got the most sun and the widest temperature range, though the authors found only a weak link between growing conditions and the cup overall. A 2020 Cenicafé panel rated the average Castillo, Cenicafé 1 and Tabi sample as standard.

plant.stature: short (dwarf): about 147 cm at two years in a 2016 Cenicafé trial, a little taller than Caturra (142 cm)
plant.yield: high: similar to or above Caturra and Colombia in Cenicafé's trials; about 7.9 kg of cherry per tree a year against 5.75 kg for Colombia
plant.rust: resistant at release, much of it partial (incomplete) resistance; since 2020 Cenicafé has found rust that can grow on all its lines. Over half the material tested showed resistance to coffee berry disease, which Cenicafé calls probable tolerance
plant.beanSize: large: about 80–84% Supremo (beans held on a 17/64-inch screen)
plant.altitude: Colombia's whole coffee zone; Cenicafé says its yield and bean size pay off especially in higher regions

family.parentsText: Caturra (mother) × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343 (father)
family.line: Cenicafé self-pollinated the offspring and selected them family by family over several generations, then blended the best advanced (F5–F6) lines, which carry different rust-resistance genes, into one variety.
family.type: Composite (multiline) variety, with the same Caturra × Timor Hybrid parentage as the Catimors

grownIn.text: Colombia, where by 2012 more than 90% of renewed coffee land had been replanted with it; its seed is certified by Colombia's farm authority, the ICA.

story.text: Cenicafé begins breeding coffee for rust resistance, the program Castillo later came out of.
Its first result, the Colombia variety, is released: like Castillo later, a blend of Caturra × Timor Hybrid lines.
The growers' federation officially releases Castillo, bred for bigger beans and higher yields than Colombia.
Of 234,000 ha renewed, more than 90% have gone to Castillo, and rust-resistant varieties cover 54% of Colombia's coffee land.

About 3.3 billion trees had been replaced with rust-resistant varieties by May 2015 in the growers' federation's renovation program, Global Coffee Report says; Castillo has been grown high up only since the outbreak of around 2008–09.

For the first time Cenicafé 1 is the single variety with the most seed handed out (41%, against 29% for Castillo General and 14% for Castillo El Tambo), and Cenicafé finds rust able to grow on every Castillo line.
Cenicafé delivers Castillo 2.0 for release, with rust resistance from sources never used before in Colombian varieties.

sections.title: The regional Castillos
body: Besides Castillo General, Cenicafé picked regional versions at its experiment stations, each from the lines that did best there: Naranjal, Paraguaicito, Santa Bárbara, Pueblo Bello, El Rosario, La Trinidad and El Tambo. A 2009 Cenicafé study found all of them cupped like the traditional varieties, with 80.8–84.3% Supremo beans.
Castillo El Tambo was 14% of the seed Cenicafé handed out in 2020, second among the Castillos only to Castillo General (29%).

sections.title: In competitions
body: In 2010 the top lot at a Colombian Cup of Excellence auction, La Loma, was listed as Caturra and Castillo and sold for $40.09 a pound, nearly three times the next lot, Sprudge reported. In the 2021 Colombia Cup of Excellence a natural Castillo from El Zafiro, Cauca, placed third at 89.46 points, the only Castillo among 25 winning lots.

sections.title: Rust is catching up
body: Castillo's defense is diversity: its lines carry different resistance genes, which Cenicafé says keeps the variety stable, and it watches each line and swaps out any that get badly attacked.

That defense is under strain. In 2020 Cenicafé found rust that could grow, to varying degrees, on every component of Castillo, Cenicafé 1 and Tabi, and its 2024 report says rust races have grown more diverse and more virulent (better at getting past resistance) since 2010, especially on lines from Timor Hybrid 1343. Castillo 2.0 is its answer: new sources of resistance and, for the first time, resistance to a highly aggressive strain of coffee berry disease, with yields comparable to current varieties.

records.name: Colombia
records.summary: Cenicafé's first rust-resistant variety: a blend of Caturra × Timor Hybrid lines.
records.lede: The first composite rust-resistant variety: a seed blend of many short lines from Caturra × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343, each carrying different resistance genes. Cenicafé delivered it in 1983, and in 2017 it called the variety still resistant more than 30 years on. Castillo, from the same kind of cross but with bigger beans and higher yields, has since taken over new plantings, and the Colombia variety wasn't among the four varieties with seed certified by Colombia's farm authority, the ICA, in Cenicafé's 2017 guide.

facts.label: cherry per tree a year in Cenicafé's comparison, against 7.89 kg for Castillo
still rust-resistant after release, Cenicafé said in 2017
cup score in a Peruvian trial at 1,250 m (4,100 ft), published in 2018, best of three rust-resistant cultivars

cup.text: Cenicafé says its cup tests on Colombia and Castillo lines have shown no difference from Caturra. In farm samples from the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta reported in 2002, 27.3% of Colombia samples rated excellent, level with Tabi and above red Caturra (18.2%). In a small trial in Peru's Perené valley at 1,250 m (4,100 ft), published in 2018, it scored 82.05 on the SCA's 100-point scale, ahead of Costa Rica 95 (80.89) and a Catimor (79.93), with the most body and acidity of the three.
cup.why: Cenicafé argues that Timor Hybrid offspring can cup like other Arabicas when breeders remove the poor-cupping lines, and says its cup tests on the Colombia lines have shown no difference from Caturra.

plant.stature: short (dwarf), grouped with Caturra and Castillo
plant.yield: high when released, but below Castillo: about 5.75 kg of cherry per tree a year against 7.89 kg in Cenicafé's comparison
plant.rust: resistant; Cenicafé called it still resistant more than 30 years after release (2017), though its 2024 report says rust races have grown more diverse and more virulent (better at getting past resistance) since 2010, especially on Timor Hybrid 1343 lines like this one
plant.beanSize: smaller than Castillo: about 53% Supremo (range 38–75%), against 83% for Castillo

family.parentsText: Caturra × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343
family.line: Selected by Cenicafé over several generations and sold as a blend of similar-looking lines with different rust-resistance genes (a multiline), which Cenicafé credits for its lasting resistance.
family.type: Composite (multiline); same Caturra × Timor Hybrid parentage as the Catimors, but from Timor Hybrid line 1343 rather than 832/1

grownIn.text: Bred for Colombia; also grown in Peru, where a 2018 study confirmed it in the Perené valley of Junín.

story.text: Cenicafé begins breeding coffee for rust resistance.
Cenicafé releases the Colombia variety, the first composite variety with genetic resistance to rust.
Castillo, from the same Caturra × Timor Hybrid 1343 cross, is released with bigger beans and higher yields, and takes over renewal plantings.
Cenicafé says its strategy of blending lines has been proven by more than 25 years of resistance in the Colombia variety.

The ICA, Colombia's farm authority, issues its coffee-seed rules (Resolution 4266); by 2017, Cenicafé says, only Tabi, Castillo (general and regional) and Cenicafé 1 have certified seed, and the Colombia variety isn't among them.
Cenicafé's variety guide calls the Colombia variety still resistant more than 30 years after release.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Cenicafé's own numbers show why growers moved on to Castillo: in its comparison the Colombia variety gave about 5.75 kg of cherry per tree a year and 52.8% Supremo beans, against 7.89 kg and 83% for Castillo.

In Peru's Perené valley, at 1,250 m (4,100 ft), a trial published in 2018 and run without a formal statistical design found it yielding 1.75 t of parchment per hectare, between a Catimor (1.65 t) and Costa Rica 95 (2.20 t). Rust was low on all three, though higher on Colombia (6.2% incidence) than on the Catimor (1.7%).

sections.title: How its resistance held
body: Because the Colombia variety is a mix of lines with different resistance genes, one new rust race is unlikely to beat every tree in a field. Cenicafé credits this with the variety staying resistant for more than 30 years, and used the same design for Castillo, Tabi and Cenicafé 1.
The pressure is rising: Cenicafé's 2024 report says rust races have become more diverse and virulent since 2010, especially on lines from Timor Hybrid 1343, the variety's resistant parent.

family.parentsText: A composite of pure lines whose ancestry includes SL28, SL34, Rume Sudan, N39, K7, SL4 and the Timor Hybrid
family.line: Single-tree selections at the fifth generation from the male parent of some Ruiru 11 lines, made at the Coffee Research Station in Ruiru; Royal Coffee calls it a reformulation of Ruiru 11.

grownIn.text: Above all Kenya, where Royal Coffee calls it the country's most-planted tree; small plantings elsewhere, such as Finca Floripondio near Samaipata, Bolivia, at about 1,710 m (5,600 ft). WCR has also trialled it at 23 sites in 15 countries.

plant.yield: high; full yields often by year 2 or 3; reported at release (Coffee & Conservation, 2011) as up to 5 t/ha under optimal management, against a Kenyan average of about 2 t/ha
plant.rust: intermediate resistance (tolerance) to leaf rust; resistant to coffee berry disease; susceptible to nematodes
plant.beanSize: very large, with a high green-coffee outturn per cherry
plant.altitude: suited to all of Kenya's coffee-growing altitudes, according to a Kenya News Agency report on the Coffee Research Institute

cup.text: Ozone Coffee finds Kenyan Batian can be more restrained than the most intensely acidic SL28 lots, with fruit, sweetness and solid body; some lots show citrus or berry notes, others lean toward spice and deeper fruit. Coffee Review's tasters, reporting on Kenyan coffees in 2020, said the few pure-Batian samples they cupped kept the savory depth but not the juicy, sweet brightness of SL28.

feel.acidity: can be more restrained than the most acidic SL28 lots

cup.why: Cup quality was one of the breeding goals, and its ancestry includes SL28 and SL34; Ozone adds that results vary a lot with growing conditions, picking and processing.
cup.prized: WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude very good, and some of the top-scoring Kenyan coffees in Coffee Review's 2020 report (94–95 points) included at least some Batian, with Ruiru 11, in the variety mix their importers reported.
cup.watch: It isn't SL28: Ozone says it wasn't meant to replace SL28 or SL34 in the cup, and Coffee Review's tasters missed SL28's juicy brightness in pure Batian lots.

story.text: Coffee berry disease, which attacks the coffee fruit and can cause severe crop losses, was first reported in Kenya.
The Ruiru breeding programme released Ruiru 11, the dwarf hybrid from whose breeding lines Batian was later selected.
The Coffee Research Foundation, now part of KALRO, released Batian in Kenya.
World Coffee Research cited an estimate that, by 2019, around 300,000 Kenyan farming families had replanted with improved varieties, Batian and Ruiru 11 among them.
In KALRO's trial of 31 varieties at Koru and Ruiru, judged by four trained cuppers, Batian had the highest overall cupping score across both sites and years.
Royal Coffee described it as the most-planted coffee tree in Kenya.

sections.title: Batian or Ruiru 11?
body: Both came out of Kenya's response to coffee berry disease, and many top Kenyan lots list the two together. Ruiru 11 is a dwarf hybrid whose seed has to be made by hand pollination, which Royal Coffee says limits how fast it can be multiplied, and it has a poor reputation with specialty cuppers. Batian is a tall tree that, Ozone notes, can be grown from seed like an ordinary variety, and it suits smallholders because it tolerates low management.
World Coffee Research recommends planting it at 2,000–3,000 trees per hectare, with several stems per tree.

sections.title: Switching an old farm
body: Kenya's Coffee Research Institute encourages farmers to convert old trees rather than replant: its director, Elijah Gichuru, told the Kenya News Agency that Batian or Ruiru 11 can be grafted onto the stems of old trees, so farmers keep harvesting from some old stems while the grafts come into bearing, whereas replanting takes almost three years. He says the switch saves around 30% of production costs because the resistant trees don't need spraying against disease. The agency's report adds that both varieties suit all of Kenya's coffee altitudes, and the institute sells scions (grafting shoots) from its farm.

sections.title: Beyond Kenya
body: Batian has travelled a little. Ozone points to a natural Batian from Finca Floripondio, a farm near Samaipata, Bolivia, at about 1,710 m (5,600 ft), where more than 50 varieties have been planted and tested; the exporter Agricafe lists it with notes of sweet milk, banana, brown spice, pineapple and a buttery texture. WCR's international trial has measured its yield and rust resistance at 23 sites in 15 countries, and WCR warns that its rust performance depends on the rust races present locally.

sections.title: What was claimed at release
body: When Batian came out, Julie Craves of Coffee & Conservation reported in 2011 that it comes into bearing in two years rather than three, can be planted at up to 2,500 trees per hectare (about twice the density of typical Kenyan varieties), and can yield up to 5 tonnes per hectare under optimal management, against an average of 2. The Coffee Research Foundation also said Batian cups far better than Ruiru 11 and even its SL parents, a claim Craves suggested taking with a grain of salt.

Later results are mixed: KALRO's 2021–22 trial at two sites gave Batian the highest overall cupping score of 31 varieties, while Coffee Review's tasters in 2020 missed SL28's juicy brightness in the few pure-Batian lots they cupped.
